Instagram began cracking down on AI-generated profiles in August, after launching a label for AI accounts earlier this year, but misleading AI content like celebrity deepfakes remains an issue. Earlier this month, Mosseri said Instagram is “actively working out what to do” about AI fakes, but he noted, “I don’t think it’s practical for us to try and ban AI content from the platform.”
Mosseri said Instagram is “now starting to require AI accounts to label themselves, because we think it’s important that people know if what they’re looking at is real or not real.” He also acknowledged there are fears around AI, including from creators:
I think people are concerned about a lot of things. I think they’re concerned about owning their content and models getting trained on their content. They’re concerned about job displacement, having AI displace whatever it is they do, if you’re a content creator or an engineer or a mathematician. Ex-Israeli diplomat calls opposition's refusal to work with Arab parties 'reckless'
Former Israeli diplomat on what the Israeli election says about Netanyahu's power
The strong showing by Arab-led parties in Israel's election has raised a question for the opposition: Will its leaders work with them to form a government?
Political observers doubt such a partnership will materialize, given the unwillingness of several opposition leaders to work with Arab-led parties. Alon Pinkas, an Israeli political analyst and former diplomat who advised former Prime Ministers Ehud Barak and Shimon Peres, called that reluctance "myopic and reckless."
Pinkas told Morning Edition that opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot could either form a coalition with the parties or establish a minority government with their outside support, allowing them to back major legislation and confidence votes without formally joining the coalition.
But both Eisenkot and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have rejected working with Arab-led parties, which draw much of their support from Palestinian citizens of Israel. Netanyahu went further, calling the prospect of a government relying on their support "a shame and a disgrace."
Speaking with NPR's Steve Inskeep, Pinkas challenged arguments that relying on Arab-led parties would undermine Israel's identity as a Jewish state. He questioned why the same reasoning would not apply to ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties, which he said describe themselves as non-Zionist.
Pinkas attributed growing support for Arab-led parties to rising crime and murder rates in Arab communities, particularly violence involving organized crime groups. He said Netanyahu's government had "willfully ignored their plight" by failing to deploy police or investigate the killings.
As for Netanyahu's chances of forming a government, his assessment was emphatic: "Mr. Netanyahu cannot. I repeat, cannot form a government."

A shouting match between American and Cuban officials broke out on the floor of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, with a member of the Cuban delegation calling a Trump official a "liar."
The confrontation unfolded as U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz spoke against the annual resolution condemning the U.S.' decades-long economic embargo against the island country, which is due to be voted on this week. Waltz had taken the podium to argue that member states should not support the measure.
As he detailed years of alleged corruption by the socialist government, members of the Cuban delegation, including Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez, began to slam on their designated table and yell for a point of order. U.N. officials then sought to tone down the outbursts.
But Rodríguez walked down the aisle to the head of the General Assembly and yelled to Waltz, “You are a liar!"
Waltz responded, “You understand who you’re dealing with? This is America. Back up.”
The exchange was a break from the diplomatic decorum traditional to the U.N., and it came amid heightened tensions between Cuba and the U.S. as President Donald Trump's administration seeks to force changes to Cuba's political system by increasing its already punishing economic campaign.
Trump, a Republican, announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to Cuba. The warning has effectively cut off fuel to the island, leading to widespread power outages that affect basic activities such as cooking, the water supply and internet and telephone services.
The Caribbean country, already facing the dire impact of longtime economic and financial troubles, is now being pushed to a breaking point.
Cuban officials have also repeatedly stressed that as U.S. officials demand that Cuba open up to private investment, Washington keeps piling on sanctions that stymie the very economic opening it has sought for decades.
Tuesday's outbursts came a week after a similar interaction between Waltz and his Cuban counterpart, Ernesto Soberón Guzmán, outside a U.S.-hosted panel with Cuban dissidents and former prisoners that sought to highlight allegations of the oppressive behavior of the island's government.
Waltz and other U.S. officials have been using these public events and gatherings at the world body to try to persuade U.N. member states to vote on Wednesday against the annual resolution. The measure is aimed at calling out the U.S. government's “maximum pressure policy” against Cuba.
For the past 34 years, the resolution has received overwhelming support. Last year, the vote was 165-7, with 12 abstentions. Argentina, Ukraine and Hungary opposed the measure for the first time.
While such resolutions are not legally binding, they do reflect world opinion.

On March 18, 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio handed the reins of the US Agency for International Development to Jeremy Lewin, a 28-year-old graduate of Harvard Law School, former investment banker, and affiliate of Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency. At the time, Lewin’s appointment drew criticism because of his lack of experience in government, diplomacy, or foreign assistance. But for career staff inside the agency, the issues surrounding Lewin’s new role were much more alarming than his thin résumé.
For at least two months, USAID senior staff had no knowledge of how Lewin, who appeared at the agency one day as a policymaker on an obscure detail from the General Services Administration, could have suddenly begun wielding the powers of the agency’s top official.
Internal USAID emails reviewed by WIRED reveal that during the three-week period of March 18 to April 4, during which Lewin began canceling lifesaving aid programs and personally signed off on the termination of thousands of USAID employees, he did not sign the paperwork typically required by law to begin work at the agency, despite repeated requests. In fact, his appointment was so mysterious that USAID security was unable to issue him an ID card because they had no records of his employment.
Lewin, currently director of policy planning at the State Department, tells WIRED that prior to Rubio delegating powers to him, he was “both detailed and dual appointed to work at USAID by Secretary Rubio according to well-established authorities and with the advice of State Department and White House counsel.”
Experts, though, say that while Lewin performed the duties of a top USAID leader under the title Rubio handed to him—deputy administrator of policy and programming and chief operating officer—it isn’t clear that he had the legal authority to do so. Questions about how DOGE affiliates like Lewin stepped into top roles at many federal agencies, including USAID, remain key to dozens of active lawsuits targeting DOGE and the Trump administration over federal workforce reductions, firings, and agency dismantlings.
Lewin has said, in a declaration submitted to the court in J. Doe 4 v. U.S. DOGE Service, that he began serving at USAID as a senior adviser as well as a director for strategy and programs on January 28, 2025. On March 18, according to court filings, Rubio, in his role as USAID’s acting administrator, delegated the authority of the deputy administrator of policy and programming and chief operating officer to Lewin, and also signed a document appointing Lewin an “officer of the United States.”
According to the emails reviewed by WIRED, on March 20, two days after Rubio placed Lewin atop the USAID hierarchy, White House liaison to USAID Adam Korzeniewski notified HR to begin the process of onboarding Lewin as a senior adviser performing duties as deputy administrator. Four days later, the emails reveal, after prompting from HR, Korzeniewski provided a proposed start date—March 18—and the next day, Lewin was sent a temporary job offer.
By March 26, the emails show, Lewin still hadn’t accepted the job offer, and had not filed his OF-306, the federal government's standard pre-employment background screening form; without this document, a federal agency cannot lawfully issue a final job offer or consummate an appointment. An HR executive noted in an email dated March 31 that Lewin had not completed the onboarding tasks required to initiate “the security reciprocity process,” which recognizes the transfer of an employees’ security clearance from one agency to another. (A detailing agreement between the GSA and USAID dated February 14—two weeks after Lewin says he began at USAID—specifes that “commencement of the detail is contingent upon the Detailee’s successful adjudication and receipt of any necessary security clearances and other pre-employment screening required by USAID.”)
On March 28, Lewin signed a letter terminating all remaining USAID staff. And as he executed sweeping powers to liquidate all 60 of USAID’s overseas missions and cancel thousands of lifesaving projects worldwide, HR repeatedly followed up with Korzeniewski.
More than a week after Lewin’s appointment, the emails show, a USAID official told Korzeniewski that the agency’s office of security was “unable to issue a USAID ID card to Jeremy Lewin as SEC [the agency’s secure database] did not have a record of Jeremy as an employee.”
“Until you’re onboarded at USAID, you aren’t even in the system,” says Natalia Machuca, a 15-year agency veteran who hired many staff. “You can’t get a badge, get into your computer, or even walk around the building.”
Lewin tells WIRED, “I was a regular government employee with a valid security clearance held by the State Department during this entire period. USAID HR was confused about this paperwork for a period of days, but this issue was cleared up once they were made aware of the dual appointment and my State Department position.”
But according to a top executive in HR, no one from their office saw any delegation documents until late April 2025. As one longtime HR executive at the agency, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said of Lewin: “He was the equivalent of an administrative ghost.”
“I think this creates a huge accountability problem if you have these actors who are making really consequential life-or-death decisions who didn't go through any standard confirmation process,” says Don Moynihan, a public policy professor at the University of Michigan, “or in this case didn't even complete their paperwork to become a formal employee.”
Lewin—who a White House official says submitted all the paperwork required for employment and clearance—provided WIRED with two documents, both dated March 18, 2025. One is an appointment and compensation waiver, signed by Rubio, naming Lewin director of strategy and planning, and stating that he would not be paid “pursuant to, among other provisions of law, 22 U.S.C. § 2385(b).” The other is a standard appointment affidavit naming Lewin USAID’s director of strategy and programs. A signature on the form appears to be Rubio’s, with the title given as “HRO”—usually an abbreviation for human resources officer. The State Department did not answer questions about this document.
To one former senior USAID official, Rubio’s use of 22 U.S.C. § 2385(b)—an obscure provision traditionally reserved for rapidly deploying emergency-response staff to disaster zones abroad—to appoint Lewin looks like a legal contortion.
“It is so unconventional that I’d never seen it used before I got to USAID,” the official said. “It was created for the purposes of scaling up really quickly if there was some outbreak of a virus somewhere and they needed to bring people on, then let them go.”
Brian Feinstein, a law professor at the Wharton School of Business, acknowledged that while using 22 U.S.C. § 2385(b) to appoint Lewin is complex, it appears to him to be legal. “Because Lewin's appointment is consistent with this law regarding USAID personnel,” he says, “his unusual status should not be a factor.”
Outside of this point, legal questions also remain about Lewin’s actions at the agency before he was appointed by Rubio, and his failure to complete the onboarding required to begin his initial detail period at USAID. During this time he was part of a team that issued sweeping orders, including one to then acting administrator Jason Gray to lock all USAID staff worldwide out of email and all communication systems, which could have put many staff’s lives at risk, and to terminate 57 of the agency’s top officials.
David A. Super, professor of law and economics at Georgetown University, describes Lewin’s failure to complete his onboarding as much more than an administrative slip-up. “You can’t just walk in the door of a federal agency and become an employee,” he says. Under federal law, a cabinet secretary can only assign the authority of a Senate-confirmed position such as USAID administrator to a subordinate official—an agency employee or officer who works under the supervision of a higher-ranking officer. These regulations, Super says, are a way for Congress to guarantee that “someone walking off the street should not be given these enormous powers.”
Nina Mendelson, who teaches law at the University of Michigan, agrees. She says the administration appeared to be trying to bypass the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, a federal statute that dictates how temporary vacancies in Senate-confirmed executive branch positions are filled. “The FVRA specifies who may fill in, for a limited time, when a Senate-confirmed post is vacant,” she says. “The possibilities are a first assistant, someone holding another Senate-confirmed post, or a longtime civil servant in the particular agency. Lewin doesn’t seem to have been any one of those.”
Lewin being placed atop USAID came in a specific context. In February 2025, shortly after the arrival of Lewin and other DOGE affiliates at the agency, two dozen current and former USAID employees and contractors sued Musk and DOGE in Maryland District Court. They successfully secured a preliminary injunction on March 18, on the grounds that special government employees—temporary hires from outside USAID and the government—lacked the authority to execute sweeping federal actions. That same day, Rubio delegated powers of the agency’s top job to Lewin.
On March 28, the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals granted the Justice Department an emergency stay, pausing the injunction based on the administration’s argument that the actions were taken by Lewin in his role as a federally appointed official. In his declaration, Lewin wrote: “I am not, and have never been, an employee of Elon Musk or USDS,” adding, “I report directly and only to Acting Administrator Rubio” in his role at USAID.
The ruling gave Lewin the green light to fire thousands of career civil service and Foreign Service staff that very day, but the legal battle didn’t end there. The district judge has since allowed thousands of affected employees to sue DOGE and the administration as a group and ordered the government to hand over a trove of internal documents.
Kevin Byrnes, a veteran federal employment law attorney representing more than 170 former and current career USAID staff in a separate suit challenging DOGE’s role in the mass firings, says the fact that Lewin had not completed mandatory onboarding paperwork raises even more questions about the authority of nonconfirmed agency leadership, and potentially exposes Lewin personally.
“If Lewin didn’t even fill out the papers and was not authorized to take these actions, then he could be exposed to personal liability,” says Byrnes, who is asking the court to reinstate all the plaintiffs to their USAID jobs, with back pay.

It's a good day to be a Kindle fan. Amazon announced the arrival of a new generation of devices earlier this month, and the new Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft are available today. A question now presents itself: Should you upgrade?
The most intriguing reason to upgrade isn't the devices themselves—the Paperwhite and Colorsoft both have base plastic versions with 16 GB of storage and aluminum-backed Signature Editions with 32 GB of storage and extra features—but the little extras could go a long way for certain readers. Namely, the ability to add page-turn buttons with the new Kindle Page Turn Cover ($80)—which is compatible only with the new Signature Editions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft.
Color also plays a big role in the Signature Editions compared to the new base models. Not a color screen, to be clear—that's still Colorsoft only—but the color of the device itself, which Amazon has said was a huge driver for Kindle users to upgrade to a new model after the brand released colors like Matcha and Raspberry in 2024. The 2026 line has one color for each of these 7-inch e-readers that's only available with the Signature Editions.
It's worth noting that while the price of these new models is the same as the 2024 editions, it's because Kindle raised the prices of its 2024 versions back in August. At first, it seemed like this was intended to make Amazon sales look better than they actually were heading into Prime Day and Black Friday, but now it's clear it was probably a way to make these new models feel worth buying, since you won't find a cheaper model as easily. And it's a valid move: These models will be my new picks, because if you're spending the same amount, why wouldn't you want the latest model?
But that doesn't necessarily help you decide if it's worth upgrading. It might be worth it if you're desperate for page-turner buttons, which is easily my favorite part of this new line of Kindles. If you don't have a Kindle already and are on a mission to select your first one, this latest version of the Paperwhite remains a good choice unless you're determined to splurge on a color screen. The warm light is a big benefit for anyone who reads in the evening, and you'll have to choose one of these two models from Kindle's lineup to get it anyway.
The Base Lineup
The Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft are, to some degree, the same device. You'll see a similar laundry list of features: a 7-inch screen, a front light with adjustable brightness and warmth, and 16 GB of storage in the base models. Both have the same new look of a flush-front screen and ever-so-slightly-smaller body when compared to the 2024 Paperwhite and 2025 Colorsoft (the first Colorsoft in 2024 was later renamed the Signature Edition, and a cheaper base model came out in 2025).

I’ve never listened to a full episode of the Happy Wife Happy Life podcast, hosted by Jordan Myrick and Kendahl Landreth, but I’ve sure seen all the clips.
My Instagram Reels algorithm recently served me, along with 5 million other viewers, a brief rant from Myrick about feeling bamboozled by the health care system. Then, I spent the next hour scrolling through the show’s other snippets on Reels, loving the couple’s snarky banter. Still, I never followed the duo to a different platform to watch the full-length podcasts.
On Monday, Instagram announced plans that might have turned me into a regular listener of the show. Instagram will expand tests in the US that let creators upload long-form content up to 90 minutes and flip a video’s orientation to horizontal. Creators can also link their short clips directly back to full-length videos.
“Our belief here is that entertainment and creativity are not limited to a three-minute video,” Tessa Lyons, vice president of product at Instagram, tells WIRED. She wants to build the “best place for social entertainment” with this overhaul of Instagram video. The social media platform may soon feel like a streaming service, as more viewers watch longer videos on their big screen.
Instagram is also expanding its creator tools for turning Reels into episodic content. “We want to be able to say, ‘Wow, Reece loved episode 3. So, as soon as episode 4 drops, we've got to make sure to show it to him,’” Lyons says. This Reels feature, called “Series,” is already available for some creators in the app, and it's being tested for TV viewing as well.
Instagram is focused on the experience of watching videos on your TV. It's hunting for ways to make that TV experience feel social, like showing your connections what you’ve been watching via the Friends tab. The company also plans to turn your smartphone into a TV remote.
Lyons sees the video-focused update as avoiding one of IGTV’s core mistakes—IGTV was the company’s previous attempt at more expansive content. In that instance, many viewers desperately wanted to flip the screen. IGTV failed to connect with users, in part, because it only allowed vertical videos. Meta discontinued the app a few years after its 2018 launch.
While Instagram’s latest changes challenge YouTube’s TV dominance, they also try to leverage its current strength as a platform for clips. Bite-sized clips, often of two people sitting behind podcast microphones, feel inescapable on social media right now, with many creators using them to boost visibility. Even WIRED’s own podcast now records videos for social media clipping.
Instagram is streamlining a viewer’s potential fandom journey. Rather than viral clips and long-form content existing on different platforms, Instagram is positioning itself as a centralized experience where I can stumble on Myrick’s health care rant in the morning and then open the app on my TV later that night and get a nudge to stream the full podcast episode.
“What we're seeing right now is that a lot of great short-form content is vertical, and a lot of great long-form content is horizontal, and we have the design challenge of figuring out how to make that all work cohesively in one product,” Lyons says. “TV becomes a great destination for watching long-form, horizontal content, and mobile becomes a great place for discovering that content.”

Naukri parent Info Edge has approved the sale of its entire stakes in healthtech startup MedCords and employment platform Unnati Online for about ₹5,000 each, marking its proposed exit from two investments it had already fully impaired. Info Edge’s board approved the divestment of its 14.18% stake in MedCords Healthcare Solutions and 31.64% stake in Unnati Online, both held by its wholly owned subsidiary Startup Investments (Holding) Limited (SIHL). MedCords stake will be sold to the startup’s promoter and director Shreyans Mehta. Meanwhile, Unnati Online’s promoters and directors Eral Ravi and Aashutosh Chaudhary will acquire Info Edge’s holding in the employment platform. The company expects to enter into the sale agreements within 30 days and complete both transactions by January 27, 2027. Info Edge had booked provisions for full impairment of its MedCords investment in FY24 and its Unnati Online investment in FY20. The proposed sales would therefore formalise its exits from investments already fully provided for. Following completion, MedCords will cease to be a joint venture of Info Edge, while Unnati Online will cease to be an associate company. The Unnati stake is calculated on a fully converted and diluted basis, excluding the ESOP pool. Founded by Nikhil Baheti, Saida Dhanavath and Shreyans Mehta, MedCords built a healthcare platform connecting patients, doctors and neighbourhood pharmacies. As Inc42 reported in 2020, the startup expanded from digitising medical records and facilitating teleconsultations into a hyperlocal healthcare marketplace, using its Sehat Sathi app to bring local pharmacies online. Info Edge had agreed to invest ₹7 Cr in MedCords in March 2020, taking its proposed aggregate shareholding to 16.89% on a fully converted and diluted basis at the time. Meanwhile, Unnati Online operated Unnati Helpers, a platform connecting informal sector workers with employers. Founded by Shantanu Singh, Eral Ravi and Aashutosh Chaudhary, the Gurugram-based startup catered to hiring needs across households and businesses, including drivers, domestic workers, delivery personnel and factory workers. Info Edge invested ₹4 Cr in Unnati via convertible preference shares to acquire about 28.5% of the company on a fully converted and diluted basis. Alongside the proposed exits, Info Edge’s board approved an investment of up to ₹150 Cr in its wholly owned subsidiary Redstart Labs through an equity subscription. The infusion will take place in one or more tranches within 18 months of approval. Info Edge said the money would support Redstart’s working capital requirements, investment opportunities and other general purposes. Redstart, which is Info Edge’s deeptech focused investment arm, reported a loss after tax of ₹2.99 Cr in FY26 and net worth of ₹76.93 C, with nil turnover. Besides the aforementioned developments, Info Edge also announced a major leadership rejig today with CEO Hitesh Oberoi departing from his operational role and founder Sanjeev Bikhchandani taking extending his role to include CEO, MD and executive director of the company effective December 3. On the financial front, Info Edge also announced an 87% jump in its Q2 FY27 net profit to ₹649.8 Cr. While the company's top line only increased by 12.2% YoY to ₹903.9 Cr, its other income almost tripled YoY to ₹428.4 Cr.

Srinagar, Oct 28: The Pashmina Testing and Quality Certification Centre (PTQCC) at the Craft Development Institute (CDI), Srinagar, has recorded a sharp rise in the testing of Geographical Indication (GI) products, especially Kashmir Pashmina, Kani and Sozni embroidered shawls, during the current financial year.
The surge reflects stronger institutional capacity, upgraded laboratory infrastructure and growing demand for authentic GI certification and QR coding.
In a detailed press statement issued here today, a spokesman of the Handicrafts and Handloom Department, Kashmir stated that the testing rate which was 40-45 per day in 2024-25, has now risen to 170 per day in 2026-27. “In 2024-25, PTQCC conducted 13,369 tests at an average of 40-45 tests per day. This rose to 22,351 tests in 2025-26, with the daily average increasing to 75-85 tests. In the current financial year, PTQCC has already performed approximately 21,000 tests.
With another 21,000 tests projected between November 2026 and March 31, 2027, the annual total is expected to reach around 42,000 tests, nearly doubling the testing rate achieved in the previous year,” the spokesman explained. 
To support this expansion, the spokesman further stated that Pashmina Laboratory has been strengthened with advanced equipment, including a Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) and two High-Resolution Digital Microscopes.
“The Department is in the process of procuring another OFDA 2000 fibre analyser and an additional digital microscope during FY 2026-27 under CAPEX. These additions are expected to further accelerate testing, improve precision in fibre identification and quality assessment and meet the rising demand for GI testing and QR coding of certified products,” he said, adding that those GI Authorised Users who submit hand-spun, hand-woven Pashmina products with Sozni embroidery are being given preferential treatment.
In order to bring greater transparency in GI testing, certification and QR coding at PTQCC, the Department has developed an in-house Online Appointment Token Management System to further streamline the operations across all testing labs of the Department including IICT and QCD (Quality Control Division). “The web application has been developed by the Resource Cell of the department which shall be operational shortly on pilot basis,” he added.
The Directorate is in the process of augmenting additional manpower to operate the machines for which technical staff is being sent to Wool Research Association (WRA), Thane Maharashtra for technical training. “With trained manpower, we shall have more teams in place to conduct tests in PTQCC so that the rising demand for GI testing and QR coding post aggressive media campaign, by GI Authorised Users is met. “The enhanced testing capacity strengthens the authentication of Kashmir’s prized handicrafts, protects the interests of artisans and weavers and builds greater consumer and buyer confidence in genuine GI-tagged products,” the spokesman stated.
Faster and more reliable certification is particularly important for exports and premium domestic markets, where authenticity is a key differentiator for Kashmir Pashmina and related handicraft products, the spokesman concluded.

Healthy snacking brand Troovy has raised ₹100 Cr ($10.5 Mn) in a Series B funding round led by existing investor Fireside Ventures, with participation from Sharrp Ventures. The startup will use the fresh capital to expand its manufacturing capacity and fuel its research and development (R&D) for product development. The D2C brand will also strengthen its distribution across quick commerce and offline channels. Besides, the startup plans to expand its portfolio into categories like namkeen, biscuits and cookies by January 2027, Baranwal said. “We will also launch more products in existing categories and build our R&D capabilities. We’re planning to develop new products with parents, as well as innovators from across the country,” cofounder Mansi Baranwal told Inc42. Founded in 2021 by husband-and-wife duo Mansi Baranwal and Aditya Mukherjee, Troovy initially entered the market with clean-label ketchup and later expanded into the healthy snacking category. Its portfolio of products includes chips, puffs, sauces, spreads, millet-based pasta, cookies and milk mixes. Chips and puffs are Troovy’s hero categories, together accounting for around 60-70% of sales, as per Baranwal. Troovy Doubles Down On Offline Expansion Marketplaces and quick commerce account for roughly half of Troovy’s sales, while sales from its own website brings in about 30%. Offline retail, which the startup recently entered in Delhi NCR, accounts for close to 6% of revenue. Troovy has begun building its offline distribution network, starting with Delhi NCR and neighbouring areas. It plans to expand into select metro and Tier I markets, initially focusing on Delhi NCR, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, with some presence planned in Punjab and Haryana. Baranwal said the startup is taking a measured approach as it works out its distribution strategy for offline retail. “We’re very much in learning mode. We’re trying to figure out the playbook and experiment with different things,” she said, adding that North India is an important market for chips. The latest fundraise follows Troovy’s $5 Mn Series A round in January this year, led by Fireside Ventures. “Troovy grew 5X in the eight months following our last investment, and that is what made us double down,” said Ankita Balotia, principal at Fireside Ventures. The latest fundraise announcement comes months after the startup came under the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India’s (FSSAI) scrutiny over the use of the word “Healthy” in the names of its Veggie Chips, Ragi Chips and Moong Dal Chips. The regulator said the product names could mislead consumers, despite the products containing other ingredients. Responding to a question on the food regulator’s crackdown, Baranwal said stricter enforcement of food labelling rules could benefit brands that have invested in product formulation and ingredient transparency. “I strongly think that this is great for the sector as well as for consumers and the country at large. These regulations exist for the benefit of the consumer, and tighter implementation is always better from a consumer perspective,” she said. However, she said compliance could add to the costs and operational challenges faced by startups that lack adequate testing infrastructure. “We do a lot of lab testing, and it puts a lot of pressure on startups like us that don’t have the correct infrastructure,” Baranwal said. She added that Troovy was also working to reduce sodium levels in its products and limit the use of ingredients it considers undesirable.

An investigation by Dutch nonprofit Global Rights Compliance has revealed new details about the exploitative tactics of a Russian labor-brokering platform that employs North Korean workers in violation of international law — benefiting Moscow’s war effort in Ukraine.
The report, released Thursday, offers striking detail into the practices of Moscow-based businessman Vladimir Sokolov, who directs the Black Horse group of companies and KNDR.su, an online platform that helps Russian employers source North Korean workers.
Sokolov’s businesses specialize in importing Chinese and European manufacturing equipment and include at least two sites connected to Russia’s military-industrial complex and an agricultural commodity export business catering to the North. Sokolov was sanctioned by the European Union earlier this month “for promoting and facilitating commercial and industrial cooperation projects involving” North Korea.

- Bandai Namco confirmed a data breach through its email provider, YmirLink.
- The exposed information does not include passwords, credit card details, or purchase history.
- Bandai Namco has suspended the affected email service as investigations continue.
The studio behind iconic titles like Tekken, Bandai Namco, has confirmed a data breach through its third-party email service provider, YmirLink. This has exposed the email addresses and internal IDs of around 346,000 members of The GUNDAM base. The incident is part of a much larger data leak at YmirLink, which has exposed more than 51.62 million records.
While the breach is concerning for affected users, there is some good news. The official statement released on October 28, 2026, which has now been taken down, stated that the exposed information is limited to email addresses and internal Bandai Namco ID numbers. Passwords, credit card details, names, addresses, and purchase history were not leaked, unlike Sony’s latest data Breach.
Additionally, as stated by Bandai Namco, the exposed email addresses could still pose a threat, as they can be used for phishing scams or impersonation attempts. To mitigate the risks, the company has warned users to remain cautious of suspicious emails and said that emails regarding the incident will not contain any URLs in their body.
Following the incident, the company has also suspended the affected email distribution service and reported the breach to Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission. The company also stated that no secondary damage, such as unauthorized use of personal information, had been confirmed at the time of announcement.
However, it will continue investigating the incident alongside YmirLink to determine its full impact. This data breach is part of a much larger data leak at YmirLink. According to Japanese news outlet NHK One, YmirLink initially reported around 9 million leaked records on October 19th, but further investigation increased the number to over 51.62 million.
This data breach primarily consists of email addresses and affects various other organizations using YmirLink’s services, which includes Japanese railway operators JR Central, JR West, and JR Kyushu, who have also reported potential data leaks.
With the investigation still ongoing, the full extent of the breach and the number of affected records could increase further. For now, the best strategy for everyone affected would be to avoid clicking suspicious links, especially given that Capcom was also breached last week.

The Franklin County board of elections building at 1700 Morse Street in central Columbus, Ohio, is an early voting site for next week’s midterms. It is also located in the middle of the large Somali American community that was targeted by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency’s Operation Buckeye last December. The campaign was designed, the agency said, to find “the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens.”
The result was a paltry number of arrests, months of sustained harassment, and a lingering feeling that ICE agents could return at any minute, especially around election time.
“Here in central Ohio, our early voting location is located in a neighborhood that's been the hardest hit by ICE, and it's an immigrant community neighborhood,” Liliana Rivera Baiman, an organizer with the 614 ICE Watch group and the Ohio Good Neighbor Network, tells WIRED. “So we knew that that neighborhood was at risk and that people were going to be going to vote there, and a lot of the community there, like our Somali community that can vote, our Latino community, they walk to the location.”
Baiman’s group is responding to the threats from the Trump administration to target immigrant communities during the midterms. Dozens of volunteers are already patrolling near early voting sites in Columbus every day, Baiman says, and the figure will rise to around 250 on Election Day. They have been trained to document, record, and report any sightings of federal immigration agents, sharing the information in dozens of Signal and WhatsApp groups.
“We teach people that they have to observe the behavior. We show them what to look out for, what does ICE look like, this is the type of uniform that agents wear, these are the types of vehicles that they drive,” Baiman says. “We show them examples so that they can get familiar with what they might see.”
These efforts are being repeated in towns and cities across the country. WIRED spoke to a dozen people taking part in this effort, whose groups are working together to combat what they see as an existential threat to American democracy. Central to this response are training sessions run by massive national groups like Common Cause, the American Civil Liberties Union, and Indivisible, as well as local groups like Living United for Change in Arizona and NorCal Resist, that have created massive groups of people who can document and record what ICE is doing, understand voters rights, and in many cases, prepare for worst-case scenarios.
Officially, the Department of Homeland Security has said that it has no plans to deploy ICE agents to polling locations on Election Day. “ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED, but added: “ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.”
For the past six months, President Trump and his allies have declined to rule out possible deployments to voting locations during the midterms, even though they would be illegal under federal law. When asked in May if he would deploy the National Guard or ICE during the midterms, Trump said: “I’d do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections. We have to have honest elections.”
“Why are there objections to sending ICE officers to polling places?” Todd Blanche, then acting attorney general, said in July. “Illegals can’t vote.” The White House did not respond to requests for comment.
Some election experts simply don’t believe it will happen: “ICE and troops will not be at the polls,” David Becker, a former Justice Department trial attorney who is now head of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said at a recent media briefing. “It won't happen. If it happens at all, it will be isolated. It will be accidental. It just won't happen.”
But for organizations on the ground interacting with voters in communities that have been targeted by ICE during Trump’s second term in office, the reality feels very different. Hundreds of different groups are part of the fight against possible ICE intimidation at the polls, and they are all working in coordination with each other.
“I've been up and down this state, in and out of Reno, in and out of Las Vegas, into our rural counties, and the number one question I get is about federal agents at polling locations,” Cisco Aguilar, the Nevada secretary of state, tells WIRED.
Beatriz Lopez, the executive director of Voto Latino, a group encouraging Hispanic and Latino citizens to register to vote, agrees, particularly when it comes to the communities her organization is focused on.
“We know that Latino voters are in the crosshairs of this administration because we know our electorate, our voting bloc, is what's going to shape and determine the elections of so many competitive races,” Lopez tells WIRED. “There is legitimate fear among our community.”
Lopez’s group, like many others WIRED spoke to, will be operating a war room on Election Day, with the specific goal of identifying and debunking viral disinformation that could dissuade citizens from voting. But they are also preparing for more troubling, real-world concerns.
“One of the scenarios that we're anticipating is that at the same time that we're trying to get people out to vote, there might be home raids by ICE in some of these neighborhoods, which has a real chilling effect on people,” Lopez said.
To combat this scenario, groups like 614 ICE Watch in Columbus are organizing patrols in neighborhoods near polling locations. “We send our folks in pairs or in groups. We never want to send anyone alone; we always want to have multiple people there so they can help take control of the situation,” Baiman says, adding that they have trained volunteers in a unique method of de-escalation: “If it starts to get very tense, we teach our folks to hum, to sing, to calm themselves down.”
The goal is not to interact with ICE agents but to document what they are doing so that events can be properly recorded and shared publicly. In January, just days after Alex Pretti was shot and killed in Minneapolis, more than 200,000 people logged into an “Eyes on Ice” Zoom training session, designed to teach people how to properly document ICE activities. Those skills are now being deployed during the midterm elections, Ezra Levin, cofounder of Indivisible, a group founded to stop the rise of authoritarianism in the US, tells WIRED.
On a much smaller scale, Living United for Change in Arizona has been training volunteers to become “constitutional defenders” in person, as the group prepares for next week’s vote. To track ICE activity, the group created a heat map that volunteers use to log and track ICE activity. The map is not available publicly, but WIRED was given access to the website and reviewed hundreds of recorded incidents of ICE activity in Maricopa and Pima counties.
Groups are also using social media to draw attention to what is happening. Last week in Sutter County, California, six ICE vehicles showed up in the parking lot of the Yuba City board of elections building, where a ballot drop box is located. Following a call from a local resident, NorCal Resist, a mutual aid organization, was able to send one of its trained volunteers and post an alert on Instagram.
“They don't like the attention, [and] when there's more community attention, they do often leave,” Giselle Garcia, programs director with NorCal Resist, tells WIRED.
DHS denied it was conducting immigration enforcement at a polling location, and said its agents were conducting a targeted enforcement operation against an illegal immigrant from Mexico. “ICE parked in front of a polling center—with permission from a representative of the center—while waiting for the target to exit the courthouse,” Chandler Rebel, a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED.
Much of this work, however, is being done in private, a move Lopez says is necessary to protect the online infrastructure they have put in place over the course of the past two years. Levin said that Indivisible’s leadership team would be hunkered down in an Airbnb in an undisclosed location on Election Day, on alert to deploy their sizable resources wherever they are needed.
Despite the fear that pervades minority communities about what Trump and his federal agents will do next week, every group leader, activist and volunteer WIRED spoke to in recent weeks has repeated one central belief: They are prepared.
“You have all this traditional election protection infrastructure that's really, really robust, but then there is this grassroots infrastructure,” Jill Garvey, executive director of States at the Core, which combats authoritarianism and political extremism, tells WIRED. “They've done all this tactical documentation training. They know how to be constitutional observers, and I'm pretty confident that when and if we have an uptick in federal enforcement at the polls, it's going to get documented really, really quickly, and it's going to be beamed out to the world that it's happening.”

Sergio Perez will remain with Cadillac until 2029 after signing a multi-year contract extension.
The 36-year-old, who is set to celebrate his 300th Grand Prix start in his home race in Mexico City this weekend, joined the American Formula One team last August before their debut season on the grid, racing alongside fellow veteran Valtteri Bottas.
Perez made his Formula One debut in 2011 and has won six grands prix – five for Red Bull between 2021-24 and one for Racing Point (now Aston Martin) in 2020.
He finished third in the 2022 drivers' championship and second behind team-mate Max Verstappen in 2023.
Despite having two years left on his contract, he was dropped by Red Bull at the end of the 2024 season after the team felt he had run out of time to prove he could support Verstappen.
Perez sits bottom of the 2026 standings, with three 14th-place finishes – in Barcelona, Silverstone, and Azerbaijan – his best performances. Neither he nor Bottas has earned a point for Cadillac.
"Joining Cadillac from day one was a project I truly believed in, and extending my commitment feels like a natural continuation of this chapter," said Perez.
"Building a Formula One team from the ground up takes time, relentless work and patience, but the progress we are making together is incredibly rewarding.
"There is still a lot of work ahead of us and I am fully committed to the next three years."

India's cartoonists built an audience online - now their posts are being restricted
- Published
For the second time in three weeks, Indian cartoonist Satish Acharya found himself effectively invisible on Instagram in his own country.
The 55-year-old discovered on Tuesday that his account had once again been briefly blocked in India, allegedly with no explanation from the platform.
Just a few weeks ago, another cartoonist, Manjul, had found that Instagram had restricted a post criticising India's election commission over its controversial revision of voter rolls. His profile remained accessible.
The cases have raised concerns about the use of legal orders to restrict political satire in India, with cartoonists saying they are often given little explanation for why their work has been blocked.
Acharaya's account was first restricted from 28 September to 6 October, when users in India could neither find his profile through search nor access it through a web link.
Anyone trying to access his profile saw a message saying it was unavailable under India's Information Technology Rules.
The rules allow authorities and courts to order social media platforms to remove or restrict content.
The government says they help tackle unlawful material, but artists and free-speech advocates warn they can stifle India's rich tradition of political satire.
"Meta platforms have been restricting the reach of my cartoons for some years," Acharya told the BBC. "But when my entire profile was restricted in India, I was a little sad."
He wrote to Meta, Instagram's parent company, but received no reply. He says he was preparing to go to court when his account became accessible again in early October, only to be blocked again earlier this week for three days.
In a statement, Meta told the BBC that it may temporarily restrict accounts to comply with India's IT Rules but did not explain the specific reasons for restricting Acharya's account or Manjul's post.
Critics say the restrictions come as humour and satire play an increasingly visible role in political dissent in India, particularly among younger people.
Memes and Gen-Z humour helped fuel protests over education and jobs in July, which led to the resignation of India's education minister. Online debate has also intensified over a controversial revision of voter rolls that removed 130 million names.
The political significance of social media has not been lost on the government. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has urged ministers to strengthen their online presence and connect with younger audiences.
At the same time, technology policy expert Prateek Waghre says the government is increasingly using legal orders to regulate online content.
The Indian Express reported, external that government agencies sent nearly 195,000 blocking and content-restriction orders to platforms including Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July through the federal government's Sahyog portal.
The figures, obtained through a right-to-information request, do not show how many posts were ultimately restricted or removed. The BBC has not seen the original response.
Waghre says that some platforms, particularly Meta, "seem more willing to comply", he says, while X appears more willing to push back. But limited public data makes comparisons difficult. Meta declined to comment on his assessment.
The government has also reportedly sought greater scrutiny of how social media platforms recommend content.
Earlier this week, several media outlets reported, external that authorities had asked Meta to ensure its systems did not steer users towards "a single or limited set of narratives" and strengthen checks on content that could "cause public disorder or incite violence".
The BBC has sought comment from India's IT ministry on the restrictions and reported instructions to Meta but has not received a response.
Of course, political satire has a long history in India - as do attempts to curb it.
Cartoons have been a fixture of Indian journalism since independence, with RK Laxman's Common Man becoming one of its most recognisable characters.
But cartoonists have also faced censorship. During the Emergency in the 1970s, when civil liberties were suspended and the press was tightly controlled, Abu Abraham continued drawing, even as dozens of his cartoons were stamped "not passed by censors".
In 2012, cartoonist Aseem Trivedi was arrested on sedition charges over cartoons allegedly mocking the Indian constitution. The charges were later dropped.
Today, concerns about restrictions on political expression extend beyond cartoonists. India ranks 157th in Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index, while critics accuse the government of putting growing pressure on independent media. The government rejects the criticism, saying India's media remains free and vibrant.
Comedians have also faced controversy over political satire. Kunal Kamra, known for his jokes about Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his party, has faced threats, cancelled shows and legal action.
For cartoonists, however, challenging those in power is central to their work.
"We are among the default opposition," says Sandeep Adhwaryu, a cartoonist at a leading Indian newspaper.
"The nature of the craft is to oppose," he says, adding that cartoonists, like journalists, must question whoever holds power.
Acharya says he has followed that principle throughout his career. Before 2014, many of his cartoons targeted the Congress-led government and were shared by BJP leaders.
"I never faced official restrictions on my cartoons during the previous governments, though there would be some trolling occasionally," he says.
Now, with the BJP in power, much of his satire is directed at Modi's government.
Social media has allowed independent cartoonists like Acharya to reach audiences without relying on newspapers or other traditional outlets.
"We are not associated with newspapers or any mainstream media. That's why we can draw," says Manjul.
But that freedom comes with a new vulnerability - dependence on platforms that can restrict their work or cut off access to their audiences.
No one knows this better than Rachita Taneja, the creator of the hugely popular Instagram comic Sanitary Panels.
"My career would not have existed without the internet," she told the BBC. Yet she describes social media as a double-edged sword.
"At the end of the day it's a for-profit endeavour that answers to advertisers," she says.
Taneja says that Meta's compliance with Indian government requests reflects the company's commercial priorities rather than concern for users' rights. Meta declined to comment.
Even cartoonists working in traditional newsrooms face pressure. Adhwaryu says artists may soften captions, avoid certain subjects or think twice before submitting a cartoon. Over time, he says, such self-censorship can become normalised, even without explicit instructions.
Still, cartoonists have found ways to support one another.
When Acharya's Instagram account was first restricted, Taneja drew a stick-figure cartoon in solidarity. "Seeing people on the front lines creating communities, protesting, running campaigns, tirelessly fighting for their own rights and the rights of others is what keeps me going," she says.
Adhwaryu believes satire will continue to adapt. He compares cartoons and humour to a "shape-shifting virus".
"It keeps mutating in response to its environment," he says. "It will find its way."

New India Foundation announces shortlist for 2026 Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay NIF Book Prize
The award presentation has been scheduled for December 12 at the Bangalore Literature Festival 2026.
The New India Foundation (NIF) on Wednesday announced the shortlist of five books for the 2026 Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay NIF Book Prize (KCBP), the foundation said in a statement on Wednesday.
The winner, who will receive a cash prize of ₹15 lakh, will be announced in December, with the award presentation scheduled for December 12 at the Bangalore Literature Festival 2026.
“We are delighted with this year’s shortlist. The five books demonstrate the value of rigorous, imaginative non-fiction in deepening our understanding of India and are exceptional in their ability to bring important aspects of the country’s experience into focus,” chair of the jury and political scientist Niraja Gopal Jayal said, according to the statement.
“The NIF Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay Book Prize embodies the New India Foundation’s mission to foster high-quality research and writing on all aspects of the world’s largest democracy,” the statement said.
The five shortlisted books for the award this year are “A Man for All Seasons: The Life of K.M. Panikkar” by Narayani Basu; “Shattered Lands: Five Partitions and the Making of Modern Asia” by Sam Dalrymple; “Assembling India’s Constitution: A New Democratic History” by Rohit De and Ornit Shani; “A Sixth of Humanity: Independent India’s Development Odyssey” by Devesh Kapur and Arvind Subramanian and “The Secret Master: Arun Kashalkar and a Journey to the Edge of Music” by Sumana Ramanan.
The books examine different aspects of India’s political, constitutional and cultural history including the making of the Constitution, the country’s development since Independence and the partitions that shaped modern Asia.
An eminent seven-member jury, including Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran, former foreign secretary Nirupama Rao and entrepreneur Manish Sabharwal, selected the shortlist.
The statement said the KCBP, instituted in 2018, celebrates original non-fiction works written in or translated into English. Based in Bengaluru, NIF supports original research and scholarship on post-Independence India through fellowships and literary awards, the statement said.

While Amazon India and Flipkart have cut commissions to attract more sellers, higher cancellation penalties, platform fees and logistics costs are denting their margins just as festive demand peaks. Meanwhile, subdued discretionary spending and rising logistics costs are adding to their woes. But what’s really happening? Flipkart’s Penalty Shot: Flipkart’s zero-commission push across fashion categories in July has nearly doubled seller onboarding. However, its new penalty structure charges sellers ₹30 for delayed dispatches and another ₹60 for cancelled orders, regardless of order value. This flat fee is hurting smaller sellers and low-value orders, taking the shine off its zero-commission model. Amazon Plays Spoilsport, Too: The ecommerce giant has followed suit. It has revised its cancellation fee structure, linking charges to order value instead of slapping a flat fee. Amazon’s flat tier-based penalty for cancelled orders can go up to 10% of the order value for orders up to ₹10,000, falling to 8% for orders between ₹10,001 and ₹50,000, 5% for orders between ₹50,001 and ₹1 lakh, and 2% for orders above ₹1 lakh. An additional 18% GST applies to these charges. Deliveries Turn Costlier: Rising logistics costs are also adding to the festive-season strain, with Amazon raising closing fees and Delhivery introducing a surcharge on D2C shipments. Flipkart is also considering a revision in seller fulfilment fees. Quick commerce is adding to the pressure, with frequent, smaller shipments increasing vehicle requirements and waiting times at distribution hubs. Sellers In A Tight Corner: The shift to value-linked cancellation fees adds to the cost of doing business on marketplaces, particularly for those operating on thin margins. Sellers have also flagged the difficulty of contesting such charges, saying the process can be cumbersome even when they have evidence of timely dispatch. With penalties, surcharges and logistics costs piling up, here’s how ecommerce sellers are paying the price. Bengaluru-based AI startup Live2.ai has raised ₹130 Cr ($13.7 Mn) in a pre-Series B funding round led by IvyCap Ventures. The fundraise comprises both a fresh issue as well as a secondary component providing partial liquidity to undisclosed early investors. The AI-powered SaaS startup’s board features backers like Sony Innovation Fund, SOSV and Duane Park. The startup, which offers enterprises a SaaS platform that helps them monitor engagement for campaigns across channels, will use the fresh capital to build its AI platform further, strengthen its go-to-market strategy for enterprise customers and global consumer brands and expand regional cloud infrastructure. It also plans to hire across engineering, data science and customer success teams in North America, Europe, Singapore and India. “Brands today are drowning in signals and starved of action. Every conversation, creator post and trend spike is a revenue decision waiting to be made, and most are made too late or not at all. This funding lets us close that gap, with detection, decision and activation running in one governed loop for enterprise customers across North America, Europe and APAC,” said CEO and cofounder J Venkat. Founded by Venkat, Neha Suyal and Yash Arora, Live2.ai’s social intelligence platform monitors brand conversations across Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, X, and review sites. It combines social listening and trend identification with influencer content auditing, campaign compliance, social publishing, and performance tracking. It also enables brands to convert content into shoppable experiences across channels. The platform’s major differentiator lies in how it runs eight AI agents, including tools for crisis detection, trend identification, campaign auditing and automated responses, with governance controls and human review mechanisms. Live2.ai said its revenue grew fourfold in the past 12 months, with only 10% of its revenue coming from the Indian market. ATO could have done better on credit card ban, Mulino says
Sarah Basford Canales
The assistant treasurer, Daniel Mulino, says the tax office was dealing with a “complex” problem when deciding how to address the ban on credit card payment surcharges but, with the benefit of hindsight, it could have done better.
Speaking on ABC’s Radio National this morning, Mulino said the tax commissioner, Rob Heferen, said the reforms were really important and the Australian Taxation Office had been concurrently trying to negotiate with credit card companies while determining an adequate transition period.
The ATO stopped accepting credit card payments after the ban came into effect at the beginning of October. Heferen previously warned it would cost the ATO about $200m a year if it could not pass on the banking and credit card fees on to customers.
The ATO will now extend accept credit card payments for an extended transition period until the end of June next year.
Overnight, Heferen told a Senate estimates hearing he first realised the Reserve Bank’s surcharge ban would be a “real issue to grapple with” back in April.
The tax boss said he had received a letter from Mulino on 28 April informing the tax office of the RBA’s reforms, which brought the proposal to a “sharp head”.
Heferen told the hearing:
If we accept credit cards, it needs to be funded, and ceasing credit cards will have an effect on people who use credit cards. And some of our discussion was, ‘OK, what’s the appropriate transition for people up to transition through?’ And so that awareness, fair to say, around June, July [2026], we had staff before that who were already thinking about the issue, already formulating proposals.
Darwin teen to face court on charges of collecting documents likely to facilitate a terrorist act
An update from the AFP as the prime minister urges the Senate to pass his government’s latest social media reforms.
A teenager in Darwin is set to appear in children’s court today over charges of collecting documents likely to facilitate a terrorist act, as well as schematics for 3D-printed guns.
The Australian Federal Police said officials began an investigation earlier this month. They allege the teen was the operator of several social media channels which accessed, discussed or reposted violent extremist material.
A search warrant was undertaken on Wednesday, where officials allegedly found documents and electronic devices that contained violent extremist material and instructions for the making of 3D-printed firearms.
The teen faces several charges, which carry a maximum sentence of between 5 and 10 years imprisonment each.
NSW government says it’s not ‘sitting back and waiting for rain’ at Menindee
The NSW water minister, Rose Jackson, says “no one is underestimating the challenge at Menindee this summer” after water volumes at the Menindee Lakes fell to their lowest point in five years.
As we have reported this morning, experts have warned that unless conditions improve there is potential for fish kills in the region that suffered millions of fish deaths in 2018, 2019 and 2023.
Jackson says:
No one is underestimating the challenge at Menindee this summer, with lake levels now at their lowest point in five years and the prospect of another hot summer.
Our focus is on doing everything we can to protect water quality and native fish through the months ahead.
Significant inflows would improve conditions but we aren’t sitting back and waiting for rain.
Temporary restrictions are in place for some upstream water users. Jackson says the government has also installed a temporary fish passage to allow for better movement of native fish.

Angus Taylor, the opposition leader, said the country needs to get the “balance right” on AI, but powering datacentres with renewables only would not deliver for Australians.

Man cautioned after allegedly stalking two SA members of parliament
A man who allegedly targeted two South Australian member of parliament has been cautioned.
SA police issued stalking cautions to the 44-year-old man on Tuesday afternoon and said the cautions related to separate alleged incidents involving two MPs that were not connected.
He was also arrested for a separate alleged breach of bail.
The state’s education minister, Lucy Hood, and another Labor MP, Ella Shaw, spoke about their alleged experiences during a press conference on Wednesday.

Albanese dismisses economic criticism from ‘partisan participant’ Peter Costello
The PM is asked about criticism of the government’s handling of economic issues from former Liberal treasurer Peter Costello, who served under John Howard.

Peter Costello is a partisan participant. He’s not an observer. He’s not a commentator. I quite like Peter …

United Nations, Oct 28: The head of the UN nuclear agency said Tuesday there has been no indication Iran has tried to repair or reconstruct its nuclear facilities damaged in US and Israeli military strikes this year or last year.
President Donald Trump has said one of the major reasons the U.S. went to war with Iran on Feb. 28 was to deny Tehran the ability to develop nuclear weapons, even as he has insisted that strikes the US carried out on Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025 “obliterated” the country's atomic program.
During a UN Security Council meeting, International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi urged Iran to give inspectors access to all nuclear sites, including those damaged in the military attacks. The IAEA has not been able to verify the status of Iran's stockpile of near weapons-grade uranium since the U.S. bombed its sites last year.
However, Grossi said that “since June 2025, we have not identified any activity to repair or reconstruct any of the facilities damaged in the military attacks of 2025 and 2026."
Trump has consistently downplayed the economic impact of the Iran war, which has emerged as a liability for Republicans heading into next week's midterm elections, and has argued that higher fuel prices are worth paying to prevent a nuclear-armed Iran. The White House didn't immediately respond Tuesday evening to a request for comment on Grossi's remarks.
Iran maintains that its nuclear program is peaceful. However, the IAEA says the country has a stockpile of 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60% purity — a short, technical step away from weapons-grade levels of 90%.
The UN meeting on Tuesday was called by Bahrain, Denmark, Latvia, France, the United Kingdom and United States after the IAEA referred Iran to the Security Council for failing to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations. Russia and China, allies of Iran, tried unsuccessfully to prevent the meeting.
Under those obligations, which are part of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, Iran is legally bound to declare all nuclear material and activities and allow IAEA inspectors to verify that none of it is being diverted from peaceful uses.
Iran's UN deputy ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi attacked the council for its silence after the US-Israeli attacks, denouncing their “wars of aggression against Iran” and accusing the US of committing war crimes against the Iranian people.
He never mentioned the IAEA's unanswered questions or the demand to return its inspectors. Instead, he asserted that “Israel possesses nuclear weapons, yet your concern is the absence of inspectors in Iran.” Israel has never confirmed that it possesses nuclear weapons.
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz called Iran a “brutal dictatorship” and asked if the Iranian ambassador wanted to apologize to Bahrain's envoy, a council member, for attacking his country.
“We've heard tireless allegations against the United States, ” he said. “What we have not heard today is an explanation for Iran's continued failure to satisfy its safeguard obligations.”
The IAEA asked Iran for answers, Waltz said, and it would be smart for the Iranian representative to start providing some answers.
“Your lies are no good here,” he said.

Partial results from Israel's contentious election show no clear winner
TEL AVIV, Israel — With a majority of the votes counted on Wednesday morning, there was still no clear winner in Israel's pivotal parliamentary election, but Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was leading his main opposition rival, Gadi Eisenkot in the official tally.
However, the various opposition groups as a whole, including a significant showing by two Arab-led factions, had more votes overall than Netanyahu's right-wing bloc of parties — indicating Israelis had turned out in their numbers to express their dissatisfaction with his government.
Overnight Tuesday both leaders addressed supporters and hailed their early results, somewhat prematurely, each suggesting they had triumphed.
"We made history! The public has voted for change," said Eisenkot, a center-right former military chief of staff who has promised more diplomacy and less extremism.
Netanyahu told supporters, "The right-wing bloc has a clear, decisive majority among the Zionist public."
But such a tight race means there could now be weeks of political gridlock.
The winning party needs a coalition of 61 lawmakers in the 120-seat Israeli parliament, or Knesset, in order to form a government. The final results will depend on the math and negotiations among broader alliances.
Arab voters make up about 20% of Israel's population, and two Arab-led parties — the socially conservative United Arab List, or Raam, and the left-wing Joint List — could be kingmakers, except that both Netanyahu and Eisenkot and his allies have resisted partnering with them.
According to election officials, Israeli voter turnout on Tuesday was at more than 77%, the highest in more than two decades. Tens of thousands of expatriates flew in from abroad to cast their ballots in the first election since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack and the war in Gaza.
Netanyahu is Israel's longest-serving prime minister, with almost two decades in office across multiple tenures, but Israelis are divided over his leadership.
The issues at stake
Many question Netanyahu's ability to keep them safe after the Hamas attack, the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust. Nearly 1,200 people were killed when Hamas attacked army bases, residential communities and an outdoor music rave — and 251 people were taken hostage back to Gaza.
Israelis have been reeling from reports that the government had received repeated warnings from countries in the region that Hamas was planning a major assault on Israel.
What happened in return was an Israeli military onslaught that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza's Health Ministry, and left most of Gaza destroyed. Today, Israel is fighting back against charges of genocide while Netanyahu faces an international arrest warrant for alleged war crimes.
Israel's wars in Gaza and the region, and its policies in the occupied West Bank, have badly strained its relations with many international governments. Public support for Israel in the United States has plummeted, worrying many Israeli voters.
Still, many other Israelis are fed up with the world's rebuke over the Gaza war and more than 67 percent of Israelis in a July 2025 poll said they were not very troubled about the suffering of people in Gaza. Netanyahu's supporters have said the wars he has led across the region, from Gaza to Lebanon to Iran, have restored Israel's security.
At Netanyahu's election night party on Tuesday in Jerusalem, giant screens played Hollywood-style videos of soldiers marching, airstrikes blowing up buildings and other destruction. Some clips appeared to show massive explosions of villages in Lebanon, where Israeli destruction of civilian infrastructure has drawn condemnation from human rights groups as potential war crimes, which Netanyahu's government denies.
The videos also repeatedly showed President Trump shaking hands with and endorsing Netanyahu. The two leaders have discussed plans to potentially launch major attacks against Iran, which could take place after U.S. midterm elections. Trump urged Israeli voters to reelect Netanyahu to "finish the job that we started."
Supporters of his Likud party at the event struck a defiant tone. When asked if Israel went too far in the war in Gaza, 24-year-old Ori Hazan replied: "We will keep fighting them, and this is now the ideology, this is the policy. You fight us, we will kill you, OK? That's it."
What comes next
With the race so close, election officials told NPR they expect to finish counting votes — including hundreds of thousands of ballots from Israeli soldiers — by Thursday afternoon.
Then whichever candidate comes out on top will get the first chance to try to form a governing coalition. The party will have six weeks to do that. Both blocs are expected to engage in major horse-trading to try to form a government. This has always been the case as no party in Israel's parliamentary system has ever won outright.
Eisenkot's Yashar party includes figures from Israel's political center and moderate right. The opposition parties he would partner with range from the right and center to the liberal left. He has pledged not to join a government led by Netanyahu.
Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party, which is part of Eisenkot's bloc, called on X for the bloc to form a coalition with the Arab parties.
"We have no future here if we don't stop being afraid. And if we don't stop with the racism," he said. Even though it would help the Eisenkot bloc win, since the 2023 attack on Israel there's been heightened mistrust of Arab political leaders.
Another possible scenario is if neither side is able to form a government, leaving Netanyahu as a caretaker prime minister, with a repeat election held next year.
