Brazilian senator Flávio Bolsonaro has declared himself the country’s “true president-elect”, alleged electoral fraud in President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election and vowed to lead Brazil’s opposition from the United States, where he has arrived with his family after leaving the country.
In a lengthy statement addressed to Brazilians and the international community on Wednesday, Flávio rejected the description of his departure as a flight from Brazil, saying he had left to escape what he described as political persecution and an increasingly authoritarian political system. He also thanked US president Donald Trump and Argentine president Javier Milei for their support, portraying the United States as a place where his family could find the legal security he claimed was no longer available at home.
“I want to make this clear: I did not flee Brazil; I left for Brazil’s sake” – he wrote, arguing that remaining in the country would have prevented him from exercising political leadership.
Flávio alleged that the October 25 presidential election was marred by fraud, claiming that Lula gained more than 10 million votes between the first and second rounds in what he called a “mathematical impossibility”. He also challenged a decision to extend voting hours in some locations, accused judicial authorities of acting beyond their jurisdiction and argued that alleged campaign violations justified annulling the Lula-Alckmin ticket.
The statement, however, did not provide evidence establishing that electoral fraud had occurred. Brazil’s Liberal Party (PL), which backed Flávio’s candidacy, had earlier recognised the official election result while calling for the issues raised by the campaign to be addressed through political and democratic debate.
Flávio also accused the Supreme Federal Court of orchestrating a campaign of political persecution against him and his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro. He claimed that judicial action against him could progress from passport seizure to electronic monitoring, censorship, house arrest and eventual political conviction. He insisted that no arrest warrant had been issued against him and denied committing any crime.
The senator said he had brought his family to the US to protect them and would continue his political activities from abroad. Drawing comparisons with figures including French wartime leader Charles de Gaulle and Venezuelan opposition leaders, he portrayed his departure as a continuation of a struggle for democracy rather than an abandonment of Brazilian politics.
Addressing lawmakers and governors allied with him, Flávio said he would lead the opposition from the US, promising to speak on behalf of supporters who, he claimed, could not freely express themselves in Brazil. He named senator Rogério Marinho as his candidate for the presidency of the Senate and said he would soon outline a strategy to mobilise the opposition through what he described as peaceful and legitimate means.
The statement marks a further escalation in Flávio’s challenge to Lula’s victory. He had previously said he would seek the annulment of the election, while the PL subsequently acknowledged the result proclaimed by Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

After Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s recent visit to India, the first by a Polish PM in 16 years, the India-Polish “strategic partnership” is expected to get stronger through better economic and defence cooperation.
This comes two years after Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Poland in 2024, which was the first visit by an Indian PM in 45 years, during which the relationship was elevated to “strategic partnership”.
But the ties are improving against the backdrop of an important development — Poland distancing itself from China on many levels.
Before India, Poland had raised its relationship with China to a “strategic partnership” in the 2010s. But Poland has moved away from China due to the trade being one-sided and the Russia-Ukraine war, in which Poland sees China as an enabler, mirroring the EU’s trajectory, according to experts.
Old values, new avenues: On India-Poland ties
In January, the EU released a draft proposal to phase out components and equipment from “high-risk” suppliers in critical sectors, as part of revisions to the Cybersecurity Act, a move criticised by China’s Huawei, which is set to be among the companies affected, Reuters reported. In February, the Polish Army barred Chinese-made vehicles from entering military facilities due to concerns that their onboard sensors could be used to collect sensitive data, as per Reuters.
An official from the WB Group, one of the largest private defence manufacturing companies of Poland, told The Hindu that they do not use Chinese critical components. “We use chips from friendly countries like South Korea,” the official said. A Polish Defence Ministry source also confirmed this development.
‘China shock 2.0’
In July this year, a study published by the Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW), a Polish government research institute, and the Union of Entrepreneurs and Employers (ZPP), titled ‘Poland–Europe–China: Cooperation or Dependency Trap?’ warned that “China shock 2.0” is hitting Europe’s industrial core, including Poland.
The source of this pressure is not simple market competition, but China’s consistent, state-led industrial strategy, as per the study. In 2025, value added lost from European industry to China was $87 billion. Of this, $11.4 billion was borne by Poland, and about 45,000 jobs in Poland are at risk, mainly in batteries, automotive parts, household appliances, and steel, as per the study.
It is against this backdrop that Łukasiewicz – ITECH, a research network under the Polish government, held its inaugural conference in Warsaw in October on its ‘Asian Programme’ to strengthen Poland’s cooperation with Asian countries. The initial countries chosen for it are Taiwan, South Korea and India.
The ultimate goal of the programme is to move beyond general declarations of international cooperation and towards concrete projects, partnerships and recommendations that support the development of Poland’s “innovation capacity”, as per the institute.
During Mr. Tusk’s visit, representatives of the institute were in India.
Pawel Marczewski, Director of the Department of Strategy and Analysis, Łukasiewicz – ITECH, said the main aim of the programme is to learn from the experiences of like-minded Asian countries about how they support their innovation ecosystem and commercialisation of technological innovation.
“But also, a pretty important factor is to be independent of China. For instance, how to build independence from China in terms of critical minerals and critical technologies. China has completely restricted the supply of critical minerals for the European defence sector, including Poland,” Mr. Marczewski said.
But this was not always the case. Dominik Mierzejewski, associate professor, Department of Asian Studies, University of Lodz, Poland, said that in 1997, the then-Polish President visited China, and it was sort of an opening of doors for bilateral relations.
“The very big signal was in 2011, when we signed a strategic partnership. In December 2011, the first document was signed and the second was signed in 2016,” he said.
Mr. Mierzejewski said that in 2012 there was the “16+1” cooperation (16 Central and Eastern European [CEE] nations and China) and in 2015, Poland was one of the first countries from Europe to be part of the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) of China. “So we thought the trade deficit would be narrowed by policies from Beijing. However, it did not materialise. And particularly this disappointment came from a lack of Chinese investments in Poland,” he said.
‘India fever’
Commenting on the current state of the relationship, he said, Poland started distancing from China from February 2022, “when Russia started its war with Ukraine”, he said. “We need to recognise that Polish foreign policy towards China is based on the fact that Poland is a member of the EU. For the EU, there is a sort of growing disappointment with China. It is not just Poland, but in Germany, France, Italy, etc., there is a structural mismatch between Beijing’s approach to international relations and European expectations,” Mr. Mierzejewski said.
“Not only in Poland, but in the whole EU, the ties with India are getting closer. What I experienced in Brussels, Paris, or Berlin is that there is India fever. Previously, we had China fever. So, this is the current context. It is important for the EU to learn a lesson from its relationship with China,” he added.
Adam Burakowski, former Polish Ambassador to India, said Poland’s relationship with China was the closest around 2016. “Now Poland is politically not that close to China, but the economic relationship continues. The bilateral trade with China is about $60 billion, but it is very one-sided with around $58 billion being Chinese exports to Poland. We would like to rebalance it.”
But Mr. Burakowski said that the visit by the Polish PM to India was more about economic ties with India. “With the India-EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA) to be ratified soon, the focus of the current visit was mainly economic,” he said. Mr. Burakowski said the bilateral trade between the countries now stands at around $6 billion and both the governments are working to increase it to $10 billion.
(The writer was in Poland at the invitation of the Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs)

Naukri parent Info Edge reported an 87% jump in its consolidated net profit for the September quarter (Q2 FY27) to ₹649.8 Cr from ₹347.5 Cr in the year-ago period, aided by higher other income. On a sequential basis, net profit rose 32.6% from ₹490.1 Cr Operating revenue increased 12.2% YoY and 2.6% QoQ to ₹903.9 Cr during the quarter under review. Other income surged 164.8% to ₹428.4 Cr from ₹161.8 Cr, taking total income to ₹1,332.3 Cr from ₹967.2 Cr in Q2 FY26. Meanwhile, total expenses increased 4.5% to ₹588.6 Cr from ₹563.5 Cr. The company’s board also declared an interim dividend of ₹3 per share for FY27, fixing November 6 as the record date. Recruitment Grows, 99acres Narrows Loss On a standalone basis, Info Edge’s operating revenue rose 12.8% YoY to ₹841.7 Cr. Its recruitment solutions business, which includes Naukri, generated revenue of ₹632.3 Cr, up 13.3% YoY. Segment profit before tax increased 19.9% to ₹373.7 Cr. Recruitment billings increased 12.6% to ₹613.8 Cr. The company said quarterly growth was affected by the timing of customer renewals. AI and data products for recruiters and job seekers accounted for a high single-digit share of recruitment revenue, with an annualised run rate of around ₹240 Cr based on Q2. Meanwhile, property portal 99acres reported a 16.7% increase in revenue to ₹134.3 Cr. Its segment loss before tax narrowed to ₹1.6 Cr from ₹23.4 Cr a year earlier. Billings grew 21.2% to ₹148.3 Cr, accelerating from 16.5% growth in Q1. The company said broker resale and rental listings increased 14% YoY, new project listings rose 15%, and owner listings grew 23%. In matchmaking, Jeevansathi’s revenue increased 16.5% to ₹39.5 Cr, while segment profit before tax stood at ₹1.8 Cr. Separately, Aisle’s revenue rose 35.1% to around ₹13 Cr. Combined billings for Jeevansathi and Aisle increased 23.1%. Info Edge CEO Hitesh Oberoi said Jeevansathi added that Jeevansathi and Aisle are growing in the mid-20% range and have the potential to create shareholder value over the medium term. He said that Jeevansathi retains over 45% profile share in Hindi-speaking markets and leads in daily logged-in users across these regions. The company is testing new features, pricing formats and AI-led recommendations to improve matchmaking, with billing growth expected to accelerate in the second half. However, education platform Shiksha’s revenue declined 8.5% to ₹35.5 Cr. It reported a segment loss before tax of ₹0.8 Cr, compared with a profit of ₹1.9 Cr a year earlier. Board Approves Exits, Leadership Transition Alongside the results, Info Edge approved the sale of its entire stakes in MedCords and Unnati Online for about ₹5,000 each. The investments in the healthtech startup and employment platform had been fully impaired in FY24 and FY20, respectively. The board also approved an investment of up to ₹150 Cr in wholly owned subsidiary Redstart Labs through an equity subscription over the next 18 months. The funds will support working capital requirements, investment opportunities and general corporate purposes. Separately, founder Sanjeev Bikhchandani will take over as executive vice chairman, MD and group CEO from December 3, succeeding Hitesh Oberoi. Oberoi will step down as MD and CEO at the close of business on December 2 after nearly 27 years in a full-time executive role to “devote more time to his personal interests in education, entrepreneurship, institution building, investing and philanthropy”. He will remain on the board as an additional director in the non-executive, non-independent promoter category from December 3, subject to shareholder approval. Shares of Info Edge ended today’s trading session 1.23% lower at ₹1,205 apiece on the BSE.

Rama Rao Malla, the son of a farmer from Anakapalli, went on to earn a B.Ed., an M.Sc. and a Ph.D. in biochemistry from Andhra University. During Breast Cancer Awareness Month, Prof. Malla, of the Department of Life Sciences at the Gandhi Institute of Technology and Management (GITAM) (Deemed to be University), is leading research to develop a blood test for one of the most aggressive forms of breast cancer.
The first graduate in his family, Prof. Malla has been a teacher for more than three decades. He joined GITAM early in his career in 2001 and, after completing postdoctoral work at the University of Illinois College of Medicine, returned to set up the university’s cancer research laboratory in 2011. He has guided 14 doctoral scholars and completed several projects on breast cancer, with four more under way, he says.
His current research focuses on triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), which lacks the receptors for oestrogen, progesterone and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), the targets of certain cancer therapies. Patients are treated mainly with chemotherapy, to which many develop resistance. TNBC accounts for 10% to 15% of breast cancers, he says, and is increasingly being diagnosed in women in their mid-30s and 40s. Mammography may miss small tumours, particularly in younger women. “If we can identify this cancer at an early stage, we can successfully eliminate the tumours by surgery,” he says.
The project, titled “Exploring Serum Exosomal microRNAs as Minimally-Invasive Biomarkers for Early Diagnosis of Triple-Negative Breast Cancer”, has been sanctioned under the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)’s “Follow-on Nischayak Anveshan” Extramural Grants programme, with Prof. Malla as the principal investigator. He says the project has an outlay of more than ₹2 crore over three years.
The study will examine exosomes, nanosized vesicles released by cells, including tumour cells. Their microRNA content can reflect that of the cells from which they originate. The researchers will compare serum samples from patients with early-stage TNBC, provided by the Mahatma Gandhi Cancer Hospital & Research Institute (MGCHRI) and the GITAM Institute of Medical Sciences and Research (GIMSR), with samples from healthy women. Sequencing and digital polymerase chain reaction (PCR) will be used to identify candidate microRNAs, and a machine-learning model will be trained to distinguish patients with early-stage TNBC from healthy individuals. The ultimate objective is to develop a kit-based test.
“We hope we can achieve something after three years that will be useful for society,” he says.
The co-investigators are P. Kiranmayi, P. Vasudevaraju, A. Krishna Chaitanya and M. Srivenkatesh of the GITAM School of Science; K. Viswa Kalyan of GIMSR; and V. Muralikrishna of MGCHRI.
The World Health Organization advises that any abnormal breast lump should be examined by a health professional, even if it is painless.

Audio Technica just released its first set of wireless StreamSet headphones
This expands the lineup beyond XLR and USB-connected models.
Audio Technica just released a wireless model in its popular StreamSet category of headphones. The new ATH-M50xSTS-WL is the very first wireless version in the lineup.
These cans don't connect via Bluetooth, as StreamSet headphones are primarily intended for content creators, streamers and gamers, all of which require ultra-low latency. They connect via 2.4GHz, so there's a USB transceiver that hooks up to PCs and gaming consoles like the PS5 and Switch 2. The battery lasts for around 24 hours and is charged via USB. The headphones can still work while being charged, via a wired connection.
Otherwise, these are extremely similar to the original wired ATH-M50xSTS headphones. They feature microphones based on the company's 20 Series and audio drivers pulled from the ATH-M50x professional monitor headphones.
The headset includes adaptive noise cancellation with two selectable levels. The company says an algorithm "continuously monitors audio input to prioritize the user's voice over ambient sounds," which includes stuff like PC fans and air conditioners.
There's a cardioid condenser microphone on a flexible boom arm that instantly mutes audio when flipped up. It uses the same 45mm audio drivers found in the ATH-M50x studio monitor headphones. I've used that particular and iconic model and can attest they do indeed sound great.
They ship with two types of interchangeable earpads. There's a pair for better sound quality, which is great for listening to music, and another designed with breathable mesh for long streaming and gaming sessions. The ATH-M50xSTS-WL headphones are available right now and cost $299.

New Delhi: The Himachal Pradesh Drugs Control Administration has asked patients and the public to stop using specific batches of medicines declared ‘not of standard quality’ (NSQ) by the central drug regulator, according to the two senior government officials familiar with the matter and documents reviewed by Mint.
The alert follows the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation's (CDSCO) September 2026 report, which flagged 330 drug samples nationwide as sub-standard. Of these, 92 originated from Himachal Pradesh manufacturers.
State health authorities confirmed that 70 of the 92 failed critical efficacy parameters—specifically assay and dissolution tests—while 22 showed minor defects, such as labelling issues. To enforce compliance, the state has ordered 96 pharmaceutical facilities to halt manufacturing, either entirely or across specific sections, pending corrective actions. The state accounts for roughly a third of India's domestic drug supplies alongside large export volumes.
Himachal Pradesh is home to over 650 pharmaceutical manufacturing units, largely based in Baddi. About 70% of these are micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and 15-20% are large companies. The state accounts for about 35% of India's total domestic drug formulations, meaning every third drug on a chemist's shelf in India originates from Himachal Pradesh.
Widely prescribed medicines flagged
According to the CDSCO’s website, several widely prescribed medicines manufactured across Solan and Baddi in Himachal Pradesh were declared NSQ after failing critical active ingredient tests:
- Aspo Pharmaceuticals’ Namik-MR tablets, indicated for muscle pain or spasms failed in its aceclofenac content.
- Multiple respiratory formulations were also flagged, including Pharma Roots Healthcare’s AX Cold syrup, prescribed for allergic cough and congestion, which failed ambroxol hydrochloride levels.
- Similarly, Alventa Pharma’s Healtuss LS and Ultra Drugs Formulations’ Cufcott LS, both bronchodilator and expectorant syrups indicated for productive cough and asthma-related airway congestion, failed tests for ambroxol hydrochloride and levosalbutamol.
- Saar Biotech’s K-Coff-D syrup, used to treat dry cough, nasal blockage, and allergic cold symptoms, was cited for deficient phenylephrine hydrochloride content.
- In the topical analgesic category, Cent Cure’s Gone Gel, applied for joint pain, musculoskeletal aches, and sprains, failed the required standard for methyl salicylate.
State cites high volumes
“The volume of substandard samples must be evaluated in proportion to the state’s massive manufacturing output. Himachal Pradesh contributes to approximately one-third of domestic supplies, besides exporting big volumes of drug formulations,” Himachal Pradesh health secretary Ashish Singhmar said, pointing out that the state’s share of failed samples actually declined from 34% in July to 28% in September.
State drug controller Dr. Manish Kapoor said, “The drugs control administration, Himachal Pradesh, maintains a zero-tolerance approach towards the manufacture or distribution of substandard medicines and every effort is being made to ensure strict compliance of regulatory requirements. Following procedures laid down under the law, not only are the licences to manufacture drug formulations suspended/cancelled by the DCA HP, but at parallel, legal action(s) are also taken by the jurisdictions from where samples get drawn for the purpose of analysis/testing.”
“The enforcement is an ongoing administrative check-and-balance: these 96 actions particularly are not entirely on the latest NSQ list. It is an ongoing process where facilities are halted either due to NSQs or when other deficiencies are found during inspections. Increased detection is a positive indicator that our regulatory mechanism is strengthening," he added.
Dr. Kapoor also pointed out that drugs often degrade after leaving factories. "There are multiple stress factors in the distribution chain—storage conditions, temperature, humidity, and rough transport—that can cause quality failure. We cannot exclusively blame only manufacturers."
Queries sent to the health ministry and the Drugs Controller General of India on Tuesday remained unanswered at the time of publishing. Queries sent to Aspo Pharmaceuticals, Alventa Pharma, Ultra Drugs, also remained unanswered, while Pharma Roots Healthcare couldn't be contacted.

Why James Comey is getting charged again
A third time is probably not the charm for Trump’s ceaseless revenge campaign.
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump’s revenge campaign is getting increasingly desperate.
What’s happening? On Monday, we learned that Trump’s Justice Department is criminally charging former FBI Director James Comey for a third time, in the latest installment of Trump’s ongoing efforts to prosecute his enemies.
Unlike two previous instances, the charges are not in the form of an indictment. Instead, the DOJ filed a two-count criminal information, which allows prosecutors to lodge charges without getting a grand jury involved (but, crucially, does not allow the government to try Comey on those charges unless he waives his right to a grand jury).
What is Comey charged with? The charges allege that in October 2016, Comey unlawfully transmitted national security information about US email surveillance to a journalist. They were filed earlier this month on October 5, exactly 10 years after the alleged disclosure, after which point the statute of limitations would have expired.
Comey denies the charges, and said in a video posted Monday that the case “would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice.”
What’s the context? Comey, whom Trump fired as FBI director in 2017, has long been at the top of Trump’s second-term enemies list. He was indicted on scanty allegations of lying to Congress in September 2025, and again this spring for an alleged threat against Trump, in the form of a photo of seashells arranged to spell “86 47” (“86” is broadly understood to be service industry slang for rejecting or removing something or someone).
The first set of charges quickly fell flat after a judge found that the US attorney who brought them — former Trump lawyer Lindsey Halligan — was illegally appointed. Comey is still seeking to have the second set dismissed.
What’s the big picture? It’s unclear if this third set of charges will stick, though the Trump administration says it still plans to seek a grand jury indictment. But their existence underscores how dramatically Trump has succeeded in politicizing the Justice Department.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

Cyclone Arnab: Naidu writes to Shah, says no loss of life, reports crop damage
Naidu cited preliminary estimates and reported crop damage across approximately 70,900 hectares in the state
The very severe cyclonic storm Arnab, which crossed the Andhra Pradesh coast on Wednesday morning, did not cause any human casualties, but considerably damaged crops, properties and other infrastructure, chief minister N Chandrababu Naidu said in a letter to Union home minister Amit Shah.
Naidu cited preliminary estimates and said the cyclone and rainfall damaged agricultural and horticultural crops spread across approximately 70,900 hectares, including paddy. “Of this, crops on about 10,450 hectares had been reported inundated or damaged,” he said.
He added about 180 houses were reported damaged, mostly in the Konaseema district. Over 220 trees fell on state roads, of which over 170 had been cleared by Wednesday afternoon, he added. Naidu wrote damages to road infrastructure were reported in coastal areas.
Deep Dive
Naidu underlined that the figures are provisional and likely to change as assessment teams completed their field surveys. “The state government will share a detailed damage assessment with the Centre after verification,” Naidu said.
He sought continued support from the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and other central agencies. Naidu urged an early deputation of a central team to assess the damage.
Naidu said the cyclone’s impact was particularly concentrated along the Godavari delta coast, covering Konaseema, Kakinada, East Godavari and West Godavari, and Krishna and Anakapalli districts. Four wards in Visakhapatnam were inundated.
Fire and Emergency Services personnel attended to over 220 emergency calls, mainly involving the removal of fallen trees.
Naidu said the state government mobilised its disaster-response machinery throughout the night, deploying 16 NDRF and 11 State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) teams across 14 districts.
Naidu wrote that over 28,000 people were shifted to relief shelters as a precautionary measure. He added that all fishing boats were brought back to harbour.
Naidu said medical teams, ambulances, relief supplies, power restoration crews and road-clearance teams had been positioned in affected districts, with collectors leading operations on the ground.
He added the administration would focus on assisting displaced families and those whose houses were damaged. Relief and response teams would remain deployed until the threat from rainfall and storm surge had passed, he said.
Naidu thanked Shah for the continued support and said the state would watch for rainfall and flooding in the days ahead.

Heavenly Creatures killer Pauline Parker dies in Orkney, aged 88
- Published
To her neighbours and friends, Hilary Nathan was a quiet, religious woman who ran a riding stable in the small Orcadian island of Burray.
But her death in an island care home last week at the age of 88 closes a chapter on an extraordinary life that began 70 years ago on the other side of the world with a sensational murder trial.
As a 16-year-old and under her birth name of Pauline Parker, she was convicted alongside her schoolfriend Juliet Hulme of the murder of her mother Honora Parker.
The case shocked New Zealand – and the rest of the world.
The court heard the girls had become inseparable at Christchurch Girls' High School. Fearing that they'd be separated following the divorce of Juliet's parents and a planned move to South Africa, they plotted to kill Mrs Parker, who they believed stood in their way.
They lured her to a park and bludgeoned her to death with a brick inside a stocking.
By the time filmmaker Sir Peter Jackson was born in 1961, both girls had served five years in prison, been released, given new identities, and left New Zealand for good.
"It was known for its tabloid sensational aspect. I know a lot of English tabloids flew to Christchurch, New Zealand, to cover the case of the 'evil schoolgirl killers'," he told the BBC's Late Show in 1995.
"Repeating that stuff would have been easy, but that's not what we wanted to do. We wanted to understand more about Pauline Parker and Juliet Hulme, and what made them become friends."
His film Heavenly Creatures starred Kate Winslet as Hulme and Melanie Lynskey as Parker. It showed how their intense friendship spilled over into a strange shared fantasy life which culminated in the brutal murder.
The defence argued insanity, but both girls were found guilty of murder and only avoided the death penalty because of their age.
In 1960, having served five years in separate prisons, they were given new identities and moved away from New Zealand.
The court ordered that they should never meet again, and yet they lived part of their lives about 80 miles (129km) apart.
When the film came out in 1995, Juliet was living in Portmahomack in Rosshire, where she'd become a crime writer living under her new name, Anne Perry.
She told the Late Show that she didn't plan to see the film.
"It would be too harrowing," she said. "What was close to the truth would be distressing and what was far from the truth would be even more distressing."
"It's a bit like being stripped naked in the High Street for everyone to come and look and pick and poke. I'd rather put my clothes on and go back home, thank you."
During filming, Kate Winslet said she had no idea where the two women were, and after Anne Perry's identity was revealed, the actress expressed the hope that Pauline Parker would be able to retain her anonymity.
"These are two women who, for the last 40 years, have had to overcome so much in order to get on with their lives and just survive," she said.
"I hope she is never found."
But in 2011, Parker was found by lawyer and true-crime author Peter Graham, who had written a book about the case called So Brilliantly Clever, its title taken from her diary, which was used as evidence in court.
She, like Juliet, had come to the UK, where she had settled in a small village in rural Kent and opened a riding school. By 2011, and now known as Hilary Nathan, she had moved to Orkney, running another stable.
For both women, religion and small tight-knit communities provided a haven. According to an interview her sister gave to the New Zealand Women's Weekly, Nathan was a devout Catholic who led a reclusive life.
Perry was a Mormon, enjoying the support of her own community when reporters began to arrive after Heavenly Creatures was released.
She said: "The media descended on Portmahomack. I was horrified, especially since my mother lived in the village. It's not just the people the film is about, it's all the people around them. I felt it might ruin my family."
Although her books were hugely successful in America, she never really found the fame she merited here in the UK, partly because of her reticence to do any promotion.
Prime Suspect creator Lynda La Plante expressed interest in a TV version of Perry's books, but the author vetoed the plan for the same reason.
In 2001, I visited Perry in Portmahomack for a rare interview for Newsnight Scotland. At that stage, she was a glamorous author, with a back catalogue which had sold 15 million copies around the world.
"I think after 51 years, you can let it go," she told me. "It's not who I am now. It's not who I have been for decades."
We didn't talk about the murder directly, but you don't have to look far in her books for insight into what happened and how her life had turned out. Her detective, the Victorian policeman William Monk, suffers from amnesia, and sometimes wonders exactly who he is.
"Monk sees himself as just himself but because of his memory loss, he has to deal with the fact that he may be someone else. That comes from my own sense that other people view me as a monster," she admitted.
"Of course it affects what I write. I have far more compassion and understanding for people who do wrong things than I'd ever have if I hadn't been in that position.
"The questions of right and wrong and compassion and forgiveness concern me in a way they wouldn't have, had I not had the life I had."
Anne Perry died in Los Angeles in 2023 at the age of 84.
Hilary Nathan's death last week brings their strange story to a close.
How they reinvented themselves out of the world's harshest headlines, and found redemption in the smallest of Scottish communities.
"I would say if you had something which harrowed you, or caused you to feel shame, you should never give up," Anne told me.
"There's more forgiveness, understanding and help out there than you might think."

Sony has a collection of colorful, translucent cosmetics for its PlayStation consoles and controllers. Announced Wednesday, the Prism collection brings three new, gorgeous color options that conjure a nostalgic, transparent tech feel.
They come in Flare Orange, Emerald Green, and Graphite Gray. (Based on the pictures, the gray looks more like a blue to me.) You can get Sony’s DualSense PlayStation 5 controllers in the Prism design or opt for PS5 console covers. On the controllers, translucent plastic wraps around almost the entire device’s frame, letting you view the components inside. On the console cover version, the transparency is more limited—you can see only the fan and a few other components.
The Prism Collection DualSense wireless controllers cost $85, while the console covers cost $75. Preorders start on November 10, but the collection won’t ship until February 4. Those are roughly the same prices as existing controllers and covers, though on the higher end. Basic color controllers start at $74 on the PlayStation website. Covers start around $59. The more colorful options on both products go up from there.
Apple’s original iMac largely popularized translucent, colorful tech that lets you see inside the machine. The look was en vogue for a while in seminal devices like the PlayStation 2 and Nintendo’s Game Boy Color.
That see-through aesthetic was a signature in the early 2000s. (My first CD player had a translucent top, and you could see the disc spinning around the whole time.) Twenty-some years later, it’s being revived as nostalgia bait in a transparent tech renaissance. You can find the transparent look in everything from gaming handhelds to a Theragun. Sony also has a transparent pair of earbuds.
Reminiscing about the good ol’ days might also remind you that Sony’s old consoles used to have disc drives. In July, Sony made a controversial decision to end production of physical game discs starting in 2028. Ownership advocates have decried the choice, noting that Sony’s own terms of service state that buying a digital copy of a game does not mean the customer owns it. It’s yet another move toward the end of physical media.
Still, the Prism collection sure looks pretty.

The Fitbit Edge is a $179.99 fitness tracker with a 1.34-inch AMOLED display, built-in GPS, ECG, replaceable battery, and up to seven days of battery life. It also offers Google Maps navigation, Gemini-powered coaching, advanced health tracking, and a special Stephen Curry edition.
The fitness world may be in a “to screen or not to screen” state, with fitness bands without screens gaining popularity, but Google is clearly keeping its Fitbit feet in both screen and screenless fitness trackers. Days after launching its Fitbit Air screenless tracker in India, the Search giant has launched the Fitbit Edge, a fitness tracker with a display that sits right in the middle of the Fitbit Air and the Pixel Watch 5, both in terms of pricing (it starts at USD 179.99, well above the USD 99.99 of the Fitbit Air but well below the USD 399.99 of the Pixel Watch 5) and display size. Only time will tell whether it will hit the golden middle ground between “lots of display” and “no display at all,” but while we wait for the Fitbit Edge to hit stores later this month (and indeed, hopefully arrive in India soon), here are twelve points worth noting about the latest Fitbit in fitness town:
Table of Contents
A big display in an increasingly no-display zone
In a fitness band world that seems to be aiming to become more and more screen-less, the Fitbit Edge comes with a big-gish display for a fitness tracker. It has a 1.34-inch AMOLED, always-on display, which is 46 percent bigger than the one on the Charge 6, its predecessor. It is also much brighter and has Gorilla Glass 3 protection. Fitbit actually claims it is the brightest and biggest display on a Fitbit fitness tracker. Should the Fitbit Air be jealous?
Wear it without Wear OS: Fitbit OS onboard
It comes from Google and also has a display on board like the Pixel Watch 5, which has led many to assume that the Fitbit Edge must be running on Wear OS, but that is not the case. The Fitbit Edge actually runs on Fitbit OS. And like all Google fitness devices, it also uses the Google Health app to keep track of your data and give you fitness inputs. While this means you get relatively less distraction and only basic notifications, it also means you do not get access to third-party apps on the device.
Bye bye Haptic, Hello real button!
One of the biggest headaches of the Fitbit Charge 6 was its pressure-sensitive, haptic touch button, which many of us struggled to use (it almost had a vibe of its own). Thankfully, the Fitbit Edge fixes that and brings a physical button on the side for controls. We couldn’t be more glad. The haptic control on the Charge 6 was a bit of a pain and messed up what was (and still is) a superb fitness tracker.
A battery that can be removed and replaced
Most modern devices have given up on the concept of a removable battery, which was sad because once the battery of a device died, it tended to render an otherwise perfectly good device useless, unless one went in for complex engineering. That, however, has been changing thanks to regulations from the EU, and the Fitbit Edge comes with a removable battery. Which means you can simply remove the battery and replace it if its health deteriorates, increasing the life of the fitness tracker.
Very Air-y battery life
In terms of battery life, the Fitbit Edge rather surprisingly has the same battery life as the display-less Fitbit Air – about a week. However, keeping the always-on-display feature on reduces this to a rather low two days.
Metal frames that can take an ECG…and save your life (in select countries)
The Fitbit Edge’s metal frame can be used to take a 30-second manual ECG. This can highlight heart rate irregularities and can also spot signs of AFib. The tracker also has an optical PPG heart rate sensor that continuously tracks one’s heart and pulse rate and alerts the user if their heart rate is unusually high or low. The catch is that the ECG is only available in select countries, but it is still great to see an ECG on a fitness tracker – a feature seen generally in premium smartwatches.
Take it swimming
Much like its screen-less sibling, the Fitbit Air, the Fitbit Edge too is pretty sturdy. The device comes with 5 ATM water resistance, which means you can easily take it along for your swim sessions. The device also features IP68 dust and water resistance, and as we mentioned earlier, Gorilla Glass 3 protection.
Comes with GPS and is stair-worthy
The Fitbit Edge has an improved and built-in GPS, something the Air lacks, so you do not need to carry your phone along to cover outdoor workouts and activities. It has multi-constellation support, which is paired with a new antenna and chip, making the device up to 40 percent better at tracking locations than the Charge 6. The Edge has another edge over the Air – an integrated altimeter, which can detect changes in altitude, and comes in handy not only while counting stairs but also during hikes and trekking, where you can accurately measure altitude change.
Get Google Maps directions on your wrist:
The Fitbit Edge might not have Google Wear, but it works in sync with Google Maps on your phone and can show you turn-by-turn directions on your wrist. The feature requires you to have an active Bluetooth connection between your phone and the Fitbit Edge, and directions will start popping up on your tracker screen when you start walking, running, cycling, or even driving. That big display really helps!
Quick Notifications, quicker actions but no call support:
The Edge has a mixed relationship with your smartphone. It is a few steps ahead of the Air in terms of notifications, or some might say behind it in terms of a distraction-free experience. You get basic call, message, and app notifications on the tracker, and also get quick reply and navigation access on it. However, you cannot use it to handle calls because the device does not have a mic or a speaker. You can accept a call from the tracker, but it will be directed to your smartphone.
Google Health Guardian’s on your wrist
Earlier limited to the more expensive Pixel Watches, Google’s Health Guardian is available on the Fitbit Edge. This comes with cardiovascular tracking and alerts, alerts for potential breathing and pulse issues, and tracking of trends in the background to create monthly reports on blood pressure and even insulin resistance. It also unlocks premium features of the Google Health app, like personalized coaching and deeper tracking and analysis.
Gemini present, but cannot be summoned:
The Fitbit Edge comes with personalized Gemini coaching to help you meet your health and fitness goals. But complete access to all of Gemini’s features requires a subscription, and you cannot summon the AI assistant on your tracker – you have to use your phone for it.
And one more thing: There is a Stephen Curry edition:
The Google Fitbit Edge comes with a special edition, designed in collaboration with 4-time NBA champion Stephen Curry. It pairs the regular tracker with a Satin Pyrite aluminum case and also features a custom moisture-wicking, water-repellent, recycled polyester yarn band. Also on board are special basketball watchfaces. Mind you, all that extra goodness will set you back by an additional USD 40 – the Stephen Curry edition starts at USD 219.99.

Barbara Barrie, who received a Tony nomination for her role in Broadway’s original Company, an Oscar nomination for her performance in Breaking Away and wide recognition as the wife of Hal Linden’s police captain on TV’s Barney Miller, died October 28 at her home in Manhattan. She was 95.
Her death was reported to The New York Times by her daughter Jane Harnick, who said Barrie’s death was medically assisted and that the actor had been diagnosed with terminal cancer.
Following her breakthrough Cannes Film Festival award-winning performance in 1964’s One Potato, Two Potato, Barrie built a career that encompassed the stage, film and television, making marked contributions to each. She appeared in 11 Broadway productions, including original stagings of Stephen Sondheim’s Company, Neil Simon’s The Prisoner of Second Avenue and California Suite, Harvey Fierstein’s Torch Song Trilogy and a 2004 revival of Fiddler on the Roof.
Her film credits included, in addition to Breaking Away in 1979, an uncredited role in the classic 1956 drama Giant and as the mother of Goldie Hawn’s character in 1980’s Private Benjamin.
Barrie was most prolific on television, with credits stretching back to the 1950s anthology dramas and such popular 1960s series as Route 66, The Twilight Zone, The Fugitive, Ben Casey and Ironside, among many others. In 1974 she flirted with Gavin MacLeod’s Murray Slaughter on a memorable episode of The Mary Tyler Moore Show, and the following year began her five-season recurring role on Barney Miller, even as her character was largely absent beyond the first season as the sitcom increasingly focused on the police precinct-workplace comedy rather than the title character’s domestic life.
In addition to her portrayal of Barney Miller‘s Liz Miller, Barrie is probably best known to TV audiences for her series regular role on the 1996-2000 sitcom Suddenly Susan, in which she portrayed “Nana” Keane, grandmother of Brooke Shield’s title character Susan. Barrie appeared in 92 episodes during the show’s five-season run.
Born Barbara Ann Berman on May 23, 1931, in Chicago, Barrie was moved to New York City after college to launch her show business career. She made her Broadway debut in the 1955 play The Wooden Dish, returning four years later in The Beaux’ Stratagem by George Farquhar. She appeared in various Off Broadway productions as well, including 1958’s The Crucible as well as regional and touring productions.
Her signature stage role arrived in 1970 when she originated the character of Sarah in Company, starring opposite Elaine Stritch, Dean Jones and Beth Howland, among others, in what would prove to be a seminal Broadway musical. She was noninated for a Tony Award for the performance.
Barrie’s most recent Broadway performance was in Joshua Harmon’s Significant Other in 2017.
In film, Barrie landed her first leading role in 1964’s groundbreaking One Potato, Two Potato, portraying a divorced woman who marries a Black man and in so doing risks losing custody of her child. Both the film and Barrie’s performance were acclaimed highlights of the year’s Canne Film Festival.
Perhaps Barrie’s most beloved and memorable film performance came in 1979’s Breaking Away when she portrayed the mother of the main character played by Dennis Christopher, a young small-town man who dreams of becoming a competitive bicycle racer. Barrie received an Oscar nomination for Best Supporting Actress for her performance (she lost to Meryl Streep in Kramer vs. Kramer). Barrie would reprise the Breaking Away role for a TV series adaptation, earning an Emmy nomination.
Among her numerous other TV credits, Barrie appeared in Family Ties, Law & Order, Pushing Daisies, Nurse Jackie, Kate & Allie, Once and Again and Army Wives. She was Emmy nominated three times, for Breaking Away, Law & Order and Law & Order: Special Victims Unit.
Barrie was the author of two children’s books: 1990’s Lone Star and 1994’s Adam ZigZag. She wrote two memoirs following her diagnosis of colorectal cancer: Second Act in 1997 and Don’t Die of Embarrassment in 1999.
Barrie was married to Jay Harnick, the founder and artistic director of TheaterWorksUSA, from 1964 until his death in 2007. In addition to her daughter Jane Harnick, she is survived by son Aaron Harnick and three granddaughters.

Tanzania celebrates first natural gas discovery in more than 10 years
- Published
Tanzania has announced a significant discovery of natural gas in the Mnazi Bay area in the south of the country - the first such find in a decade.
Energy Minister Juma Homera attended a ceremony at the Kasa-1X ST2 well, which is jointly owned by state-owned Tanzania Petroleum Development Corporation (TPDC) and French oil firm Maurel & Prom, to mark the occasion.
He said the estimated 223 billion cubic feet (6.3 billion cubic metres) discovery was a "major milestone" in the development of the small oil and gas sector in the East African nation.
The new well is expected to start production early next month and is intended to boost domestic supplies.
Tanzania has existing natural gas reserves of 57.54 trillion cubic feet.
"The discovery is important in ensuring the country has reliable, clean and safe energy at affordable costs, particularly at a time when demand is increasing due to industrial growth and other economic activities," Homera said.
Natural gas accounted for nearly 80% of Tanzania's sources of electricity generation, according to government statistics for 2024.
In recent years, the country has also encouraged the use of compressed natural gas to power vehicles, with natural gas plants and filling stations set up mostly in the largest city, Dar es Salaam.
Some Tanzanians have been converting their vehicles to a dual-fuel system - with the locally available natural gas allowing for cheaper prices than petrol.
Tanzania made its first natural gas discovery in 1974 on the Songo Songo Island in the south-east Lindi region, followed by a second discovery at Mnazi Bay in neighbouring region of Mtwara in 1982.
The commercialisation of these discoveries began in 2004. This propelled further gas exploration both onshore and offshore, with the largest single discovery of 2.7 trillion cubic feet of natural gas in 2016.

It's "ACOTAR" time, people.
On Tuesday, Sarah J. Maas released "A Court of Splintered Harmony," the sixth book in the "A Court of Thorns and Roses" series. The book is the first volume in a larger story arc within the world of "ACOTAR," which Maas has titled "The Valkyrie Cycle."
Maas took readers back to Prythian in the novel, picking up after the events of "A Court of Silver Flames" and "House of Flame and Shadow," the third book in her "Crescent City" series. High Lord Rhysand, High Lady Feyre, and their Inner Circle are working to protect humans and keep Koschei, a death god, from escaping the enchanted lake where he's trapped. There's plenty of turmoil for the Inner Circle at home, too, though, from power struggles to love triangles.
Luckily, parts two and three of "The Valkyrie Cycle" come out in January 2027 in one volume called "A Court of Forgotten Melody," so fans won't have to wait too long to see what happens next in "ACOTAR."
In the meantime, "ACOSH" was packed with plot twists and shocking reveals, so read on for a look at the most important details you may have missed.
Spoilers for Maas' works ahead.
Koschei the Deathless
Koschei was positioned as the looming villain in Maas' latest novel, though the character has yet to physically appear on page. (He made a brief appearance in a shadowy form in "A Court of Silver Flames.")
In "ACOSH," Vassa, a human queen trapped by Koschei, tells Feyre and Rhysand that he projects his voice to others rather than allowing anyone to get close to him, with the notable exception of Feyre's father, according to Lucien.
Vassa also shared that all the women Koschei keeps as prisoners are distant descendants of the fae warrior who initially trapped him at the lake.
It's not the first time Maas has alluded to the mysterious female fae who trapped Koschei and his sister Stryga. The Bone Carver, their brother, spoke of her to Feyre and Cassian, Rhysand's general, in "A Court of Wings and Ruin," saying, "Clever, that fae warrior. Her bloodline is long gone now — though a trace still runs through some human line." He also said she could have been his "salvation," though he doesn't explain how.
The Bone Carver said her name had been forgotten to history, but perhaps Koschei will reveal her identity in future Maas works.
The Bone Carver also said he and his siblings came from another world, much like the Asteri (known as the Daglan in Prythian). It's possible they originate from the world on which Maas' "Throne of Glass" series takes place, considering Maas has been tying her three fantasy worlds together in her recent works.
Azriel's shadows
"ACOSH" offers readers a more in-depth look at Azriel's shadows. Through his narration, Maas reveals that the shadows are sentient, exploring the world for Azriel and telling him everything from the weather to how people are feeling.
They also display feelings toward different characters throughout the novel, investigating intruders in the Night Court or avoiding others, such as the shadow creature Erebos.
They seem either unable or unwilling to come anywhere near Elain Archeron. They won't enter any room she is in, whether that be a dining room or a temple.
Azriel thinks his shadows' disappearance is "a gift," but their absence puts him in danger twice in "ACOSH."
First, he does not sense the creature Bryaxis approaching during baby Nyx's naming ceremony, thinking to himself that his shadows weren't there because "Elain had chased them away." Bryaxis was able to attack the Inner Circle in part because Azriel didn't feel her coming.
Hours later, Azriel's shadows do not warn him that Lucien, Elain's mate, is outside her bedroom, as they had "fled the moment he'd sought out Elain," again leading to trouble for the Shadowsinger. He and Lucien physically fight during the interaction, and Rhysand kicks Azriel out of the house. Morrigan, Rhysand's third and the object of Azriel's longing for years, also scolds him, and the interaction marks the last time he sees Elain in the novel, who ends up fleeing Prythian in the aftermath.
In contrast, his shadows are thrilled to see someone else a few pages later: Gwyn. Azriel ventures to the House of Wind to retrieve some of his belongings after the incident, and when he hears singing, his shadows "surged past his feet, a black tide racing ahead," sprinting to Gwyn. The shadows then gather at Gwyn's feet, watching her until Azriel summons them back.
Perhaps Maas will explore what Azriel's shadows know about each female in future works.
Nesta and the prison
As she is in "A Court of Silver Flames," Nesta Archeron is central to the plot of "ACOSH," quarreling with the Inner Circle and ultimately saving them when Bryaxis comes back to town.
She is also drawn to the prison throughout the novel, which she explored extensively with Bryce Quinlan in "House of Flame and Shadow." During their journey there, they discovered that the prison had once been an eighth court that could have served as the Dusk Court.
Maas leans into dusk imagery each time Nesta visits. During one trip to the prison, she looks "to the purpling eastern sky. To the first star of evening. To the darkness, the night growing beyond it."
She also sees that the prison is along "that northern horizon, stained with a dazzling blend of encroaching night and lingering day."
It also appears that Nesta and Rhysand may share a connection to the prison. When Nesta tries to winnow to the island, she almost drowns and sees something "glimmering" on the floor below, believing it is calling, "Find me," to her. Rhysand saves her, telling Nesta he heard her mentally scream, "Find me," to him.
It's possible Nesta was confused and shouting out mentally for aid, but it's also possible Nesta and Rhysand were being beckoned by the same Made object. Rhysand controls the prison through his bloodline, so it's plausible that a Made object associated with it is calling to them both.
In addition to the dusk imagery she associates with her, Maas also ties Nesta to the word "splintered," which appears in the novel's title. Nesta asks her house for guidance on her relationship with Cassian, and the house offers her a pile of splinters from a punching block she broke during her training. For Nesta, the demonstration is meaningful.
"The House couldn't have chosen a better symbol of where she and Cassian stood," she thinks to herself. "The training, the determination, the love that had grown between them — all shattering not due to some outside force, but because of her."
The splinters lead her to open up to Cassian about her feelings, but they also may indicate that "Splintered Harmony" in the title has a lot to do with Nesta and Cassian.
Other imagery
Nesta isn't the only character Maas associates with specific imagery throughout the book.
Maas repeatedly associates Elain with spring. Azriel describes Elain as "a whisper of spring" and "as lovely as a spring dawn." Lucien says she has a "floral scent," and she is seen tending flowers and decorating Nyx's naming ceremony with them in the book.
Maas also introduces the concept of Feyre and her son, Nyx, as a flash of silver in the night court.
Clotho made "a braided, silvery piece of fabric" for Feyre and Rhysand to use during Nyx's naming ceremony, telling Nesta it was one of a kind as she gave it to her to pass on to the High Lord and Lady. Later, when Lucien is dining at their home, he notices a tapestry Feyre has hung on the wall, saying his magical eye can see the silver thread moving in it.
During his chapter, Lucien also says his magic eye has shown him a silver aura around Feyre since the moment he met her, describing it as a "silvery brightness" that intensified as Feyre found love and joy at the Night Court.
Gwyn's power
During both passages in which Gwyn appears in the novel, she is singing, which seems significant given the musically themed titles of books six and seven in the "ACOTAR" series.
Maas gives indications that Gwyn's music may have magical properties.
Nesta notices that Gwyn's singing voice is more powerful than the voices of her fellow choir singers, saying, "Gwyn could have carried the entirety of the song herself, that mezzo-soprano voice so rich and resonant that it seemed to effortlessly burst from her."
Likewise, Azriel describes Gwyn's voice as "otherworldly" and "strange and yet familiar," adding that "starlight spilled down the steps, almost in answer to the song" as she sang.
Maas also seems to liken Gwyn to light, particularly when she's singing.
When Nesta watches Gwyn sing, she notes that she "shone" and seemed to "radiate light," thinking to herself that "the candlelight seemed to bend toward" her friend. Similarly, when Azriel sees Gwyn at the House of Wind, he describes her hair as "shining in the starlight," remarks on her "bright gaze," and notes that her eyes were lit by the stars above.
Similarities between Azriel and Gwyn
Throughout "ACOSH," Azriel describes himself as a monster because of his shadow-wielding abilities and talent at extracting information from enemies. He says he was often called a monster or a demon in his youth, and he came to think of himself that way.
"He was a monster — merely a creature," Azriel thinks of himself in the text. "Best left skulking in shadows. Most suited to collecting information through subterfuge or pain."
Other characters in "ACOTAR" have said people think of them as monsters, like Rhysand, but the only other character in "ACOSH" who seems to genuinely think of herself as monstrous is Gwyn.
In a chapter told from her perspective, Gwyn reveals that she has been avoiding training with the Valkyrie and the world outside the temple because she relished killing enemies during the Blood Rite. Her chapter ends with her thinking she hears Bryaxis laughing at her, "like it knew it wasn't the only monster down here."
Maas also highlights parallels between Azriel's and Gwyn's powers in "ACOSH."
Azriel talks about his Siphons, which help control his magic, repeatedly in the book. He notes that they are all "a cobalt bordering on turquoise," for a reason he has never known.
Later, Gwyn throws her Invoking Stone at Azriel when he startles her, which he says "glittered with turquoise fire." Gwyn's eyes are a similar shade, described as teal throughout Maas' works.
In addition to the similar coloring of the Siphons and the Invoking Stone, Azriel notes that the Stone has a similar magical feel, thinking he "never realized how much presence it seemed to have, like his Siphons, but wholly different," he said.
Azriel quickly returns the Stone to Gwyn after their brief interaction, but Maas may explore the similarities between the two down the line.
Parallels with Mor
At the end of "ACOSH," Elain begs Mor to take her with her to Vallahan, and Mor agrees, seeing that Elain needs space from Azriel, Lucien, and the Inner Circle to figure out what she wants.
It's not the first time Mor has helped an Archeron sister get some distance from a male causing her problems.
In "A Court of Mist and Fury," Mor whisks Feyre away from males twice. First, she rescues Feyre from the Spring Court after Tamlin traps her in his house. Later, Mor winnows Feyre to the cabin after she discovers that Rhysand had been keeping the fact that they were mates a secret.
She does the same for Nesta in "A Court of Silver Flames," winnowing Nesta to Emerie's home when she needs a break from Cassian. She brings Gwyn to the house, too, so Nesta has the support she needs during her turmoil.
For Feyre and Nesta, that time away allowed them to figure out how they felt about the males in their lives, positive or negative. Hopefully, Elain gets the same clarity from her space.

Naukri parent Info Edge said founder and vice chairman Sanjeev Bikhchandani will take over as executive vice chairman, MD and group CEO from December 3, 2026.

Revenue from operations grew 12.2% YoY and 2.6% QoQ to ₹903.9 Cr. Other income rose 164.8% YoY to ₹428.4 Cr from ₹161.8 Cr, contributing to the increase in net profit.

- The claim that U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., was married to her brother is unfounded.
- The latest rumor stems from a New York Post story claiming Omar's father's name was Nur Said Elmi — not Nur Omar Mohamed — and the Omar has a sister in the United Kingdom named Leila Nur Said Elmi who allegedly lived with Omar's ex-husband Ahmed Elmi, suggesting they were all siblings. A legal motion from the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia also referred to Omar as "llhan Nur Said Elmi."
- Snopes found that the claims lack evidence because they appear to be entirely circumstantial and unsubstantiated. Having possibly similar names does not prove that Omar is related to Leila Nur Said or Ahmed Elmi. Additionally, the claims did not confirm Ahmed Elmi's parentage or his relationship to Leila Nur Said. The claims also ignore Somali naming conventions in which children receive first names tied to their paternal lineage.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have reached out to Omar, the U.S. attorney's office and an individual believed to be Ahmed Elmi, and are waiting for responses.
For years, U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has been the subject of claims that she committed immigration fraud by marrying her brother, which Snopes has determined were unfounded. In October, President Donald Trump's administration reopened an investigation against Omar in which it claimed to have more evidence about her family history and alleged she had committed identity fraud, leading to federal agents raiding her home in Washington, D.C.
Following this development, Snopes readers asked us to once again determine whether Omar married her brother to commit immigration fraud and whether the U.S. government had DNA evidence to substantiate that claim.
The accusations continued to claim that Omar had married her brother, a man named Ahmed Elmi. New reporting from The New York Post claimed Omar's father's name was actually Nur Said Elmi, not Nur Omar Mohamed. According to the Post, a U.K. marriage certificate showed that Omar's ex-husband lived in London with a woman named Leila Nur Said, who was believed to be Omar's sister and whose father's name also also Nur Said Elmi.
A Fox News story, citing anonymous sources, claimed Omar's real name is Ilhan Nur Said Elmi. Motions filed by Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, related to the search warrant also referred to Omar as "Congresswoman Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar."
In an X post, responding to allegations about her name, Omar wrote: "So let's make it crystal clear. My name has always been Ilhan Omar."
A NewsNation report claimed the federal agents went through Omar's garbage in the hopes of obtaining DNA samples during the raid on her house. Omar told MSNOW that she did not believe they had taken DNA samples, nor was she asked to provide any. Without DNA testing Elmi and Omar, there is no definitive proof they are siblings.
In an interview with MSNOW, asked directly whether she was related to Elmi in any way, Omar said, "Not to my knowledge."
We found that this was not evidence enough to support the claim she married her brother or committed immigration fraud. We have reached out to Omar's office for a response to the above allegations, as well as to Pirro's office, and will update this report accordingly.
Below, we break down all the claims about Omar's past marriages, her father's name and her alleged sister:
What is the timeline of Omar's marriages?
As we have reported previously, Omar was married twice before her current marriage to Tim Mynett: to Ahmed Hirsi (who was Ahmed Aden before he gained U.S. citizenship) and to a U.K. citizen, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi — the subject of the above claims.
According to a statement Omar released in 2016, she and Hirsi applied for a marriage license in 2002. The couple married in an Islamic ceremony but never completed the process for a civil marriage, according to Hirsi. By 2008, Hirsi and Omar had separated (per Islamic custom). After that relationship ended, Omar had a civil marriage with Elmi in 2009. When that relationship ended, Elmi moved to England and they divorced per Islamic practice in 2011, but without receiving a legal divorce.
Omar and Hirsi reconciled in 2011 and remarried in an Islamic ceremony, according to her statement. In 2017, Omar formally petitioned for divorce from Elmi, and legally wed Hirsi in 2018. Minnesota court records show Omar and Elmi's marriage was legally dissolved on Dec. 4, 2017. Minnesota court records show Hirsi and Omar legally divorced on Nov. 22, 2019. Hirsi and Omar have three children together, according to court documents.
Who is Omar's father?
Nur Omar Mohamed died in 2020 from COVID-19 complications, according to a report in Sahan Journal, a Minnesotan news organization focusing on immigrant communities. The obituary described him as a prominent Somali military officer during the late-1970s Somalia-Ethiopia war.
The report noted Mohamed was a colonel during the dictatorship of Mohammed Siad Barre, who was removed from power in 1991, after which the country descended into civil war. Mohamed and his family subsequently became refugees.
In a statement announcing his death, Omar referred to her father as Nur Omar Mohamed. However, in a deleted 2013 tweet about Father's Day, Omar referred to her father as "Nur Said." Many jumped on this as evidence that Omar's father could also be the father of her ex-husband Ahmed Nur Said Elmi.
In 2019, after Omar's account deleted the tweet about her father, Omar's spokesperson said (archived):
When people write vile things on posts about people she loves—including posting disturbing doctored images of her father—she takes them down. Nur Said means 'Happy Light' and it's been her dad's nickname since he was a kid. He has a public page with the same name. She isn't deleting it for the disturbing and hateful reasons that are being implied by conspiracy theorists.
According to the Defense Language Institute Foreign Language Center, part of the Defense Department, Somalis have names with three or more components and don't commonly use hereditary surnames. A Somali often receives a personal first name at birth, followed by their father's first name, and then their grandfather's first time. So most children, male or female, share their father's and grandfather's first names. However, many Somalis also have additional names based on their lineages or clans. The institute noted, "Because all three names come from a shared pool of personal names, many Somalis have names that are the same or similar."
Omar's tweet referring to her father as "Nur Said" on its own does not establish that Ahmed Nur Said Elmi was her brother. The names Said, Nur, and Elmi are extremely common among Somali Muslims. Further, according to a 2016 profile of Omar, her paternal grandfather's name was Abukar.
Snopes was unable to find Mohamed's original Facebook account. It is likely the account has been deleted.
Is Omar related to Leila Nur Said?
The New York Post connected Omar's father's Facebook account to Leila Nur Said, saying she frequently left "hearts" on his pictures. Snopes was unable to locate either account and thus cannot independently verify this connection.
The Post's pool of evidence that established these connections is flimsy. A U.K. marriage certificate obtained by the Post for Leila Nur Said lists Nur Said Elmi, a military officer, as her father. Ahmed Elmi is not mentioned on this certificate. The Post reported: "Elmi's parentage is not known, but he lived in London with Leila Nur Said, a Somali woman who is thought to be Omar's sister, who possibly raised him."
Neither the Facebook connection to Omar's father, nor the marriage certificate, can effectively establish Ahmed Elmi's relationship with Leila Nur Said.
Media reports claim Elmi is a doctoral researcher at the University of Bristol. We reached out through an email listed on the university website and will update this post accordingly.
Our previous coverage
As we reported before, Omar showed a reporter from the Minnesota Star Tribune photos of documents from her family's entry into the U.S. after fleeing the civil war. She did not provide the reporter with copies of these papers but showed that they listed her father and showed her as the youngest of seven children. There was no one named Ahmed Nur Said Elmi listed in the documents.
We previously noted that Omar and her siblings all arrived in U.S. with refugee statuses. Omar was a minor when she became a naturalized U.S. citizen. How one sibling could end up with a completely different immigration status from the others remains unexplained by the claims.
According to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services policy, immigrants can apply for permanent residency status (opening the pathway to naturalization) if they are siblings of a U.S. citizen, or if they are married to a citizen. Any sibling of Omar would not have to marry her in order to secure a path to citizenship. If Elmi desperately wanted U.S. citizenship, he would not have immediately returned to England after his split with Omar.
In sum …
There is not enough evidence establishing familial ties between Elmi and Omar. Media reports are relying on similar names to establish connections — disregarding Somali naming conventions in which unrelated people can share common names. Until we know more, we leave this claim unrated.
For further reading, we are have reported on numerous rumors about Omar, including that she allegedly fled to Morocco after the raid on her home and that she changed her birth year in official records.

క్లెయిమ్: లెఫ్టినెంట్ జనరల్ గిరీష్ కాలియా, చైనా అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్లోని అసఫిలా, లాంగ్జు, తక్సింగ్ సర్కిళ్లను తన ఆధీనంలోకి తీసుకుందని, కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం ఈ విషయంలో తగిన చర్యలు తీసుకోవడం లేదని తెలిపిన వీడియో.

Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.
The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.
The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.
AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.
The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.
The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.
The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.
“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.
The US has banned humanoid robots from China, citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.
As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.
But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.
Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.
“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.
China’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from 1 December, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets.
Wang added that there was still optimism in other technology sectors, such as AI research and satellites, the latter because their links to the military indicates long term state support for the sector. And globally the AI boom is expected to last for at least another year.
On Monday, US AI company Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, filed paperwork ahead of a planned IPO that could be the biggest stock market debuts of all time. The company is expected to bring in as much as $100bn.
China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon. And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China.
This week the top officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum, an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. The Congress is expected to anoint Xi Jinping, China’s leader, for a fourth term. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilising policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy.
Any stimulus measure would be “high risk”, Wang said. “What if it doesn’t work out? Then whoever came up with that policy, that guy would be held accountable”.
