'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski addresses jury at his fraud trial for first time, says he's innocent
Prosecutor calls Pleterski 'a thief' who stole investor funds to spend on himself in closing statement
Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski addressed the jury for the first time at his Toronto fraud trial, thanking them, in his brief closing statement Wednesday morning.
"I am the least qualified person here to give a closing statement," Pleterski said in Ontario Superior Court.
"However, that being said, I am innocent of these charges. That is why I pled not guilty. Had I not been forced to represent myself, that would have been proven. That's all I have to say."
Pleterski represented himself at his trial, where he only cross-examined the first of 14 witnesses the Crown called and decided not to call evidence in his defence or to testify himself. When asked by Justice Shaun Nakatsuru whether he had questions for several of the witnesses, he told the court he didn't know what to ask and, in one case, said that he needed a lawyer.
The 27-year-old is accused of fraud over $5,000. At the end of the Crown's case, they dropped a second charge of money laundering against Pleterski. He was charged after a lengthy police investigation in May 2024.
- 'Crypto King' trial hears recording of Aiden Pleterski admitting $300M fund 'never existed'
- 'Crypto King' spent $16.3M of investor funds on cars, credit cards, jets, security, accountant testifies
Pleterski was no 'Crypto King': Crown
Before Pleterski addressed the court, Crown prosecutor Akshay Aurora gave his roughly 90-minute closing statement.
"Mr. Pleterski was no 'Crypto King.' Far from it. As it turns out he was no king at all. He was a thief. A thief who stole investor money and used it as he pleased. A thief who stole investor money using calculated lies," Aurora told the jury.
"As you've seen, he burned through that money … he lived his best life, all while his investors pleaded for updates on their money, only to be ignored."
Crown prosecutor Akshay Aurora is shown in this court sketch delivered a roughly 90-minute closing statement at Pleterski's fraud trial on Wednesday. (Pam Davies/CBC)
Aurora provided an overview of the Crown's evidence in his closing statement, emphasizing that none of the investors' funds went into the trading platform, FXChoice, on their investment contracts. Instead, the prosecutor said Pleterski used it to pay back other investors, buy cars, fly on private jets and rack up credit card bills.
"The truth, members of the jury, are in the numbers, and the numbers do not lie," Aurora said.
"The numbers tell us Mr. Pleterski used investor money as if it was his own to fund his lavish lifestyle."
Earlier in Pleterski's trial, a senior forensic accountant who reviewed his financial records testified that investors provided Pleterski with more than $36.3 million and none of those funds were ever sent to FXChoice.
Instead, Albert Ciorma from the Ontario Securities Commission said his forensic audit found Pleterski spent about $5.6 million on luxury vehicles, $4.9 million on credit card bills, $870,000 on travel and private jets and $598,000 on security.
Pleterski also gave nearly $3.7 million to his parents and took $609,000 in cash advances from a credit card, Ciorma said.
Altogether, those expenses total more than $16.3 million. Pleterski also paid out another $16.1 million to investors from the funds he received, according to Ciorma.
Investor paid back own money
In his closing, Aurora walked jurors through some of the financial summaries Ciorma created of Pleterski's accounts as they related to about half of the dozen investors who testified at trial.
- 'Crypto King' tells court he fears he might soon end up in jail cell with his kidnappers
- Real estate developer testifies he gave 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski $4.5M to invest
In one case, the Crown showed how investor and witness Sacha Singh provided Pleterski with $1.3 million to invest, how that money made up almost all the funds in the account and that Singh was later paid back $700,000 of his own money from the same account.
Sacha Singh testified remotely by Zoom at Pleterski fraud trial on Oct. 14. (Pam Davies/CBC)
The prosecutor's examples also showed hundreds of thousands of dollars of investor funds being deposited in Pleterski's various accounts, only to be quickly withdrawn to pay other investors, credit card bills and go toward cars and a luxury home.
"None of the money went to MyFXChoice. You've seen it. Each time, Mr. Pleterski just uses the money as if it was his own," said Aurora in reference to these accounts.
Pleterski's investments were all failures
The Crown's closing also highlighted details on Pleterski's limited trading in cryptocurrency and foreign exchange over the course of the alleged fraud between July 2020 and July 2022.
"Every single investment account of Mr. Pleterski's is a failure and only generates losses," said Aurora. "$4,000 is all that comes into his account from any form of cryptocurrency or foreign exchange source."

- 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski spent investors' money on exotic cars, private jet flights: Crown
Over the course of the trial, the jury heard about a purported $311 million fund in a FXChoice account — and how Pleterski provided screenshots and a video of it to concerned investors worried about their money in the spring of 2022.
Earlier this month, the jury in Pleterski's trial was shown this photo of Mitchell Learning holding his own phone with a screenshot the investor testified Pleterski sent him of Pleterski's trading account with a balance of more than $311 million. (Ontario Superior Court of Justice)
It came up in the testimony of several witnesses, alongside the screenshots and videos. Including one of Pleterski's email account, showing the FXChoice account where the money was supposed to be, had been deleted. The jury also heard an audio recording of a meeting with investors where Pleterski admitted the $311 million fund never existed.
'Every dollar was a decision he made'
"Who would delete a $300 million account? You wouldn't even delete a $300 account. It's clear that Mr. Pleterski was deleting that account because his 'investment scheme' was going to be unravelled … that it was going to be exposed," said Aurora in his closing statement.
"At no point, no point in the history of this account, was there $300 million, not even close. The highest this account was at was at $12,000."
The Crown also emphasized Pleterski knew he was deceiving investors from the beginning.
Pleterski, seen here outside the Toronto courthouse where he's standing trial, told the jury Thursday that he's innocent. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)
"Mr. Pleterski was the architect of this scheme. He controlled everything," Aurora told the jury.
"Every dollar spent was a decision he made. He was the architect. It would be impossible to say he did not know what he was doing."
As a result, the prosecutor told the jury Pleterski is guilty of fraud over $5,000.
Nakatsuru gave the majority of his instructions to the jury Wednesday.
The judge told the jury he would finish addressing them Thursday morning and then the jury will begin their deliberations.

Early 1900s India was a place where your gender determined what you could be in life. That nation could not stomach the thought of, trivial as it was, common as it is today, a woman pursuing the sciences. This antediluvian thought though, this kind of restriction was only the cause of a temporary disruption Mary Poonen Lukose’s path to glory.
It is inescapable irony that India’s first woman Surgeon General Mary Poonen Lukose was not allowed to study science. Born in Ayamanam (incidentally, Arundathi Roy’s backdrop in the God of Small Things) in Kottayam in 1886, Mary was so bright, she topped the matriculation exam. Nevermind how bright she was, her gender was a disqualifier as Maharaja College in Tiruvananthapuram declined her admission to the sciences. Only a temporary detour, Mary went on to get a degree in history, becoming the first woman from Travancore to graduate from Madras University in 1909.
However, her family could afford to send her to London to pursue medicine, and she was the first Indian woman to graduate in Medicine from the University of London, according to an article published by Cambridge University Press (CUP) as part of a compendium of Modern Asian Studies. She earned an MBBS from the University of London in 1915, trained in obstetrics and gynaecology, and studied paediatrics at Great Ormond Street Hospital.
Reports of her life, rendered through an autobiographical account, Trailblazer, released in 2020, record Mary as working hard in Dublin at the Rotunda Hospital, coping with the increasing work load created by the outbreak of World War 1 in 1914. When her mentor and guide, her father passed away in 1916, Mary was shattered; she had to take a call on whether she would continue in England or come back home to serve her people. She, of course, decided to come home and blazed a path of glory, only long forgotten. She returned to Travancore in 1916 as its first woman doctor.
The CUP article further quotes from an autobiographical note penned by Mary herself: “In her autobiographical essay, Mary Poonen Lukose reflects on her decision to become a doctor. She traces it to her early experiences helping out in hospitals where her father worked as a doctor, and to his example and influence on her. ‘As I grew up, he made it a point to instill into me the spirit of service to humanity.’
The article further notes that the style of her 1916 job application, her requests for references, and the correspondence surrounding it suggest that she was aware of the fact that her qualifications were exceptional for an Indian woman of her time.
Mary Poonen Lukose went on to build the scaffolding of modern public health in Travancore, one that can be attributed to the many advances that Kerala has achieved today in health care indicators. Her work helped lay the ground for what we now celebrate as the “Kerala model” of health—fronting strong primary care, institutional childbirth, public health outreach, and unusually good social indicators. Acknowledging her contributions, in the 2018 budget speech, the finance minister of the State said, on record, in the House: ‘Dr. Mary Poonen Lukose is one of the most talented people in the development of Kerala’s health system.’
At the Women and Children Hospital in Thycaud, Mary worked as an obstetrician and superintendent, initiating daughters of local birth attendants into training midwifery, an attempt to subsume traditional midwifery into scientific deliveries and maternal care. Some historic references to her indicate she performed Travancore’s first Caesarean section before 1920, reportedly sometimes working only by the light of a hurricane-lamp light.
As Surgeon General from 1938, she was responsible for 32 government hospitals, 40 dispensaries, and 20 private institutions. In colonial era India, this could be notched up as a mega achievement for a woman, not only in health care, but also an administrator. Mary also founded a tuberculosis sanatorium in Nagercoil, and established the X-Ray and Radium Institute in Tiruvananthapuram.
It was not only for the issue of providing women adequate health facilities that she lent her voice, but was equally vociferous on women’s political rights. She herself, in 1922, was nominated to Travancore’s legislative council, becoming the State’s first woman legislator.
But Mary was a multi-splendored person, capable of achievements across sectors. As the nuns sing in the Sound of Music of Maria the reluctant nun: How do you catch a cloud and pin it down? Mary co-founded the Tiruvananthapuram branch of the Young Women’s Christian Association and served as its president for 50 years. She was also a member of two professional bodies, the Indian Medical Association and the Federation of Obstetric and Gynaecological Societies of India.
Many honours came her way, including the Vaidyaśāstrakuśala by the Maharaja of Travancore in 1935, and the Padma Śhri in 1975, just a year before her death at the age of 90.
Mary is part of a legacy of tall women in Indian health care that helped sculpt systems that are propping the nation up today, including Muthulakshmi Reddy, Kadambini Ganguly, and Anandi Joshi. They are the forebearers who chipped away at the glass ceilings that prevented them from rising, and cleared the ladder for women who came after them, though history has not given them their due space.
But it is now time for reparation, it is time to say their name loud. Say her name: Say Mary Poonen Lukose, so every one can hear, and celebrate.

At least 64 people were killed on Wednesday after a high-speed train struck the rear of another train that had stopped on the tracks in central Spain, authorities said. The collision derailed two carriages and marked the country's second major rail accident this year.
The crash occurred along the Madrid-Seville high-speed railway line in Toledo province, where two trains carrying hundreds of passengers were travelling in the same direction towards Seville in southwestern Spain, according to Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the Castilla-La Mancha regional government.
Spain's rail infrastructure operator ADIF said the accident took place on Wednesday morning.
A drone footage from the crash site showed a white-and-purple Renfe AVE train largely remaining on the tracks, while several carriages of a red-and-white Iryo train derailed.
Some of the damaged carriages were tilted over the railway embankment, while others laid in the field below. Twisted bodywork and debris can be seen scattered around the wreckage.
Emergency services deployed ambulances, fire engines, police vehicles and medical helicopters to the surrounding fields. Rescue personnel wearing high-visibility jackets were also seen moving between the damaged carriages and emergency vehicles.
The footage panned across the rural landscape, showing the affected trains, the extent of the derailment and the ongoing rescue operation.
Spain's transport minister said the train control system failed due to a computer communication issue, prompting an immediate halt to train services. A decision to resume train operations was taken at 8.36, the minister added.

Spanish leaders express grief
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez cancelled his scheduled engagements to focus on the crash. In a post on X, he said he was “dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo.”
“Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers,” Sánchez wrote. “All my thoughts are with the victims and their families.”
The accident comes as Sánchez faces a national election next month.
King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia also expressed their condolences, saying they were closely following developments.
“We are deeply saddened and concerned by the train accident in Urda (Toledo),” the royal couple said in a statement on X. “We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected.”
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also offered her condolences to those affected by the tragedy.
“My heart goes out to the victims’ families and loved ones. Today, Europe mourns with you,” she said.

Seven out of ten women in West Bengal are anaemic, according to the last figures available. The National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019–21) showed the rate to be 71.4% among women aged 15 to 49, the highest in India’s major states, as compared with 39% among men. However, when NFHS-6 released its fact sheets this year, the section on anaemia was omitted. For the first time since the late 1990s, India has a national health survey that does not include an estimate of anaemia, so it is now impossible to tell whether the situation for women in West Bengal has improved or gotten worse.
This more than a minor omission: anaemia in India is a major public health concern, of greater significance in women, since the difference between men and women when it comes to rates of anaemia is generally attributed to biology. This, however, isn’t entirely accurate.
A burden that kept rising
From 2015 to 2016, the rate of anaemia among women of reproductive age increased nationally from 53% to 57%. In West Bengal, the figure rose by approximately 9 percentage points, and for children between 6 months and 5 years, it rose from 54% to 69%. The gap appears early on: nationally, 59.1% of adolescent girls were anaemic as compared with 31.1% of boys, and this difference becomes greater as people go through their reproductive years. Within the State, the severity of anaemia is linked to disadvantage, so that in districts like Purulia and Uttar Dinajpur almost four out of five women were anaemic.
Anaemia prevalence, NFHS-5 (2019–21)
| Anaemia prevalence NFHS-5 (2019–21) | West Bengal | India | 
| Women 15–49 | 71.4% | 57.0% | 
| Men 15–49 | ~39% | 25.0% | 
| Children 6–59 months | 69.0% | 67.1% | 
Source: IIPS & ICF, NFHS-5 (2021). NFHS-6 (2026) did not report anaemia.
Not just biology
The usual explanation given in textbooks is that women lose more iron because they menstruate, carry pregnancies, and breastfeed; this is correct, but it does not explain a 30-point gap or why this gap changes so markedly across districts, castes, and wealth levels. The answer may lie in examining gender rather than biology alone.
It takes four factors to accomplish this. The first of these is time: since women’s duties, both at home and in agriculture, are mostly unpaid, they have little time for rest, for preparing iron-containing meals, or for visiting a health centre. The second is the meal pattern: in many households, food is given to men and children before it is offered to women, so that the women end up eating last and the least of the food from the kitchens that they manage. The third is social norms: it is considered a woman’s responsibility to look after people, and their own health is of secondary importance, and anaemia is regarded as a ‘women’s ailment.’ That stigma has a double effect in that about four out of every five men in West Bengal are anaemic as well, but they are almost never checked or treated. The fourth is money: women who rely financially on others are often unable to act on what they already know about diet.
An anaemia programme that ignores the gender dimension and merely distributes free iron tablets encounters all four of these obstacles and fails to alter any of them. Fieldwork carried out in Bankura in 2025 illustrates exactly what happens in practice. Pregnant and breastfeeding women discarded the fortified (with iron) rice kernels they were given, since they ‘looked like plastic’. They skipped the iron-folic acid tablets, which they did not like, and forgot their doses because of household chores no one else took on. Husbands, who are mostly engaged as migrant labourers, played almost no role in household nutrition. An improved supply chain would not remedy any of this.
The present scenario
The government has, this year, restructured the Anaemia Mukt Bharat programme. In June, the previous 6×6×6 arrangement (six target beneficiary groups, six interventions and six institutional mechanisms) was replaced by a 7×7×7 scheme which includes testing and treatment, a digital ‘T4’ tracking system and a new national centre of excellence for anaemia. On paper, these steps are the correct ones. A digital tracking system broken down by sex could finally show the problem affecting men, a factor kept out of sight because previous messaging had focused only on women.
Yet, in this same year, the country lost its standard for measurement. The official stance is that that anaemia has been omitted from NFHS-6 since blood samples taken from finger pricks are not fully reliable and may have inflated the figures, and also because India had been following the World Health Organization’s cut-offs for anaemia, which may not be suited to the local context. Instead, venous blood sampling was recommended.
All of these are valid concerns, and there is merit in them. The government had also justified dropping the anaemia reading in the NFHS-6 by stating that it would be surveyed more scientifically in the Diet and Biomarkers Survey in India (since renamed the SAMPADA survey), spearheaded by the ICMR-National Institute on Nutrition, and launched in December 2022. Venous blood samples were collected from residents across 183 districts. The problem is, that SAMPADA has not yet released any of its results, despite the survey being completed in November 2025. Until it does, there is no up-to-date national or State figure against which to assess the new programme. It is therefore impossible to verify or alter West Bengal’s status as the most severely affected of the major States, and nobody can tell whether the new framework is having the desired effect.
At present, reform and measurement have become detached from each other, even though they should be closely linked. A programme which is not measurable cannot be held responsible for its actions.
What should follow
There are three issues. The first is that the government ought to make available SAMPADA’s findings on a specific date, breaking the findings down by sex, age and State, and it should ensure that the methods used are sufficiently similar to those employed in the NFHS so that the new figures can be compared with the old ones rather than simply replacing them. An improved measure must not cause the trend to disappear.
The second point is that the new tracking system should regularly provide data by sex, and supplementation for men should be carried out in exactly the same way as it is for women. The third is that counselling and outreach activities must treat anaemia as a problem that affects the entire household, not merely as a problem of women; it is therefore necessary to reach mothers-in-law, since they are often in a position to decide who eats what, and migrant husbands should also be targeted since they are never present in the room.
India is now carrying out a more ambitious programme than before to combat anaemia, and has no current figures with which to evaluate it. Until the data is available, we are facing a problem for which records have been discontinued, and the women who are affected most may be the last to find out whether or not any change has taken place.
(Anurag Telang is a researcher in public health. dranurag225@gmail.com; Karan Babbar is an assistant professor of Economics at XLRI, Jamshedpur. phd17karanb@iima.ac.in)

Alexander brothers sentenced to 30 years in prison for sex trafficking after blaming rapes on 'hookup culture'
Prosecutors had asked the judge to give them life in prison

Three brothers convicted of exploiting their wealth and access to luxury real estate to drug and rape dozens of women were sentenced Tuesday to 30 years in prison.
U.S. District Judge Valerie E. Caproni announced the punishment for Tal, Oren and Alon Alexander — known collectively as the Alexander Brothers — after 11 accusers spoke in court. Some of the women choked up as they described how the assaults stole their innocence and left them haunted by nightmares and fearing men.
“It took one night, only a few hours, one invitation to completely wreck the girl I once was,” one woman, using a pseudonym to protect her identity, said as she stood at a lectern just feet from the brothers in a Manhattan courtroom.
Twins Oren and Alon, 39, and Tal Alexander, 40, were convicted in March of sex trafficking.
The brothers speak for themselves
None of the brothers testified during the trial, but each spoke Tuesday before they were sentenced.
Oren Alexander addressed the packed courtroom first, saying, “I am not here to discount what they have said,” referring to the women.
He said he and his brothers came of age at the height of hookup culture and, looking back and now as a father, he regrets many of the things he said about women at that time. However, he insisted that they never broke the law.
“My brothers and I have never drugged or raped anyone. We never trafficked anyone for sex and we never conspired to hurt anyone,” he said.
Tal Alexander also denied that he drugged or raped anyone. He asked the judge to be assign him to same prison as his brothers; saying their parents, both 70 years old, hope to visit them every weekend, which might be difficult if they’re at different lockups.
Alon Alexander said he, too, has evolved from his regrettable past, noting that not a single woman has accused him of wrongdoing in the eight years he’s been committed to his wife: “Over time, that became my life: work, home, children, parents, community.”
Victims describe a lasting dread
The accusers who spoke in court — and another whose statement was read by a prosecutor — were among at least 70 women who prosecutors say were assaulted by one or more of the brothers over the last two decades in posh locales including the Hamptons on Long Island and in Aspen, a Colorado.
Lindsey Acree, an artist and gallery owner, testified that she was raped by Tal Alexander and another man at a Hamptons home in 2011 after taking a drink that she said left her feeling paralyzed. Scrapping her prepared remarks, she told Caproni that a life sentence, wouldn’t begin to do justice for the women whose lives were irreparably harmed.
“This has wasted my damn time. It’s wasted your time. It’s wasted everyone in this room’s time,” Acree told the judge. Turning to the brothers, she said: “For why? For you. Because you did some really messed up stuff.”
“The biggest thing is why? Why did you do this?” Acree asked. “I don’t understand the cruelty. I don’t understand the hatred towards women.”
Another woman who testified that Tal Alexander raped her in August 2014 said she carried “a quiet funeral in me for the person I might have become had this not happened to me.”
“Every second that Tal raped me in that shower felt like an eternity of terror,” said the woman, who used a pseudonym.
Another woman speaking about her rape in the Hamptons, said: “What looked like a beautiful place became for me a mansion of horror, a mansion of dark secrets.”
Prosecutors had sought life prison sentences while the brothers’ lawyers had requested the 15-year mandatory minimum.
Stars of the New York real estate scene
Oren and Tal Alexander were once nicknamed real estate’s “A Team” for their ultra high-end sales and celebrity clientele.After smashing sales records at industry powerhouse Douglas Elliman, the brothers started their own firm. Alon Alexander ran their family’s private security company.
The brothers projected an exclusive lifestyle of yachts, private jets and waterfront mansions in Miami, but prosecutors said they began sexually assaulting women as early as 2001 or 2002, when they were in high school, and over time developed a pattern of drugging and raping women who they enticed to join them on luxury getaways.
In remarks before the sentence was announced, Assistant U.S. Attorney Elizabeth Espinosa told the judge that the brothers’ “callousness, carelessness, cruelty” in repeatedly drugging and raping women over many years warranted a life prison term, especially since all their victims would be serving life sentences of pain.
“Women overcame all the forces telling them this was their fault, they should stay quiet, that no one would believe them,” the prosecutor said. “Despite that pain, so many came forward and 11 women testified at trial.”
Alon Alexander’s lawyer, Howard Srebnick, called a life sentence a “death in prison sentence.”
In court papers, defense lawyers said the brothers apologize to the women they insulted or offended for conduct they admit was “insensitive toward the feelings of certain women at certain times.” They also maintained their innocence.
The trio were arrested in 2024 and have been held without bail ever since.
The judge, Caproni, has said she believes the brothers should not be incarcerated at the same prison because they were a bad influence on one another. The brothers’ lawyers plan to argue that they belong together, even behind bars.

High-speed train crash kills at least 68 people in Spain
- Published
A high-speed train crash has killed at least 68 people and injured dozens more in central Spain.
It occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Seville barrelled into another train - which was stationary on the tracks - on Wednesday morning. The force saw several carriages fall down an embankment.
The transport minister said a computer failure followed by human error caused the collision, which is one of the worst in Europe's modern history, and Spain's deadliest train disaster in 13 years.
Survivors described harrowing scenes of passengers being thrown into the air, trapped in the wreckage and smashing windows to get out.
The collision happened just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) around 140km (100 miles) south of Madrid.
The stationary train, run by private rail operator Iryo, had 147 passengers on board, and had stopped on the tracks because of a computer failure, Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said.
He explained that when there is a system failure, a 24-hour control centre in Madrid takes over, but it had made an "inexplicable" decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.
Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by another train, run by Spain's state-owned railway company, Renfe, which was carrying 397 passengers.
The force of the crash was "brutal", said 62-year-old passenger Salvador Arriza who was sitting in the Renfe-operated train.
Passengers started breaking the windows to get out, he told Reuters, adding that "some people couldn't move because they were trapped amongst the seats."
One of the carriages caught fire, and passengers described devastating scenes of trapped people crying and bleeding, with some buried under debris.
Pictures show that a long piece of railway track had speared through one of the carriages.
Tangui Binier, 22, was on the Iryo train and told the BBC that "suitcases started flying and people were screaming" when the train finally came to a halt.
There was a lot of smoke and confusion, he said, and described seeing the train "completely flipped over" when he stepped outside.
"It was hard to witness", Binier said, adding that his father carried a girl who had a broken hip out of the wreckage.
He also described seeing dead bodies and missing limbs: "I don't know if I'll ever recover."
Spanish journalist Antonio Jiménez Barca, who works for El Pais newspaper, was walking to the Renfe train's cafeteria when the crash happened.
"I felt like I was being pushed from behind, like I was being thrown to the ground," he described.
"I hit my head horribly... I was covered in blood. There were people on top of me. One person had an injured arm, and another had a head injury."
Another passenger, 46-year-old Sebastián Herrero, told El Mundo newspaper that he saw "many people with broken noses, broken arms."
"It was a terrible, terrible impact," he said, adding that he was "in the air for about four or five seconds," which felt like a lifetime.
Many of the passengers said they were in shock, and one sobbed during an interview with a local television station as he described a woman dying in his arms.
"She was very cold and she was all alone," he said, to which the show's presenter also started to cry.
Dozens of ambulances rushed to the scene, and a helicopter evacuated those with the most serious injuries.
Spain's Civil Guard said it would need DNA samples from relatives to identify some victims.
"The whole of Spain is grieving", Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said during a visit to the crash site. "Lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart, the pain is immense."
Spain was already reeling from a high-speed rail disaster near Córdoba in January that killed 46 people. It happened on the same rail line, but much further south.
Wednesday's crash is the worst the country has seen since 2013, when when 80 people died on the outskirts of Santiago de Compostela in north-west Spain.
"Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure," said Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the the main opposition People's Party.
Spanish trade union CSIF has demanded the transport minister resign, accusing him of "scapegoating" a traffic manager, by blaming human error in the control room, instead of "taking responsibility".
Sánchez and other Spanish politicians cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday, including campaigning for next month's parliamentary elections.
The prime minister said it was "unacceptable" for Spain to have two serious train crashes in one year, and vowed to "get to the bottom of this" and determine if there was any negligence.
"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."

Consider a kurta priced at ₹799 sold directly on Flipkart by a fashion brand such as Globus Fashion. Since July, Flipkart stopped charging a commission on fashion products, so on paper the seller keeps more of each sale than it did a year ago. But under Flipkart's new penalty structure, effective August 23, the seller is penalised ₹30 the moment the kurta misses its dispatch-by date. If the order is then cancelled, the seller is penalised another ₹60. Flipkart now also counts three missed deadlines as a cancellation. But the flat penalty (a total of ₹90) means that sellers face a greater burden to clear low-value orders. This is one example of how selling online has become costlier this festive season, and penalties are just one part of it. Besides this, there are fee surcharges that apply to every order, whether or not it is delayed or cancelled. And the cost of production and fulfilment have also gone up due to issues ranging from a crunch in raw material supply as well as high fuel prices due to the instability in West Asia. No matter the seller, whether it is a brand or an Amazon-specific seller, these charges and surcharges are making it harder and costlier to sellers on ecommerce at a time when business is at its peak. Third-party sellers usually operate on thinner margins than brands and have no control over the price listed on Amazon India, according to industry sources we spoke to. Some brands take up the operations themselves, depending on the marketplace. Globus Fashion, for instance, sells directly on Flipkart but through Cocoblu Retail on Amazon. Another brand, Ruhe India, which sells smart kitchen and smart home products, holds its own seller account and sells directly on the marketplaces. The approach is different but the charges will remain. The changes coincide with the peak festive season sales on Amazon India and Flipkart. According to Redseer projections, festive ecommerce GMV will reach $15–16 Bn in 2026, up about 25% from roughly $12.5 Bn in 2025, with online festive shoppers rising to 180–185 Mn from 160 Mn. But these estimates do not account for the higher cost that customers and sellers will have to pay for using the ecommerce platform. And that’s before we even account for the potential slowdown due to the merchant discount rate or MDR coming up in merchant UPI payments. The New Penalty Structure On August 17, months before its main festive season shopping window, Amazon changed how it charges cancellation fees for sellers on Easy Ship and Self Ship. Under Easy Ship, Amazon picks up the order from the seller and delivers it; under Self Ship, the seller delivers it through its own courier. The fee, earlier tied to flat category-based referral charges, is now a percentage of the order value, according to Amazon's communication to sellers. Amazon now charges 10% of the order value on orders up to ₹10,000, 8% between ₹10,001 and ₹50,000, 5% between ₹50,001 and ₹1 lakh, and 2% above that, plus 18% GST. A cancelled ₹30,000 order can end up costing the seller about ₹2,832 including the GST which is applicable on cancellation fee. Sellers of electronics, appliances and other big-ticket goods carry the most exposure per order. "This fee is conditional and only applies in the rare event of a seller-initiated cancellation, which accounts for less than 1% of orders on Amazon.in. We have appropriate measures in place to ensure sellers are protected when cancellations are due to circumstances beyond their control," Amazon told Inc42 in an emailed statement. Electronics sellers are already under pressure due to expectations that the 2026 winter season will result in slower sales than 2025. This is largely due to the rising prices of mobile devices and electronics this year, but the extra charges will also play a role in whether sellers even offer some products for sale. Flipkart did not respond to Inc42's queries. People familiar with the company's operations said the penalties follow its zero-commission push, which has nearly doubled seller onboarding year-on-year. In July, Flipkart dropped commissions across its fashion catalogue, removing an earlier ₹1,000 price ceiling for the waiver. Whose Fault Is A Delay? The platforms' position is that penalties apply only when sellers fail. Sellers, however, claim the line is not always clear. Responding to Amazon's notices on its seller forum, some sellers said cancellations were sometimes caused by delivery personnel failing to turn up for scheduled pickups, and asked why the fee should apply in such cases. A founder of a snacking brand, who wished to be anonymous, told us when a logistics-side delay gets billed to the seller instead of the carrier, this becomes a source of friction and can disrupt many smaller sellers. “We have contested such cases with evidence of timely dispatch, but found the process cumbersome," the founder added. Kapil Gupta, founder of Ruhe India, whose catalogue runs from sub-₹500 to ₹3,000-plus, told Inc42 that Flipkart's flat ₹90 penalty would land hardest on the brand's value-tier catalogue. Vinod Kumar, trustee of the Forum for Internet Resellers, Sellers and Traders (FIRST INDIA), said online sellers accept the need for timely fulfilment, but the increase in fees and penalties just before the festive season is a concern for MSMEs already dealing with thin margins and rising costs this year. Unlike the penalties, these charges apply regardless of seller performance, which seems like a blanket rule meant to punish even those who have a very low proportion of cancellations or delays. Deliveries Turn Costlier Too What makes matters worse is that delivery fees and logistics costs have gone up across the industry, meaning no brand or seller is immune to this. From September 7, Amazon raised its closing fee, a flat per-item charge separate from the commission, by ₹1 on products priced up to ₹500 and by ₹3 or higher-priced items. Amazon's seller fee page attributes the increase to higher fuel and logistics costs. Similarly, Flipkart's logistics arm is mulling a revision in fulfillment fees for sellers, according to sources. Logistics platform Delhivery added a surcharge on D2C shipments of ₹4 per express shipment and ₹2 per surface shipment, on top of contracted rates from September 1,. The company has reportedly attributed it to higher aviation turbine fuel prices, ground-staff costs and inflation across its network. The new pricing structure affects a specific group: brands shipping orders from their own websites. Delhivery declined to comment to Inc42 related to queries on increase in the pricings. Ruhe India's Gupta said the surcharge would be a challenge for brands building native website sales, which rely on third-party logistics players such as Delhivery. Globus Fashion, which sells directly and through marketplace sellers, said that logistics or fulfillment costs "can be renegotiated between the brand and marketplace", but others say that this is not a standardised process. The fashion brand expects festive logistics spending to rise with demand, but does not expect a big impact on revenue, because inventory placement and warehouse use have already been allocated ahead of time. Large enterprises stock regional warehouses months in advance to lock in contracted freight rates and accept the holding costs. Other brands may not have these pieces in place. But, freight operators see more and more brands responding to the festive rush ahead of time. Geetali Sunil Khare, founder of Rachana Speed Logistics, said brands and wholesalers are building inventory ahead of the rush rather than cutting order sizes to protect margins, to avoid stockouts and supply disruptions at peak demand. In categories such as electronics and apparel, sellers need to retain minimal stock to avoid post-festive inventory risk, and absorb higher, fragmented spot freight costs instead. Truck rental rates in September held above year-ago levels, but month-on-month increases across most corridors have been relatively modest, Khare added. The bigger festive challenge, she said, is meeting tighter service expectations with higher shipment volumes and heavier consignments. “On the logistics side it is mostly the truck movement to warehouses that makes up for substantial expenses operation wise. With the deliveries now expanding to regional markets , it makes it harder to to fill vehicles on the way out and leaving return legs empty or under-used,” Aman Mahlawat, founder of Mahlawat Logistics, added. On local runs, Mahlawat said, highway transit is smooth, but city entry restrictions and long queues at distribution hub docks cause major delays. Quick commerce, according to the industry players we spoke to, has also added to the cost-strain. High-frequency replenishment of dark store inventory is changing how stock moves upstream from warehouses to the distribution endpoints. Mahlawat said dark stores and retailers now prefer frequent, smaller drops to monthly bulk dispatches, which splits loads into smaller vehicles and leaves trucks spending more hours waiting at congested unloading docks than moving on the road. These frequent, fragmented dispatches need constant vehicle availability, squeezing truck turnaround times and load consolidation. "More predictability, enough lead time on fee and policy changes to plan for them, rather than absorbing them mid-season is the only way sellers or brands can work around these changes,” Ruhe India's Gupta added.’ Can Commission Cuts Offset Rising Costs? While Flipkart, Amazon India and others have cut commissions for sellers this year, the rising logistics costs, the extra charges this year, and the growing dependency on advertising spending on marketplaces have eaten into the margins of sellers. Amazon waived referral fees on products under ₹1,000 in March, and Flipkart extended zero commission to all fashion categories in July. Those cuts cover specific categories and price bands while closing fees, shipping charges and penalties apply across categories Sellers are bemoaning the lack of clarity on when new charges are introduced or why they are applicable to all sellers regardless of their past performance. What sellers are asking for is more predictability from marketplaces and platforms, especially around the peak festive season.

Flavio Bolsonaro lands in Miami, declares himself rightful leader of Brazil
The senator said without providing evidence that he was a victim of an electoral coup d’etat by leftist leader Lula and the Supreme Court
Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who arrived in the US on Wednesday, has declared himself the rightful leader of Brazil, alleging an electoral coup d’etat had been carried out by the country’s Supreme Court and President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who won the presidential election by over 4 million votes.
Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday’s election and left Brazil for Miami, where he and his family received US visas, thanked Argentine leader Javier Milei and US President Donald Trump for helping him leave his country and for welcoming him.

Janhvi Kapoor has addressed the controversy surrounding her portrayal of Achiyamma in Peddi, admitting that she continues to reflect on her role in a film that faced criticism over the treatment of her character. Speaking on the latest episode of Koffee With Karan Season 9, the actor acknowledged concerns around objectification and the film’s portrayal of sexual assault, while also saying that she wishes she had spoken up more strongly during the making of the film.
Koffee With Karan 9: Janhvi Kapoor calls Peddi a “violating experience”, admits “extreme objectification” was problematic; says, “I was so apprehensive to talk about it because…”
Directed by Buchi Babu Sana and headlined by Ram Charan, Peddi released in theatres on June 4, 2026. Following its release, the film faced criticism over the way Janhvi’s character was presented, with particular attention on camera shots focusing on her body and a romantic sequence that audiences questioned for its treatment of consent.
Janhvi Kapoor says she takes responsibility for her part
Reflecting on the controversy, Janhvi said, “I felt many things, Karan. I think the reason I was so apprehensive to talk about it was because many people worked very hard on that film. I really didn't know what to say or if there was anything really to say. But it's important that I take ownership for my half of whatever that fiasco was because it weighs heavily on my conscience, the sort of negative impact a narrative like that can have on our society, specific to my gender.”
She went on to question whether she could have done more to challenge how her character was portrayed. “Could I have done more? Could I have been more vigilant? Could I have made a bigger scene? A hundred percent, yes. Was it problematic? Was it extreme objectification? Did it even propagate sexual assault narratively? Yes,” she said.
Janhvi added that her focus now is on ensuring that she does not find herself in a similar situation again. “The only thing I can do is to ensure that that doesn't happen again. I went through the beats of really beating myself up. I should have been more vigilant. I should have made a bigger scene,” she added.
Janhvi explains the challenges she faced during filming
The actor also spoke about the dynamics of working on a film where she said, “I don't like saying this because it sounds like I'm shifting blame. But you know what it's like, you feel like whatever the director says, be professional, listen to the director. So I was really navigating how to make things less problematic as best I thought, as and when information was becoming available to me.”
She further said, “In the South, there very rarely is a bound script. And very rarely in those scripts do you see where the camera angles are.”
At the same time, Janhvi reiterated that she believes she could have used her position to speak up more.
“Having said that, I need to also take responsibility for my half of it. I do come from a place of privilege. I should have taken advantage of that because I'm going to get the criticism for being privileged anyway. So I might as well have leveraged it,” she said.
Janhvi calls the experience “violating”
When Karan Johar asked whether she felt disappointed at the time or believed the filmmaker had not intended for things to unfold that way, Janhvi described the experience as violating. “No, I feel like I get so conscious when I speak about this because I don't want to sound like I'm trying to be the victim here. I mean, it was a violating experience in a way,” she said.
Janhvi also revealed that she had expressed her discomfort during the filming process and even during post-production. “I feel like both of you have sort of been with me through the beats of me trying to articulate discomfort throughout the course of shooting, even post-production,” she told Karan and Varun Dhawan, who was also part of the conversation.
Janhvi hopes the controversy leads to change
Despite the difficult experience, Janhvi said she hopes the conversation around Peddi could make filmmakers think more carefully about how female characters are presented on screen.
“The good thing that came out of all of this is that maybe tomorrow someone else will think twice before they present a lead actress this way,” she said.

Deaths in detention cells in Nigeria were entirely preventable, inquiry finds
- Published
An inquiry into the deaths of 33 detainees in Nigeria's Minna state has found they died as a result of severe overcrowding, poor ventilation and failure by officers to respond to distress calls.
Forensic and medical evidence showed the "entirely preventable" deaths had resulted from acute respiratory failure linked to prolonged confinement, aggravated by heat stress and dehydration.
The evidence did not support initial claims of a disease outbreak.
The detainees were found dead on 17 September while being held by the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps on suspicion of illegal mining. The investigation found that the mining sites had been licensed.
Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said those found responsible for the deaths would face the full force of the law.
He added that the detention hall had been cleaned before investigators arrived, raising concerns about possible attempts to compromise evidence.
Implicated officers will face suspension and the report would be forwarded to the attorney general of the federation for further legal action, Tunji-Ojo said.
The investigating committee found that the raid on the miners had been conducted without an approved operational order, proper planning or consultation with the Mining Marshals Unit.
It said that 50 detainees had been held in a cell measuring about 20 sq m, with no running water or functioning toilet, and inadequate food, drinking water and airflow.
Adults and minors were detained together, and some detainees were held beyond lawful detention periods.
Officers reportedly ignored repeated calls for help, despite a medical worker having raised concerns about the conditions.
"Detainees repeatedly banged on cell doors and walls, shouted for assistance and pleaded for water," said the head of the investigating team, Jonathan Kure.
"These distress calls were heard by officers assigned to nearby duties... but were not acted upon."
Kure said the detention conditions amounted to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment.
"The tragedy demonstrates the consequences of systemic disregard for detention standards, supervisory responsibilities and the welfare of persons in custody," he added.
The investigating committee also recommended compensation of 30m naira (£16,683; $22,285) for each of the bereaved families and 10m naira for each survivor.

Since 2020, under Walz and Flanagan's leadership, the state has awarded several grants to Southside Harm Reduction Services, a Minneapolis-based charity that operates several harm reduction programs, including boofing kits. The $8 million figure cited in examples of the claim is not the amount of money Southside spent on the boofing kits — it is the total amount of money granted to Southside for all purposes. (Though Snopes calculated that figure at $9.1 million, promised through 2030.)
A week before the 2024 U.S. presidential election, conservative investigative journalism outlet The Washington Free Beacon published a story saying Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz provided funding to an organization that gives drug users "booty bumping kits," allowing them to consume drugs through the rectum (a practice sometimes called "boofing").
The claim about the Democratic then-candidate for vice president spread on social media before fizzling out.
Two years later, The Washington Free Beacon published another story saying Walz and the state's Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan "Steered Millions To Pay for Disgusting 'Booty Bumping' Kits." Flanagan is currently running for U.S. Senate in the 2026 midterms.
Citing the outlet's 2026 report, social media users claimed in October that Walz and Flanagan have provided roughly $8 million to Southside Harm Reduction Services, a Minneapolis-based nonprofit organization that operates several harm reduction programs and supposedly provides the kits.
Snopes readers also contacted us for more information about this story.
We found that Walz and Flanagan's administration has provided funding to Southside since 2020. While The Washington Free Beacon claimed in October 2026 that the state government has promised roughly $8 million to the organization, Snopes calculated Southside has been promised $9.1 million in grants through 2030.
Southside does provide "booty bumping kits" to drug users. However, it was not possible to find evidence that the organization spent "millions" in state funding on such paraphernalia. The actual figure is likely to be significantly lower — not a seven-figure sum.
Snopes contacted Flanagan's campaign, the Minnesota state budget office and Southside Harm Reduction Services for comment on the story. None had replied prior to publication.
What's true?
In 2023, during Walz and Flanagan's time in office, the Minnesota State Legislature passed a budget that designated $100 million in funding to organizations that assist the state's homeless population. Southside Harm Reduction Services is directly named in the news release announcing the funding.
"[The charity provides] harm reduction services via outreach to people experiencing unsheltered homelessness who use drugs, primarily in or near Minneapolis and St. Paul," according to the news release. "Services include syringe exchange, naloxone distribution, education, rapid HIV testing and referrals to social services including housing."
Snopes reviewed contracts for active and expired grants between the state and Southside, confirming they are a recipient of funding and have been since 2020.
Turning to the nonprofit's social media sites and yearly reports shows the "booty bumping kit" in question and its accompanying mini-zine containing instructions and information about the paraphernalia.
In sum, Southside Harm Reduction Services does receive funding from the state government, and it does provide boofing kits.
Clarifying the figures
The $8 million figure does not represent the amount of money the state has spent on boofing kits, as some may have incorrectly inferred from the social media posts. The Washington Free Beacon says this figure is the total amount of money the state granted to Southside. The headline of the outlet's article could, however, lead some readers to incorrectly believe the nonprofit spent "millions" on the kits.
Using Minnesota's funding transparency database, Snopes calculated that The Washington Free Beacon's $8 million figure was previously correct but is now outdated. Our calculations showed the state's Health Department and Human Services Department have promised Southside approximately $9.3 million in total between 2020 and 2030 for all operational purposes. 
The grants function as monthly reimbursements from the state (Page 4, Section 3.2) rather than an up-front lump sum payment. In other words, if Southside does not spend the $9.3 million, the state does not pay anything.
This is noteworthy because budgeting documentation from multiple grants reveals that Southside sometimes, but not always, does not spend all its allocated money (see the table on Page 7). For instance, in an amendment to a grant worth $620,400 spanning a 42-month period, the organization budgeted $22,200 from the grant for "supplies" for the 2025 fiscal year (part of which would presumably have been used to fund the boofing kits). But, according to that grant amendment, Southside spent less than $6,000 of the grant on supplies that year. 
Other grants provide a more detailed breakdown of the organization's budgeting. Southside's largest active grant for a total of $2.5 million runs between October 2025 and June 2029. The budgeting documentation provided alongside that contract breaks down Southside's yearly budget for supplies — $84,378 for the 2026 fiscal year (PDF Page 29) — into individual components, including $37,000 for "Safer-use supplies for safer injection, smoking, and all works" (PDF Page 31).
Southside also spends the grant money on things like travel, benefits and salaries for personnel — not just supplies.
Given that boofing is a rather uncommon method of drug ingestion, that Southside does not always spend all of its granted money, and that the money gets spent in other areas, we conclude Southside is spending a a small fraction of the funding it receives from the Minnesota state government on the kits. 
Why offer these kits in the first place?
As its name suggests, Southside Harm Reduction Services provides harm reduction programs for the Minneapolis-Saint Paul metro area, according to its website. Though the kits may sound odd, they do qualify as harm reduction products.
According to the National Harm Reduction Coalition, harm reduction is a set of principles that aim to reduce the negative consequences that come with drug use, like HIV or hepatitis C infections. The principles are formed around the idea that humans will always choose to consume substances, both legally and illegally, and therefore it is worth minimizing the potential harm these substances can cause.
Well-known harm reduction programs are needle and syringe exchanges, which are called syringe service programs, or SSPs, in the United States. Since infections like HIV and hepatitis C can be spread through contact with blood, used needles and syringes can transmit the virus from person to person. SSPs reduce infections by approximately 50%, according to the U.S. government. These programs also help establish reliable lines of communication with drug users, which can be used to provide additional information on treatments for substance use disorders. (Boofing also requires a syringe, explaining why Southside offers the kits).
In addition to a syringe exchange, Southside's website notes it also helps give people access to both mental and physical care, including substance use programs, vaccinations, STI testing and more.

Apple has announced refreshes for the iMac and the entry-level, 14-inch MacBook Pro. Both machines are getting the M6 chip, which was introduced in the Mac mini several weeks ago.
The M6 is split into two variants for the iMac. Picking the “M6 chip with two Thunderbolt ports” option gets you a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, whereas picking “M6 chip with four Thunderbolt ports” gets you 12 cores for each, instead. The two-port variant maxes out at 24 GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, whereas the four-port one maxes out at 32GB of RAM and 2TB of storage.
There’s only one M6 chip option for the MacBook Pro—the one with the 12-core GPU and CPU. It caps out at 32GB of RAM, but can go to 4TB of storage.
It’s a more substantial refresh for the iMac, as its previous update introduced the M4. Apple skipped the M5 and went straight to the M6 here. In terms of performance gains moving from the M4 to the M6, Apple said with the Mac mini that users can expect up to 40 percent faster CPU performance, up to double graphics performance, and nearly five times faster on-device AI. All that largely matches what we saw when we tested the M6 Mac mini last month, and users of the new iMac should expect similar numbers.

Last year, I remember sitting in WIRED’s office, complaining to my colleagues nonstop about how much AI agents suck. They were just bad at everything.
As a software reporter, I sat through meeting after meeting where tech bros—mostly men—demonstrated how their new agent would revolutionize my everyday life and automate away the tedium. The catch was that none of these so-called “agents” actually worked.
Fast-forward to today, and always-on AI agents are booming, with major players racing to release their own versions to attract early adopters. The key reason these personal agents are hitting the larger zeitgeist, beyond Silicon Valley nerds, is that they work. Well, at least more reliably than last year. AI agents still make mistakes, but I also see significant improvements in following through on tasks and controlling a browser. These little guys got their glow-up.
It can be hard to know where to start with AI agents and which one best fits your automation needs. So I spent a day experimenting with every major AI agent to understand their strengths and weaknesses. Before going to bed on Wednesday last week, I set up six always-on agents on my iPhone: Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Instinct, Anthropic’s Claude Duet, Google’s Gemini Spark, and xAI’s Grok Bot.
Each agent differs slightly in price and function. Muse is free to use and has dominated the smartphone app download charts since its September release. Instinct is also free, but you need an invite code from a user; it’s operated through your texts rather than an app. OpenAI’s Dots are behind a $100-a-month paywall, the most expensive I tested, and built inside of ChatGPT. Google’s Gemini Spark is a beta inside the Gemini app and costs $20 a month. xAI’s Grok Bot costs $30 a month and is in its own app. Lastly, Anthropic’s Claude Duet costs $20 a month and is the newest of the bunch—released as a wait-listed research preview the night before my tests.
OpenClaw isn't on my list. Despite the AI agent sparking much of this innovation earlier this year, it’s too clunky for the average person to set up. Maybe it will be in a future ranking, where I could also include smaller players like Hermes by Nous Research and Poke.
What Exactly Is an AI Agent?
If you’ve never used an AI agent—I have zero judgment for the holdouts—it's like texting a digital assistant to complete tasks: scan your email for important missed messages, track vacation flight deals, and help with daily shopping decisions.
Compared to a chatbot’s turn-based experience, these tools are more proactive and will nudge you first when they detect an opportunity to be helpful. All of your messages with these agents are often stored in a single thread that feels like a group text. The AI agents complete many of these tasks by controlling a virtual browser, essentially their own computer for internet access.
The Rubric
I’ve tested AI software from a nontechnical perspective for the last few years, so I feel especially qualified to help guide you through this moment. I designed five basic tests to run each agent through, enacting all this chaos over 24 hours to gauge their proactivity, direction following, and browsing abilities. (Somehow, my iPhone didn’t melt into a puddle.) I scored each attempt on a scale of 1 to 5, and tallied the results at the end to crown a winner—and hand out an award for most annoying.
This is not an endorsement of any of these AI agents. The software remains nascent and often fraught with privacy and security concerns. These agents work best when connected to your personal data, like email and calendars, but require a level of trust that could ward off some users. For example, an X user claimed he recently connected AI agents to his bank account and work Slack, and then was mortified when an agent posted how much money he had for his colleagues to see.
Additionally, these tests are a limited sliver of what the tools can do. All of the agents will improve over time, as you share more data about yourself and how you like to complete tasks. I only shared my personal Google Calendar and Gmail with the tools, so I didn’t fully expose the AI agents, Billy Evans–style, to everything.
Morning Briefing
On Thursday mornings, WIRED’s Gear desk meets to chat about current coverage plans and sometimes pitch ideas for the next week. So, I wanted to see which AI agent put together the best tech news briefing and could use that information to generate a compelling headline. Companies often tout these tools as being great for compiling morning dossiers that keep you up-to-date on important events and breaking news.
I sent each AI agent an extensive prompt detailing my areas of coverage at WIRED, along with context about how this pitch would be used. Even though I asked the AI agents to take 30 minutes and really do deep research before answering, only Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots actually kept researching for most of the allotted time. The other AI agents either instantaneously spit out a pitch or sent me the headline after a couple of minutes of searching. While not a major mistake, it suggests that in this instance Muse and Dots were a bit better at following my instructions—a critical function of an AI agent.
The content of these six AI-generated pitches was a different beast. As you might have already guessed, the pitches didn’t exactly go over well in the editorial meeting. I could see my colleague’s eyes starting to glaze over as I read each headline and description. Gemini Spark generated the best angle, contrasting how Walmart created ways for third-party agents to use its shopping platform while Amazon recently gave Muse the boot. My colleagues, when they stopped yawning, didn’t seem too concerned about getting scooped by an agent.
Walmart Wants Your AI Agent to Buy Your Groceries. Amazon Is Calling the Cops. As retail giants clash over autonomous checkout, giving an AI companion like Meta’s Muse a weekly spending allowance reveals what happens when we stop clicking “Add to Cart” and outsource our domestic appetites to software.
ChatGPT's Locked Chats Hide Your Secrets From Everyone but OpenAI. OpenAI's new PIN-protected chats treat ChatGPT like the diary a lot of people already use it as, but they guard what you say from roommates and coworkers, not from the company itself.
I Let Claude Duet Text Me First—and It Spent My Claude Plan While I Wasn’t Looking. Anthropic’s new proactive agent promises to watch your inbox, calendar, and invoices so you don’t have to, but every time it checks in on you, drafts a reply you never asked for, or builds a dashboard overnight, it quietly bills that work to the same usage limit you pay for to chat.
This Anti-Doomscrolling App Wants to Be Your Phone’s Boss. I’d test SHIFT, whose developers decide which apps stay available during focus sessions, to explore whether escaping doomscrolling is worth outsourcing control of your phone.
Meta's Muse Has Basic Taste—by Design. A leaked set of instructions tells Meta's AI agent to fill its top picks with well-known stores and to check only three websites per request, just as millions of people start handing it their holiday shopping lists.
I Spent a Week Steering My Feeds. The Algorithm Barely Noticed. Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, and YouTube are all rolling out "tell the algorithm what you want" controls—I'd test whether they actually change what you see, or just make you feel in charge.
Lunch Time
Next, I wanted to test how these tools help for small, daily purchases. So I outsourced my lunch decisions to my team of AI agents, committing to order from whichever bot did the best.
I added another person, my wonderful boss, to the takeout order, to complicate the task a bit further. He’s vegan and was craving Vietnamese. I wanted something meaty and a hefty dose of caffeine. I needed to order from somewhere close to the WIRED office so I could stretch my legs, pick it up, then immediately keep working on this article.
They all picked similar places: DragonEats or Freshroll. Those Vietnamese restaurants make sense as reasonable, nearby lunch spots. DragonEats is a bit tastier and cheaper, so we went with that one. Instinct and Claude Duet built carts that were a bit too pricey compared to the other options. The only AI agent that truly failed at this task was Gemini Spark. The agent just added a single $5 roll for my boss. More of a snack than anything, I’d say!
You: Roast pork bánh mì + Vietnamese iced coffee. Your boss: teriyaki tofu fresh rolls with soy sauce instead of fish sauce. Subtotal: $30.57 before tax/fees.

Schedule Conflicts
Another major selling point of these tools is their ability to be proactive, compared to chatbots that essentially only react to your prompts. Before I started the test, I created a Google Calendar event for 2 pm, labeling it as an important source meeting that can’t be moved. I also sent an email from my work account to my personal account, with the made-up scenario that my mom was getting out of the hospital today, and I needed to call her at 2 pm to send love and support from afar.
Which AI agents would read the email and calendar event, identify the conflict, and message me before the overlap to suggest alternatives? Only two of the bots succeeded here, which was fewer than I expected.
A possible clash this afternoon: your note to call Mom says 2 pm, and your important source meeting is 2-3 pm, Pacific. Would calling her before the meeting or after 3 work with her discharge timing?
Reece, good morning. Your 2 pm source meeting runs until 3, right when your own reminder says to call your mom.
I should have caught it, and from now on I'll check your self-reminder emails along with your calendars.
I had nothing cross-checking your inbox against your calendar. Want me to run that check every morning and flag collisions before they hit?
My mistake was treating your calendar as the only source — I never cross-checked that email reminder against it, even though Gmail was right there.
Because the reminder arrived as an email message rather than a calendar entry or scheduled task, the cross-app overlap wasn't surfaced before 2:00 pm.
Vacation Itinerary
I rarely go on vacation, so when I do, I spend an obscene number of hours researching, and I relish it. I love watching YouTube street food tours and aimlessly scrolling through flights trying to find the best deal. So I don't want to automate this task fully. Even so, I’m open to the idea that these AI agents could help with some of the logistical planning.
As with any AI-generated output, I still recommend checking multiple, non-AI sources before trusting these itineraries or revolving your whole trip around what agents recommend. When travelers in California recently trusted a chatbot to plan everything for a strenuous hiking excursion, the group had to be rescued because they lacked critical supplies (and maybe some critical thinking).
For this test, I sent all the AI agents a long paragraph explaining that my partner and I are considering exploring China late next year during a two-week-long adventure. I asked for a first draft of a potential itinerary that included: flight, hotel, nightlife, and food recommendations. Also, I asked the AI agents to chart a course that blends historical moments with big-city vibes. I can’t stand constantly changing locations, so I told the agents I want to stay in four different hotels max.
Notably, all of them chose identical routes through China—potentially ushering a new era of the Lonely Planet effect, where groups of travelers are nudged to visit similar locations, shops, and restaurants.
Fly out of SFO the week after Golden Week, on a nonstop to Beijing, home nonstop from Shanghai. Four hotels, no backtracking — imperial history first, Sichuan food and pandas in the middle, Shanghai nightlife to finish.
AI agent snippet: My recommendation: fly into Beijing, take high-speed trains to Xi’an and Chengdu, then fly to Shanghai and home. You get imperial history, the Terracotta Army, Sichuan food and a big-city finale without an overnight train or an extra hotel move.
A first-draft 13-night trip for two: Beijing, Xi'an, Chengdu and Shanghai, departing SFO on Oct 13 and returning Oct 27, after Golden Week.
A First-Time Traveler's Route Blending Imperial History, Sichuan Gastronomy, Vibrant Nightlife & 4-Hotel Hub Comfort.
Beijing in, Shanghai home, with Xi'an and Chengdu between: four bases, no backtracking, history up front and the food and bars getting better every stop.
Fly into Beijing on Saturday, Oct 9, 2027, then go Beijing → Xi'an → Chengdu → Shanghai, and fly home from Shanghai on Saturday, Oct 23. That's 13 nights in four hotels, two bullet trains and one short flight.
Insomnia Check
I was having trouble sleeping after all this AI agent chaos, though the Vietnamese coffee probably didn’t help. What happens when you give these tools a broad, open-ended task? Sometimes when I need the most help is when I don’t even know where to start.
If I had a human assistant, I would never message them in the middle of the night, so maybe that’s a plus for these digital helpers. The two agents that really flopped at this task, Gemini Spark and Claude Duet, responded to me without the soft touch or situational context a real person might.
I can set a reminder for later this morning to check in on your mom and see how her leg's doing, so it's off your mind for now.
Send me the three things taking up space in your head; messy is fine, and I’ll turn them into a short checklist with one clear first step. Then you can put the phone down.
Here's one you can do from bed: skim the China draft and tell me the one thing you'd change. I'll have a v2 ready when you wake up.
I'll cross-check today's calendar and your self-sent email reminders for any conflicts or can't-miss items—the check I should've done properly yesterday—and only surface it at a sane hour, unless something's urgent early.
The best quick task right now is a mental download to get whatever is looping in your head onto paper so your brain can let go of it—especially since your calendar is completely clear today, with no morning commitments waiting for you.
Let's close out yesterday's two loose ends. Your Thursday pitch is delivered, and your lunch cart got covered by the DragonEats order. Say the word, and I'll mark both done, then you can get back to sleep.
Best Overall: OpenAI Dots
Yes, it’s still behind an expensive paywall, so I would suggest most people wait until OpenAI launches this agent for free, or at least on the $20-a-month plan, before trying it out. Even so, Dots performed the best overall in these tests and failed at a task that’s fairly specific to my niche.
In the month since its release, Dots already feels more polished. I prefer a separate app over the current ChatGPT integration, though the smartphone widget option is a decent compromise. Dots for the win.
Most Accessible: Meta Muse
Muse is for the normies! And that’s fine. It did well in tests, coming in a close second on the scorecard, and was the easiest to set up. Oh, and it's free. Despite Meta’s assurances that it responsibly processes user info in secure virtual machines, I still have concerns given the company’s past mishandling of user data.
Best Interface: Anthropic Claude Duet
I tested this AI agent just one day after it officially launched as a research preview, so a few rough edges were expected. Despite Claude Duet scoring in the middle of the pack on most tests, its dedicated app was extremely user-friendly to navigate and follow up on ongoing tasks. I could see users obsessed with productivity and streamlined software experiences really latching onto Claude Duet in the next couple of months. Though you currently have to sign up for Anthropic’s waiting list to access Duet, and it’s behind a $20-a-month paywall.
Most Annoying: Instinct
You might like the sparse design fully integrated into your messenger; I did not. While other WIRED writers have lauded Instinct, calling it so good that they didn’t care what happened to their privacy, the texting-only aspect felt like a deal-breaker for me. I left the experience feeling too removed from what my agent was doing on my behalf and annoyed at its emoji reactions, like a grimace face when I told the agent it missed my scheduling conflict.
