A Delaware proposal to let companies be operated by AI agents would help the firms’ human owners evade legal responsibility for reckless and harmful actions taken by the AI, US Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) told Delaware Governor Matt Meyer in a letter yesterday.
Comer, chairman of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, told Meyer that the committee “seeks assistance obtaining documents related to your state administration’s efforts to establish a new form of corporate entity to be known as an Artificial Intelligence Company (AIC).”
Comer said the proposal is ripe for abuse. “We are concerned that Delaware’s AIC proposal could be used to protect powerful AI companies and their investors from responsibility for reckless harmful actions, while also protecting non-transparent forces seeking anticompetitive regulatory capture behind state AI initiatives,” Comer’s letter said.
Comer suggested he may propose a federal law that would limit states’ regulatory authority. He said the committee’s probe of Delaware’s plan would “inform possible federal legislative efforts including proposals to appropriately limit state AI regulatory initiatives.” Citing the Oversight Committee’s “jurisdiction to study intergovernmental relationships including those of states,” Comer asked for documents related to development of the proposal and potential AI safety risks.
AI-run companies could operate in just about any industry except banking. “An AIC may have any lawful purpose, regardless of whether for profit, except for the business of banking,” according to a draft bill that may be submitted to the Delaware state legislature.
The draft bill says AI agents could be “designated to manage the business and affairs, and to conduct the business, of the AIC.” The bill proposes a “regulatory sandbox” that would exist for 30 months to test the idea. Allowing AI-run companies would bring more revenue via taxes and fees to Delaware, which is already a top destination for business entities of all sizes.
“The answer is to wrap AI in legal form”
In July 2026, Delaware’s Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez co-wrote an op-ed in Fortune announcing the proposal. The op-ed said that “nothing in the law of several states clearly prevents an AI agent from operating a company with no human at the helm,” and that states should develop legal frameworks for autonomous software that is able to contract, pay suppliers, and make transactions with no human involvement.
“The answer is not to try to prohibit the activity; any effort to do so is just as unlikely to succeed as the technology and its enablers are likely to push the boundaries of the law,” the op-ed said. “The answer is to wrap AI in legal form. Give an autonomous system a recognizable legal identity and you make it legible to law. You create a deﬁned target to which responsibility and damages can attach. You make the agent’s conduct visible, traceable, and accountable.”
The op-ed explained how an AI-run company will shield humans from legal liabilities:
A Delaware AIC will be a separate legal entity whose day-to-day aﬀairs are managed by an AI agent rather than a person. At the agent’s direction, the AIC can sue and be sued in its own name, hold and dispose of property, and incur obligations. It has a single member, a person or an entity, responsible for keeping the AIC adequately capitalized, and the AIC must keep a log of its activities. That member is shielded from the AIC’s debts, except where it fails to capitalize the company or uses it to commit fraud or a willful violation of law.
Under the proposed law, the “member” is an individual or a corporation that would fund the AI-run company and benefit from any profits, but designate an AI agent to manage the actual business. The draft bill says, “The member is not liable for any act or omission that the AIC takes or fails to take, or that another person takes or fails to take at the direction of the AIC.” There are exceptions for when a person uses the AI-run company “to engage in fraud or any willful violation of law,” or “caused or allowed the AIC to conduct business when the member knew or should have known the conduct was outside the AIC’s statement of purpose.”
Citing Patibanda-Sanchez’s announcement, Comer wrote that an AI-run company would provide “the human or entity capitalizing the AIC with liability protections from potential harms to business partners, consumers, and the public, perpetrated by the controlling AI.”
A spokesperson for Gov. Meyer told Ars today that “we have received the letter and are in the process of reviewing it.” A spokesperson for Patibanda-Sanchez declined to comment, saying that the governor’s office is handling press requests on the matter.
Patibanda-Sanchez’s op-ed said Delaware’s planned regulatory sandbox will “pilot agentic commerce in daylight, under supervision, with capital tied to liability and the ability to shut a system down.” The 30-month testing period would give the state legislature “a full record for deciding how to legislate” AI-run companies, it said.
Delaware home to most Fortune 500 companies
A future state law allowing AI-operated companies would be especially impactful in Delaware, as about two-thirds of Fortune 500 companies are incorporated in the state. Although Elon Musk now prefers Texas, many corporations choose Delaware for its low corporate taxes and business-friendly legal framework. Patibanda-Sanchez boasts that Delaware provides “the most predictable and business-focused legal home in the world,” and that 334,461 new entities were formed in Delaware in 2025.
Patibanda-Sanchez collaborated on the sandbox plan with a private company that says it makes legal AI agents for businesses. “The framework for industry engagement with AICs is being developed in Delaware as part of a public-private partnership led by Norm Ai,” said the op-ed co-written by Patibanda-Sanchez and Norm Ai founder and CEO John Nay.
Meyer, a Democrat, publicly supported the idea of letting AI agents incorporate in a response to an April 2026 social media post by Mark Cuban. Cuban wrote, “If I was the governor of a state looking to grow their revenues, I would add the ability for anyone to incorporate using an AI agent and stablecoins. And charge a premium for the service. Post the agent in the marketplace/connectors that the big LLMs have, to simplify it for everyone. First to market makes a killing.”
Meyer’s official X account replied, “On it!” and posted a link to Meyer’s July 2025 announcement of the plan for an AI sandbox in which “artificial intelligence technologies can be safely developed and deployed across high-impact sectors, including corporate governance, biotechnology, healthcare, chemicals, and financial services.”
In July 2025, Meyer signed a legislative resolution “to create a regulatory sandbox framework for the testing of innovative and novel technologies that utilize agentic artificial intelligence.” This resulted in the Delaware Artificial Intelligence Commission forming a Sandbox Subcommittee to work on a “draft regulatory framework that would create a regulatory sandbox that would test and evaluate agentic artificial intelligence and its application to corporate governance,” the commission said in its December 2025 annual report.
The commission said the Sandbox Subcommittee was working on “potential draft legislation,” and had received a briefing from Patibanda-Sanchez “on the work of a group she has formed to investigate a potential structure for a regulatory sandbox.”
AI-run firms can do “anything that a company can do”
In June 2026, the draft legislation was detailed in a Spotlight Delaware article that said the bill is likely to be introduced in the state legislature next year. The article said:
The principal drafter of the proposed legislation, John Mark Zeberkiewicz, said the measure could allow AI agents to engage in just about any business activity—from providing coding services to signing contracts, or even filing and defending lawsuits.
He also noted that it seeks to protect owners of new Artificial Intelligence Companies from facing legal liability from actions the AI might take. “Anything that a company can do, the AIC can do as a company,” said Zeberkiewicz, a corporate attorney at Wilmington’s Richards Layton and Finger.
Patibanda-Sanchez said at a Delaware AI Commission meeting in June 2026 that the state would benefit from fees paid to form the new type of AI-run companies, according to the Spotlight Delaware article. “Should a new entity form be created out of it, that’s really a huge benefit to our state’s revenues,” Patibanda-Sanchez was quoted as saying.
UC Berkeley law professor Andrew Baker told the Financial Times that the Delaware proposal seems likely “to be an overly generous liability shield, which seems unwarranted without some underlying policy rationale that hasn’t been developed or justified well.”
Martin Petrin, a law professor at York University in Toronto, told Bloomberg that “other states will likely move ahead with similar proposals to compete in this area. If they are serious about this, a federal framework could help address concerns about safety and a regulatory race to the bottom.”
Jon is a Senior IT Reporter for Ars Technica. He covers the telecom industry, Federal Communications Commission rulemakings, broadband consumer affairs, court cases, and government regulation of the tech industry.

New Delhi, Oct 28: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Wednesday held talks with US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to take stock of India-US defence ties and explore ways to advance them further.
The meeting took place in Cebu, Philippines, on the margins of a multilateral conclave.
Singh and Hegseth are in Cebu to attend a meeting of ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting Plus (ADMM-Plus) grouping.
ADMM-Plus is a platform comprising 11-nation ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) and its eight dialogue partners: India, China, Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Republic of Korea, Russia and the United States.
Ways to further shore up bilateral defence ties were expected to be the main focus of the Singh-Hegseth talks.

Stenzin Tankyong’s debut feature “Kakthet” (Idiot), set in the remote high-altitude region of Ladakh, has been selected as the winner of the inaugural INR40 lakh ($42,000) feature film co-production fund run by Humans of Cinema and Safarnaama Pictures.
The Ladakhi-language project was selected from nearly 400 entries after an extensive screening and evaluation process.
The film follows the precarious future of a government school and the community around it – both dependent on one reluctant grade 10 student who has never passed an exam, and whose teachers must attempt the impossible: save the school by saving the one student determined not to be saved.
Tankyong has spent eight years making films that bring Ladakh’s stories, landscapes and culture to international audiences. His short films “Sekool” (2019) and “Last Days of Summer” (2023) have screened at festivals including the International Film Festival Rotterdam, the Clermont-Ferrand International Short Film Festival and the Dharamshala International Film Festival.
“Kakthet” is produced by Ritu Sarin and Rajesh Thanickan, alongside French co-producers La Belle Affaire Productions. A filmmaker and producer whose career spans more than 30 years, Sarin co-founded both White Crane Films and the Dharamshala International Film Festival. Thanickan’s credits include Neeraj Ghaywan’s “Homebound,” executive produced by Martin Scorsese and premiered at Cannes in 2025; “Santosh,” which premiered at Cannes in 2024; and “Our Share of Sand,” which premiered at the 2026 Venice International Film Festival’s International Critics’ Week, where it won the Audience Award.
The project had already attracted international industry attention before the fund selection, winning the Co-Production Features Grant at WAVES Film Bazaar in 2025 and being chosen as one of 30 projects for the 2026 Asian Project Market, held alongside the Busan International Film Festival.
The fund was launched by Humans of Cinema founder Harshit Bansal and Safarnaama Pictures founder Nazim Momin, a U.S.-based engineer and producer. Filmmakers Vishal Bhardwaj and Shaunak Sen are attached as mentors, with Sen also serving as executive producer of the winning project. The jury comprised actor Imran Khan, filmmaker Arati Kadav, “All That Breathes” producer Aman Mann and festival director Aseem Chhabra.
“The past few months working on this fund have been both unbelievably challenging and incredibly rewarding. We were pleasantly surprised by the sheer number of brilliant projects we received from across the country, and we’re even more convinced how desperately initiatives like these are needed in South Asia right now. It was definitely a testing process, but we couldn’t be happier with the result. Stenzin is an exciting new filmmaker with a distinct voice, and we’re excited to be an ally in his journey of making his debut feature,” Bansal said.
“Stories like ‘Kakthet’ remind us why it is important to create opportunities for voices that emerge from outside the mainstream. I’m glad to be associated with this initiative and look forward to seeing Stenzin Tankyong bring his vision to life,” Bhardwaj said.
“The ‘Kakthet’ script mobilizes lightness, absurdity and humor to tell the story of a slow lamentation underwriting several lives in Ladakh. The story of Singay and the motley group of students and teachers always stays curious and sensitive, while never lapsing into judgement. I look forward to supporting the team in realising this project,” Sen said.
“I want to congratulate the Humans of Cinema and Safarnaama team who have worked tirelessly to create this fund. I was amazed at the passion, rigour and love they’ve put in selecting the winner. I want to congratulate the winning film and above all, I want to applaud all the filmmakers who applied. So many stories represented fearlessness and fierceness, and I was really inspired by them,” Kadav said.
“I’m delighted that ‘Kakthet’ has been selected for the inaugural HoC x Safarnaama Pictures Co-Production Fund. For independent filmmakers in India, finding support for stories rooted in our own regions, languages and lived experiences can be challenging. The fact that this support comes from within our own country makes this recognition especially meaningful for us. For a film in Ladakhi, grounded in the culture and realities of Ladakh, this support offers real encouragement to tell a story that might otherwise struggle to reach the screen and a wider audience. Initiatives like this create valuable opportunities for newer voices in independent cinema, bringing the diverse cultures and experiences of our country to wider audiences. I’m glad Kakthet (Idiot) is part of this first edition, and I thank HoC, Safarnaama Pictures, the jury and mentors for helping us take the film forward,” Tankyong said.
The screenplay is in its fourth draft. In July 2026, the team completed a three-week recce across the Changthang region and Leh for location scouting, production planning and the capture of visual and sonic material for a proof-of-concept teaser. Principal cast, crew and shooting locations are now in place, with the team focused on securing additional financing and establishing co-production relationships across Asia, Australia and Europe.

Waking early, I put a small jar of my sauerkraut into my messenger bag, hop on my bicycle, ride to Seattle's King Street Station, and board a train heading to the Portland Fermentation Festival, the yearly gathering affectionately nicknamed “Stinkfest.”
Usually the sheer existence of a festival like this is enough to get people revved up to come together and talk about their favorite ferments, but in an interesting twist, fermented foods are enjoying a popularity boost from a different crowd. The MAHA movement, and particularly the Donald Trump cabinet, are big into fermented food, eating meat, usually steak, with fermented sides like kimchi or sauerkraut at every meal.
I've come to Portland, Oregon, wondering if there was going to be any overlap in the Venn diagram between festival attendees and the MAHA steak-and-ferment crowd. I mentioned this to my cousin-in-law Erick, who's been part of the Portland food scene for years, and he laughed out loud.
“It'll be more like a Venn dumbbell,” he said, making a pair of thumb-and-forefinger circles and tracing a line in the air between them. “No overlap, but food will be the bridge.”
Still, I was curious. I’d check.
The festival is almost exactly what the fermentation-friendly might hope to find. Right inside the main door next to the check-in desk is a bacterial petting zoo—a common thing at this sort of event—and a table where attendees can drop off their own ferments to share. Further on, lining every wall of the main room, are exhibitors who have paid a grand total of 25 bucks for a table, handing out free samples of fermented foods.
The space quickly fills up–several hundred people flow through over the course of the evening–and it appears that there's both a line in front of each exhibitor and perhaps a more organic continuous line with people flowing clockwise from one exhibitor to the next. People are notably excited and happy. There's a kid walking around with a tray of handmade pickle pins he's giving people to wear and there's a collective gasp when 20 or 30 minutes in, Dillon T. Pickle, the mascot of the Portland Pickles West Coast League baseball team, walks into the room. At one point, a big baby crawls across most of the main floor, unhindered and happy.
In the middle of it all is festival co-organizer, journalist, and cookbook author Liz Crain. She explains that the Fest, now in its 14th installment, was started in 2009 by friends who love to ferment. There were members of a little company called Pickleopolis and a club called The Kraut Collective, and, with some help from author and fermentation rockstar Sandor Katz, they launched a Portland tradition.
When I ask how the festival has evolved since its first year, she gets a little philosophical.
“Cheap. Portland. Weird. People get excited,” she says in a tone where several punctuation options would be in the spirit of the festival. “People lined up on the sidewalk all the way around the building for the first one. I poured hard cider that I made from a tree in my backyard.”
“There's nothing for sale, and that gives it a potluck-y party style. Most big festivals have consumers and purveyors, but without those distinctions here, it makes conversations a bit deeper, a bit more personal,” she says. “There's no gatekeeping, no secret recipes. It's always been wacky and fun.”
She isn't sure how much MAHA crossover I'll encounter, but she has an openness to it.
“RFK is certainly infatuated with sauerkraut and steak. There's some good to be found in the overall MAHA tenets, but so much of it has been muddied by the anti-vax stance and ludicrous conspiracy theories,” she says, though she believes it's important to “look closely and critically at pesticides and favor less-processed foods.”
“But a diet that's based solely on meat, particularly beef, animal fats, and sauerkraut … well that's not a very diverse diet,” she says. “Let's just say I wouldn't want to sit next to that person on a plane or be stuck in an elevator with them.”
I pick up on these ideas with Chris Curtin, a fermentation microbiology researcher at Oregon State University.
“Historically, everything has shown that narrowing the scope of your diet misses some things. They don't turn out to be the best in the long run,” he says. An Australian living in the US for the last decade, he can clearly see the way trends are moving and notes that registered dietitians have consistently put fermented foods at the top of their superfood lists for the past decade.
Curtin describes his work as caring about what happens when we mess around with microbes to see what happens to the raw material. As he puts it, "I'm interested in tinkering if it involves microbe wrangling." He also gets the festival's popularity among those who ferment.
“Fermenting is such a readily accessible scientific experiment that you can do in your kitchen. People go, find foods they like and want to make in their own kitchens. It's accessible and tactile.”
This plays out at the festival as I begin to sample the merchandise. The first thing I taste is an “orange whey Julius” that includes whey and OJ and is pleasingly reminiscent of the Orange Julius I'd get as a treat as a kid at the Mall of New Hampshire.
Next to that is Nat West's booth with Peruvian corn beer called chicha. West has run a cider company, dabbled in politics, driven a TriMet city bus in Portland, and now runs the Vancouver, Washington, farmers’ market. In a chicha, the fermentation starts by the brewer chewing ground field corn. At the festival, attendees are drinking what West has chewed. As people in line joke about drinking this guy's spit, or at least the byproducts of it, West interjects, “nobody's died yet!”
“The ptyalin enzymes in the saliva kickstart the starch-to-sugar process,” he explains as I take a sip and gaze longingly at the draft beer in the hands of someone who's wandered into the show from the Hotlips pizza next door.
Further along, Portland's Jorinji Miso has a double booth with samples of miso soup with bonito flakes along with koji (rice fermented with Aspergillus oryzae spores) and amazake, a koji-based drink.
The couple who run Maypop Wine Co. have their hands full at the Fest. The company’s cofounder Vince Kelsea explains that they make “anything but pinot” in the Willamette Valley—a lush north-south valley in Oregon renowned for its pinot noir. Making unfiltered, low-intervention wines like Maypop in a region famous for its pinot sounds like they're making things hard for themselves, but the attendees maintain a several-deep line at the booth all night long.
In one corner is Kiyomi Hasagewa, a third-generation Japanese bean purveyor. She’s sharing tastes of a 15-year-old miso she dehydrated and ground so she could bring it from Hokkaido to the festival. She sprinkles it over the rice and tops it with a wedge of sun-dried daikon which her elderly mother fermented in a mashed pumpkin paste. It is easily the most interesting bite in the room.
Back in the entry hall are my personal favorites, the ferments that attendees have brought to share. Liz Crain has brought along plum and dandelion wines, pickle brine, a blackberry-blueberry-lemon water kefir, and a monster jar of sour dills. I note with pride that the jar of sauerkraut I brought is next to Liz’s pickles, near-empty. Nearby is another giant jar of “fermented carrot coins, cherry bomb, garlic, ginger, horseradish,” which I anticipate as a pleasant assault on my senses, but it's really just pleasant. A garlic blast for sure, but one with all of the harsh edges smoothed by time and beneficial bacteria into something lovely.
Also at the community table are Portland occupational therapist Eva Ortega and her fermentation buddy Letti Kittel who drove down from Seattle.
“I've only made unsuccessful ferments so far,” says Ortega, undeterred. “I'm here to learn.”
Kittel says she's been nerding out on fermenting for about a year and has brought a kombucha starter with its bacteria-and-yeast scoby for others to bring home and try. And while both of them have no comment about the MAHA connection, Ortega puts some of Kittel's starter in a little jar and drops it into her purse.
I'm expecting another round of “no comment” when the MAHA diet comes up with three other fermenting friends, Megan Andricos, Josh Monifi, and Desiré Demarest, but Andricos, aka DJ Sappho, followed a similar diet 20 years ago in what they call their “fermented-pickled food and protein phase,” which consisted of “mostly kimchi and meat.”
They're off that diet now, but they liked being on it. “Kimchi evens out my gut biome. I felt better. Not superhuman, but better.”
Also on the community table is something called “Higgins Kraut,” made with Napa cabbage, carrots, garlic, and ginger, which, with a lovely melding of flavors, won my personal Best-in-Show award.
Turns out it's made by one of the show’s other founders, George Winborn, who was involved for the first 10 years. He'd been farming in Dallas when he moved to Portland, to a place that had no yard and nowhere to farm.
“Doing the Fest helped scratch the itch,” he says. He's now getting Wellspring Farm in Gresham, Oregon, off the ground and noted how the festival has become a bit more commercial, a bit less homemade. But all that's relative, considering we're standing here over our jars of sauerkraut, and the exhibitors are very small businesses, if they're businesses at all.
“I still love the DIY and starter tables,” he says. “It reminds you that everyone can do this.”

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

The first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine in the outbreak gripping the Democratic Republic of Congo began Friday (October 23, 2026), the head of the World Health Organisation said.
Also Read: Congo’s Ebola outbreak records more than 4,000 deaths
The DR Congo's worst-ever Ebola outbreak has passed the 9,700-case mark, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,600.
Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the epidemic.
Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will be put through a full-scale human trial in the DRC to see if it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo.
The trial began with the first shot of Ervebo being administered in Bunia, the capital of the DRC's northeastern Ituri province, which is the epicentre of the outbreak.
"Science gives us hope. Today, in Bunia DRC, the first participants were vaccinated in a new Ebola vaccine trial called Tumaini, which means 'hope' in Swahili," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on X.
"This trial will help us understand whether any of the vaccine candidates designed for Bundibugyo virus work," he said, adding that in the meantime, the existing Ervebo vaccine would be tested.
"WHO is supporting this DRC-led effort to find answers and save lives."
Two vaccines in the pipeline
The so-called Tumaini trial is a single trial framework that can test the safety, efficacy and immunogenicity of multiple vaccines.
The trial will use a ring vaccination approach: immunising contacts deemed to be at high risk of infection.
It is gearing up to incorporate two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which are currently advancing through earlier-stage, smaller-scale clinical trials.
One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab being developed by the University of Oxford; the other, by the U.S.-based Moderna group, uses mRNA technology.
Both have received funding from the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, and are expected to enter the trial "shortly", CEPI said in a statement.
"Tumaini will work closely with affected communities, health authorities and outbreak response partners to generate robust evidence on vaccine performance that could contribute to curtailing the epidemic, saving lives, and strengthening preparedness for future Bundibugyo outbreaks," said CEPI.
The trial will include pregnant women and children aged 12 years and older, generating evidence for populations that are often excluded from clinical trials.
'Important step'
WHO emergencies director Chikwe Ihekweazu said the trial was set up to generate the rigorous evidence needed to determine whether the participating vaccines could protect people at risk.
"If successful, this would be the first time we have clear evidence of vaccine efficacy against Bundibugyo virus — a major advance that could transform how we respond to this outbreak and prepare for future outbreaks and help save lives," he said.
Ebola, which spreads through contact with bodily fluids and causes a haemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.
"Bringing this trial into the Ebola response is an important step towards addressing the urgent needs of affected communities," said Steve Ahuka-Mundeke, the DRC Ebola response incident manager.
The DRC declared its 17th outbreak of Ebola on May 15, and the WHO, two days later, triggered a public health emergency of international concern, its second-highest alert level.

Where does Fleetwood beating Arsenal rank in biggest cup upsets?
- Published
Arsenal suffered a shock Carabao Cup exit at the home of Fleetwood Town, as the League Two side recorded one of the biggest upsets in the competition's history.
Mikel Arteta's Premier League champions lost 5-3 on penalties to a Fleetwood outfit ranked 84 places below them in the English football pyramid.
Following Fleetwood's victory, BBC Sport looks at some of the biggest shocks of all-time in the FA Cup and League Cup.
This isn't an exhaustive list, and you can leave your thoughts in the comments, rank the historic upsets and share your results.
Fleetwood 1-1 Arsenal (5-3 on pens, League Cup, 2026)
Fleetwood Town celebrated the biggest victory in the club's history as they stunned Champions League finalists Arsenal to reach the EFL Cup quarter-finals at Highbury Stadium.
The League Two club stunned the visitors when Aaron Loupalo-Bi gave Fleetwood, who sat 19th in English football's fourth tier, a 21st-minute lead.
Viktor Gyokeres pulled Arsenal level after the break - but they could not kick-on and were reduced to 10-men in the 86th minute when teenager Max Dowman kicked out following a challenge by Harrison Neal.
In the shootout, Fleetwood goalkeeper Jay Lynch saved Bruno Guimaraes' spot kick before Conor Haughey scored the winning penalty to spark scenes of ecstasy on the pitch and in the stands.
Grimsby 2-2 Man Utd (12-11 on pens, League Cup, 2025)
An upset as astonishing for its manner as it was for its proportions. Grimsby Town, a League Two side, beat top-flight Manchester United.
Not only did they win, but they were 2-0 up after 30 minutes following goals from Charles Vernam and Tyrell Warren.
The visitors pulled one back through Bryan Mbeumo with 15 minutes to go and United looked like they might squeeze through when Harry Maguire went on to level in the 89th minute.
But an incredible shootout followed, with Clarke Oduor for Grimsby and Matheus Cunha for Manchester United missing the only penalties as each side's 11 took one.
The players then went again and, after Darragh Burns scored to make it 12-11, Mbeumo struck his second spot-kick against the crossbar.
Plymouth 1-0 Liverpool (FA Cup, 2025)
Arne Slot made 10 changes to his Liverpool side after they had won an EFL Cup semi-final in their previous game and the Reds were made to pay.
Eight minutes after the interval, the Pilgrims were awarded a penalty after Harvey Elliott's handball and Ryan Hardie drilled home from the spot in emphatic fashion.
Hardie almost added a second shortly afterwards when his shot was turned on to the post by Liverpool keeper Caoimhin Kelleher.
The bottom club in the Championship held on, with Conor Hazard making crucial late saves, to beat a team who would go on to win the Premier League title.
Chelsea 2-4 Bradford City (FA Cup, 2015)
Bradford ranked 49 places below their opponents as they travelled to Stamford Bridge to take on Chelsea, who at that point were top of the Premier League.
Gary Cahill and Ramires netted to put the hosts 2-0 up and give Chelsea firm control of the fourth-round tie.
Bradford had other ideas, though, as Jon Stead pulled one back before Filipe Morais side-footed in an equaliser.
Andy Halliday then blasted the Bantams ahead before Mark Yeats slotted a fourth to inflict a crushing defeat on Jose Mourinho's side.
Oldham 3-2 Liverpool (FA Cup, 2013)
Premier League giants Liverpool had ample strength at Boundary Park, with the likes of Luis Suarez, Raheem Sterling and Daniel Sturridge all starting.
League One hosts Oldham were in the midst of financial problems but produced a spirited display against the odds, with Matt Smith nodding in a Youssouf M'Changama cross to open the scoring.
Suarez levelled, but Smith soon took advantage of an error from Liverpool goalkeeper Brad Jones before Reece Wabara netted a back-post header to give the Latics a 3-1 lead.
Joe Allen volleyed home to pull one back and Liverpool brought on Steven Gerrard, but it was not enough to avoid defeat.
Bradford City 1-1 Arsenal (3-2 on pens, League Cup, 2012)
A fourth-tier side against Premier League opposition in the quarter-finals of the league cup - Arsenal were clear favourites.
Bradford had already caused an upset in the tournament, beating Wigan on penalties in the round before.
Up for a fight at home to Arsene Wenger's Gunners, Garry Thompson volleyed the Bantams ahead before Thomas Vermaelen headed home a Santi Cazorla cross with just two minutes of normal time remaining.
Just as Mbeumo missed the decisive kick for United against Grimsby after scoring in normal time, the same happened for Vermaelen here as Bradford prevailed 3-2 on spot-kicks.
Liverpool 2-2 Northampton (2-4 on pens, League Cup, 2010)
Another surprise cup exit for Liverpool.
This one happened in the League Cup - at Anfield.
Milan Jovanovic fired in an opener for Liverpool but Billy McKay equalised and Michael Jacobs tapped in to give the Cobblers a lead early in extra time.
David Ngog scored from a late header to set up the penalty drama, but Northampton were the victors from the spot, with Abdul Osman keeping his cool to slot in the decisive spot-kick.
Man Utd 0-3 York City (League Cup, 1995)
Ruben Amorim is not the first Manchester United to suffer a shock in the League Cup - even Sir Alex Ferguson has faced the same.
The United boss didn't take the game lightly and made just four changes from the league game which they had played three days before, with the likes of David Beckham, Lee Sharpe and Ryan Giggs starting.
Paul Barnes, father of Newcastle winger Harvey Barnes, scored twice for Alan Little's visitors, including one from the penalty spot, before Tony Barras headed a third to inflict a crushing defeat at Old Trafford.
United put out another strong team at Bootham Crescent for the return leg two weeks later, with Eric Cantona in their squad, but despite getting two goals from Paul Scholes and another from Terry Cooke, the Minstermen went through 4-3 on aggregate thanks to a strike from Scott Jordan.
Wrexham 2-1 Arsenal (FA Cup, 1992)
Arsenal were reigning Premiership champions and second in the top flight.
Wrexham were 24th in the Third Division.
The Gunners made the trip to Wales as firm favourites and were just 10 minutes from securing a spot in the fourth round after Alan Smith's first-half opener.
But Mickey Thomas sent a 25-yard free kick past David Seaman before Steve Watkin's strike earned victory for Wrexham just two minutes later.
Sutton 2-1 Coventry (FA Cup, 1989)
Sutton United had a memorable cup run in 2016-17, beating three EFL teams - including Leeds United - before losing to Arsenal in the fifth round.
They have also produced one of the biggest shocks of all time.
The non-league side took on a Coventry team who were then in the First Division and had won the FA Cup in 1987.
The part-time side upset the odds at home, with Matthew Hanlan volleying home the winner just before the hour mark.
Hereford 2-1 Newcastle (FA Cup, 1972)
Top-flight Newcastle were beaten in the third round of the FA Cup by non-league opposition when they took on Hereford United in 1972.
Hereford took the tie to a replay after a 2-2 draw at St James' Park, but Newcastle looked destined to make it to the fourth round thanks to a late goal by Malcolm McDonald in the rematch.
However, the non-leaguers had other ideas and Ronnie Radford popped up to score the most famous 30-yard goal in FA Cup history to take the game into extra time.
Substitute Ricky George scored the winner - amid scenes of wild celebration at Edgar Street - as Hereford became the first non-league club to defeat a First Division side since 1949.

Dolores Huerta, influential labor leader, feminist and civil rights icon, dies at 96
Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers union to improve working conditions in the nation's fruit and vegetable fields and coined the phrase "Sí, se puede!" that became a widespread rallying cry, has died. She was 96.
Huerta's family said in a statement through her foundation that she died Wednesday at home.
She kept a busy schedule well into her 90s, marching in protests and speaking in cities across the country about race, poverty, LGBTQ+ and women's rights on behalf of her Bakersfield, California-based foundation.
Huerta's resolve cemented her place in history as one of the nation's most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists. Her three-word Spanish-language slogan — which translates to "Yes, it can be done" — was grounded in the belief that people could affect change.
Her work over the decades earned her a number of accolades, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor. When then-President Barack Obama presented the award in 2012, he praised Huerta as a tenacious leader and joked that he had stolen her slogan for his 2008 campaign.
This year, Huerta sent shockwaves through the Latino community when she revealed that she was sexually abused in the 1960s by the farmworker movement's co-founder, César Chavez, leading to the birth of two children, a secret she kept for 60 years and long after he died.
From the early 1970s on, Huerta's life partner was Richard Chavez, César's brother, and together they had four kids. She also had seven children from two earlier marriages.
Huerta said she had kept silent for so long because she feared that coming forward would compromise her life's work and unravel all the progress made for workers.
When asked during a 2026 interview with the news organization Latino USA about keeping the secret, Huerta said: "It was my personal pain, it was my personal problem and, you know, I think it was worth it because it was my cross to bear. I'll say it that way."
Homegrown activism
Huerta was born Dolores Clara Fernandez in 1930 in Dawson, New Mexico. Her father was a miner and union activist who went on to win a seat in the state Legislature. Her parents divorced when she was 3, and her mother took her and her brothers to California.
Immersed in a melting pot of Mexican, Filipino, African American, Japanese and Chinese working families, Huerta learned from her mother — who owned a restaurant and hotel — about independence, compassion and activism.
Huerta was a young, energetic elementary school teacher in the farm-rich San Joaquin Valley when she decided to answer another calling after growing frustrated by her students' poor living conditions.
"I couldn't stand seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes," she said in a 2017 PBS Independent Lens documentary on her life. "I thought I could do more by organizing farmworkers than by trying to teach their hungry children."
Huerta's early work with a civil rights group in Stockton resulted in her meeting Chavez. The two wanted to focus more on the plight of farmworkers, so in 1962 they started the National Farm Workers Association, which became United Farm Workers of America a few years later. She was a key leader and negotiator for the union for years.
She was among those who joined Filipino grape pickers on the picket line in what became the five-year "Delano Grape Strike." With Chavez, she negotiated collective bargaining agreements and contracts with big growers, winning the first health and benefit plans for farmworkers.
Chavez, who died in 1993, once described her as fearless, committed to the cause and tough when it came to negotiations.
On the campaign trail
She met U.S. Sen. Robert Kennedy of Massachusetts during his visit to Delano in 1968 and became a volunteer on his presidential campaign, registering Mexican Americans in California to vote. Huerta was on stage with Kennedy after he won the California primary and he publicly thanked her moments before he was shot.
The assassination devastated Huerta, but she kept organizing for farmworkers' rights.
Huerta was jailed 22 times for union demonstrating. In 1988, she was seriously injured while protesting Republican presidential candidate George H.W. Bush's opposition to the UFW grape boycott during his visit to San Francisco.
Caught in a crowd, she was struck by a police officer's baton, suffered three broken ribs and a pulverized spleen, and required more than a dozen blood transfusions. She reached a settlement with the city to resolve her claims.
After a long recovery, Huerta shifted focus and hit the road to campaign for women's rights and encourage Latinas to run for office.
She also campaigned for Democratic Presidents Bill Clinton, Obama and Joe Biden. California Gov. Gavin Newsom considered her a close friend.
Fueled by courage
Emilio Huerta, one of Dolores' 13 children, once pointed to his mom's courage during an interview, saying it was one of the most significant drivers of her life's work.
"To dedicate your life to building a dream of a union for farmworkers, to take on agriculture, which to this today is still a powerhouse. ... That took a lot of guts," he had said.
Huerta learned the art of lobbying politicians. She secured financial aid for the unemployed and disability insurance for California farmworkers. She spoke out against toxic pesticides, pushed for amnesty for immigrants in the country illegally and fought federal guest worker programs.
By directing nationwide boycotts of grapes and lettuce in the early 1970s, she helped to create the economic pressure and political climate necessary for California to pass what would be the first state law recognizing farmworkers' right to collective bargaining.
Her work earned her many accolades. She was the first Latina to be inducted into the National Women's Hall of Fame and she's received nine honorary doctorates from U.S. universities.
Schools are named in her honor in California, Texas and Colorado. Her image graces many murals, and streets bear her name, but she didn't always win favor with more liberal activists.
In 2016 when she endorsed Hillary Clinton instead of Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont in the presidential Democratic primary, actor Rosario Dawson — a Sanders supporter who played Huerta in a 2014 movie about César Chavez — said Huerta had become "an instrument of the establishment."
Dawson and Huerta eventually reconciled.
Guitarist Carlos Santana later oversaw a documentary based on Huerta's life after the pair had a late-night conversation about music while in Hawaii. Santana, a Miles Davis fan, discovered Huerta was a huge fan of bebop legend Charlie Parker.
"I even met Charlie Parker. That's my claim to fame," Huerta joked during an interview with The Associated Press when she was 87.
It was her work as a leader within the labor movement that reverberated through the U.S. and beyond, making her name synonymous with civil rights. In the 2025 documentary "Seeds of Change: The Life and Legacy of Dolores Huerta," she recounted her decades-long journey in activism and talked about the inspiration she drew from the women's movement during the 1970s, saying it provided validation that she too could stand on the stage with other labor leaders.
"I hope that my legacy will be one of an organizer that organized to fight injustice," she said in the film. "We want to give our children an inheritance of justice, right, not jewels or property or money because they'll just fight over it. So the main thing to do is to give them this love for justice — and that is the greatest gift I think that any of us can have."

Why Zimbabwe tycoon 'Sir Wicknell' was loved and hated in Africa

Wicknell Chivayo, the Zimbabwean tycoon who died in a helicopter crash along with his wife Lucy Muteke last week, divided opinion in life and continues to do so in death.
He called himself "Sir Wicknell", a nod to the embellishment that epitomised his lifestyle - and a nickname some used for the 45-year-old who packed enough controversy into his short life to last several lifetimes.
He was relentlessly self-documenting, building much of his public persona on social media, where he posed with piles of cash and announced the cars and money he gave to people whom he considered deserving.
Chivayo delighted in displaying his access to heads of state across Africa and showing off his possessions, conducting video tours of his fleet of expensive cars, mainly Rolls-Royces, with vanity plates, watches and a vast collection of designer shoes.
His admirers saw a fabulously wealthy man sharing his good fortune. His detractors recoiled at the ostentatious displays, questioned the origins of his money and his political connections, and saw his lifestyle as a stark illustration of inequality.
But Chivayo remained tone-deaf to such criticism. As his fortunes rose, he became ever more unapologetic about flaunting his wealth in a country where nearly half the population lives below the international poverty line, according to the World Bank.
"He gave to those few on an island of wealth in a sea of poverty," Pedzisai Ruhanya, director of the Zimbabwe Democracy Institute think-tank, told the BBC, explaining how his donations were mainly to influential people.
He dismissed Chivayo's generosity as grandstanding for the ruling Zanu-PF party - an attempt to ensure the support of key politicians and even church leaders.
Nonetheless, there has been an outpouring of grief, especially from recipients of his largesse, and tributes from politicians, religious leaders and business figures.
Among the mourners gathered at the Chivayos' opulent home in the capital, Harare, ahead of their burial on Thursday, was Cleopas Mukungunugwa, a young and prominent Zanu-PF social media influencer and recipient of two luxury cars from Sir Wicknell.
Standing outside the mansion, where a massive poster of the couple is displayed, he told local media that he was devastated by his patron's death, external, explaining how "Sir Wicknell" often dictated what he should write in his posts.
"He was criticised by many on social media and our goal was to bolster his reputation as a philanthropist," he said.
Chivayo dropped out of high school aged 15 because his family could no longer afford the fees after his father died when he was 10.
His first job was as a wages clerk for a bus company. From there, he moved into his first independent hustle - selling mobile phones and dealing in foreign currency, often on the black market at the height of the country's hyperinflation crisis.
In 2005, he was sentenced to five years in prison for money laundering involving 837,000 South African rand (then worth $137,500, £72,000). He served three years at Chikurubi Maximum Prison after two years were suspended.
Details of his career following his release are murky, but he went into the energy business, becoming what one state-run newspaper described as a "tenderpreneur" -making money by getting government contracts.
He headed the firm Intratrek Zimbabwe, which partnered with Chinese electrical giant CHiNT Electric. This was at a time when legislation required all companies in the country to cede economic control to black Zimbabweans, under a policy known as indigenisation.
In 2014, Intratrek was selected to build a 100MW solar power station in the southern town of Gwanda. A contract worth more than $170m was signed the following year. It became one of the biggest controversies of Chivayo's business career.
Zimbabwe Power Company, the state-owned utility that awarded the contract, sought to terminate it when Intratrek failed to deliver, but the courts ultimately ruled that the agreement remained valid.
A parliamentary inquiry later described Intratrek as a "briefcase company" being used as a front to attract investment.
Chivayo acknowledged that Intratrek lacked expertise in solar construction, describing it as the local partner while CHiNT provided the technical muscle.
Intratrek received an advance of more than $5m for the Gwanda solar plant, but it remains unbuilt to this day.
Just weeks before Chivayo's death, Intratrek received a government notice to proceed with the project and was given 24 months to complete it.
As the accusations flew, the businessman just smiled and sweet-talked his way through the maelstrom - even winning over President Emmerson Mnangagwa, who was initially unimpressed by him when he first came to power.
In 2018, Mnangagwa cited Gwanda as a lesson in the dangers of doing business with "fly-by-night briefcase businessmen", adding ominously that "Chikurubi is not full". The state-run Herald newspaper reported that the warning was directed at Chivayo.
Yet within a few years, that relationship transformed into a bromance. In one of several photographs capturing the remarkable informality between them, Chivayo lounges, almost lying, on a sofa beside Mnangagwa, apparently entirely at ease in the president's company.
His access was not confined to Zanu-PF - he also posted photographs with opposition figures, including the late Morgan Tsvangirai and Nelson Chamisa.
But he became a conspicuous presence around Mnangagwa, speaking glowingly of the president and making no secret of his support for Zanu-PF.
He faced allegations over the procurement of materials for the 2023 elections, in which Mnangagwa was voted in for a second term.
Investigations alleged that South African supplier Ren-Form grossly inflated prices and subsequently paid hundreds of millions of rand to a company linked to him. Chivayo denied wrongdoing, and Zimbabwe's anti-corruption commission later said it had found no evidence linking him to procurement fraud. Ren-Form denied any wrongdoing.
In April, he offered the country's 360 legislators $10,000 each, prompting accusations that he wanted to influence an impending vote on a controversial constitutional amendment to extend what would have been Mnangagwa's final five-year term by two years to 2030.
He was forced to withdraw the offer following a backlash and denied it was intended to influence the vote.
When the legislation was signed into law several months later, Zanu-PF posted a video clip of him with the caption, external: "Billionaire Sir Wicknell Chivayo celebrates… singing '2030 Ndeya Emmerson Baba!' while cruising at 51,000 feet aboard his Gulfstream G550".
Access to power became part of Chivayo's social-media persona. In June, Eswatini's King Mswati III granted him citizenship of the southern African kingdom and a diplomatic passport - photographs and videos showed him kneeling before the monarch, external.
He had an impressive camera roll, with snaps of him posing with other African presidents such as Nigeria's Bola Tinubu, external, Tanzania's Samia Suluhu Hassan, external, Malawi's Peter Mutharika, external, Mozambique's Daniel Chapo, external, Zambia's Hakainde Hichilema, external and he was part of the delegation that met South Africa's Cyril Ramaphosa, external when he visited Mnangagwa's farm earlier this year.
Some relationships extended beyond formal meetings. In August, Chivayo and his wife attended the engagement of Kenyan President William Ruto's daughter Charlene at the president's family home.
Afterwards, Ruto personally drove the couple to their waiting helicopter. Chivayo filmed the journey from the passenger seat, external. True to form, he gloated: "Being driven by the president of the republic. God is the greatest."
Ruto wrote on X following the death, external: "I will remember him for his friendship, his energy, and his deep conviction in the possibilities of our continent."
But in Kenya the Zimbabwean businessman was viewed with great suspicion because of his closeness to Ruto - something expressed loudly on social media since his death.
Many of the comments are not printable but as Kenyan blogger Cyprian Nyakundi put it, external, listing some of the controversies surrounding Chivayo: "As a Kenyan, I distance myself completely from President Ruto's glowing tribute to Wicknell Chivayo. Those condolences and that 'dear friend' language are his own, not mine, as a Kenyan."
One commentator on X said his death had "united Africans in celebration", external.
"When a man's passing brings more relief than sorrow, the reaction itself tells a powerful story. It is time for those in power to reflect and reevaluate!"
At home there has also been pushback against those who say speaking ill of the dead is un-African - as the topic of the tycoon's death is the trending topic in Zimbabwe these days.
At a shopping centre in Harare over the weekend, Christabel Moyo voiced what many have been saying.
"What is African - getting rich from inflated state contracts and using that money to support Zanu-PF?" the 42-year-old accountant asked.
"He was busy doling out cars and cash to the rich while the Zimbabwean public health system is collapsing."
The extraordinary gifting spree for which he will be remembered began around 2023. Musicians, sports and business figures, politicians and religious leaders were among the beneficiaries of cars and cash in what some might see as a blatant attempt to buy support for the ruling party.
He started with relatively modest Toyota Aquas, but the gifts soon became dramatically more expensive.
Top musician Jah Prayzah, who is close to Zanu-PF was given three luxury cars, along with about $400,000, over three years.
The musician postponed his wedding - scheduled to take place last weekend - because of the helicopter crash, saying: "Wicknell was more than a friend to us."
Another key recipient was Bishop Nehemiah Mutendi, head of the Zion Christian Church that is fiercely loyal to Zanu-PF. The cleric received millions in cash donations and four luxury cars.
Chivayo regularly attended the Johane Masowe weChishanu African apostolic church, one of the biggest in Zimbabwe, whose followers can often be seen worshipping outdoors wearing white robes.
It also received scores of cars, buses and cash from the businessman as he pushed the influential sect closer to the ruling party, taking along Mnangagwa as guest of honour to a massive church gathering in August.
But not everyone accepted Chivayo's largesse. Eunor Guti, widow of Zimbabwe Assemblies of God Africa founder Archbishop Ezekiel Guti, declined a luxury vehicle and $250,000 in cash.
In 2024, veteran musician and government critic Thomas Mapfumo, who is based in the US, rejected Chivayo's offer of a luxury car and house, saying he could not be "bribed" and later describing his money as "dirty".
However, this year, he did accept $1m to perform at Jah Prayzah's wedding and Chivayo's birthday party in November.
Some long-time admirers of Mapfumo, who arrived in Harare on the eve of the helicopter crash, accused him on social media of compromising his principles, though this was denied by the 81-year-old musician.
Chivayo's generosity was not confined to individuals - he also donated 20 ambulances to Zimbabwe's failing public health system and gave buses and other assistance to schools.
Those close to him say his philanthropy was not always performed for an audience. Prominent lawyer Wilson Manase said following the tycoon's death that when he had fallen seriously ill in Dubai, Chivayo flew over to visit him.
In an interview with state broadcaster ZBC, the lawyer, who was promised a car in Chivayo's last tweet, described him as "pure hearted" and deeply religious.
The tycoon had two young children with his first wife Sonja Madzikanda, from whom he split in 2024 and was still embroiled in a messy court case over the divorce settlement.
He was also keen not to forget his roots. On the day he died, he had visited his rural home in Gandami, south-east of Harare, where he was building a $1m eight-bedroom mansion to be officially opened in November for his birthday.
He boasted it would bring "Borrowdale Brooke to Gandami" - a reference to one of Harare's most exclusive residential estates. He had also pledged $500,000 to improve the local primary and secondary schools and a clinic.
Chivayo's death leaves Zanu-PF without one of its most colourful campaigners.
But he also leaves behind unanswered questions - with many of his countrymen continuing to wonder how exactly he rose from such humble beginnings to becoming a multi-millionaire with the means to dole out such extravagant gifts.
Ish Mafundikwa is a freelance journalist based in Harare

EU dropping associate membership title for its closer alliance with Canada: sources
Carney says it's the substance of Canada-EU relationship, not its name, that matters
The European Union is backing away from the idea of making Canada an associate member of the 27-nation bloc, sources tell CBC News.
A joint statement expected to be released at the 21st Canada-EU summit in Montreal on Friday will instead use softer language promising closer ties, according to sources who have seen the latest draft of the statement.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen surprised many last month when she announced the EU would begin the process of making Canada its first "associate member" — a status that does not exist within the bloc — raising questions among some members and Canadian politicians about what that would look like.
News that the summit's joint statement won't mention associate membership was first reported by Politico.
Sources with knowledge of the draft statement between Canada and the EU told CBC News the term "associate member" has been removed and the draft now calls for an "ever closer association."
They stressed the statement is still a draft and could change before the week's end.
A source speaking to CBC News on the condition they not be named because they weren't authorized to speak publicly added that this doesn't mean the substance of the agreement changes.
Another source said some EU countries opposed the term "associate member," particularly Germany who called it a red line.
Speaking to reporters on Tuesday before a cabinet meeting, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the title of Canada's relationship to the EU shouldn't matter as long as it delivers for Canadians.
"The good news is it doesn't matter about specific names or nomenclature," he said.
"What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians … and Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation, so we can live our lives as we choose."

Doctors tell the BBC about the targeting of Sudanese hospitals by paramilitary fighters
A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.
UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing".
Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.
The health minister of the group's civilian-affiliated government, Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, dismissed the allegations as propaganda.
The BBC's Africa correspondent Barbara Plett Usher speaks to two doctors who support the claims of systemic targeting of hospitals.

The Osaka Prefectural Police arrested three people Wednesday on suspicion of attempting to smuggle Indian star tortoises, an internationally protected species, from Thailand into Japan, in violation of the customs law.
The suspects include Takayuki Fukushima, a 57-year-old construction worker from Tondabayashi, Osaka Prefecture, and a 17-year-old high school student from the prefecture who purchased the animals in Thailand.
A 26-year-old man who was also arrested allegedly paid for the trip to Thailand.
They are suspected of conspiring to smuggle three Indian star tortoises and 13 crayfish from Thailand into Kansai International Airport in Osaka Prefecture on May 8.
Police have not disclosed whether the suspects have admitted to the allegations.
According to the police, Fukushima allegedly asked the student, who sold fish, newts and other animals through social media, to smuggle Indian star tortoises into Japan.
The student reportedly bought the animals in Thailand and brought them back in a suitcase. The attempted smuggling was discovered during a baggage inspection by Osaka Customs.
The tortoises had been wrapped in damp cardboard, police said.
Fukushima is suspected of intending to resell them at a high price.
International trade in Indian star tortoises is regulated under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, commonly known as the Washington Convention.

Shares of Jio Platforms, the telecom and digital services arm of Reliance Industries, listed at ₹1,358 apiece on the BSE and the NSE, a 21.36% premium to the issue price of ₹1,119. The debut gave the company a market capitalisation of ₹12.5 Lakh Cr (about $131 Bn) as against the ₹10.3 Lakh Cr (about $108 Bn) capitalisation at the issue price. The listing follows India’s largest IPO, which was subscribed 22.19X when bidding closed on October 23. Jio Platforms had set a price band of ₹1,065-₹1,119 per share for the ₹30,213 Cr offering. The IPO comprised a fresh issue of up to 27 Cr equity shares, with no offer-for-sale component. Ahead of the public issue, Jio Platforms raised ₹8,109.8 Cr from anchor investors by allotting about 7.25 Cr shares at ₹1,119 apiece. Participants included HDFC Mutual Fund, ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund, SBI Mutual Fund, BlackRock, the Government of Singapore, and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority. Jio plans to use ₹27,500 Cr from the IPO proceeds to prepay certain borrowings of its telecom subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm (RJIL), with the remaining proceeds earmarked for general corporate purposes. The debt repayment makes the offering partly a balance sheet exercise, while its growth prospects depend on expanding beyond telecom connectivity into broadband, cloud services, enterprise solutions, and AI. RJIL had 533.3 Mn customers as of June 30, 2026, while Jio’s network carried around 60% of India’s wireless data traffic in FY26. During the quarter, Jio’s average revenue per user (ARPU) rose 3.26% to ₹215.60 compared with ₹208.80 a year earlier. Monthly data consumption also increased to 43.7 GB per customer from 37 GB. This comes as the company has been working on extracting revenue from customers beyond its mobile connectivity offerings. Jio’s fixed broadband customer base grew from 11.2 Mn in March 2024 to 28.6 Mn in June 2026, including 14 Mn JioAirFiber customers, giving it an avenue to deepen household engagement. On the financial front, Jio Platforms’ operating revenue rose nearly 15% YoY to ₹1.47 Lakh Cr in FY26, while net profit increased 15.1% to ₹30,049 Cr. Earlier today, Motilal Oswal initiated coverage on Jio Platforms with a ‘BUY’ rating, setting a target price of ₹1,350 per share. The brokerage expects Jio to sustain its leadership in wireless connectivity and home broadband, while expanding its digital services business across cloud, enterprise communications, IoT and managed services.

The PlayStation 5 just might be Sony’s final Blu-Ray player
Sony has long been a pioneer of physical media, but that could be coming to an end.
It's ironic coming from a company that has such a rich history of excellent CD, VHS and DVD players, but it looks like Sony is now committed to getting out of the disc business. With recent news of the firm discontinuing its sole remaining dedicated 4K Blu-player in its native Japan, and PS5 ditching game disc production from January 2028, the future looks bleak for Sony fans who love physical media.
Thanks to pesky disc rot, your Blu-ray collection won't last forever, and now it's possible the entire Blu-ray market could be at risk going forward. With the discontinuation of Sony's last dedicated UHD player, the writing may be on the wall for Blu-ray as a continuing format. Will the PS5 really be Sony's last remaining device capable of playing 4K movie discs? Will the PS6 even have a disc drive?
Understanding Sony's Blu-ray player discontinuation
Sony officially confirmed it was discontinuing its last 4K Blu-ray player on Oct 22, 2026. The Sony UBP-X700/K, which was released in spring 2025, was the company's final standalone UHD player on the market. Though the UBP-700/K will no longer be sold in Japan, at time of writing it appears to still be available from retailers elsewhere, like Grooves Land and Walmart.
The news was first released by Japanese Sony-affiliated blog Kunkoko (with additional Western reporting by FlatpanelsHD). As a translated version of the blog post read: "Sony ends shipments of Ultra HD Blu-ray player UBP-X700/K. Following the end of Blu-ray recorder sales and the announcement that PlayStation game disc production will cease, the PS5 will be Sony's only UHD Blu-ray player in Japan."
As it noted, the standard disc-equipped PS5 (as well as the Slim or Pro PS5 with the disc drive add-on) plays both 4K and 1080p Blu-ray discs. However, the PS5 can't handle Dolby Vision in 4K movies that support the format, so Sony's current-gen console isn't as accomplished a player as the UBP-X700K.
4K Blu-ray always beats 4K streaming for picture quality, yet dwindling sales of both Blu-ray players and discs show that folks care more about easy streaming access than they do the quality of Blu-ray bitrates. For hardcore audio/visual dweebs like me, it'll be a sad day when 4K movie discs are no longer manufactured. Yet from a sales standpoint, I can reluctantly see where Sony is coming from.
When will the PS5 stop supporting new game discs?
Back in July, Sony confirmed that beginning January 2028, physical PS5 disc production will be halted for new PS5 titles. Moving forward, you'll only be able to buy new releases digitally from the PlayStation Store or from retailers via redemption codes. Existing discs will continue to work, but games released after this cutoff won't see a physical release.
At the time, we lamented how PlayStation had struck a massive blow to game preservation. Now the company also appears to have landed a haymaker to the hearts of film lovers who cherish owning a physical copy of their favorite movies.
This is pure speculation from someone with a large collection of both standard and 4K Blu-rays, but the killing of Sony's Blu-ray line could spell an end for the format in the not-too distant future. LG stopped production of its Blu-ray players in December 2024, while Samsung pulled out of the market way back in 2019. That leaves Panasonic as the last major manufacturer that hasn't abandoned Blu-ray (though small enthusiast brands like Magnetar & Krovatar continue to produce players). With the vast majority of big firms now out of the Blu-ray market, it's hard to envisage a long-term future for UHD discs.
Will the PS6 have a disc drive?
Right now, it's hard to say. But it's difficult to be optimistic for a future where next-gen PlayStation consoles still sport disc drives. With the PS5 ditching game discs from early 2028, the sales incentive for Sony to incorporate an optical drive into the PS6 doesn't make much sense.
That said, an exclusive report from Insider Gaming claims the company will launch the PlayStation 6 with a detachable disc drive. According to the site's anonymous sources, "customers will be able to buy the console individually as a 'digital console', bundled with the PlayStation 6 as a 'traditional console', or upgrade later by purchasing the detachable disc drive separately."
To be clear, such PS6 disc drive speculation isn't being widely reported anywhere else, so it's easy to be skeptical. And while some of that wording is a bit confusing, the notion of a detachable drive would follow the PS5 playbook. Sony first gave gamers the option of buying an attachable optical drive when the PS5 Slim launched on October 10, 2023, selling the add-on for $79. Skip forward to November 7, 2024 when the PS5 Pro hit the market, and the supercharged console also supported the same optical drive.
Viewed through that lens, it's definitely possible Sony could launch a PS6 Digital Edition with an optional drive. From a manufacturing perspective, producing one console that supports an attachable disc drive makes more sense than separate disc and discless versions of the same machine. It could also technically be feasible for the PS6 to support the existing PS5 drive, assuming no advancements in disc tech happen by then.
Even if past leaks have claimed that the PS6 could triple the performance of the PS5, don't go betting the farm on the PlayStation 6 having a disc drive. Sony sadly seems committed to an all-digital future, and as an ardent fan of both game discs and 4K Blu-rays, that makes me mighty sad.

In a show of gratitude towards its employees, a pharmaceutical company in Haryana has gifted four brand-new Kia Sonet SUVs to its top-performing employees just days before Diwali, the festival of lights. MK Bhatia, a social worker and founder of MITS Healthcare in Panchkula, handed over the keys to the cars to the employees. Images and videos of the gesture are now doing the rounds on social media. In the video, Bhatia arrives at the dealership in a BMW 3 Series Gran Limousine, where four SUVs stand covered in black cloth. The employees unveil their respective vehicles one by one as their colleagues cheer them on. The celebrations then continue with cake-cutting and dancing. According to a report by Cartoq, the initiative aims to recognise employees' strong performance. One of the employees said he had been with the company for five years before being selected for the reward. The company reportedly covered the initial down payment for the vehicles, while the monthly instalments are deducted from the employees' salaries. The cars have been registered in the names of the respective recipients. MITS Healthcare has also launched a lucky draw for employees who have completed at least 18 months with the company. Open to staff at all levels, from security guards to senior officials, the initiative aims to give more employees an opportunity to win a car. This is the fourth consecutive year that the pharmaceutical company has rewarded its employees with cars. In October 2025, Bhatia gifted 51 vehicles to high-performing employees as part of the company's Diwali celebrations. Bhatia credited his employees for the company's success, saying their dedication and hard work deserved recognition. MITS Healthcare has also rewarded its staff with vehicles in previous years. In 2024, the company gifted cars, including Tata Punch and Maruti Suzuki Grand Vitara SUVs, to 15 employees, The Indian Express reported. Mining is half of Minecraft’s essence, yet somewhere along the way, I stopped wanting to explore the caves or start digging at random locations and see what it leads me to. Once you know the best levels, the right pickaxe, and the most efficient ways of mining, getting every ore feels a lot less like a reward feature but more like working a night shift. That’s why I wasn’t expecting the Minecraft Ice Caves to impress me this much.
While Ice Caves may sound like just another cave biome on paper with cooler features like more ice blocks and some frozen mobs, I feel it would reignite the joyful feeling we used to get while mining. The Minecraft 26.4 update could easily be one of the best recent drops because it just makes mining exciting again.
Ice Caves Turn Diamond Mining Into an Actual Treasure Hunt in Minecraft
What immediately sold me on Minecraft’s Ice Caves wasn’t the blue scenery; it was the danger that makes the biome worth exploring.
The past few updates this year brought the Sulfur Caves in Minecraft, but they don’t generate any Stone variants for ores exclusively unless surrounded by massive Cheese caves. So, ordinary ore hunting becomes inconvenient.
Whereas the Ice Caves have placements for diamonds, iron, lapis lazuli, redstone, and more ores. These are found in stone and deepslate blocks that generate in pockets of Ice Caves.
Let me tell you another reason why you should be invested in these areas. Firstly, the Ice Caves have a very rare chance of being generated with an opening to the Overworld. Secondly, diamond generation is massively reduced when blocks are exposed to air.
Naturally, Ice Caves become one of the best spots to look for diamonds in the game. Moreover, with the fast-breaking ice blocks in Minecraft, tunneling becomes far easier, and you might fall in front of diamond veins faster than you could’ve imagined.
This Frozen Gold Mine Wants Me Dead
The clever part of Ice Caves is that Mojang isn’t handing you an icy ATM and politely asking you to make withdrawals. The Ice Caves bite back, or at least let’s say the environment does.
The most dangerous element here is the Frostbite mobs in Minecraft. These are the frozen zombie variant that can fight at range with Ice Balls before switching to melee punches when close. The worst part is that their melee punches apply a Freezing effect. Not only does it freeze you, but it also deals some damage over time.
Additionally, you would find other cave Minecraft mobs such as zombies, spiders, skeletons, and strays. Apparently, Mojang might’ve thought, dodging one projectile while sliding on Ice wasn’t enough cardio. So, they added Icicles and Brittle Ice blocks to Minecraft as environmental hazard elements.
For years, cave survival revolved around carrying a torch because, obviously, how are you going to see through the dark? However, if you hold on to your torches long enough, the Icicles can fall on your head and remove a chunk of your health.
On the other hand, the floor in the Ice Caves doesn’t quite support you, either. The Brittle Ice blocks generating in the crevasses can break when stepped on and send you into the freezing water below.
These aspects are what make this Minecraft biome click for me. Better mining rewards require me to work my way to them.
Mojang Finally Finds a Better Way to Make Mining Rewarding in Caves
The Deep Dark creates tension and makes me terrified of making a noise. Dripstone Caves biome is literally a pincushion, and the Lush Caves are so beautiful that most of the time I forget the actual purpose of my visit. Ice Caves seems to borrow the best of the three and doesn’t hold to any singular aspect.
However, I’m not yet crowning this biome as the flawless one ever. It’s still in its experimental phase and is set to release in December 2026. In the meantime, I’m excited to see what more features Mojang has in their sack for us.
I hope there are just enough rewards to justify the trouble of throwing myself on the Frostbites, Strays, collapsing Icicles, slippery terrain, and the Minecraft Brittle Ice blocks under my boots.
So, what are your thoughts on this biome till now? Let us know in the comments section below.

Son of Zambian bishop detained in post-election raid fears for his father's safety
The son of detained Zambian opposition politician Bishop Trevor Mwamba has told the BBC he is concerned for his father's safety after the former Bishop of Botswana was detained along with 10 other opposition figures by authorities.
Eno Mwamba said his father, who is leader of the United National Independence Party, has been charged with treason following President Hakainde Hichilema's disputed election victory.
The opposition politicians have been held since a raid by security forces on 14 August.
Opposition leader Brian Mundubile, head of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP), had gone into hiding after disputing the election result, but has since also been detained by the authorities.
The government accuses the opposition of planning an armed insurgency and have charged the detained politicians with treason. They have denied the charges.
