Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said.
Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer.
But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India.
When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries.
Alexander’s comments show how much Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, who called this week for a “serious dialogue” on the UK’s relations with the EU, including possible re-entry, has shifted the government’s position.
Speaking to the Guardian from a trade delegation to India, Alexander welcomed the progress made since the Indian agreement came into force earlier this year, since when the price of scotch whisky in India has fallen by 10-15%.
But he said the economic benefits of trading agreements with the EU would be greater.
“In trade policy, geography still matters,” he said. “The Channel is just 21 miles wide. Our largest trading partner is and will remain the European Union in the years to come. We trade almost twice the amount with the European Union that we do with the United States, the largest single-country trading partner.”
He said: “It’s no secret that I was not a supporter of leaving the European Union, and I called out early as trade minister what I described as the ‘post-imperial delusions’ of the Brexiteers. Back in 2016, they promised a world of Britain as a buccaneering free trade nation in a world where barriers were coming down. Sadly, what we’ve witnessed in the year since is a more protectionist, more regionalised world in which barriers have been going up.
“At the time we joined the Pacific trade grouping, the CPTPP [Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership] – which undoubtedly makes a lot of sense geopolitically for the UK – our own analysis made clear that the long-term boost to UK GDP from membership is less than a tenth of 1%. If you compare that with estimates of the structural damage to the UK economy from Brexit, you get a sense of just how important Europe remains to our future trade and prosperity.
“We’re already paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours who, with almost half of total UK trade, remain easily our largest trading partners.”
Alexander was speaking in Mumbai, where he was joined by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, as well as a group of mayors from northern England. He made it clear he did not support any particular method of achieving closer relations with the EU.
The ministers spent much of their time in meetings with Indian officials as they attempt to iron out what they say have been “teething problems” with the early implementation, especially for smaller businesses.
“There are always teething problems,” Alexander said. “We’re also having a conversation at the level of regulation to see how do we overcome non-tariff barriers that can prove to be an inhibitor to the kind of progress we want to see unless they’re addressed.”
Many in the government say a bigger prize will be to reach an agreement at next month’s EU summit, where Burnham hopes to sign new trading deals for emissions, electricity and agricultural products.
One hurdle to delivering that is the UK’s desire to discuss the protectionist “Made in Europe” policy, which British manufacturers fear will shut them out of a key market. EU leaders say they are willing to discuss British entry into that scheme, though they are also pushing for the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, without which they fear the UK will become a back door into the European market.
Reynolds told the Guardian this week he would not impose tariffs simply because of pressure from Brussels.

“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” has officially premiered, and members of the film press are already calling the sixth installment a “perfect adaptation” that breathes “new life” into the franchise. “Sunrise on the Reaping” is the second “Hunger Games” prequel movie following 2023’s “The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes.”
Film critic Griffin Schiller hailed the movie as the “Rogue One” and “Andor” of “The Hunger Games” franchise, adding: “It’s [a] sobering, yet powerful story of devastating loss and the necessary cost of rebellion for a sunrise we may never see. As a massive fan of the series and especially this book, I couldn’t have asked for a more perfect adaptation.”
Filmhounds Magazine editor-in-chief and Tomatometer critic Gavin Spoors praised the film’s third act as “stellar,” writing that it “pulls the rug out underneath you.” “Anchored by terrific performances (Zada is a star), this emotional thriller nails the themes of the cost of revolution and how we all need to play our part,” he wrote on X.
Matt Neglia, Next Best Picture editor-in-chief, wrote that the film “features some of the best casting of the year” in his review. “Many of the actors breathe new life into familiar characters, making them their own, while preserving the qualities that made them so compelling in the first place,” he continued. “Glenn Close, with her horror-inducing face, is a scene-stealer as is Jesse Plemons embodying the spirit of the late great Philip Seymour Hoffman. Joseph Zada is beyond impressive in a highly demanding role that pushes him to the limit physically and emotionally, perfectly capturing the essence of Haymitch with all the sympathy, charm and bitterness Woody Harrelson brought to the role. I’m continually blown away by how Francis Lawrence continues to find more layers in this familiar structure thematically and stylistically as the production and costume design continue to be dazzling highlights. If this is to be the end of his time working on these movies, it’s a good way to go out as this latest installment brings the franchise full circle with the character that’s always been the beating heart at its center.”
“The rebellion is sparking with SUNRISE ON THE REAPING,” wrote fellow Next Best Picture editor Lauren LaMagna. “Francis Lawrence continues to breathe new life into this world. The unique production design doesn’t let familiar beats get too dull. Joseph Zada is heartbreakingly radiant as Haymitch. A star is born role.”
“One of the biggest highlights? Joseph Zada,” wrote Collider’s Perri Nemiroff. “I had high hopes for him after watching We Were Liars, but he had my jaw on the floor time and time again during Sunrise on the Reaping. His ability to capture Haymitch’s warmth and charm and then weave that into the rage and heartbreak the Hunger Games sparks is superb. SO much of this movie is on his shoulders, and he soars tackling every ounce of it. This is only the beginning for Zada.”
He continued: “Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes bolstered my rewatches of the original films, and I have no doubt the same will be true of Sunrise on the Reaping. Sparking real change can take time and demand great sacrifice. This film franchise is better off for having added Haymitch’s.”
Static Media writer Nina Starner also championed Zada’s casting, saying that it “couldn’t be better.” “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is a worthy addition to the franchise,” she wrote. “It looks and feels terrifyingly real, and it bridges the gap perfectly between the original stories and Ballad. A from me.”
Based on Suzanne Collins’ 2025 novel “Sunrise on the Reaping,” the latest “Hunger Games” movie centers on a young Haymitch (Zada, taking over the role from Woody Harrelson) as he fights to survive while competing in the 50th Hunger Games. The cast also features Jesse Plemons as Plutarch, Ralph Fiennes as President Snow, Kieran Culkin as Caesar Flickerman, Maya Hawke as Wiress and Kelvin Harrison Jr. as Beetee. New characters in the film franchise are played by the likes of Mckenna Grace, Glenn Close and Whitney Peak, among others.
“Sunrise on the Reaping” takes place 24 years before the start of the first “Hunger Games” movie. Frances Lawrence, who has directed every “Hunger Games” movie except for the first installment (that was Gary Ross), returns to helm the latest prequel movie.
Much of the buzz surrounding “Sunrise on the Reaping” has been related to the franchise returns of Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson and Harrelson as Katniss, Peeta and Haymitch. Book readers know that Suzanne Collins’ novel ends with a flash-forward epilogue featuring the trio, so it appears the film adaptation is following suit.
“It was unbelievable,” Lawrence said on the “Call Her Daddy” podcast about reprising Katniss. “It was so crazy. It was the same crew. It was the same AD, who I’ve worked with a million times because I love him. And with Josh [Hutcherson] and Woody [Harrelson] … it was so emotional. Josh and I didn’t walk to the bathroom without our arms around each other. It was so beautiful.”
“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” is set to open in theaters Nov. 20 from Lionsgate. Check out first reactions to the movie below.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration published draft guidance that would streamline approvals of some individualized gene therapies, a win for rare disease advocates who have criticized the agency approach to these treatments, STAT says. The FDA has continued to require companies to submit separate drug approval applications for each patient’s customized gene therapy, even when they use fundamentally the same approach to target different genes. Advocates argue this creates a prohibitively expensive regulatory burden. The new draft guidance formalizes a “plausible mechanism pathway,” and offers more specific rules for licensing and updating gene editing treatments.
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway warned Eli Lilly to discontinue its practice of requiring hospitals to provide claims data to receive discounted medicines under a federal program, a sign that more states are pushing back against such moves by drugmakers, STAT notes. In an Oct. 26 cease-and-desist letter sent to the company, Hanaway maintained that Lilly has “broken” its promise to sell its medicines under the 340B Drug Pricing Program to eligible hospitals in the state. As a result, she contended the drugmaker has made “false and misleading statements” and violated state law.

When AI-powered sales intelligence startup Reo.Dev raised $11.3 Mn in July 2026, its priorities reflected a growing reality for Indian startups building for global markets. The company planned to deploy fresh capital towards expanding sales and marketing operations in the US, which already accounted for nearly two-thirds of its revenue. Yet most of its approximately 75-member workforce remained in India. Reo.Dev is not alone in operating across these two markets. Bengaluru- and San Francisco-based Coreworks AI raised $5 Mn earlier this year to develop its enterprise AI platform. More recently, RapidCanvas secured $29 Mn to expand its go-to-market and field AI engineering teams across India, the US and Brazil. These companies illustrate the increasingly international nature of India's AI startup ecosystem, where the markets founders sell into, the teams they build and the locations from which they operate do not necessarily overlap. The momentum is backed by capital. According to Inc42's Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026, Indian AI startups raised $438 Mn during the July–September quarter, a 265% year-on-year increase. With $676 Mn raised in the first half, cumulative funding for the first nine months of 2026 crossed $1.1 Bn. As more startups pursue global AI opportunities, however, an important question is emerging. Does getting closer to Silicon Valley necessarily make an Indian AI startup more competitive? For Suhas Motwani, cofounder of The Product Folks, a global community of product professionals and builders, the answer is more complicated than a change of address. "The corridor is real, and for a lot of founders it is useful," says Motwani. "The harder question is what gets built on each side of it, and what gets lost when the move happens too early." Why Silicon Valley Is Becoming Harder To Ignore The attraction of Silicon Valley extends well beyond fundraising, which was the case even at the height of the Indian SaaS boom. For AI startups, just like SaaS startups before them, proximity to potential enterprise customers, experienced operators, specialised talent and the wider AI ecosystem can shorten the distance between product development and commercial validation. That matters particularly for startups building enterprise AI products, where customer discovery often requires understanding complex workflows, procurement processes, security requirements and the commercial value of automation. As Inc42 previously explored in its analysis of enterprise AI sales, winning enterprise customers is no longer simply about demonstrating technical capabilities. Startups must identify decision-makers, prove measurable returns and navigate the operational risks associated with deploying AI in live business environments. For companies whose largest potential customers are American enterprises, building those relationships from thousands of kilometres away can introduce additional challenges. Physical presence can create opportunities for more frequent customer interactions, closer feedback loops and a better understanding of how enterprise buying decisions are made. Motwani believes this proximity can be particularly useful in a sector where product capabilities, customer expectations and competitive positioning are evolving rapidly. But there is an important distinction between using Silicon Valley to accelerate learning and treating relocation itself as a competitive advantage. "A low barrier to raising in the Bay is very different from a low barrier to building a durable company," he says. "The move itself is cheap. The compounding effects are not." The challenge for founders is to determine whether their company genuinely needs a physical presence in the US, and what business outcomes that presence is expected to deliver. How AI Is Changing The India–US Equation The India–US technology corridor is not new. Indian SaaS companies have spent years building products and engineering teams at home while selling to enterprise customers abroad. However, AI is changing the economics of that relationship. The cost and complexity of developing frontier AI models continue to demand enormous capital, computing infrastructure and specialised talent. At the same time, access to increasingly capable models is making it possible for smaller teams to build AI-powered applications without developing the underlying technology themselves. The distinction is becoming more visible as the global AI industry enters a new phase. On 26 October, Anthropic publicly filed its registration statement for a proposed US initial public offering. The Claude maker reported approximately $16.3 Bn in revenue during the first half of 2026, compared with about $1.2 Bn in the corresponding period last year, illustrating the rapid commercial expansion of the frontier AI industry. Its proposed listing also comes amid questions over the enormous capital requirements and long-term economics of building advanced AI models. For Indian founders, the implications extend beyond the public market performance of companies such as Anthropic. While frontier AI development remains heavily capital-intensive, application-layer startups can increasingly build on models developed elsewhere, allowing them to direct more resources towards solving specific customer problems. This distinction is particularly relevant to India. According to the Google × Inc42 Bharat AI Startups Report, 2026, 90% of funded Indian AI startups covered in its analysis operate at the application layer. However, access to powerful models also means that technological capabilities can become easier for competing startups to replicate. A sophisticated AI feature, by itself, may no longer constitute a lasting competitive advantage. What becomes harder to replicate is a startup's understanding of its customers, its integration into their workflows, its distribution network and the trust it builds through repeated use. This is where the India–US corridor takes on a different significance. For application-layer startups, being close to Silicon Valley can offer access to frontier AI developments, customers and distribution networks. But the ability to build quickly, experiment cost-effectively and develop products for demanding users can remain rooted in India. The opportunity is no longer just about exporting Indian engineering capabilities to the US. It is about determining which parts of an AI business need to operate closer to the technology frontier, which need to be closer to customers, and where the startup can build its strongest competitive advantage. Knowing The Risks For much of the past decade, Indian technology startups have competed globally by combining engineering talent, leaner operating structures and access to international markets. AI is changing the economics of building software, but it has not eliminated the importance of these advantages. Moving an entire founding or engineering team to San Francisco can significantly increase operating costs, particularly when the startup is still experimenting with products, pricing and its target customer segment. More importantly, an early relocation can affect the company's product development process. Founders who move away from their engineering teams may find themselves managing critical product decisions across time zones. The resulting separation can make experimentation, communication and decision-making more complex at precisely the stage when startups need to move quickly. There is also the question of which users influence the product roadmap. A startup developing AI products for American enterprises may benefit enormously from spending more time with US customers. But the same approach could prove counterproductive for a company building for Indian consumers, small businesses or enterprises with distinctly local requirements. Motwani argues that the environment in which a startup develops its earliest products can influence the capabilities it prioritises and the problems it learns to solve. India, for instance, exposes AI products to considerable variation in languages, devices, connectivity, user behaviour and willingness to pay. A product designed around affluent, English-speaking users with reliable connectivity may not necessarily work as effectively for consumers using regional languages, shared devices or less predictable networks. These constraints can force teams to improve reliability, usability and cost efficiency much earlier in the product development cycle. The risk is not that an Indian founder builds for the US. It is that the founder changes markets without deliberately reassessing which customers, capabilities and advantages should shape the business. An Opportunity Too Large To Overlook The case for maintaining a strong presence in India is also increasingly supported by the size of the domestic opportunity. According to the Google × Inc42 Bharat AI Startups Report, 2026, India's AI market is projected to reach $126 Bn by 2030. Enterprise AI expenditure is estimated to grow from $11 Bn in 2025 to $71 Bn by 2030, while consumer AI expenditure is projected to rise from $13 Bn to $55 Bn over the same period. For application-layer startups, this represents a significant opportunity to build products that address specific customer problems, integrate into existing workflows and earn sustained adoption. There are, however, important differences between market opportunity and commercial readiness. India was already the world's second-largest market for AI application downloads in 2024, accounting for 177 Mn downloads. Yet the Bharat AI report estimated consumer AI monetisation at just $12 Mn during that period. In other words, significant user adoption does not automatically translate into strong monetisation. For Indian AI founders, this creates two different opportunities. The US offers access to enterprise customers with established software budgets, while India offers a large and diverse market in which startups can build products around local workflows and underserved customer segments. Choosing between them should depend on the problem being solved, rather than the assumption that one market is inherently superior. There are also alternative routes to global customers that do not require startups to abandon their Indian operating base. An earlier analysis published on Inc42 examined how India's Global Capability Centres (GCCs) could become an important route to multinational enterprise buyers, offering Indian AI startups access to global workflows and potential decision-makers within the country itself. The major implication is that access to international customers does not always require shifting the entire centre of product development overseas. The Case For Building Across Two Markets Rather than viewing Bengaluru and Silicon Valley as competing destinations, Motwani sees merit in founders using the two ecosystems for different purposes. Through his work with The Product Folks, he has observed differences in the priorities that dominate conversations among founders and product professionals in the two markets. In San Francisco or the Valley, discussions tend to centre on distribution, pricing and category creation. In Bengaluru, they are often more focused on engineering teams, product positioning, capital efficiency and the immediate challenges of building a sustainable business. Both perspectives matter. A startup can build a technically capable AI product in India and still struggle to reach the right international customers. Equally, access to American buyers and investors does not guarantee that the company will develop a defensible product or sustainable business model. This is where a two-market operating strategy becomes relevant. For founders serving US enterprises, customer-facing functions may need to be closer to those customers, while product and engineering teams can continue operating from India. Reo.Dev offers one illustration. As Inc42 reported in July, the startup was expanding its American sales and marketing operations while retaining most of its workforce in India. But operating across two markets brings its own challenges. Founders must establish clear ownership of product decisions, maintain communication between customer-facing and engineering teams, and ensure that feedback from international customers translates into improvements rather than endless customisation. There is also a less visible challenge: access to the right relationships. Entering a new market requires more than understanding its customers. Founders often need introductions to experienced operators, potential partners, investors, early hires and advisors who understand the practical challenges of building across borders. Motwani has been working to address some of these gaps through The Founder Folks, an invite-only founder initiative emerging from The Product Folks network. Built around the India–US corridor, the initiative seeks to connect founders with experienced operators, potential customers and advisors, alongside offering practical guidance on US market entry, fundraising and managing cross-border teams. Its emphasis reflects a broader challenge in the ecosystem: founders looking to build global businesses need more than access to capital. They also need access to relevant experience, networks and market-specific knowledge. Ultimately, a US presence can accelerate customer discovery, but whether that learning becomes a competitive advantage depends on how effectively it informs the product being built. The Real Test Is Product-Market Fit The debate over where Indian AI startups should operate ultimately connects to a larger challenge facing the sector. AI has made it easier for startups to develop prototypes, experiment with new capabilities and launch products. But these improvements do not automatically make it easier to build businesses that customers depend on. Motwani believes founders must distinguish between what an AI product can demonstrate and what users will actually trust it to do. "The shift from demo to daily use is not about adding features," he says. "It is about deciding what work a user will actually trust the system to do." This distinction becomes particularly relevant when founders enter new markets. Customer expectations around product reliability, workflow integration, support, pricing and accountability can vary considerably between India and the US. A product that performs well during a demonstration may still struggle when deployed within an enterprise workflow that requires multiple approvals, integration with legacy systems or verification of AI-generated outputs. These challenges are becoming more consequential as investor expectations mature. Inc42's Q3 2026 investor survey found that 63% of institutional investors surveyed saw some degree of froth in Indian AI startup valuations. At the same time, 39% believed vertical AI applications would capture the greatest value over the next five years. The findings suggest that while investor interest in AI remains strong, the ability to build commercially viable, differentiated applications will increasingly matter. For founders, the priority is not simply to reach a larger market. It is to understand which problems customers will pay to solve, how the product fits into their existing processes and whether the business can deliver value consistently. A startup may need to be in San Francisco to understand those requirements. Another may discover its strongest opportunities by working more closely with Indian enterprises and consumers. Neither outcome can be determined by geography alone. Where Will India's Next Global AI Companies Be Built? India's AI startup ecosystem is entering a phase in which global ambitions are becoming more closely intertwined with domestic capabilities. As frontier AI companies prepare to face greater public market scrutiny, the application layer offers Indian startups an opportunity to participate in the global AI economy without necessarily matching the capital or infrastructure investments of the largest model developers. But it also raises the competitive bar. Building products is becoming faster. Access to underlying AI capabilities is expanding. What will distinguish companies is their ability to identify valuable problems, reach the right customers and develop products that become indispensable to their workflows. Access to US capital, customers and talent can help startups accelerate their growth. At the same time, India's engineering ecosystem, domestic demand and operating advantages continue to offer meaningful opportunities. The challenge is to combine those strengths without assuming that a particular operating model will work for every company. For some founders, relocating to the US will be commercially necessary. For others, maintaining customer-facing teams abroad while building from India may offer a more effective structure. And for startups addressing domestic problems, staying close to Indian users could be fundamental to product-market fit. The decisions will also evolve as companies grow. What makes sense during initial customer discovery may not be the right structure after a startup finds product-market fit or begins scaling internationally. Motwani's argument is that founders should approach these choices as deliberate business decisions rather than signals of ambition. "The corridor is a tool," he says. "Like any tool, it rewards the founders who are clear about what they are using it for and punishes the ones who confuse motion for progress." As Indian AI companies compete for opportunities on both sides of the Pacific, the differentiator may ultimately be neither their headquarters nor their ability to access Silicon Valley. It will be whether they can use the strengths of both markets to build products customers value, businesses that endure and competitive advantages that are difficult to replicate.

Anger in Kenya over extradition hearing delay for ex-British soldier accused of murdering woman
- Published
The family of a Kenyan woman allegedly murdered by a former British soldier 14 years ago has expressed outrage after being told an extradition hearing for the accused had been postponed until May 2027.
Relatives of Agnes Wanjiru, whose body was found in a septic tank near a British army training camp in Kenya in 2012, described the delay as "completely unacceptable" and have accused the authorities of failing to keep them informed.
Robert James Purkiss was arrested in the UK last November and is fighting extradition to Kenya to face trial for the murder of the 21-year-old mother.
He denies the allegation. His hearing was due to be held in London next month.
- Murdered Kenyan's friends want UK soldier to face justice 
  - Published21 September 2025
Wanjiru's niece, Esther Njoki, told the BBC that the family had learnt of the postponement through the UK embassy and had received no official explanation.
"We have exercised patience and endured uncertainty for years, but our patience is now being taken advantage of," she said in a statement.
"Agnes deserves justice. Her daughter Stacy deserves answers about what happened. And as a family, we deserve to be treated with dignity and kept informed about proceedings that profoundly affect our lives."
The family said it had already raised money and made arrangements to travel to the UK for the hearing, which was due to take place in three weeks.
It is now calling on the authorities to expedite the proceedings, warning that the latest postponement means the case will enter its 15th year without a trial.
The family said a UK court was expected next week to give the reasons for the hearing delay.
Wanjiru disappeared in March 2012 after spending an evening at a hotel in Nanyuki, about 200km (124 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi, where British soldiers were stationed for training.
Her body was found nearly three months later in a septic tank at the hotel. She had suffered stab wounds to her chest and abdomen and left behind a five-month-old daughter.
A Kenyan inquest concluded in 2019 that she had been unlawfully killed by one or two British soldiers.
In September 2025, a Kenyan High Court issued an arrest warrant for a British national after prosecutors presented evidence they said justified bringing murder charges.
Purkiss' lawyers said he intended to contest his extradition to Kenya.
He appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court in February via video link, where he was further remanded in custody.
Last year, the then British Defence Secretary John Healey met Wanjiru's family during a visit to Kenya and pledged his government's support for efforts to secure justice.
The UK government has previously said it remains committed to helping the family, but would not comment on ongoing legal proceedings.

The US ambassador has suggested Canada could be blamed if Republicans perform poorly in next week’s midterm elections, the latest intervention from a controversial figure who has been accused of inflaming a bitter dispute that has angered and baffled residents of both countries.
On Wednesday, CTV news reported that Pete Hoekstra told business leaders at a closed door meeting that if a number of swing races – including Maine and Michigan – go to the Democrats, it could make things harder for Canada because Donald Trump might try to blame the loss on it.
“That’s an interesting way of framing it,” the prime minister, Mark Carney, told reporters when asked about the allegations.
For months, Canada and the US have been locked in a bitter tariff war, with Ottawa retaliating against illegal US tariffs and targeting goods in states that rely heavily on trade with Canada.
Carney said that Canada “will pursue” such a deal if it presents itself, but that Ottawa’s trade negotiators are “not in that position right now”.
Hoekstra is a deeply polarizing figure in Canada, particular for his response to Trump’s rhetoric about making Canada the 51st US state. Speaking to a Michigan radio station last year, he described the threats as a “sign of affection” and questioned why Canadians were offended by what he characterized as a “generous offer”. He had previously described Canada’s 2025 federal election as “anti-American”.
This year a House of Commons petition signed by more than 225,000 Canadians called for his expulsion, suggesting his statements violated diplomatic protocols, including the prohibition on diplomats interfering in the internal affairs of a host country.
More recently, Hoekstra has accused Canadian officials of interfering in US elections, pointing to Canadian politicians who have criticized the tariffs in US media, and the province of Ontario’s anti-tariff advertisement that ran on US television.
“We see all of that. We are monitoring it. We are evaluating it. And if some of it becomes election interference, America will respond to it,” Hoekstra, who comes from Michigan, recently told a Canadian podcast, adding that Canadians should “keep your nose out of American politics”.
Canada’s industry minister, Mélanie Joly, who was a target of Hoekstra’s comments, told reporters in Ottawa that her country “would never do that” and said Canada would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada”.
Carney, while in Turkey, told reporters there was “no merit” to the claims of interference and that he was “disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions”.
Roland Paris, the director of the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs at the University of Ottawa and a foreign affairs adviser to the former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, said the remarks were an “extraordinary thing” for a US ambassador to say about his host country and looked like an effort to “manufacture a pretext for the Trump administration’s own political difficulties”.
“The job of an ambassador is to represent the interests of his country, but it’s also to maintain channels of communication and build relationships and manage disagreements,” he said.
“His comments have repeatedly aggravated tensions instead of helping to manage them. I don’t think that he’s serving American interests very well. I’m not even sure that he’s serving the interests of his president.”
Paris points to polling in the US that shows voters have increasingly linked tariffs, the war and cost of living. There is also widespread confusion over why the White House has chosen to treat Canada as a trade adversary.
“It’s certainly not working in Canada. It’s on the contrary. It seems that every time Mr Hoekstra opens his mouth, the Canadians are more determined than before to stand up to the bullying of the Trump administration,” he said. “That’s not serving American interests.”
The US embassy denied Hoekstra said Canada would face blame for a poor Republican showing, suggesting the remarks were “grossly taken out of context” from a broader discussion.
“The ambassador has consistently said that the Canadian media is attempting to overstate the relevance of Canadian issues in American elections. As we have previously stated, Americans will decide American elections based on issues that are important to them,” the embassy said in a statement.
At a Canadian American Business event last year, Hoekstra delivered what witnesses say was an expletive-laden tirade at Ontario’s trade representative after the province ran a series of anti-tariff ads in the US that featured Ronald Reagan. Ontario’s premier called the outburst “absolutely unacceptable” and “unbecoming of an ambassador”.
Last week, Barack Obama noted the unusual choice to attack a longtime ally while speaking at a Democratic campaign rally in Detroit, mocking Trump’s fixation on Canada and jokingly referring to his northern neighbor as a “well-known evil empire”.
“That historical adversary of ours: Canada,” the former US president said. “It’s your neighbor! It’s a few minutes drive over the bridge. These are the people who gave us Martin Short … and maple syrup. They are the nicest people. And somehow we’ve gotten them so mad.”

The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.
“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”
Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba.
“The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.”
Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets.
The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians.
The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital.
Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month.
“The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia.
Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead.
“The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source.
When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm.
Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.”
US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.”
Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño.
Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.”
Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater.
“In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old.
US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”.
Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000.
Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland, is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half.
His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba.
Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says.
The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled.
Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient.
“They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks.
Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”.
Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets.
Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said.
Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.”
Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter.
“It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.”
Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided.
Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes.
Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region.
Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year.
David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.”
The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.”
Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia.
Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger. Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them.
Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart.
Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.”
In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery.
Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea.
El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine.
Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year.
Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night.
For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness.
“She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived.
Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse.

Forty Iranian sailors rescued off Sri Lanka coast after medical emergencies
- Published
Sri Lanka's foreign ministry says it has coordinated efforts to treat and repatriate 40 Iranian sailors suffering from unspecified medical emergencies in international waters off the island's southeastern coast.
Ministry spokesperson Thushara Rodrigo told BBC Sinhala they received a distress call on Saturday from Iranian ships "regarding an urgent medical need".
The rescue operation was planned by the Iranian Embassy in Colombo, he said.
Iranian ships have been stranded at sea due to a US naval blockade. Sri Lanka stresses it is neutral in the conflict, but has at times offered help to Iranian sailors in what it says is an obligation to international law.
A BBC Sinhala report last month found that there were 21 Iranian vessels located in international waters near Sri Lanka.
The 40 rescued sailors served on different ships - though Sri Lankan authorities do not have information on how many ships they belonged to, Rodrigo said.
The sailors were brought ashore and taken to Colombo for medical treatment before being sent back to Iran by plane on Saturday night, he added.
He said that several agencies were involved in the operation, including local shipping companies.
According to Rodrigo, Sri Lanka was obliged under international law and humanitarian grounds to provide the necessary facilities for medical emergencies.
"This does not mean that we will provide assistance to those ships," he said. "It is generally an internationally accepted tradition to respond to a distress call after receiving it."
"We have dealt with such cases before. This is a normal process that continues to be implemented."
The ongoing conflict in Iran started when the US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on the country in February. Iran responded by attacking Israel, US bases and allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a critical international trade route.
Attacks by both sides have persisted as negotiations stalled.
Sri Lanka has sought to remain neutral in the conflict, having rejected military access requests from both the US and Iran and urged both parties to prioritise dialogue.
It has also offered assistance to Iranian ships caught in the conflict on what it argues are humanitarian grounds.
In March, Sri Lankan authorities said they responded to a distress call from the Iranian ship the Iris Dena, which had sunk off its coast after a US torpedo attack.
More than 80 crew members were killed in the attack, and injured survivors were taken to a hospital in the Galle Harbour.
The following day, Sri Lankan authorities allowed another Iranian naval vessel to dock at one of its ports, with President Anura Kumara Dissanayake saying that they would "never hesitate to protect humanity".
Sri Lankan authorities said earlier this month they had no immediate plans to send aid to 19 Iranian ships near its coasts which had reported shortages of food, water and fuel. The authorities said they had to prioritise national interests, the Associated Press reported.

The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.
As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.
“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said.
“Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.
“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.
Kaseya said leaders around the world should realise that although the brunt of the health crisis is affecting Africa at the moment, the situation could change. “We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”
This outbreak, the 17th in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history.
Ebola is a highly contagious, severe, and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies, such as during funeral preparations.
On 15 May, DR Congo’s health ministry declared an outbreak in Ituri province, though sequencing shows it had begun in February. It has now spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last week, in west Africa, Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.
France is the only non-African country to have confirmed a case of Ebola so far – a doctor who had returned from DR Congo – in June.
The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way. The results should be available in three to six months, said Kaseya.
Of the total 10,091 cases, 10,060 have occurred in DR Congo, with 4,887 deaths. Two people have died in Uganda, and two in Kenya.
The response to the crisis has been hampered by inadequate protective equipment and unpaid health worker wages, leading to strikes. Conflict in DR Congo as well as mistrust towards officials in affected areas, misinformation and global aid cuts have further complicated the situation.
Kaseya will convene a meeting of African health ministers on Wednesday to urge greater cross-border cooperation. He wants governments to introduce screening and testing for people coming from affected regions at points of entry and exit.
“The main message to ministers is that they have to understand they could be affected, and we don’t want them to be surprised by what could happen,” he said.
At a meeting in November with African heads of state, Kaseya will call for a “corridor of peace” in conflict areas. “Currently, we have colleagues in Ituri who want to go and support the population, but they cannot because of insecurity,” he said. “I have to say to leaders, this outbreak is not for rebels, it’s not for the official army, it’s for everyone. Ebola can affect everyone … We need to come together to have a kind of agreement on how to protect each other.”
Kaseya called for a global effort to fund the response. He said governments had pledged $3bn (£2.3bn), but that more than $2bn was still outstanding. African countries had committed $120m, he said, while the rest is meant to come from international donors including the US, the UK and the EU.
“We need this money now,” he said. “We must understand that failure to provide funding now to African countries [will result in more being spent] because the outbreak will continue to move. If we have other countries affected we’ll be talking about trillions of dollars because it will require a lot of support to stop this outbreak.”

Shendi, Oct 28: More than 100 people were killed in a Sudanese military drone strike on a busy market in Nyala, the capital city of the South Darfur province in southwestern Sudan, said Emergency Lawyers, a rights group tracking violence in the country, in a statement Tuesday.
The strike, which it says happened Monday evening, also injured 113 people. The group said many of those killed and injured were women and children. The group blamed the Sudanese military for the strike on the market, condemning the attack.
“This massacre transformed a civilian marketplace into a scene of mass killing and injury and is an assault that threatens the lives of residents and compounds their suffering amid the ongoing war,” the group said in a statement. It called for an independent investigation into the strike.
Doctors Without Borders, which is also known as Médecins Sans Frontières, or MSF, said earlier that 36 bodies arrived at its hospital in Nyala and reported seeing 150 injured in its emergency room. Nyala, the capital of South Darfur province, is controlled by the paramilitary group Rapid Support Forces, which has been fighting with the Sudanese army since 2023.
Drone warfare has been a staple of this war but in recent weeks, a massive escalation of drone strikes by both the RSF and the Sudanese army has killed hundreds. Both warring parties have increasingly launched explosive-laden drones that, in multiple cases, targeted civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, dams, schools, markets and displacement camps. Drone strikes have become the deadliest threat to civilians in this conflict, according to the UN.
The conflict has created the world's largest humanitarian crisis, with about 34 million people — almost two out of every three Sudanese — needing assistance, according to the UN.
Sudan's war started in April 2023 when tensions between the military and the RSF exploded into open fighting in the capital, Khartoum, and spread across the country.
Previous strike leaves parts of Sudan without power
Large parts of Sudan's capital were without electricity for more than 12 hours Tuesday after a drone strike on a major power substation, according to an electric company official.
The attack left hospitals and bakeries dependent on generators and limited water supplies across Khartoum.
The state-run Sudanese Electricity Distribution Company acknowledged “serious damage and technical faults” to the distribution network and several main stations and power lines but didn't explain the reason in a statement. It apologized to residents across Khartoum state for repeated and prolonged outages.
A company official, speaking to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the media, said a drone attack hit the Al-Markhiyat transformer station in Omdurman, on the outskirts of Khartoum. He said it is the second to hit the station this year, blaming it on the country's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The RSF has been at war with the Sudanese military for more than three years. Sudan's war began in April 2023, when simmering tensions between the military and the RSF exploded into open fighting in Khartoum and spread across the country.
Deadly drone attacks across Sudan have been carried out by the two rival forces. But those attacks have become rare in Khartoum since the Sudanese military took control of the capital in May 2025, after years of brutal fighting between the military and the RSF.
The UN has expressed concern over the use of drones across Sudan, saying they have been killing civilians, including children, and are disrupting essential services.
The official who spoke to AP said technical teams are still assessing the damage, describing the strike as major. He estimated that 60 per cent of the power supply in the capital could be affected, predicting that water stations will be most affected.
A resident living near the Al-Markhiyat transformer station in Omdurman said he heard a drone shortly before the blast.
“At around 4:30 in the morning, on my way to dawn prayers, I heard the sound of a drone very close by, and just moments later a huge explosion, and the power went out,” Abdel-Hafiz Abdel-Mutaal told AP. “I saw fire burning at the transformer station.”
The city descended into darkness after sundown.
Adel Ali, a resident of south Khartoum, said he was without power and water for 17 hours.
“My main concern is how to preserve my insulin supply which needs a fridge,” Ali, a diabetes patient, said. “Life without electricity is totally paralyzed, and a bread crisis is emerging as many bakeries have shut down.” He said this would drive the price of bread even higher.
The electricity company, in its statement, said power rationing would be longer than usual in all areas until repairs are finished. It did not say when that would be. Technical teams were working around the clock to restore power, it added.
The conflict has killed at least 59,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED, though aid groups say the true toll is likely higher. Over 67 per cent of the country's population is dependent on aid, while 825,000 children face acute malnutrition.
The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, or IPC, a global food crisis monitor, warned last week that the “deteriorating humanitarian situation” across greater Darfur and Kordofan states is worsening, with food insecurity putting these areas at risk of famine.
In a joint statement, over 30 countries, including the United States, United Kingdom and the European Commission, urged parties to the conflict in the country “to lift all impediments on humanitarian assistance.”

Quick Answer
You can build a portfolio website for free without coding using AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Google AI Studio, or Perplexity. Simply provide your details or resume, ask AI to create a personalized website, download the HTML file, and publish it for free using Netlify Drop or GitHub Pages.
A resume is a standard way to showcase your skills and experience while applying for jobs. Most companies still evaluate candidates through resume screening. However, resumes follow a standard template and don’t truly visualize users’ skills.
On the other hand, portfolio sites have become popular for showcasing candidates’ creative skills. However, most portfolio sites were previously limited to developers with web development and website-publishing skills. But thanks to AI, that restriction no longer applies to regular users.
Anyone can now create a personalized portfolio website to showcase their skills and experience creatively without writing code. Web hosting services like Netlify and GitHub also make it easy to publish a simple portfolio site for free.
If you are a beginner, have never written code, and want to publish a portfolio website to showcase your skills and stand out, this guide will show you how to create one for free.
I will show you how to create a free portfolio website using Claude, ChatGPT, Google AI Studio, or even Perplexity, then guide you through a detailed, step-by-step process to publish it for free without writing code.
Table of Contents
How to Create and Publish a Portfolio Website for Free Using AI
How to Create a Free Portfolio Website Using Claude
You can create a portfolio site using any free AI model. First, let’s create one using Claude. If you’re not aware, Claude also offers a limited free version, enough for most users to create a great portfolio site.
Step 1: Go to Claude.ai and sign in or create a free account.
Step 2: Once you’re done, paste this prompt into the prompt box and press Enter. You can modify the prompt to add or remove details, or to guide how your portfolio website looks. Remember that the possibilities are endless. Even if you generate a site, you can edit and customize it later, but the free version is very limited. So, ensure that you specify every detail before submitting your prompt.
Step 3: Now wait for Claude to create your portfolio site. You will see a message such as “Creating site.html” with a timer. Leave the tab open until it finishes creating.
Step 4: Once it’s done, Claude shows a preview of your website in the side panel canvas. You can preview what Claude built. You can also see how it looks on different devices, including mobile, and whether it’s responsive.
Step 5: Next, you need to download the file. To do that, in full screen, click the small arrow icon next to the copy icon at the top right of the screen, then choose Download as HTML and save the file locally on your device.
Once the site is created, you can publish using the steps below. You can also create portfolio websites with other free AI tools like ChatGPT, Google Gemini AI Studio, and more. Those offer better free rate limits than Claude.
How to Create a Free Portfolio Website Using ChatGPT
Unlike Claude, ChatGPT offers a completely free version with much more generous rate limits, letting you create a fully personalized portfolio website.
Step 1: If you don’t have a ChatGPT account, go to chatgpt.com and sign in with your free account.
Step 2: Now, enter the prompt in the prompt box and press Enter.
Step 3: Wait for ChatGPT to plan, build, and write the code.
Step 4: In my case, building a portfolio site took six minutes. You can tap the HTML file to preview it. Like Claude, ChatGPT also opens it in a preview.
Step 5: However, it also offers a direct download option, and when it’s done, click on the download portfolio.html, and it opens a preview, and click on the download icon at the top panel, and select HTML option, and save it locally on your device.
How to Create a Free Portfolio Website Using Google AI Studio
Next, let’s build a free portfolio site using Google AI Studio.
You can also use Gemini to create a website, but here I am using Google AI Studio. It gives access to the latest models, is free to use, and offers plenty of customization options. However, if you are a beginner, it can sound complex, so we created this simple guide to help you understand Google Gemini AI Studio.
Step 1: To create a portfolio website using Google Gemini AI Studio, go to aistudio.google.com and sign in with your Google account. Next, in the sidebar, under the Build section, tap on New app.
Step 2: Now Google AI Studio directly shows the preview on the right side. Since Google offers free rate limits, you can re-enter the prompt and make the changes you want. To proceed, click the code icon at the top of the preview.
Step 3: Now find the index.html option. Google AI Studio creates several project files, but index.html holds your entire website. In the file list, hover over index.html, click the three-dot menu next to it, then click Download.
Step 4: Once downloaded, open the file from your downloads folder and check that everything works properly without breaking anything. However, I highly recommend skipping the Export and Publish options here. Export lets you download the whole project, while Publish hosts the app within Google; both steps are unnecessary if you want to publish a simple portfolio site.
How to Create a Free Portfolio Website Using Perplexity
Next, you can also build a website using Perplexity. The free version allows you to create a simple portfolio site.
Step 1: To do that, go to Perplexity.ai, sign in with your free account, and click on the Ask Anything box.
Step 2: Paste the prompt and tap Send.
Step 3: Wait for Phubloxity to create a portfolio website. Once done, it will show you the portfolio.html file. Click on it to preview.
Step 4: After you check the preview, click the download option, download it as an HTML file, and save it locally on your device.
How to Publish Your Portfolio Website for Free
To publish your portfolio site, there are plenty of options, but in this guide, I will show you two free, reliable options: Netlify Drop and GitHub Pages.
Method 1: Publish Your Portfolio Website Using Netlify Drop
Step 1: Create a free Netlify account. First, go to netlify.com and sign up with your email. You can also sign up using Google or GitHub.
Step 2: Go to app.netlify.com/drop and drop the index.html you created using Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Google AI Studio from your downloads folder, or click the file and select it.
Step 3: Next, it automatically creates a free address. After a few minutes, your project shows as published with a random address such as sunny-tulip-tf52.netlify.app in my case. You can also click on that link to see the live site.
Step 4: However, if you think it can have a better name, open the project settings and change the project name to something short, such as meera-ai. Your address becomes meera-iyer.netlify.app. Make sure your site name is unique, since there will be hundreds of free Netlify sites out there.
Step 5: Once you have hosted the site successfully, you can share your link. Your portfolio is now live for anyone on any device to access it.
Method 2: Publish Your Portfolio Website Using GitHub Pages
Now let’s look at how to publish it for free using GitHub Pages.
GitHub also lets you host a simple website for free, and you can do everything on the GitHub website without installing anything. However, it takes a few more clicks than the Netlify Drop process.
Step 1: First, create a GitHub account. To do that, sign in to your free account at github.com, then go to github.com/new and create a new repository. For example, you can create ramesh.portfolio and set it to public. Remember that free accounts need a public repository for Pages to work. Turn on “Add a README” and finally tap on Create repository options.
Step 2: Once done, you can upload a file to the repository. Click Choose your files or drag and drop the index.html file, and at the bottom type a short message such as “Add portfolio website” and click on the Commit changes button.
Step 3: Once done, open the repository and go to Settings. Then click Pages in the left sidebar. Under Build and deployment, set Source to Deploy from a branch, pick main and / (root), and click Save.
Step 4: Now wait until GitHub says the changes can take up to 10 minutes. Wait for your site to go public, refresh the page, and wait for it to update. Once it’s done, click Visit site.
That’s it. GitHub will create your page under your name using a GitHub subdomain.
Final Thoughts
This is how you can use free AI tools to create free portfolio websites. Whether you are a beginner and have never written code before, you can follow this simple step-by-step process to create your first portfolio website.
If you have never built one and don’t even have an idea of creating profile sites, you can simply upload your resume into the AI tool and ask it to convert it into a portfolio website and generate an index.html page. If you have any issues while deploying the site, let me know in the comments, and I am happy to guide you.

Meta weighs delaying 'alarming' new business terms as backlash grows
The company says it won't make "policy changes" until it consults with publishers.
As Meta faces an escalating backlash over its new terms for businesses, the company says it might push back their implementation as it plans "a full consultation" with publishers. But the company still hasn't changed the language of the terms, which gives the company the authority to scrape the websites of businesses that use Facebook.
The controversial new terms were originally supposed to go into effect October 30, but Meta later delayed it to November 20 after an outcry. Now, Meta spokesperson Andy Stone says that the actual implementation could be pushed back yet again, though Meta still lists November 20 on its website. "We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders," Stone said in a post on X. "We're committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we'd delay implementation of the updated terms. Until then our existing terms remain in place."
We've heard publishers' feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders.
We're committed to getting this right, and as we expect this... https://t.co/t91Q1QU8mu
— Andy Stone (@andymstone) October 28, 2026
Stone's statement comes as Meta has faced an intensifying backlash against the update, which gives it the right to scrape the websites of companies that use Facebook. The new terms state that Meta has the authority to "use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents)" to access businesses websites "in order to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products."
Publishers have raised significant concerns, with one industry group describing the change as "outrageous and probably illegal." A group of Norway-based outlets have also filed a lawsuit against the company over the new terms. This week, California Senator Adam Schiff became the second lawmaker to call on Meta to walk back the changes.
"The breadth of these updated provisions is extraordinary," he wrote in a letter addressed to Mark Zuckerberg. "Meta asserts an alarming opening to bypass technical measures essential to the economic security of news organizations and subscription-based creators, including paywalls, registration gates, and digital subscriber barriers. Meta's updated terms provide no mechanism for businesses to opt out of scraping while maintaining their account presence."
But while Meta is acknowledging the backlash, the company hasn't made any substantive changes to its terms since it removed the word "train" and added a reference to "advertising and business products" earlier this month. Stone has said that the new terms are "not about scraping news sites" and that the company will respect content owners' robots.txt preferences.
But, as legal experts and publishing groups have pointed out, robots.txt preferences are not legally binding. And AI companies regularly ignore these instructions. Meta also makes no reference to robots.txt in its terms, as Schiff points out in his letter. "Without the insertion of specific language codifying Meta's policy to respect robots.txt signals into the latest contractual terms, users lack any reliable means by which to protect their content," the senator wrote.
Meta didn't immediately respond to questions about whether it was planning further changes to its terms.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

The number of registered medical practitioners (RMP) in Keralam has crossed one-lakh mark, and 32.75% of them got their registrations between 2021 and 2025, data collected from the Kerala State Medical Councils (KSMC) till October 8, 2026, show.
According to RTI data collected from the KSMC, there are 1,13,023 RMPs in the State. As many as 31,446 doctors were registered between 2021 and 2025. A total of 5,981 doctors got registered in 2021, 5,734 in 2022, 5,283 in 2023, 7,065 in 2024, and 7,383 in 2025. As many as 2,695 doctors registered with the KSMC till October 8 this year.
K.V. Babu, Kannur-based ophthalmologist and public health activist, who gathered the information, says that 95,993 doctors were added to the list in the last 27 years. “Keralam’s population is around 3.62 crore. Among the above-mentioned doctors, at least some may have migrated to other States or abroad seeking better opportunities. However, if at least 80,000 of them are here, there is one MBBS doctor for a population of 450 people already,” he says. Dr. Babu claims that the consequences of this trend could be unemployment among medical graduates and commercialisation of health care.
Seats fall vacant
“According to reports, hundreds of MBBS seats have fallen vacant in [deemed-to-be universities] in Tamil Nadu this year [after the final round of counselling for the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test for undergraduate medical courses]. A similar phenomenon could happen in Keralam as well. The government should study this issue before giving permission for new medical colleges,” he says.
M.N. Menon, president, Indian Medical Association (IMA), Kerala State branch, says around 5,000 graduates are coming out of medical colleges in the State every year. “Another 2,000 are passing out from other States and countries. Unemployment among new medical graduates is already high. Instead of granting sanction for new medical colleges, the government should improve the infrastructure in the existing ones and deploy qualified faculty members. Also, we are seeing shortage of doctors and faculty members in government hospitals and government medical colleges. The focus should also be on appointing necessary staff there,” Dr. Menon adds.
