Police are questioning staff at a control centre in Spain after at least 68 people were killed and 77 injured when two high-speed trains collided in the country’s second major rail crash this year.
There were 544 people on board the two services between Madrid and Seville when they crashed at around 9am Wednesday morning. The incident is one of Spain’s deadliest rail disasters, and the worst since 78 people were killed when a high-speed train derailed near Santiago de Compostela in 2013.
Passengers were travelling between Madrid and the southern Andalusia region when an express train operated by Iryo was struck by a train operated by Renfe in Toledo. The Iryo train had been stationary due to a signal fault, a person briefed on the disaster said.
Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, suggested that the accident may have been caused by human error, as one of the trains had been told to resume its journey.
“It was the control centre, through its operators, that made the decision to resume traffic, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” he said. “Clearly, it was a wrong decision.”
Local media reported that the Civil Guard and the Railway Accident Investigation Commission are questioning the control centre operator who was managing traffic on the line at the time.
Footage showed a derailed train with several carriages remaining on an elevated section of track while twisted metal, broken panels and wreckage could be seen strewn across an embankment beneath the line.
Survivor Jesús Jerónimo, 54, told El Pais that people were thrown from the train by the “brutal” impact of the collision. He had been travelling in carriage two of the high-speed train en route to Seville, where he often goes for work meetings as a medical consultant.
“I was working on my laptop when I felt a very strong acceleration and I crashed into the seat in front of me,” he said.
“People were thrown from the train. We thought we had derailed. Then, little by little, we got out and saw that our train was tilted. There were many injured people and a lot of people shaken up. I saw papers on the floor and a child who was fine.
“Right now, we were helping the emergency services, holding IV bags with our hands… The firefighters, however, are working on the most damaged section of the train.”
Eduarda, a passenger on the Iryo train, told Cadena SER radio she had initially thought it was making an emergency stop as she was thrown forward by the strong impact. She only realised the seriousness of the accident after seeing injured people and being told to evacuate.
After climbing down an embankment to safety, she saw what she described as a catastrophic scene, with part of the train hanging down the slope and a fire in one carriage.
Emergency responders, including a helicopter, police and ambulances, arrived within about 20 minutes. “I saw dead people,” she said.
Miguel, a passenger travelling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains, said he heard a “massive roar” from the impact.
“We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail. Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train – I imagine it must have been the other one,” he told Reuters.
Andalusian politician Juanma Moreno declared three days of official mourning in Andalusia, from 2pm on Wednesday until 2pm on Saturday.
“We are devastated,” he said. “All of Andalusia stands with the victims of this new railway accident.”
Jesús Pérez Martín, mayor of the nearby town of Los Yébenes, told RTVE he’d heard reports of “mutilations and very serious injuries”. Meanwhile, health minister Mónica García amplified calls from Madrid authorities urging people to donate blood amid the tragedy.
Renfe said it had activated a special line for families of victims and expressed its condolences, while Iryo activated emergency protocols.
Mr Puente said the fatal train crash occurred after a Renfe high-speed train was authorised to continue its journey despite an active red signal because of a stationary train on the tracks ahead, breaking protocol.
Politicians cleared their agenda for the day following the serious crash, with prime minister Pedro Sanchez offering support to all the victims and their families.
“Shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo,” he wrote on X. “I remain in constant contact with the Minister of Transport, and with the president of Castilla-La Mancha.
“Emergency services are working on the ground to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations. My affection, solidarity, and support to all the victims and their families.”
British foreign secretary Ed Miliband said he was “deeply saddened to hear of the terrible train crash”.
He added: “My thoughts are with the people of Spain and all those affected by this tragedy. The UK stands in solidarity with you”
It was the second major train collision this year on Spanish railway lines, after 46 people were killed and more than 120 injured after a high-speed train derailed and collided with an oncoming one on 18 January near Adamuz, in the province of Cordoba.
That incident is still under investigation, but a preliminary report by Spain's Civil Guard in February pointed to defects in the track, rail, or weld between two sections of track as the main hypothesis for it. That crash triggered a debate about the level of investment in railway maintenance in recent years.
Following the latest crash, Jose Trigueros, president of the Association of Roads and Civil Engineers in Spain, renewed these criticisms of Mr Puente.
“It’s unacceptable that our infrastructure is being managed by incompetent people who should be focusing on their Ministry instead of tweeting. The state of our infrastructure is a disgrace. I hold the Minister responsible,” he told Europa Press.
Mr Puente has refused to say whether he’ll resign after a second fatal train collision this year. He said that the railway system is “reliable and safe” but had “some limits”, like every system of transport.

Republicans have an Epstein problem
The ghost of Jeffrey Epstein is haunting the GOP in scores of ads this midterm season.
Eighteen years after his first conviction, and seven years after his much-debated death, the ghost of the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein is suddenly inescapable again.
He’s the subject of scores of midterm campaign ads, each more lurid than the last. A second bill mandating the release of the Epstein files is currently kicking around Congress. And on Monday, House Democrats released a new report alleging that the Justice Department helped cover up details of Epstein’s relationship with President Donald Trump, calling — very aspirationally! — for an independent criminal investigation.
Of course, no one really expects Trump’s attorney general to name a special counsel to investigate the Trump administration. In a statement, one White House spokesperson panned the report as “a desperate attempt by crazed Democrats to distract Americans.” (The timing, just one week before the midterms, does seem pretty fortuitous.)
The document, which runs to 50 pages, draws on public accounts and staff interviews with an unspecified number of survivors, including a former pageant queen who alleges that Trump raped her in 1993. The woman had previously accused Trump of groping her, which a Trump spokesperson dismissed at the time as “fake.”
Go a little deeper
When it comes to Epstein, however, Democrats don’t need a lot of new material to damage Trump. The scandal, and his administration’s handling of it, continue to cast a long, dark shadow over Republicans.
That’s surprising to me, candidly, because the decades-old dealings of even a very despicable sex offender don’t have any bearing on Americans’ day-to-day costs or experiences. And Trump has been able to brush off a lot of other unsavory behavior and associations.
But the Epstein story has lodged in the brains of some voters who helped elect Trump — including young voters whose growing disillusionment could make a big difference in next week’s elections.
Many of these young voters “resent the fact that Trump’s basically become part of the establishment” and see the Epstein files as evidence of that, the political analyst Rachel Janfaza recently told Vox. Some also feel burned by Trump’s campaign promise to release the government’s investigative files on Epstein…and his about-face once in office.
Democrats, sensing an opening, are hammering the issue. Relentlessly so. According to data from the tracker AdImpact cited by NBC News, there are currently more than 500 campaign ads airing across the country that include the words “pedophile” or “predator.”
Many of them reference Epstein or the so-called Epstein files, and three-quarters are backed by Democrats. One recent ad featuring an Epstein survivor, and targeted at Kansas Republican Roger Marshall, slams the incumbent senator’s September 2025 vote to block a procedural measure that would have released the Epstein files. (The Senate later moved to release the files by unanimous consent.)
Another ad, this one in Maine, claims that Epstein’s “business partner” funneled $3 million to Sen. Susan Collins’s super PAC. (Importantly, the connection between Epstein and this purported partner is so tenuous as to be nonexistent.)
These ads will fade after Tuesday, of course. But you haven’t heard the last word on this. Should Democrats win control of either chamber, they’ll gain the power to subpoena witnesses and documents for yet more Epstein investigations.
Some Democratic leaders in the House are already salivating over that prospect.

A company called Steakholder Foods has launched a line of products under the brand name Perfecta. While the meat is 3D-printed, it is made from a formulation of plant material like other plant-based meats are. It is not made from cultured animal cells, which is often what people refer to when they mention "lab-grown meat." It is not clear which grocery stores or retailers are selling Perfecta-branded food, though the company has said its products have reached shelves in certain Northeastern U.S retail locations.
Between September and October, social media users claimed that 3D-printed, lab-grown meat had started being sold in U.S. stores from early September.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) claims the 3D-printed meat "has federal clearance" but will not have a "lab-grown meat" label on its packaging. The post reads, in part:
The first 3D printed 'meat' has federal clearance and is about to be sold in the United States.
Packaging will not say 'lab-grown meat' because there is not a law that requires the packaging to say it was printed.
3D-printed plant-based food is already on shelves in the U.S.
Federal labels for cell-grown chicken and pork fat must be pre-approved and have used the words "cell-cultivated."
The printed food was in stores on September 3 of this year.
The company Steakholder Foods put its Perfecta line into Northeast supermarkets.
The rumor has appeared elsewhere on Facebook (archived) and on Instagram (archived). Numerous Snopes readers also emailed us to ask if the story is true.
In short, on Sept. 3, Israeli company Steakholder Foods, which specializes in making 3D-printing technology for plant-based meats, announced the launch of its 3D-printed, plant-based meat products in Northeastern U.S. retailers under the brand name Perfecta. Therefore, the claim is true.
Steakholder Foods' news release says its "Premium Plant-Based Meat" products were launched at retail locations in the Northeastern United States on Sept. 3, "marking the brand's first commercial placement on U.S. store shelves."
According to the webpage, the launch "focuses on building awareness and consumer trial throughout the Northeast U.S. market while establishing a foundation for broader expansion across additional regions."
It is not clear which grocery stores or retailers have started selling or stocking the products.
Snopes reached out to the company via a contact form on its website for more information. We will update this article if we hear back.
According to Steakholder Foods, the company uses plant-based ingredients and cultivates cells to create what ultimately becomes the 3D-printed meat.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service do regulate "lab-grown" meat and require a label for such products. However, this regulation is specifically for food made with cultured animal cells, not for food made with other kinds of cells, which is what Perfecta products consist of.
Snopes reached out to both the FDA via contact form and the FSIS via email to confirm that there are not similar kinds of regulations for food made with other cultured cells, such as plant cells. Additionally, we asked both agencies to confirm if Perfecta products had received federal approval, as the above Facebook post states. We will update this story if we receive responses.
Based on how the product boxes appear on the website, there does not appear to be any text identifying the food as 3D-printed or made with cultured cells. The boxes do clearly identify the meat as "premium plant meat" and "plant-based."
Manufacturers of plant-based meat products usually have to process their ingredient mixes in a way that allows them to mimic the texture of conventional meat. According to the Good Food Institute's Asia-Pacific website, the most common processing method requires putting shear stress on the ingredients to align them into a meat-like texture. There are several other methods of processing plant-based meats, including 3D-printing.
For further reading, Snopes previously fact-checked a claim that a plant-based meat manufacturer was 3D-printing meat products in the Netherlands in 2024.

If you were anything like me as a kid, trick-or-treating meant one, maybe two, pillowcases full of candy every Halloween.
Republicans are coming for your blue M&Ms
Why your Halloween candy might be a little less colorful this year.
And as fun as collecting all that candy could be, the real fun began when I got home and dumped my winnings onto my bedroom floor. That’s when the sorting began.
I had some very specific rules: The usual suspects — think Smarties, Tootsie Rolls, and Dum Dums — went into one pile. Fun-size chocolates, like Snickers, Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups, and Baby Ruths, went into another. And then there was my prized pile: Skittles, Warheads, Starbursts, and Sour Patch Kids. Those were meant to be eaten slowly throughout November. The rest was fair game.
The ways we sort and eat our Halloween candy are decided by some very particular, personal rules. But Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. would like to add another distinction: Which candies are made with artificial dyes?
Kennedy’s ire for synthetic food dyes is years old, and they’ve become a major target of his Make America Healthy Again movement. Last year, he announced a plan to remove “petroleum-based synthetic dyes” from foods, arguing that companies “shouldn’t be feeding it to the rest of us.”
That plan has become a multimillion-dollar problem for Mars, the maker of M&Ms, which promised customers last year that they would create an all-natural version of their tasty chocolatey treats. As the Wall Street Journal reported this summer, however, its latest offering is missing one of the most iconic colored M&Ms — the blue M&M.
M&Ms aren’t the only snack food in Kennedy’s crosshairs: He has called out Doritos, Cheez-Its, Cap’n Crunch, and gummy bears, saying their ingredients include “a lot of poisons.” On Fox News, he described what children eat as “food-like substances” and also said that “some of it was made in petroleum refineries.”
In reality, the evidence is more complicated, because the Food and Drug Administration has long considered many of these approved synthetic dyes to be safe under its rules, while acknowledging that some children may be sensitive to them. Kennedy’s sweeping accusations go much further.
Still, pressure from Kennedy and those in the MAHA movement has led many companies to rethink the recipes of your favorite snacks. But producing those alternatives isn’t easy or cheap, as the story of the blue M&M illustrates.
Jesse Newman, a food reporter for the Wall Street Journal, went inside a Mars factory in Topeka, Kansas, to see the process for herself. She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about why blue is so difficult to produce naturally, and what changing a candy’s color actually accomplishes.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
The Secretary of Health and Human Services, RFK Jr., has some issues with the blue M&M. What, what exactly happened? How did it draw his attention?
He is not a fan of any sort of chemical. He’s really concerned about toxins in our food. And Blue 1, which is the food dye that makes blue M&Ms blue, is a synthetic chemical.
He really takes issue with artificial dyes. He believes that they cause hyperactivity in kids, some neurological challenges. He thinks artificial dyes are linked to cancer.
As a member of the Trump administration, he formally set out to get them removed, didn’t he?
Oh yeah. He’s been putting a lot of pressure on the industry to strip artificial dyes from all kinds of products.
What do we know factually about artificial dyes? We hear that they’re bad for us. We hear that a lot of things are bad for us. We’re all still alive and kicking. Are artificial dyes really detrimental to our health?
The FDA for decades has said that there are nine artificial dyes approved for use in food. And they said that those artificial dyes are safe and have said so for years and years and years, as have other global bodies, so long as they’re used in accordance with some of the standards that the FDA laid out.
A California state agency has found that dyes are linked again to hyperactivity in children. And the FDA itself has said, ‘Okay, we think that these dyes are safe for the vast majority of kids, but some kids might be more sensitive to them than others.’
So I think the real issue is that it’s a chemical doing it. They’re purely cosmetic. They don’t do anything except color food. There is no nutritional benefit that you are getting from these dyes. And so do we need them? Absolutely not.
I think one of the issues is that if you’re looking at the ways our food contributes to health problems, artificial dyes are probably pretty low on the list.
You went inside a factory where they make M&Ms, and you looked at how they’re trying to make this happen. Tell me everything.
I went to this plant in Topeka, Kansas, to see how they were made. And it’s a massive industrial food plant, where they mix these colors and spray them onto these small chocolate orbs, which they refer to as lentils.
The M&Ms move through the plant, and they arrive at these massive [machines] that they call pans, but they look like big tumble dryers. And the M&Ms just tumble around in these pans, and the color is sprayed on. It’s a very, very industrial process, millions of M&Ms a day. And the challenge that Mars has now is making that happen with a natural dye instead of an artificial one.
A blue natural dye is the challenge. What are the problems?
They’ve been working on this for years. And they went with a product called spirulina, which is made from algae. But spirulina comes with a host of problems that they are now dealing with.
Blue 1, which is the artificial dye, arrives at the factories as a liquid. And they pour it into these mixers and they mix it up with this sugary syrup and it’s pretty easy to handle. Spirulina arrives as a powder. So now you’re mixing a powder into this same mixture, into the same recipe, and that is very different.
Because spirulina is a protein, the resulting mixture becomes a lot thicker. What they found was that the mixture containing spirulina would really clog up the piping. It was getting stuck. It moved less smoothly through the pipes.
Also because it is a protein, it was starting to coat and build up on the inside of the machinery. And when that happens, it’s a food safety hazard. It can mold; it can cause problems. For many reasons, it was a challenge to handle.
How much did this all cost?
I should say it’s not done. Mars wouldn’t give me an official figure for how much they spent. But they said that they are spending millions and millions of dollars.
They’re having to retrofit their plants, essentially. Mars said that they’re having to change about 300 types of machinery in their plants. It’s a real investment. And at the end of the day, it all comes down to cost.
What did they actually end up getting done? What was the outcome here?
Mars said what they committed to was that they were going to release a new version of their M&Ms and a few other of their products this year that were made with natural dyes instead of artificial dyes.
They didn’t come out and say we’re eliminating artificial dyes. And so folks should be really clear about that: Their artificially dyed M&Ms aren’t going anywhere. They are still on shelves.
What they said is that they’re going to come out with an option that is naturally dyed. So they tried to do that. And what they found was that they couldn’t do it at a cost that was acceptable to them. With the blue and with the spirulina, it would have been far too expensive to make it work at scale. We’re talking millions and millions and millions of M&Ms per day.
They had problems making the green, the blue, and the brown M&M because, if you go back to your elementary school color theory, they needed blue to make all of those M&Ms. Ultimately they said, “Okay, we can do green. There’s little enough spirulina in the green to make the green M&M.” But blue and brown, they are not able to get there yet due to the amount of spirulina that those colors require.
And so earlier this year, they launched their naturally dyed version of M&Ms with red, orange, yellow, and green M&Ms. And if you take a look at this bag, my colleague referred to these as autumnal. They look very autumnal.
They look sort of muted. 
You know, it really isn’t the same. It looks like a mature person’s M&M.
At the end of the day, what are the changes to the M&Ms? Let’s say I go online and get the natural dyed ones. What does that mean for my health? Am I now a healthy and virtuous person if I’m eating the autumnal M&Ms?
It means very little.
I would say you are, hopefully, still enjoying that sugary treat and the pick-me-up in the afternoon as you’re starting to tire. But you’re still eating candy; you’re still eating sugar. It really hasn’t changed very much.

A shark went astray and captured Korea's heart - will she finally make it back to sea?
- Published
As soon as a large shark was spotted in a canal in Busan - a bustling shipping hub and beach city on South Korea's south-eastern tip - marine biologist Kim Hyun-woo was drafted in to rescue it.
He got the call in mid-September, on his way home from a business trip tracking shoals of mackerel to aid fishing vessels. Despite being one of the country's leading shark experts, he never thought he'd be asked by the coastguard to actually save one.
South Korea is no stranger to sharks but one this size, in a shallow, concrete canal right by the world's seventh busiest port, was unheard of - until now.
With an excited crowd already gathering at the waterfront, his team from the National Institute of Fisheries Science had to move fast.
The first task was to determine the species.
Some sharks are more dangerous than others. The star of the 1975 blockbuster Jaws, the great white shark, is known to attack and kill humans.
The specimen in Busan was found to be a female dusky shark, a species linked only to two deadly attacks. Still, Kim feared someone in the crowd might jump or fall into the canal.
The shark had to return to sea.
A small coastguard ship made an initial attempt using an electrical deterrence device, which generates a weak current that sharks avoid.
They're usually used after sightings near popular beaches. But after five hours, officials determined this particular shark was too large and fast for the device.
Kim changed tack, deciding instead to wait for the shark to let herself out. But that did not happen.
As authorities looked for ways to guide her out of the canal, the stranded creature went viral.
Just hours after she appeared, the council had sent everyone in the city an emergency text alert, urging pedestrians and residents to "exercise caution for their safety".
People rarely visited the park along the canal but because of the message, the place was soon brimming with people eager to spot the shark.
Adoring fans named her Bukangi, from "buk hang", the Korean name of the nearby harbour. Within days, a business trademarked it and Bukangi pins, plushies and T-shirts began selling online.
City authorities joined in, livestreaming the shark and making her their official mascot.
A banner was hung at the entrance of the canal, asking the public to sign a petition "on behalf of Bukangi" to demand the national government's support for the construction of a new 30,000-seater baseball stadium by the canal.
Shark spotting became a team effort among locals and visitors. The unspoken rule was that children were given the front row, and whoever saw Bukangi had to point her out to newer arrivals.
Some self-appointed defenders even patrolled the canal at night to make sure no-one was shining torches or lasers at Bukangi.
More than 1.6 million visitors ultimately flocked to the canal.
The local mayor said the shark brought "the kind of publicity even billions of dollars cannot buy" to the port.
"It's really rare these days for people to come together," said Kim Joo-eun, who came to see the shark with her two nieces. "I feel that Bukangi brought us all together, cheering for her… It's a lot of fun."
But officials couldn't leave Bukangi in the canal.
As September drew to an end, she hadn't been seen feeding for days and was spotted with bloody abrasions on her snout from bumping into the concrete walls.
Prominent marine biology professor Choi Yoon told local media that experts were particularly worried about a "critical" injury around the shark's eye.
At the end of September, Kim's team mounted another rescue attempt. The marine biologist looked back to a 2004 incident in Massachusetts, when water jets were used to drive a great white shark away from a shallow pond.
But when the team tried this on Bukangi, she kept circling back.
On 2 October, they decided to install a net spanning the width of the canal to stop her from returning. She managed to swim around the net and was back within hours.
At this point, Kim started thinking the shark might have problems with her snout's electromagnetic sensors, which she uses for navigation. Or she might have become confused by the loud noises emitted by ships in the harbour.
The reason Bukangi was even in the canal may be a sign of warming seas, the oceans ministry suggests.
It believes she may have followed plentiful fish to warmer waters. Some 50 large sharks were recorded off South Korea's east coast in the first half of the year; four times as many as last year.
With each failed attempt some of Bukangi's newfound fans began demanding she be left in peace.
On Thursday, several showed up with placards and shouted "leave Bukangi alone" and "remove the net".
When a security guard told them to stop, one man cried: "I love you, Bukangi!"
"I am obsessed with her," said Jeong Yo-won, a woman in her 40s. She called the shark a "source of hope and joy" and insisted, "I don't think we should evict her mercilessly like this."
Others thought it was time for her to return home.
"I would stare at her for hours because I was so enamoured by her," a woman said after sighting the shark on her third attempt. "I hope Bukangi would stay, but I prefer that she lives a long and healthy life."
People joked the council should "make an official ID for Bukangi and give a pension", Shin Seungmin said.
"She brought so much fun with her. But she should go and live her normal shark life."
Staying in the canal would seriously jeopardise Bukangi because of falling autumn temperatures, Kim explains. Usually this prompts sharks to migrate to warmer waters further south.
"This canal is far from something we can call a habitat," he adds. "A wild animal cannot stay in a space made strictly for humans."
Eventually, as public scrutiny grew, the oceans ministry took over the rescue operation from the fisheries institute. Around 40 personnel, including divers from Busan's aquarium, were mobilised. A vet was on standby, along with an ambulance in case the divers were attacked by Bukangi.
On Wednesday divers installed two layers of nets, and Bukangi was successfully herded out of the narrow canal into open water. But overnight, she swam back into the canal, diving under the outer net.
This left her trapped between the two layers.
Then on thursday, rescuers removed the outer layer, and Bukangi was seen swimming further and further towards open sea.
Although she did occasionally circle back, the rescue operation had ended.
There have been no sightings of Bukangi in the last few days, which experts say is a positive sign.
Prof Choi believes she may be adjusting to wider, deeper waters.
She is unlikely to have travelled far, he adds, and could reappear over the coming week.
But he is also worried about any injuries she may have sustained. Trapped in the canal, it "kept scraping against [the walls], stripping the skin off its snout and even its pectoral fins", he told local media.
For now, South Korea is holding its breath, hoping Bukangi can find her way back to her home - the open sea.

On October 17, Saturday, even as 19 people were killed and several injured in a stampede at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal in Kolkata, a different scene of chaos unfolded a few kilometres away at Jadavpur.
A bulldozer was brought in by the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) and Kolkata Police to demolish bookstalls of Left parties set up near 8B bus stand of Jadavpur. While locals and Left workers, including CPI(M) and AISA activists, protested through the night to thwart the attempted demolition, the authorities succeeded in bringing down certain bookstalls and damaging others.
Left book stalls have come under threat both from Right-wing fanatics and the administration after chief minister Suvendu Adhikari issued a warning. “You consider Sanatan Dharma to be merely cultural. You do not say Durga Puja; You call it ‘Sharadotsab’. I will tell all Durga Puja committees that if these so-called communists come to set up stalls and do not write Durga Puja, do not allow a single stall,” Adhikari had announced earlier.
Alt News has already reported on alleged attacks on book stalls by BJP workers in several parts of the state.
Same Stalls Set Up For Years
Left organisations, including the CPI(M), AISA, SUCI(C) and Association for Protection of Democratic Rights (APDR), have historically set up bookstalls in and around the 8B bus stand area of Jadavpur. The CPI(M) has been setting up its bookstall there for over 40 years, while AISA’s stall has been set up for more than 10 years. The APDR has been setting up a bookstall for the past four to five years. This year, an RSS bookstall was set up right between the CPI(M) and AISA stalls.
Around 6 pm on Saturday, a joint team of Kolkata Police, Central Armed Police Force personnel and KMC arrived with a JCB earthmover to demolish the Left bookstalls. However, the RSS stall was left untouched.
According to the KMC personnel present at the spot, the Left stalls lacked the necessary permissions. Left parties, however, denied this allegation. Representatives of the Left parties argued that they had paid the required fees to the KMC to set up the stalls.
The administration, however, maintained that paying the fees did not necessarily mean that permission had been granted to set up the stalls. The Left parties, in turn, asked the authorities to show which documents they lacked, while also asking what documents the RSS stall possessed that made it legal. Their requests were repeatedly rejected, representatives told Alt News.
‘Authorities Passed the Buck’
“Police and the KMC workers were only passing the buck on each other. Police said the KMC had sought their help to demolish illegal structures. When confronted, KMC workers said that police had asked them to help demolish our stalls,” said DYFI Kolkata district committee member Sainik Sur.
“We asked police and KMC time and again to show the demolition order. But all they said was that there was immense pressure from higher levels to demolish all the Left stalls,” added Sur.
A similar claim was echoed by AISA state president Ritam Maji. “Police and the KMC made it very clear that the Left bookstalls were illegal, whereas the ‘Sanatani’ stall that came up this year for the first time was legal. We have paid the required fee to KMC and have the receipt of the same, yet they claimed that our stalls were illegal. When we asked them to show documents of the RSS-backed stall, to figure out what permissions we lacked, the police simply said that the top brass of the KMC had requested that the space be cleared,” said Maji.
Besides the earthmover, the administration had also brought a KMC dumper truck near the stalls, generally used to collect and dispose of garbage, allegedly to collect the debris from the stalls and the books, representatives of the Left said.
Hundreds Gather Around Bulldozer
After an APDR stall was partially demolished, nearly a hundred people — locals in the area and Left party workers — gathered near the bulldozer in the evening to prevent it from demolishing stalls. Armed with flags, books and posters, they formed human chains around the bookstalls, forcing the authorities to retreat. CPI(M) central committee member and former Jadavpur CPI(M) MLA Sujan Chakraborty also reached the spot to join the resistance.
Around 1 am on October 18, Sunday, personnel from Kolkata Police, CAPF and KMC workers started assembling near the bookstalls again. An hour later, they again started dismantling the APDR stall.
The SUCI(C) bookstall, set up near Gate 2 of Jadavpur University, was also demolished around this time. The area surrounding the stall was cordoned off by security personnel, and party workers could not prevent the demolition.
CPI(M) Kolkata district committee member Sudip Sengupta, who is in charge of the party’s bookstalls, documented the resistance against the demolition as scores of people stood in front of the JCB earthmover, through his Facebook Live.
After the SUCI(C) stall was brought down, the administration tried to demolish both the APDR and AISA stalls, which were interlocked in a single bamboo structure. Around 3 am, Left activists were again seen forming human chains around their stalls. A section of the activists sat inside the AISA stall as the police and central forces tried to demolish it, ultimately compelling police to retreat.
As the administration tried to bring down the APDR stall around 4:30 am, CPI(M), AISA and APDR workers tried to resist the advance in a unified manner. SFI general secretary Srijan Bhattacharya was seen resisting the administrative forces, who tried to tear down the bamboo scaffolding of the APDR stall.
Subsequently, individuals identifying themselves as KMC workers used machetes to cut the ropes of the APDR stall and bring down the structure, despite the efforts of protesters.
After the APDR stall was demolished, protesters formed a human barricade in front of the CPI(M) stall. Actress Ushasie Chakraborty was among the protesters who held the barricade.
As the standoff continued, CRPF personnel wielded the baton briefly, but it failed to scatter the crowd. Around 5 am, the forces left the spot.
Although the CPI(M) stall was mostly left untouched, the AISA stall suffered extensive damage. AISA activists tore down a section of the stall and rebuilt it on Sunday morning. SUCI(C) and APDR also rebuilt their stalls, and books were sold through Sunday.
“The police informed us that if we dismantled our stall for repairs, they would not allow us to rebuild it. However, we repaired it nonetheless and carried on with our programme,” said Maji.
Trinamool Congress MLA Kunal Ghosh visited the CPI(M) stall on Sunday evening. “I have visited the 8B stall quite a few times in the past. Maybe this time I might have skipped coming here. But after what happened last night, I feel it is my duty to come here and show solidarity,” said Ghosh, with CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh standing by his side.
West Bengal Congress President Suvankar Sarkar also visited the CPI(M) stall on Sunday evening. So did CPI(M) state secretary Md Salim.
Chief Minister’s Warning
On September 10, Adhikari urged Durga Puja committees to deny the CPI(M) space for bookstalls if the party used the term “Sharodotsav”, or autumn festival, instead of Durga Puja. He alleged that the term was part of a concerted attempt to dilute the religious character of the festival and impose communist culture. He reiterated his stance two days later while inaugurating a Ganesh Puja pandal in Keshtopur, a northern suburb of Kolkata.
Following Adhikari’s warnings, on October 14, a division bench of the Calcutta High Court overturned the order of Justice Sougata Bhattacharya’s single bench and declined the CPI(M)’s plea to organise a bookstall in front of its party office in Bongaon in Jessore Road of North 24 Parganas district — a spot where a bookstall by the Hindu Jagran Manch had allegedly been set up.

An analysis of data from wearables, such as daily steps and minutes of physical activity, showed a consistent pattern where one's genetic risk was less strongly linked to depression severity among more active adults.
"Depression is one of the leading causes of disability worldwide, so understanding how we might reduce its burden is important," author Denver Brown, assistant professor in the school of health sciences at Kansas State University, US, said.
"As we move toward more personalised medicine, understanding a patient's genetic risk could help inform conversations about lifestyle, including the potential role of physical activity in helping prevent depression or manage its symptoms," Brown said.
Adding physical activity to a daily routine could therefore be especially beneficial for individuals with a genetic predisposition to depression, potentially helping reduce their risk and ease their symptom burden, the researchers said.
The study, published in the journal Nature Mental Health, analysed data from 23,517 participants of the All of Us Research Program, a nationwide effort in the U.S. to better understand how differences in biology, lifestyle and environment influence health.
"... these findings suggest that genetic and behavioural factors contribute largely independently to MDD (major depressive disorder) onset but interact in shaping symptom expression, highlighting PA (physical activity) as a potential modifier of genetic vulnerability in depression and a potential target for precision mental health interventions," the authors wrote.
The researchers analysed survey responses, electronic health records, genetic data and long-term physical activity data from Fitbit devices.
At the neurobiological level, physical activity enhances neuroplasticity by supporting synaptic plasticity and hippocampal function -- the systems are often dysregulated in depression and implicated in genetic vulnerability pathways, they said.
Exercise also regulates inflammation and improves immune signalling, which the team said is relevant, given growing evidence linking genetic risk for depression to immune and inflammatory signalling.
Further, the researchers said being physically active influences stress reactivity, potentially reducing the impact of genetically mediated stress sensitivity on depressive symptoms.

Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers.
The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II, an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well.
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot, which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.
The Cat Has Left the Bag
The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week.
With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language.
“This vulnerability in the ICMP parser of the EDK2 network stack is interesting in terms of how it affects the chain of trust and the broader ecosystem,” said HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at security firm Dragos. “An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint’s TPM. This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario).”
CVE-2026-97631 is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), which is responsible for allowing servers, storage equipment, and other devices to boot using code downloaded from a local network. During this process—known as the pre-execution environment boot—the driver uses a network listener to monitor for ICMP errors. Because the driver doesn’t enforce a memory copy limit of 504 bytes, overwriting adjacent data, a malicious insider or a hacker who has gained low-level access to a local network can send an error message that appends code past this limit. The IUEFI module running on the CPU then becomes corrupted.
As the official advisory puts it:
The malicious error can be delivered through a simple unicast sent from any network distance to a target device’s IP address, as long as it’s sent during the PXE boot sequence. An attacker can deliver a denial-of-service by causing the boot sequence to hang. When the attacker knows what the target firmware build is, it can plant a “counterfeit event” that executes the malicious code on the CPU in its UEFI firmware environment. The code runs in ring 0, a CPU’s most privileged execution level. Because exploits bypass attestation processes designed to cryptographically prove to remote servers that the hardware is secure, they present a key opportunity for elevating limited privileges.
Yet Another Forever Day
CVE-2026-97631 joins a long list of previously discovered vulnerabilities in UEFI or code that works closely with it. The most severe of them, LogoFail, stemmed from logo images included in the UEFI of just about every hardware maker. Rendering bugs allowed attackers to subvert the chain of trust UEFI enforces and go on to install malicious components before the OS loaded or Secure Boot ran. PixieFail was a vulnerability similar to CVE-2026-97631. It, too, was the result of faulty PXE boot flaws in EDK2. Following discovery of the vulnerability, researchers embarked on multiple fuzzing projects designed to surface other critical flaws in the open source code library. It appears those efforts failed to find this latest flaw.
Other recently discovered UEFI flaws include:
- PKFail, a supply-chain failure resulting from non-production test platform keys, public for more than a decade before they were discovered, used in hundreds of device models;
- BootHole;
- Bootkit; and
- BlackLotus.
Like CVE-2026-97631, exploitation or use of these payloads is appealing because it allows attackers to infect machines early in the boot process, before TPM and other defenses load, so they can inflict maximum damage. Given the ubiquity of CVE-2026-97631, Moore said it’s likely a “forever” bug that will live on in end-of-support systems.
There are important caveats and limitations to exploiting this latest vulnerability. As noted, some level of control over a local network is a prerequisite. That likely limits exploitation to insiders or attackers, such as nation-states or ransomware operators, who manage to gain low-level access inside a network and are looking for a way to elevate system rights. There’s no evidence yet that CVE-2026-97631 provides an initial entry point into a network. There are other hurdles to clear.
“For exploiting the vulnerability itself, an attacker needs to guess specific addresses within the target system, so it’s not something that you can throw a single exploit at any target and get RCE across a diverse range of devices, but it needs to be tuned for each target model/version/configuration since the addresses will change based on those,” Jesse Michael, a principal researcher at firmware security firm Eclypsium, told Ars.
“Unlike some of the previous, high-profile vulnerabilities like BootHole, Black Lotus, and Baton Drop, this vulnerability can be fixed with a basic code fix, which will require deploying a BIOS/UEFI update, but they don’t need to deal with revocations, pk/kek/db/dbx key management updates, or making sure to update OS and provisioning media like you do with Secure Boot bypasses in the bootloader itself.”
CVE-2026-97631 doesn’t affect home and small office users, or any other users who boot their devices solely from disk drives. Instead, it applies only to organizations with machines that boot from local networks, or conceivably from Internet-connected resources. Even then, the targeted firmware must rely on EDK2, as opposed to a different reference implementation, and use the PXE functionality (which is turned on by default).
In an email, Intel said that none of its “commercial products currently under security support” are known to be affected. “Intel does not include the affected EDK2 functionality in its reference code, though it may be integrated by an OEM board vendor or system manufacturer,” the company added. It advised customers to check with their system manufacturer for specific guidance. Publicly available Intel reference code, however, makes reference to EDK2. Further, TianoCore has said that each Intel-supplied UEFI development kit “is a fully validated implementation … for a specific revision of the EDK II source.” Many other Intel documents reference EDK2 as well.
Arm, meanwhile, responded to a list of questions with: “CVE-2026-97631 is not directly applicable to Arm’s product portfolio.” Like Intel, firmware the company makes available also borrows heavily from EDK2. TianoCore has also documented Arm’s reliance on EDK2.
While it’s possible some platforms are free of EDK2 code, it’s prudent for users of all servers to investigate if CVE-2026-97631 affects them.
Questions sent to AMD, Phoenix Technologies, AMI, Microsoft, and Amazon—likely some of the other biggest organizations affected—went unanswered when this post went live. Without concrete answers to questions about the use of EDK2 by organizations like these, it’s impossible to say what or how devices are affected and what actions, if any, these organizations, or their users, should take. Representatives from the TianoCore Project also didn’t respond.
Some readers are likely to be unhappy at the lack of detail. Sometimes—particularly in cases involving botched disclosures that break embargoes months before they’re scheduled to lift—there’s no escaping the lack of actionable information in initial reporting.
Those affected should check with the maker of the firmware being used to boot their systems and ask for guidance. Beyond that, they should consider turning off network boot capabilities at least temporarily if possible. Firmware configurations should always enable security features such as TPM and Secure Boot whenever possible, although those defenses don’t protect against this particular threat. It’s also a good idea to monitor logs for signs of exploitation attempts.

I’m a primary care pediatrician practicing in Pennsylvania. Nearly every day, I hear from parents who say: “I’m scared. How can I protect my baby from measles?”
With more than 1,300 reported cases in my state, 33% in children, the threat of measles in my community no longer feels hypothetical. It’s created a stark divide: Some parents are eager to get their child protected as early as possible, while others wonder if we are overly panicked. As a pediatrician, it is dizzying to have a family clamoring for the MMR vaccine in one room while the room next door adamantly opposes vaccination. During this measles outbreak, my colleagues and I find ourselves trying to avoid unnecessary panic about routine childhood illness, while keeping careful watch for real cases. As a result, health care and child care providers alike need to be re-educated on measles.
Some people have referred to my warnings of the danger of measles as “propaganda” or “fear porn,” perhaps reflecting a leftover pandemic-era skepticism. In early 2020, we did not know how severe Covid would be for children, and in being cautious, public health measures designed to help slow the spread of the virus created social isolation, education delays, and vaccine hesitancy.
While Covid was a novel illness, we have more experience with measles. That history is why public health organizations and pediatricians are concerned about this highly contagious and preventable infectious disease returning. Not only do health care providers worry about and need to communicate to patients the risk of hospitalization (1 in 5 cases, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) and death (1-3 in 1,000 cases) from measles, they also need to share that measles causes several complications including ear infections (1 in 10), diarrhea (1 in 10), pneumonia (1 in 20), and brain swelling (1 in 1,000).
In addition, measles can cause “immune amnesia,” where the immune system forgets its immunity to prior infections, leaving children vulnerable to all the infections they have already overcome. That could put our patients at additional risk and become a burden to the health care system.
I’m grateful that many in my area are taking this threat seriously. Day cares and school nurses send unimmunized children home with non-measles rashes because many are unsure what measles looks like. I understand: Even as a pediatrician of 18 years, I have never seen a case of measles outside a textbook. Many practicing pediatricians share this measles naivete because the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine eradicated measles in the United States in 2000. We often need to grab the most senior physician around who saw measles years ago, or consult an infectious disease colleague to determine if a measles-like rash is something to investigate further with testing.
As we enter fall viral season, the number of “measles mimickers” will only increase. The symptoms of measles sound like every illness a child could bring home from day care: runny nose, cough, red eyes, fever, and rash. This may lead to confusion, worry, and overutilization of the health care system. Therefore, understanding what measles is, and isn’t, becomes even more important.
Pediatricians can reassure families that much of their daily life will remain unchanged. No public health organization suggests major lifestyle changes during the measles outbreak. Much of the decision-making about what activities are “safe” depends on a family’s own risk-taking tolerance. For example, taking an unimmunized infant to a large, indoor family wedding may be non-negotiable to some parents whereas others may seek alternative childcare.
Pediatricians can help families navigate these decisions and guide them on how to continue living healthy lives with minimal interruptions during a measles outbreak.
First, pediatricians should urge anyone who is eligible to get vaccinated against measles with the MMR vaccine. This vaccination routinely starts at 12-15 months of age, with a second dose between 4-6 years of age. But they don’t have to wait that long.
Patients can get their second dose of the MMR as early as 28 days after the first, to increase protection against measles. This is an effective way to ensure that children are prepared if exposed to measles and that we reach herd immunity.
Second, pediatricians should recommend avoiding traveling to outbreak areas if possible. While not all travel is avoidable, measles exposure risk may be a good reason to put off that family long weekend in Amish country.
Third, they can suggest that friends and family who have a cough or cold symptoms stay away from unvaccinated children. The classic measles rash is one of the later symptoms, so sometimes measles is spread by someone who initially has a sniffle that they think is just a cold. This is a time to be more cautious about exposure to sick people.
Additionally, anyone who is unvaccinated and was exposed to measles should not consider themselves safe if they don’t get sick within a few days. Measles symptoms can appear seven to 21 days after exposure. This means that unprotected people need to stay home and away from others for 21 days after exposure.
Fourth, pediatricians should remind families to practice healthy habits with children. Nutritious meals, adequate sleep, regular exercise, and frequent handwashing can help keep germs away and immune systems strong.
Fortunately, most of my patients’ parents have expressed a desire to get their child an early second dose of the MMR vaccine during this outbreak. Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia has given over 16,000 such doses since the outbreak started. Many of these parents are looking to ensure their child is protected, but many are also vaccinating to protect the vulnerable around them: pregnant women, immunocompromised people, and infants.
The most at risk during this outbreak are the vulnerable people who can’t be vaccinated, and those who love them. When less than 95% of a community is vaccinated for measles, herd immunity is lost, meaning there aren’t enough immune people to prevent the spread of infection.
It’s also important that pediatricians’ offices make clear to families that if they are exposed to or have symptoms of measles, they need to call a health care provider first rather than showing up at a clinic. To minimize spread, health care teams need protocols to keep people with measles separate from vulnerable patients and expedite testing. Requesting patients call ahead helps ensure sick people get the right care in the right place at the right time, while protecting others.
The threat here is real. But parents don’t need to panic. We have the tools to end this outbreak. We have eradicated measles before, and through vaccination, we can do it again.
Katie Lockwood M.D., M.Ed., is a primary care pediatrician at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. She and CHOP neonatologist Joanna Parga-Belinkie, M.D., are co-founders of Pediatric Health Chat, an online initiative providing resources for families looking for good information on the latest myths and misconceptions about children’s health.

For the last several years, Readwise has been building tools for power readers. There’s the eponymous product, Readwise, which stores and categorizes your Kindle highlights to help you remember what you’ve read. There’s Readwise Reader, an app for reading newsletters, PDFs, and web articles you’ve saved for later. And now there’s Readwise Books, a full-fledged platform for buying, reading, and talking about books.
Readwise is taking on Kindle and Kobo for ebook supremacy
Taking on Kindle is hard. Beating Goodreads might be really easy.
Readwise Books is currently in beta, available through invite or to existing Readwise subscribers. I’ve been testing the app for a few days, and it’s a much bigger take on reading than most. Tristan Homsi and Daniel Doyon, Readwise’s cofounders, like to call the platform “Strava for reading” because it can track how long, how much, and how fast you read, and it can show that information to friends you make in the Readwise Books app. The app’s homepage is a feed of what other people are reading, with comments and recommendations laced throughout.
“Strava for reading” wasn’t the original goal of Readwise Books, which has been part of the Readwise plan since the beginning. “Literally, Dan and I talked about this when we first met,” Homsi says. “We feel like Kindle could be so much better. We really didn’t think it would take nine-plus years to be able to get to this point.” But it turns out, Doyon adds, that for all their ideas about innovation in books, “no one sits around wanting a better Kindle.” But there is one thing they do wish for: a better Goodreads. “Everybody hates Goodreads.”
In a sense, then, the plan for Readwise Books is to take on Kindle by first taking on Goodreads. The Readwise Books app offers a nice way to track books you want to read, are reading, and have read; it even syncs with your Kindle account to let you track books you’ve bought from Amazon by taking pictures of your starting and ending pages. You can rate and review books and see what others have said. It’s a little Strava, a little Letterboxd, and a lot nicer to look at than Goodreads.
The long-term goal, of course, is to get people to stop buying Kindle books and start buying from Readwise. Homsi and Doyon have spent the last several years working to reach deals with all five of the major US publishers in order to have a competitive library of books available. That meant endless negotiations, security reviews, DRM debates, and more — both cofounders seem exhausted just talking about the process. But eventually, by several small miracles, they got the deals done. And since those deals govern the price of books, and many things about how they’re sold and presented, they bring Readwise to a nearly even playing field almost immediately.
It all took a lot longer than expected, but Doyon and Homsi think their timing might actually be pretty good. Digital book reading continues to grow, particularly among young people; a huge amount of that reading happens on phones and tablets. Meanwhile, a new crop of E Ink devices like the tiny Xteink and the Boox Palma line have expanded the universe of available hardware for a company like Readwise.
Not long ago, Doyon says, they would have had no choice but to build an e-reader of their own. (And he says they still might.) Now, they can just make sure it runs on an E Ink-friendly flavor of Android.
After a couple of days using Readwise Books, I can say confidently I already like it better than practically all of its competition. It’s a much nicer-looking app than anything you’ll get from Kindle or Kobo; it has lots of ways to customize how books look; and at least for now, I’m finding the tracking features compel me to read more instead of annoying me. (Homsi says some early versions of the gamification features were substantially more annoying.) I’ve found a few bugs, and the half-integration with Kindle is a little confusing in spots, but it’s already a really nice place to read.
Of course, I, like millions of other people, already own a Kindle and lots of Kindle books. Switching ebook platforms is hard, and Doyon says he’s not counting on everyone to do it right away. He says he’s hopeful Readwise can persuade existing users to switch, in order to sync their notes and progress more seamlessly. He’s also hoping that the advent of AI, and the ways in which AI reliance may rot our brains, will get a lot of people back into the idea of reading more deeply again. And that a bunch of those people might be looking for a nicer, more social place to do so.

Civil aviation ministry holds fog preparedness meeting for upcoming winter season
The civil aviation ministry reviewed winter fog preparedness for Dec 15-Feb 15, 2027, directing airlines and airports to ensure flight safety.
New Delhi: The civil aviation ministry held the first Fog Preparedness meeting for the upcoming winter season to review preparedness and coordination among stakeholders for the fog season.
The meeting was headed by civil aviation secretary Samir Kumar Sinha and attended by the director general of Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) Vir Vikram Yadav, Chairman, Airports Authority of India (AAI) Puneet Kansal, senior officials from the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS), Central Industrial Security Force (CISF), India Meteorological Department (IMD) along with representatives of Delhi airport and other fog-affected airports and airlines.
The IMD officials stated that the fog season is expected to run from December 15 this year to February 15, 2027.
"The meeting focused on ensuring smooth airport operations and minimising inconvenience to passengers during fog-related disruptions. Emphasis was laid on advance preparedness, timely communication, effective coordination among stakeholders and appropriate assistance to passengers in case of flight delays, cancellations and rescheduling," a release from the government stated.
It also said that the DGCA was emphasised to ensure regulatory oversight, compliance with applicable instructions, verification of aircraft and crew preparedness, and effective passenger facilitation measures by airlines.
Also read: DGCA to carry out final airline audits this week ahead of US aviation body checks
"The AAI and airport operators were directed to ensure the readiness of Instrument Landing Systems (ILS) and Runway Visual Range (RVR) systems, airside safety, adequate terminal capacity and effective coordination for airport operations during low-visibility conditions," it said.
The airlines, in the meeting, were directed to ensure the availability of qualified crew and compliant aircraft for low visibility operations, plan realistic flight schedules and take timely decisions regarding flight operations, the government stated.
"It was emphasised that passengers should receive timely updates through SMS, mobile applications and email regarding delays, cancellations and revised departure times, so that they don’t reach the airport without adequate information about their flights," the statement read.
It said that the IMD was also directed to ensure reliable weather forecasts, regular observations and timely dissemination of weather updates to facilitate operational planning.
"Air Traffic Control and air navigation service providers were instructed to ensure safe sequencing of air traffic, adherence to low-visibility procedures and coordinated traffic management during fog conditions," the government stated, adding that the role of BCAS and CISF in ensuring safe and orderly passenger movement, including terminal re-entry and re-boarding wherever required, was also discussed.
The government also directed airlines to ensure that their respective ground handlers maintain adequate staffing, ensure efficient baggage management and aircraft turnaround, and provide necessary assistance to passengers during operational disruptions.
"Particular emphasis was laid on passenger facilitation during prolonged delays and cancellations. Preparations to be made to ensure adequate staffing at check-in counters, airline helpdesks and customer care facilities. The Secretary emphasised that airlines need to ensure that their helpline desks at the airports are manned by informed and empowered personnel who can adequately address passenger queries," the government said in its statement.
It said that the collective objective is to minimise passenger inconvenience through advance preparedness, timely information, clear operational decisions and effective passenger assistance during the upcoming fog season.

A 48-year-old man with uncontrolled diabetes developed persistent swelling in his left lower limb, followed by high fever and breathlessness. An ankle-joint sample was initially misidentified as Acinetobacter baumannii complex, while findings in his lungs raised suspicion of tuberculosis. Cultures from his blood and joint pus eventually identified Burkholderia pseudomallei -- the bacterium that causes melioidosis. His blood cultures cleared around the 21st day of treatment, and he recovered, according to a case report described by Atish Mohapatra, Assistant Professor, Department of Microbiology, Kalinga Institute of Medical Sciences, Bhubaneswar.
In another report published in 2026, Dr.Mohapatra and colleagues described a 25-year-old patient living with sickle cell disease and type 1 diabetes who developed disseminated melioidosis involving the bones and lungs, with a splenic abscess and pulmonary embolism.
Neha Rastogi Panda, senior consultant, Infectious Diseases, Fortis Hospital, described a case involving a 54-year-old man living with diabetes and chronic liver disease. He had low-grade fever for about six weeks, followed by high fever over 15 days, and a persistent cough for three weeks. He also had swelling and pus discharge from his left foot. A CT scan showed extensive consolidation in the right lower lobe of his lung. Blood cultures and samples collected during bronchoscopy grew B. pseudomallei, confirming pulmonary melioidosis with bloodstream infection.
A study published in The Lancet Global Health, led by Nitin Gupta, Department of Infectious Diseases, Kasturba Medical College, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, assessed high-risk hospitalised adults at 15 Indian tertiary-care centres between January 2023 and December 2025. Culture-confirmed melioidosis was found in 262 of 2,953 patients (8.9%). Of those diagnosed, 50 (19.1%) died in hospital.
The infection and risks
B. pseudomallei is found in soil and water in tropical and subtropical regions. Infection usually occurs when contaminated soil or water enters the body through cuts or wounds. Inhalation of contaminated dust or water droplets and, less commonly, ingestion of contaminated water can also transmit the bacterium. Human-to-human transmission is exceptionally rare.
Melioidosis can cause pneumonia, bloodstream infection, skin and soft-tissue infections, abscesses in organs such as the liver and spleen, septic arthritis and bone infections. It can also affect the kidneys, muscles and prostate. Rarely, infection involves the nervous system. Severe disease can progress to septic shock and multiorgan dysfunction.
Symptoms vary according to the organs affected. Patients may have persistent fever, cough, breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss, painful joint swelling, abdominal pain or localised skin infections. Some develop a slowly progressive illness resembling tuberculosis, while others deteriorate rapidly. The infection can also relapse if treatment is inadequate.
Diabetes is a major risk factor. Chronic kidney, lung and liver diseases, heavy alcohol use and reduced immunity can also increase vulnerability. Dr. Mohapatra says clinicians usually consider melioidosis in high-risk patients with unexplained sepsis, severe pneumonia, deep-seated abscesses or bone and joint infections, particularly when environmental exposure is plausible.
Why diagnosis is delayed
When it comes to diagnosis there are challenges at both the clinical and laboratory levels. Symptoms are often nonspecific, the disease can present in different ways and the incubation period can vary. Clinicians may not suspect melioidosis or send appropriate samples for culture, while microbiologists may struggle to identify the organism correctly.
Automated identification systems can help, but they are not infallible. Like in the above case, the bacterium was initially misidentified as A. baumannii complex. Dr.Mohapatra notes that even systems such as VITEK 2 can misidentify B. pseudomallei. MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry can aid identification, but its cost and limited availability can be barriers. Validated molecular tests, including PCR, can support confirmation where accessible.
Culture of blood, pus, abscess aspirates, respiratory specimens or affected tissue remains central to diagnosis. Depending on the presentation, urine and other clinical samples may also be tested. Multiple specimens may be necessary because infection can involve several organs, and prior antibiotic use can make confirmation difficult. Imaging with ultrasound, CT or MRI can help locate deep-seated abscesses and identify organ involvement.
Madhumitha R., senior consultant, Infectious Diseases and Infection Control at MGM Healthcare, Chennai, says clinicians should consider blood cultures in patients with persistent fever, ideally before antibiotics when clinically appropriate. If melioidosis is suspected, the laboratory should be informed so that appropriate identification procedures can be followed. A history of contact with contaminated soil or water can also help guide testing.
Experts call for better communication between clinicians and microbiologists, training for laboratory personnel to recognise suspicious organisms, and referral pathways to facilities that can confirm difficult isolates. Standardised laboratory procedures and quality assurance are important, particularly where advanced identification methods are unavailable.
Treatment and surveillance
India’s National Centre for Disease Control provides technical guidance for melioidosis treatment in its 2025 manual on zoonotic diseases of public health importance. Treatment has two phases: an initial intensive phase with intravenous antibiotics, followed by prolonged oral eradication therapy to reduce the risk of relapse.
Ceftazidime is an established option for the intensive phase, while meropenem is preferred in severe illness, including septic shock and neurological involvement. Intravenous treatment may last two to eight weeks or longer, depending on severity and the organs affected. Bone and joint infections, neurological disease and deep-seated abscesses may require prolonged treatment. The oral eradication phase commonly uses trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for several months, with longer courses sometimes required for complicated infections.
Dr.Panda stresses that treatment must be individualised according to organ involvement, drug susceptibility, kidney and liver function, tolerability and clinical response. Drainage of accessible abscesses, control of underlying conditions such as diabetes, monitoring for adverse effects and follow-up after discharge are also important. Incomplete treatment can lead to relapse even after symptoms improve. There is currently no licensed vaccine.
The multicentre study found variation across participating centres, with the highest proportions in Odisha (26%), Madhya Pradesh (22.7%) and Karnataka (19.3%) – figures describe the selected hospital populations, not State-wide prevalence. The study also found associations with monsoon admission, outdoor high-risk occupations and groundwater as the main drinking-water source. These associations do not establish causation.
Earlier reviews have found confirmed cases in several Indian States, but differences in diagnosis, awareness and reporting may affect how many cases are recorded. Dr. Mohapatra says India should move beyond identifying melioidosis only when an unusual case appears. Experts recommend a phased surveillance system, beginning with hospitals and laboratories equipped to confirm infection and expanding as diagnostic capacity improves.
Such a system could track confirmed cases, geographical and environmental exposures, antimicrobial susceptibility, treatment regimens, deaths, complications and relapse. Better surveillance, alongside improved diagnostic access and clinical awareness, would help establish the disease burden and guide public-health responses.
Prevention is important especially for people who often come into contact with soil or water. Farmers and others at higher risk should use protective footwear, cover cuts and abrasions, and clean contaminated wounds promptly. Avoiding untreated surface water and informing a doctor about possible environmental exposure may also help reduce risk and guide timely testing.
Improving clinical awareness, access to reliable diagnostic testing and systematic surveillance will be essential to identifying more cases of melioidosis in India and reducing deaths from this potentially life-threatening infection.
