When the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, visited India for the second time this year, headlines concentrated on who he met and where he went.
The fact that Rubio bypassed New Delhi and did not meet the prime minister, Narendra Modi, during his trip last week, and instead traveled to the financial capital, Mumbai, where he met India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (pictured top with Rubio), and business leaders, did not go unnoticed. Nor did his decision to travel to Jamnagar, the small Gujarati town that is home to Reliance Industries’ colossal oil refinery complex.
Bilateral ties between the two countries have come under strain under the second Trump administration, particularly over tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. Yet, Rubio’s return to India just five months after his first visit as secretary of state signals that the country remains useful for president Donald Trump’s ambitions after all.
As director of the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Milan Vaishnav has spent a decade tracking India’s place in the world, particularly its ties with the US. Vaishnav has described Trump 2.0 as “unbound” marking a new era in India-US relations.
Tracking foreign affairs, he told me, is a minefield right now. From the White House’s transactional approach to global alliances, ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and consequential elections around the world, politics is changing at a pace that means all predictions are off the table. “I think anyone who tells you they know exactly what is going on and how it fits into their neat theory of the world is lying to you,” says Vaishnav.
I asked him about the many confusing aspects of the US-India relationship, from the hostile political rhetoric to the US embrace of Pakistan, as well as Rubio’s latest visit.
Trump the deal-maker
Ahead of Rubio’s visit, several commentators noted the secretary of state’s “unusual” itinerary. Vaishnav thought the pre-visit chatter about Rubio skipping Delhi to visit Mumbai and Jamnagar was overblown. “Not every bilateral meeting has to take place in a national capital,” he says.
But that doesn’t mean it wasn’t noteworthy. “I do think the choice of venues was intentional. This administration and, particularly, this president, sees foreign policy through the lens of ‘deal-making’. And if you’re trying to drum up business deals, what better place to visit than Mumbai?” he says.
The Jamnagar visit, where Rubio met Mukesh Ambani, the chair of Reliance, also indicates some politicking. “At a time when petrol prices are extremely high in the United States and are likely to be a major issue in the 3 November midterm elections, the administration wants to show that it is doing everything it can to bring them down. India is a major consumer of oil, but it is also a major exporter of refined petroleum products,” says Vaishnav. “One of Rubio’s objectives was to encourage Reliance and, by extension, India to process more Venezuelan crude [oil],” he added.
While this could present an opportunity for India to advance relations, it’s not a given: the US president remains, after all – and to put it lightly – mercurial.
“The biggest plot twist for me has been the Trump administration’s embrace of Pakistan after the May 2025 conflict with India,” says Vaishnav. Pakistan’s standing in Washington had eroded over the years, especially under Joe Biden, who left office without ever having made a presidential phone call to his counterpart in Pakistan. “Many officials in Congress had grown exhausted with Pakistan’s double game, speaking the language of partnership on the one hand while undermining US interests on the other,” says Vaishnav.
But, after coming to power the second time, Trump thanked the country for its help in nabbing a suspect linked to a 2021 bombing in Afghanistan that killed 13 US service members. This reversal in Pakistan’s fortunes gathered pace after the May conflict with India, which Trump took credit for ending. In June, he welcomed Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, to the White House, after Munir called for the president to be nominated for the Nobel peace prize.
“I chalk up the reversal to a few factors: Trump’s well-known strongman envy, Pakistan’s savvy diplomacy, and the prospect of energy and crypto deals involving members of Trump’s inner circle,” says Vaishnav. For him, it isyet another demonstration of how much weight Trump places on deals, transactions and short-term wins. “For New Delhi, this means Modi’s personal rapport with Trump and 25 years of investment in the bilateral relationship offer no guarantee against a 180-degree reversal in US policy,” he adds.
In a recent piece, Vaishnav’s colleague Sameer Lalwani pointed out that the US relationship with India remains more resilient than the political rhetoric may suggest with quiet, but nonetheless strategic, progress being made.
As Lalwani points out, bilateral trade reached a record high between India and the US in 2025; nearly $68bn worth of AI infrastructure investment in India has been pledged by US technology companies; and the two countries have carried out record number of joint military exercises this year.
The way forward
Despite these wins, in terms of future bilateral relations, “there are at least three reasons for caution,” warns Vaishnav. First, he points to the onslaught of US actions that have dented Indian interests. Trump had imposed a punitive 50% tariff on India in 2025, which was reduced to 18% earlier this year, but without a comprehensive trade deal being reached. Second, on immigration, the White House’s H-1B visa and green card restrictions have disproportionately affected Indian workers in Silicon Valley.
“This has created a real trust deficit on the Indian side, and with good reason,” says Vaishnav. The frustration was on display earlier this month, when New Delhi branded remarks made by the US vice-president, JD Vance, about Indian professionals as “deeply offensive”. Furthermore, Vaishnav argues that while governments and private sector firms might be great at making announcements, they’re not always a guarantee of delivery.
His final caution is how political tensions can have a chilling effect. The trade negotiations offer a telling example: in January, the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, blamed the lack of a trade deal on Modi’s failure to phone Trump, a characterisation that New Delhi has disputed. Vaishnav says: “Much of the progress we are seeing is the product of decisions made years ago. It is one thing to keep existing projects moving, but turbulence in the relationship could make new initiatives a heavier lift.”
If India is serious about making its ambition to be a global powerhouse a reality, Vaishnav thinks there’s a clearcut way to win. “I would argue that the most important investment is political – ensuring India remains a robust, inclusive, participatory democracy,” he says. “On the economic front, India has made massive new investments in physical and digital infrastructure. But the returns on those investments will be limited unless the government doubles down on reforms: more efficient dispute resolution, an impartial legal system, even-handed tax enforcementand regulatory certainty.”
Ultimately, neither side can afford to treat the other as expendable. The test now is whether strategic foundations can hold at a time of global political upheaval.
What else we’re reading about
Student protests | Bikaner House, one of Delhi’s premier arts venues, asked visual artist Raihan Vadra to remove from his show more than 70 photographs that featured recent student protests. Vadra, the son of the Congress leader, Priyanka Gandhi, defended his work and also refused a request to remove images featuring the national flag. In a press statement, the venue said certain photos were “inconsistent” with its policy.
Fashion | Designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee, celebrated for his maximalist aesthetic, hosted a Diwali party at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. In September, he unveiled a high-jewellery collection inspired by the Byzantine, in collaboration with the museum.

Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Film-maker Ritu Sarin, director of the annual Dharamshala international film festival, which runs from 29 October to 1 November, suggests a film from this year’s lineup:
“Shot over three years on real locations, Anmol Sidhu’s sophomore feature, Flowers of Acacia, follows wedding orchestra dancers in rural Punjab with a gaze that allows all the large brutalities and smaller intimacies to shine through. Sidhu’s confident, consummate grasp of the medium is on full display in terrifying scenes that stretch to the edge of what is palatable. The camera refuses to look away.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
7,633
That’s the number of trees Mumbai’s municipal authorities authorised to be felled over five months this year, to make way for development works, according to the Indian Express. Of these, about 3,500 will be permanently removed, while the rest will be replanted elsewhere.
Vibe check
Prarthna Singh has consistently placed the female identity at the heart of her artistic practice, documenting Indian women’s aspirations and acts of rebellion in male-dominated spaces. When commissioned to photograph rkivecity’s menswear line, made from discarded clothes reworked into new garments, she turned that same gaze outward. The setting was the acclaimed 151-year-old Mayo College boys’ school in Ajmer, Rajasthan – Singh attended the linked girls’ school, and credits it with shaping her rebellious spirit.
“I was thinking about how I could bring a sense of intimacy and camaraderie of boarding-school life to the images, because that exists,” she told me. One image shows a pair of hands holding another boy’s jacket, the faces left out of the frame, so the garment stands in for the familiarity they share. Seeing this work against the backdrop of students taking to the streets to fight for their rights lends the series a lasting significance. “This was just my way of showing all of this is connected. These worlds are not existing separately,” said Singh.

A Christian family was allegedly attacked at their home in West Arjunda village, Panskura, East Midnapore district of West Bengal, on the evening of October 26, Monday. An FIR was registered in connection with the case on October 28, Wednesday at Panskura police station.
Parvati Hembram Soren (27) alleged that a mob of around 30 people, including members of their extended family, neighbours and others who associated themselves with the Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP), assaulted her, desecrated Bibles present in their home and threatened them to renounce Christianity and accept Hinduism.
Some of the accused named in the FIR include extended family members of Parvati and her husband, Santu Soren, namely Gorachand Soren, Balaram Soren, Sombari Soren, Mamani Soren, Arati Soren, Arjun Soren, Logen Hansda, Geeta Soren, Kanka Soren and Nera Bou.
Parvati, Santu, and his uncle and aunt had embraced Christianity over a year ago and is associated with Christ the King Mission Church under the Balichak Catholic Parish. Parvati’s sister-in-law had also embraced the faith, but since she is a minor, her conversion certificate has not yet been published.
The alleged assault comes within days of a family in Patlapur village, Paschim Midnapur district, being allegedly subjected to three days of physical assault, sexual harassment, and continuous intimidation by a group of men who identified themselves as belonging to the Hindutva outfit Bajrang Dal.
ALSO READ: Christian families in Bengal attacked, allege ‘rape and death’ threats by ‘Bajrang Dal’ members
‘Dragged, Slapped, Kicked, Clothes Torn’
Speaking to Alt News, Parvati recounted that on Monday evening, she was praying with her husband and their two children while playing Christian religious songs and carols on a speaker. At around 7:30 pm, a group of approximately 30 people allegedly barged into their home. “Initially, they verbally abused us, snatched our Bible and threw it away. Then, they locked my family members in a room and beat me. They slapped, kicked and punched me,” she alleged.
Hearing her screams, Parvati’s other family members tried to intervene but were unable to protect her because of the sheer number of people attacking her, she added.
Further, the attackers allegedly attempted to tear up the Bible and set it on fire. When Parvati tried to stop them, they allegedly grabbed her by the hair, dragged her out of her house and assaulted her again. “Sombari, Mamani, Arati, and Geeta grabbed me by my hair and dragged me out of the house. They also tore of my clothes,” Parvati alleged.
“I have endured several injuries due to this physical assault and have immense pain in my body. Even my sister-in-law was beaten,” she alleged, adding that her husband was spared the physical assault because he was holding one of their children, she said, although he was verbally abused. The assault continued for approximately an hour, after which Parvati became unconscious.
Parvati underwent medical tests at 10:36 pm on Monday. The following morning, October 27, she went to Panskura police station to lodge an FIR. “The police took my written complaint and said that they would do a preliminary investigation and then lodge an FIR,” she said.
Parvati further alleged that her sister-in-law was recording the incident, but the attackers quickly snatched the latter’s phone, deleted the videos and photographs, before throwing the phone to the ground and damaging it. “Later they took all four Bibles from my house, destroyed them and threw them into a nearby pond. The mob also tried to break open my aged uncle-in-law’s home, located next to our house,” she added.
‘Death Threats, Social & Economic Boycott’
Moreover, Parvati told Alt News that the attackers repeatedly demanded that the family renounce their faith in Christianity and return to Hinduism. They allegedly threatened to wreak havoc in their home, harm or kill family members, and impose a social and economic boycott if they refused to comply.
While Santu works as a toto driver, Parvati works on the farmlands. Their neighbours, who were also part of the assault, have allegedly forced them to plant Tulsi and Manasa plants in their courtyard and perform Hindu rituals. “To continue harassing us, they have tied two cows in our courtyard, and the cows keep littering near our water tap,” she claimed. Additionally, the neighbours are allegedly constructing barriers along the local pond’s bank to prevent Parvati’s family from using the pond water.
During the incident, the family managed to contact a local volunteer of Bangiya Christiya Pariseba (BCP) in Monirampur, who alerted the organisation’s legal team. Subsequently, advocate Aditya Tewary contacted Parvati.
However, the lawyer told Alt News that a man answered the phone after the attackers allegedly snatched it away from Parvati. “I called Parvati, but a man answered the phone, who said he was from Vishva Hindu Parishad. He told me, ‘We are here to set things right. We have received information about Christian conversion here’. As soon as I told him I’m an advocate, he disconnected the call,” Tewary said.
Not An Isolated Incident
This is not the first time that the Soren family was allegedly harassed and intimidated for practising Christianity. On October 11 around 6 pm, members identifying themselves as belonging to Bajrang Dal, along with their extended family members, arrived at their home and demanded that they renounce their faith in Christianity and return to Hinduism, Parvati told us, adding that she had then filed a complaint via email on October 12.
Even then, she named members of her extended family in the complaint as she did not know the names of the Bajrang Dal men. However, no action was initiated by the police.
Police Inaction
“When we were trying to call the police [on Monday], they told us that they [the assailants] would call the police themselves,” Parvati said.
However, she alleged that the police did not reprimand the assailants and instead schooled her and her family. “Instead, shockingly, the police told us to perform and practice our religious rituals inside our house and asked us not to use a speaker, claiming it to be an attempt to convert others,” she said. “Our Hindu neighbours keep playing religious songs on loudspeakers. We have never complained. How can playing songs on a small bluetooth speaker convert others?”
Upon being contacted, Panskura police told Alt News that they do not have the authority to brief us on any case and asked us to contact the headquarters. We then contacted East Midnapore Superintent of Police (SP) and Additional SP, but the phone went unanswered.
The FIR has been lodged under Sections 115(2), 3(5), 303(2), 324(4), 329(4), 351(2) and 76 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, pertaining to voluntarily causing hurt, common intention, theft, mischief, house-trespass, criminal intimidation, and assault or use of criminal force against a woman with intent to disrobe her, respectively. Despite the two complaints, no arrests have been made yet.
‘Don’t Give Them Loan’
Meanwhile, Parvati told Alt News that the harassment continued on Wednesday when a representative from a loan agency visited her home to process an application submitted by her and her husband. According to Parvati, her extended family surrounded the representative and allegedly pressured him not to process the loan because the couple had converted to Christianity.
“We bought a toto, but now we do not have enough money to pay the remaining instalments. That is why we had applied for a loan. Today, a person from the loan office visited my house. When he was leaving, my attackers surrounded him and asked him not to give us a loan, because we are not Hindus. If the police do not lodge an FIR and protect my family and me from this daily harassment, then we have to commit suicide,” she said, adding that even though she demanded police protection, her demand went unheeded.

Typhoon Champi was declared the strongest storm of the year so far after recording sustained winds of 185mph last week. From late Thursday to early Saturday, the typhoon battered Taiwan and Japan’s southern islands. Champi approached the east coast of Taiwan before the centre of the storm turned south along the Yilan County coastline, looping offshore and then tracking northwards away from the island. The storm brought gusts of up to 141mph and 48-hour rainfall totals of more than 620mm to parts of Yilan.
So far, the death toll remains at one, with 527 reported injured. There were widespread power outages, with more than 288,000 houses having no electricity at one point, although most had since been reconnected. Champi has been downgraded to a tropical storm as it rapidly weakens to the south-west of Japan’s mainland on Monday.
For the fourth time in October, parts of Greece are at risk of flooding. In the early part of this week, low pressure will bring severe thunderstorms and longer spells of heavy rain to much of the country, and this will be followed by a deep area of low pressure passing across southern areas.
The national meteorological agency issued warnings for Monday, with 30mm-60mm of rain forecast in a 12-hour period across central areas, and50mm-80mm in the north-east Aegean Islands. Forecast models indicate the potential for similar totals in a 12-hour period between Wednesday and Thursday, making further flooding possible.
A low-pressure system developed into a cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal this weekend. Cyclone Arnab is expected to move towards the north Andhra Pradesh and south Odisha coast by Wednesday. The India meteorological department has alerts in place for extreme heavy rain, thunderstorms and strong surface winds across the eastern side of the country.
Models are forecasting gusts of up to 85mph, and six-hourly rainfall totals of up to 100mm, as the storm makes landfall, currently expected on Wednesday. From then, the system is set to drift to the north before gradually dying out over north-east India at the end of the week.

Climate change must be declared a "global health emergency" to shape governments' policies after heat caused three million deaths between 2016 and 2023, a report in The Lancet said Wednesday.
Published by the British medical journal ahead of the COP 31 climate summit in November, the 10th edition of the report brought together 146 researchers from 30 countries to assess the impact of climate change on the health of the world's population.
It said there were a record 710,000 heat-related deaths in 2023 with more than 70% of that toll linked to human-caused climate change.
Marina Romanello, the executive director of the health and climate research project Lancet Countdown, said there were "three million heat-related deaths globally in an eight-year span since the Paris Agreement" of 2015.
"That's roughly equivalent to the entire population of Wales being wiped out in the space of eight years due to heat," she told a news conference.
And "68% of those deaths are directly attributable to climate change."
The legally binding international climate treaty adopted in the French capital aimed to limit global warming to well below 2C and pursue efforts to keep it to 1.5C compared to pre-industrial levels.
Climate change impact
Romanello said the global health emergency due to climate change should have "an integrated approach so that we're not responding to emergency after emergency".
Instead she called for "a cohesive long-term response that builds resilience, builds capacities, and builds the possibilities of countries to avoid further emergencies moving forward".
To determine the share of deaths attributable to warming caused by human activity, the researchers compiled the number of heat-related deaths recorded by states, then subtracted those that would have occurred in the absence of climate change, said Professor Ollie Jay of the University of Sydney.
Jay said the intensity and frequency of periods of intense heat were amplified by climate change, pointing out that last year an extreme drought affected more than half of the world's land surface for at least one month.
Economic cost
By reducing worker productivity, warming has cost the global economy more than one trillion dollars per year over the past three years, the researchers said.
Southeast Asia and Africa, the hardest-hit regions, are estimated to have lost the equivalent of 3.9 percent and 3.2 percent of their GDP, compared with 0.2 percent for Europe and 1.5 percent for the Americas.
However there has been concrete progress in some areas.
Since 2016, 56 of the WHO's 194 member states have adapted their health and early-warning systems to anticipate extreme events.
Investment in clean energy reached $2.1 trillion in 2025 -- double that of the amount invested in fossil fuels, which cause climate change.
However fossil fuels still account for 80 percent of global energy, causing air pollution that results in 2.73 million deaths per year, the study said.
Meanwhile, roughly 323,000 deaths have been avoided in "at least" 77 countries where air pollution from fossil fuels has fallen since 2016, according to the report.
Although funding for climate-related medical research has increased sevenfold to reach $316 million in 2024, 84% of these funds go to researchers in wealthy countries, even though the least developed nations are the most affected by the growing climate-related health threats.
Romanello said this year for the first time the researchers' work was complicated by the disappearance of certain data sources, particularly from the United States, such as fossil fuel subsidies, which have not been made public by the US authorities.
And for the past two years, global geopolitical instability has pushed global warming and its health impact into the background, she said, stressing that inaction was exacerbating the situation.

Scientists at the ICAR-Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI) have developed a new potato variety called ‘kufri jamunia’ that has higher levels of anthocyanins, vitamin C, and certain micronutrients than regular potatoes. The Central government has been promoting it of late as a means to address hidden hunger, i.e. when people consume enough calories but still do not receive the necessary nutrients.
Usually, experts who fortify foods, focus on items like rice and iodised salt, which a large number of people in India consume, often throughout the year, thus ensuring the added nutrients are delivered to a significant chunk of the population. Kufri jamunia is however a potato, which people in India generally consume much less consistently than rice or salt, and the micronutrient intake depends on preparation methods and how the body absorbs them.
What makes it different
Kufri jamunia offers nutritional advantages, but they are substantial in some aspects more than others. Questions also linger about its ability to resist disease and retain nutrients through different Indian cooking methods.
The variety reportedly has a mealy texture. In one CPRI assessment involving 64 people, 95% rated its overall acceptability ‘good to excellent’ and 56% said its taste was very good. This study cohort, though, is too small to generalise the results. CPRI researchers themselves have proposed that kufri jamunia can be used in curries, parathas, soups, baked goods, and dehydrated flours.
Importantly, kufri jamunia potatoes also have purple skin and flesh, which could affect consumer interest. Research on other biofortified foods has already shown that while people are generally willing to pay modest premiums — the national average cost of ordinary potatoes purchased wholesale is around ₹17/kg — whether they accept a new variety depends on its appearance, their awareness, taste, and of course local preferences.
How was is developed
The CPRI team developed the kufri jamunia variety by crossing two potato lines, MS/8-1148 and CP4242, in 2015. MS/8-1148 is high in vitamin C whereas CP4242 had purple skin and flesh. The result, formally called MSP/16-307, could naturally accumulate higher concentrations of specific nutrients as it grew. The team then conducted trials, including multi-location testing, in 2021-2023.
Based on the trial data, the Central Sub-Committee on Crop Standards, Notification and Release of Varieties for Horticultural Crops approved the variety in mid-2024 and the government notified it in November that year. The variety’s plants produce 10-12 medium to large tubers each and mature in around 90 days. The purple colour comes from anthocyanins — organic compounds also found in jamun and blueberries.
According to the Press Information Bureau, 100 g of kufri jamunia flesh contains around 42.75 mg of vitamin C (versus 23.15 mg in regular potatoes), 42.05 mg of anthocyanins, 2.28 mg of zinc (versus 0.28 mg), 3.22 mg of iron (versus 0.57 mg), and 161 micrograms of carotenoids. And per the CPRI team’s findings themselves, published in Potato Journal in 2025, 100 g of kufri jamunia was found to have a range of carotenoid levels, from 15.6 micrograms in Kanpur to 298.4 micrograms in Raipur, during the multi-location trials. Kufri jamunia also contains slightly less zinc than kufri neelkanth and slightly less iron than kufri manik; the latter are other coloured potato varieties developed at the Institute.
Anthocyanins are known to have antioxidant properties, although whether the same benefits will accrue when delivered by kufri jamunia potatoes is not known. And in the absence of similar studies, the same caveat goes for iron and zinc.
A 2016 study in Food Chemistry examined purple-fleshed potatoes and reported that steaming and microwaving generally preserved more of the nutritional substances than stir-frying did. However, again, research specific to kufri jamunia is not available.
Cultivation factors
Nutrient availability and delivery constitutes one half of a biofortification programme; the other half is determined by cultivation.
At the Modipuram research station, according to the Potato Journal paper, the team recorded an average yield of 49.01 tonnes per hectare after three months, across three seasons, whereas subsequent multi-location trials, including at Modipuram, recorded an overall mean of 31.96 tonnes per hectare across north (36.77 tonnes), central (33.79 tonnes), and eastern (25.91 tonnes) India.
On the other hand, at these locations, kufri manik yielded 31.52 tonnes per hectare and kufri neelkanth 36.61 tonnes per hectare. Further, kufri jamunia could moderately resist late blight, a disease caused by the water mould Phytophthera infestans, in laboratory conditions but has been reported as ‘susceptible’ in the field. Late blight is a devastator of potato crops and the CPRI team has already recommended that farmers apply fungicide.
Next, the multi-location trials also produced 29.19 tonnes of marketable potatoes per hectare, versus 33.48 tonnes for kufri neelkanth. So if the costs of cultivation were equal, kufri jamunia farmers could need a 15% premium on the selling price to attain the same gross revenue. (A study published by a CPRI in Indian Horticulture in 2020 estimated that, for regular potatoes, the seed material accounted for 40-50% of the production costs vis-a-vis regular potatoes, with a per-hectare seed cost of around ₹60,000-75,000 per hectare.)
Many unknowns
Taken together, there are many unknowns about kufri jamunia at this point to assess its overall cost-benefit ratio, including the cost of seeds and disease management, pricing, its uptake in the market, and how efficaciously it will deliver iron and zinc to the population. It would be premature as a result to deem kufri jamunia to be a proven solution to address India’s hidden hunger.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): The BJP has launched various events across the country to counter the Congress and CJP's protests against SIR, demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
The party plans to organise a march in the state capital on November 4 by mobilising 1,00,000 supporters.
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh may take part in it. Similar marches will take place in Indore on October 30 and in Jabalpur on November 20. Central minister Mansukh Mandaviya will participate in the march in Indore.
The BJP held a meeting at the residence of the in-charge minister of Bhopal, Chaitanya Kashyap, on Wednesday to discuss a strategy for the march.
BJP's state unit president Hemant Khandelwal, Member of Parliament Alok Sharma, ministers Vishvas Sarang and Krishna Gaur, legislator Rameshwar Sharma, Bhagwandas Sabnani, former legislator Dhruvnarayan Singh, district president Ravindra Yati and in-charge of the event and state vice president Nishant Khare participated in the meeting.
The party leaders told the public representatives to mobilise as many people as possible for the march. The root of the march also came up for discussion at the meeting.

In July, as supporters of the Cockroach movement took to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, incensed over exam-paper leaks and demanding the resignation of India’s education minister, the rest of the nation realised that for the first time since the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) came to power in 2014, the curse of inertia and the grip of fear had been smashed irrevocably. Prime minister Narendra Modi’s image of invincibility has been punctured.
People in India have been conditioned to believe in an idea of intense slow-burn protests that eventually bring change – but the Cockroaches have shown us that the revolution can be fast-tracked.
This time the Cockroaches are demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, following reports in the Indian Express in late September that he had pushed through a purge of voter rolls. Round one of the Cockroach protests came to an end because the BJP was willing to sacrifice the education minister. Round two does not allow for such scapegoating. If Kumar goes, Modi must go too – it would be an open admission that the electoral system has been compromised.
The response of the BJP so far has been hysterical. The repressive apparatus of the state was out in full force: detentions and arrests of journalists, protesters being roughed up and beaten, an internet blackout in the capital. The Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke’s bravado in announcing his protest plans paid unexpected dividends the first time around. The second time, the continual broadcasting on social media by the three Cockroach leaders seemed like a lack of experience in organising and strategic thinking. Police forces detained them on touchdown at Delhi airport on the morning of the protest. They alleged that thousands of their members faced preventive detention or were not allowed to reach the capital city.
So at protests on 10 October, the CJP leaders were conspicuous by their absence. Only leftwing and Congress-allied student organisations, prominent gutsy young activists (Neha Bora, Aishe Ghosh, Gurmehar Kaur) and their elected political representatives held the ground and faced the worst of the police brutality.
The absence of the Cockroach leadership on the ground notwithstanding, the protests continued in pockets, eventually reaching a crescendo on 12 October. Heeding a call by Rahul Gandhi on behalf of the Congress-led opposition bloc, the streets of Delhi were filled in an act of defiance the like of which I have not witnessed in my lifetime. The state, however, seemed to have got the memo beforehand. The Delhi police and security forces numbered 90,000, 45 metro stations were closed in the inner city and trains to Delhi were cancelled. Student activists travelling to the capital were picked up en route from their railway carriages.
The following day, a small group of Cockroaches were arrested entering Jantar Mantar, which the Delhi police had banned from being used as a protest site. Two of the group’s leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained and subsequently sent to jail for five days.
Despite the high-handed approach of the police, the people are still clamouring for battle on the streets. Every screengrab, every video, every reel reinforces the feeling that we are witnessing a carnivalisation of the protests. The songs, the slogans, the sudden bursts of dancing, the satirical placards, the sheer joy of the crowds: this is Mikhail Bakhtin’s carnivalesque. What is the cause for such celebration? This: the state is evidently in retreat. People have begun to treat power as something to be ridiculed.
One of the most popular slogans has been Jab jab Modi darta hai, police ko aage karta hai (“Whenever Modi is afraid, he pushes the police forward”). The regime’s undiluted dread was most visible at Connaught Place in central Delhi on 16 October, when the CJP had called on people to gather at Central Park for a flag-waving celebration. The New Delhi Municipal Council shut down the park for two days and an elaborate fortification followed. The park was cordoned off, security personnel formed a human chain along the metal railings and 220 companies of the Central Armed Police Forces were deployed alongside the Rapid Action Force and the Delhi police.
Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke and communist student leader Neha Bora were both detained as they made their way towards Connaught Place. Neither was allowed to contact lawyers until late into the night, and lack of knowledge about their whereabouts caused panic online. Neha was released from detention the following morning, and Abhijeet could walk free on conditional bail.
For over a decade, the regime crushed students and dissenters by branding them anti-national and punishing them under the draconian Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. The genius of the Cockroach protest lay in something very simple – how could the state frame the waving of the Indian national flag as an anti-national activity? We now have a government that is not confident of its own legitimacy; it views the tricolour as a weapon when it is in the hands of its citizens.
The powerlessness of the state could also be seen in its desperation to police the online space: it summoned Meta officials over the summer and imposed an internet shutdown earlier this month. For a party that coasted to power with post-truth propaganda on WhatsApp, its undisputed dominance on X and heavy investment in keeping social media influencers on its payroll, the algorithms (or their oligarch owners) may well have turned. It is impossible to capture the entire social media ecosystem with threats and purchasing power alone.
For the regime, it is a losing battle against the newfound visual grammar that has defined a wave of protests around the world: nothing is as seductive as young women defiantly clashing with uniformed police, or an opposition leader who climbs the barricades and waves the national flag. The German philosopher Walter Benjamin wrote about the tendency for fascism to lean into the aestheticisation of politics – today, looking at Delhi, he would be pleased to report back that the aesthetic can also be snatched back by the masses.
On 12 October, after the mass mobilisation, Gandhi addressed the media by saying: “This is tandav, Lord Shiva’s dance. There is no planning here”, and “This is the wedding procession of Shiva, anyone can join in”. These references to Shiva are a calculated manoeuvre. It is a nod to India’s majority Hindus who, time and time again, have been sold the lie that their sole protector is Modi.
Modi recently went Bhajan clubbing – a kind of rave setup with remixed Hindu devotional music – in a desperate attempt to establish his gen Z connections. But he may find the rug pulled from beneath his feet. Modi’s base rewarding the BJP election after election for weaponising their faith did not secure jobs for the next generation. And now it is their own children who are at the receiving end of the state’s violence.
Saving India cannot happen without pulling Hindus out from the vicious grip of extremist Hindutva. This is one unforeseen outcome of this protest and the wider movement. Whether it topples the government or not, it has shown it can unite people against the divisive force that is the BJP.
- Meena Kandasamy is a poet and writer based in Chennai

League Two side Fleetwood Town will face Everton or Newcastle United at Highbury in the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup.
The lowest-ranked side left in the competition have already made history by reaching the last eight after they stunned Premier League champions Arsenal on penalties on Tuesday.

A new dawn is rising in "The Hunger Games" universe (literally).
"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is set to hit theaters on November 20, taking fans back into the world of Panem. This time, they will see it through the eyes of a young Haymitch Abernathy as he competes as a District 12 tribute 24 years before the events of Suzanne Collins' original trilogy.
Fans have been eagerly awaiting the film since it was first announced in 2024, before the novel it is based on was even published.
Now, a little under a month before it premieres, the film's arrival is feeling more and more real. Tickets finally went on sale on Wednesday, and the same day, Jennifer Lawrence confirmed she'll be reprising her role as Katniss Everdeen in the film, alongside Woody Harrelson and Josh Hutcherson.
Here's everything we know about the movie so far.
'Sunrise on the Reaping' hits theaters in November 2026
"Sunrise on the Reaping" was published in March 2025, and it is the second prequel to Collins' immensely popular dystopian series, following the 2020 release of "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes." Like "Ballad," the latest installment reveals key lore about the world of Panem, while staying true to the heart of Collins' original works.
Lionsgate announced it would adapt the story into a feature film, following the success of the "Ballad" adaptation, in conjunction with the novel's June 2024 announcement.
At the time, Deadline reported that the film, "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," would be released on November 20, 2026. The film officially premieres on the 20th, though some fans were able to secure advanced screening tickets for November 18 and 19 at select theaters.
Francis Lawrence, the filmmaker who helmed every movie in the series except the 2012 original, directed the movie from a script adapted by Billy Ray.
Nina Jacobson and her producing partner, Brad Simpson, returned to produce the prequel under their Color Force banner. Jacobson told Variety in March 2025 that her team already had "a great draft" of the script and set filming locations before the book was even released.
Filming started in the summer of 2025
"Sunrise on the Reaping" has a massive cast, largely because Haymitch is reaped into the second Quarter Quell. The 50th Hunger Games has twice as many tributes competing, meaning 48 children from the districts are sent to the arena instead of 24.
In addition, the novel introduces readers to characters in District 12 with connections to the other books in the series and features appearances by "Hunger Games" favorites such as Effie Trinket and Plutarch Heavensbee.
Lionsgate revealed the film's cast on social media, showing snippets of the characters' introductions in the novel as they burst into flame, revealing the actors portraying them.
The 'Sunrise on the Reaping' cast includes:
- Haymitch Abernathy: Joseph Zada
- Lenore Dove Baird: Whitney Peak
- President Snow: Ralph Fiennes
- Effie Trinket: Elle Fanning
- Caesar Flickerman: Kieran Culkin
- Plutarch Heavensbee: Jesse Plemons
- Beetee Latier: Kelvin Harrison Jr.
- Wiress: Maya Hawke
- Mags Flanagan: Lili Taylor
- Maysilee Donner: Mckenna Grace
- Wyatt Callow: Ben Wang
- Louella McCoy: Molly McCann
- Lou Lou: Iona Bell
- Magno Stift: Billy Porter
- Drusilla Sickle: Glenn Close
- Panache: Jhaleil Swaby
- Ampert: Percy Daggs IV
- Silka: Laura Marcus
- Wellie: Rada Rae
- Maritte: Sky Frances
- Clayton: Salimou Thiam
- Ringina: Tatyana Muzondo
- Buck: John Doeble
- Kerna: Alina Reid
- Hull: Kaine Buffonge
- Willamae: Kara Tointon
- Sid: Smylie Bradwell
- Clerk Carmine: Jeffrey Hallman
- Woodbine: Serafin Mishiev
The film's star, Zada, is a relative newcomer with a handful of roles to his name. In March 2025, Jacobson told Variety her team was looking for an actor who could bring the same "mischief" Woody Harrelson brought to the role in the original trilogy without "impersonating" him.
"You want somebody who very credibly feels like they could be a young version of this character, before the trauma and grief and rage that the fallout of the Games create," Jacobson said. "Nobody can be Woody Harrelson, but Woody Harrelson."
Of the roles announced, Fiennes' and Fanning's castings arguably generated the most buzz.
Fiennes, who is no stranger to film franchises after playing Voldemort in the "Harry Potter" films, will be offering the third cinematic iteration of President Coriolanus Snow.
Donald Sutherland originated the role of the aging villain in the three original "Hunger Games" films, and fans saw Tom Blyth's portrayal of Snow as a young man in the first prequel. Snow is the primary antagonist in "Sunrise on the Reaping," as he is in the original trilogy, and he makes some chilling appearances in the novel.
Elizabeth Banks played Effie Trinket, Katniss and Peeta's handler from the Capitol, in the original "Hunger Games" trilogy, and the character appears as a young stylist in "Sunrise on the Reaping." Fans were eager to see who would step into Banks' shoes because her performance was so beloved in the films, and Fanning's casting was met with overwhelming excitement.
Plemons will take over the role of Plutarch for Philip Seymour Hoffman, and Jeffrey Wright played Beetee Latier before Kelvin Harrison Jr. Interestingly, both Plemons and Harrison previously played Hoffman's and Wright's children in other projects. Plemons was Hoffman's son in the 2012 film "The Master," and Harrison was Wright's son in "Monster," released in 2018.
Lawrence announced that filming for the project was set to begin in July 2025 at CinemaCon in April 2025, and Zada and Grace were spotted together in Spain that month.
Lionsgate released the most enlightening trailer for the movie yet in September 2026
On November 20, 2025, Lionsgate shared an official teaser trailer for the film to celebrate one year until its release.
It gave viewers a glimpse of the arena for the 50th Hunger Games, showing Zada as Haymitch standing on a podium alongside his fellow tributes in a picturesque, hilly countryside.
Importantly, the teaser showed Lenore Dove giving Haymitch a striker with a bird on one end and a snake on the other. The striker plays an important role in the book, was illustrated on the book's cover, and was unveiled as the official logo for the film in a teaser clip released in April 2025, making its appearance exciting for fans of the text.
Both the teaser trailer and teaser clip ended with Harrelson's voice saying, "I think these games are gonna be different."
On April 13, 2026, Lionsgate released the first full-length trailer for the film. It offered a more comprehensive look at the film's plot, focusing on Haymitch's reaping and his time at the Capitol before the Hunger Games actually begin.
Clips of some of the book's biggest moments appeared in the trailer, including a chariot crash during the parade of tributes, Haymitch's live TV interview before he enters the arena, and a private conversation between Haymitch and President Snow.
The trailer is also stacked with appearances from the star-studded cast. It features Kieran Culkin as Caesar Flickerman, the role Stanley Tucci played in the original trilogy, and Maya Hawke as a younger, less traumatized version of Wiress, an ally to Katniss in the 75th Quarter Quell and a mentor to Haymitch in the 50th.
Hawke as Wiress offers one of the most chilling lines in the trailer: "The arena, it's a killing machine. But all machines can be broken."
Lionsgate also released a video introducing Haymitch to viewers on July 4, which is both Reaping Day in the "Hunger Games" universe and Haymitch's birthday. It includes clips from the movie, as well as commentary from Lawrence, Jacobson, and Zada on Haymitch as a character.
Finally, the studio shared a second full-length trailer for the movie on September 16, a little over two months before the film's premiere. "Witness the beginning of a revolution," the official "The Hunger Games" Instagram account captioned the trailer.
The trailer gives a closer look at Haymitch's experience in the Capitol and the arena after he is reaped for the Games, showing glimpses of his disastrous tribute parade and his work to dismantle the arena from the inside as he competes.
It also tees up his conflict with President Snow more directly than the other trailers. In one clip, Haymitch looks directly at Snow and claps in a silent stadium, the lone voice of dissent as Capitol loyalists look on in horror at this small act of rebellion (and, in Plutarch Heavensbee's case, in awe).
Alongside the trailer, Lionsgate also released two posters for the film, coining the slogan, "Challenge authority. Capitalize power."
The tributes from District 12 pose under "challenge authority," while people from the Capitol, like Snow and Heavensbee, are on the "capitalize" poster.
The 'Sunrise on the Reaping' epilogue
Since the book the movie is based on was released, fans have wondered if the film will include the epilogue from "Sunrise on the Reaping."
The epilogue takes place in District 12 after the events of "Mockingjay," with Haymitch telling Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark about his childhood and time in the arena.
In December 2025, The Hollywood Reporter confirmed that Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson would be reprising their roles as Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark in "Sunrise on the Reaping," though the outlet didn't say whether Harrelson would return alongside them or how they would appear in the film.
On October 28, Lawrence confirmed she will appear in the film, alongside Hutcherson and Harrelson, to the delight of fans.
On the "Call Her Daddy" podcast, host Alex Cooper asked Lawrence what it was like to step into Katniss' shoes again, and Lawrence replied that it was "unbelievable."
"It was so crazy because it was the same crew," she said. "It was the same camera guys, the same AD, who I've worked with a million times too because I love him, and Josh and Woody."
"It was so emotional. Josh and I, like, didn't walk to the bathroom without our arms around each other," she added. "And Woody obviously came through the window of my hotel room uninvited cause it would not be the same. It wouldn't be the same if he listened to boundaries and used a door."
Lawrence didn't reveal any details about her appearance in the film, but "Hunger Games" adaptations have historically been fairly loyal to Collins' book, making it safe to assume the trio will be depicted in some form of the epilogue.

Budgam, Oct 28: Stressing the need to preserve linguistic and cultural identities amid globalisation, Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha on Wednesday cautioned that the disappearance of a language also meant the loss of a distinctive way of understanding the world.
Speaking at an event in Bemina, LG Sinha said a region could not be understood merely through geographical boundaries, maps and statistics, but also through its folk traditions, languages, art forms, religious heritage and the lived experiences of its people,
He said the centre would focus on cultural heritage, language preservation, manuscript conservation, digital archiving, linguistic mapping and interdisciplinary research.
On artificial intelligence (AI), Sinha said technological capabilities and emotional intelligence were not contradictory but complementary, adding that emotional intelligence could make technology more useful, responsible and humane.
He stressed that students should use modern technology to expand their capabilities while preserving independent thinking, ethical awareness, imagination and human identity.
“The future will belong to those capable of connecting different disciplines and facilitating dialogue between technology professionals, researchers and traditional artisans,” he said.
Sinha also highlighted the need for collaboration among experts in linguistics, anthropology, ecology, economics, psychology and the arts to address challenges such as climate change, migration and tourism-related issues.
He expressed confidence that the centre could emerge as a model for interdisciplinary research and attract scholars from other institutions.—(KNO)

Skip funerals of farmers who die by suicide: Shinde Sena MLA's controversial advice
Sanjay Gaikwad said people should avoid the last rites of farmers who die by suicide. The remark triggered controversy while he urged distressed farmers to seek help from elected representatives.
Shiv Sena (Eknath Shinde faction) MLA Sanjay Gaikwad has sparked a controversy with his remarks on farmers who die by suicide, saying that people should not attend their last rites so that others realise the consequences of taking their own lives.
The MLA from Buldhana in Maharashtra made the remarks while responding to a question about Vanchit Bahujan Aghadi chief Prakash Ambedkar's recent comment describing farmers as “useless”.
Gaikwad said farmers facing difficulties should approach their local MLAs, MPs or the government to seek help instead of dying by suicide. He also said farmers should consider the hardships their families would face after their deaths.
'NOBODY SHOULD ATTEND THEIR LAST RITES'
In his remarks, Gaikwad said he believed that refusing to attend the last rites of farmers who die by suicide could discourage others from taking the extreme step.
“I would say that nobody should even attend the last rites of a farmer who dies by suicide. Only then will they understand what happens when an animal eats their body. After that, no farmer will die by suicide,” he said.
He further argued that farmers who take their own lives leave their children and spouses to face severe difficulties.
“I have heard his speech. Sometimes, people speak out of anger. Why do you die? Why do you die by suicide? If you have a problem, write to the government, your MLA or MP. Inform them about your difficulties. Everyone will come together to help you,” Gaikwad said.
He added that by dying by suicide, farmers were effectively punishing their children. Referring to marriage vows, he said couples promise to remain together for seven lifetimes, but suicide cuts that commitment short.
GAIKWAD HAS FACED CONTROVERSIES OVER REMARKS
Gaikwad belongs to the Shiv Sena faction led by Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde and represents the Buldhana Assembly constituency.
The MLA has previously attracted controversy over his public statements, drawing criticism for remarks that have put his party in a difficult position.

The Keralam government will introduce a Bill in the next Assembly session to regulate high medical treatment costs in private hospitals, Health Minister K. Muraleedharan told the Assembly on Monday (October 26, 2026).
He was responding to a question from Communist Party of India (Marxist) MLA K.N. Balagopal on the steps being taken by the government to regulate the trend of some major hospitals, in which global private equity firms now have big stakes, inflating treatment costs.
The Minister said the government agreed in principle to the need to regulate private hospitals, many of which were now under the management of foreign companies. He said that while the costs for treatment as well as room rents have increased drastically, insurance companies are at times refusing claims, causing difficulties to the common people.
Health destination project
Responding to another question, Mr. Muraleedharan said the government was preparing a project to transform Keralam into a health destination which will be sought after by foreigners as well as those from other States. The Principal Secretary (Health department), Director of the Health Department and the Director of Medical Education will coordinate these activities.
A major campaign for early detection and control of lifestyle diseases is also underway. As part of this, heath workers will visit houses and identify those needing attention through a survey and preliminary screening. The pilot project will be implemented in the Vattiyurkavu, Idukki and Nilambur Assembly constituencies first and later expanded across the State, said Mr. Muraleedharan.

New Delhi, Oct 27: The Supreme Court on Tuesday sought a response of the Centre on a petition challenging provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act and the DPDP Rules on the grounds that they allegedly infringe press freedom and the right to information.
A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued the notice after hearing senior advocate Madhavi Divan, appearing for the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA).
The matter has been listed for further hearing on November 17 along with pending ones.
The plea sought striking down several provisions of the data protection law and its accompanying rules as unconstitutional, saying that the absence of an exemption for journalistic activities could seriously impede news reporting, undermine investigative journalism and compromise the confidentiality of sources.
During the hearing, Divan described the petition as perhaps the first comprehensive challenge by what she termed the “legacy media”, distinguishing traditional news organisations from citizen journalists.
“This is perhaps the first comprehensive petition by what we call legacy media. There has been some debate over citizen journalists. We are the traditional, conventional legacy media,” she said.
The senior lawyer urged the bench to issue notice on the application seeking an interim stay of the challenged provisions.
Divan said that the law’s consent requirements could make routine news gathering and reporting unworkable, particularly when journalists report on matters involving individuals who may not consent to the use of their personal data.
“If I am left to the mercy of the data principal as to whether he or she will give consent, how will news be reported?” she asked. The senior lawyer stressed that the requirements could have serious implications for television journalism and time-sensitive reporting.
“On television, it is live. Otherwise, it has to be new,” she said, adding that provisions could effectively shut down newsrooms.
“What is the point if I have to ask for permission and consent,” she asked.
The association has also challenged the amendment to Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information (RTI) Act, alleging that the change restricts access to information relating to public officials and alters the scope of information available for public scrutiny. “Section 8(1)(j), the deletion, is changing the whole concept of news,” Divan submitted.
The petition also raised concerns over the Centre’s powers to requisition information under the DPDP Act, saying that the provisions could have far-reaching consequences for the functioning of news organisations and their ability to report on matters of public interest.

Controversial Islamic cleric shot dead in northern Nigeria
- Published
A controversial Islamic cleric in Nigeria has been murdered outside his home in the northern state of Katsina.
Two assailants arrived on a motorcycle and shot Yahaya Masussuka in the town of Dutsin-Ma as he was saying goodbye to visitors on Monday evening, sources told the BBC.
The 47-year-old preacher and one of his guests, who was also shot, were rushed to hospital but both were pronounced dead by the attending doctor, police said.
It is not clear why Masussuka was targeted, but the cleric had received death threats on social media where he posted videos in which he rejected some elements of mainstream Islam, including what happens to people after their death.
It is widely believed in Islam that a person's soul will be questioned in the grave by two angels. If they answer correctly, their soul sleeps peacefully until the day of judgement - if not it will be tormented.
This understanding comes from what is known as the Hadith, a collection of texts believed to be the spoken words and actions of the Prophet Muhammad.
This serves as a key source of Islamic knowledge to help interpret the Quran, the central religious text of Islam.
But Masussuka based his teachings mainly on what was in Islam's holy book, questioned some of the hadiths - and did not believe that the dead were reawakened and questioned.
He was once jailed for nine months because he teased some respected scholars over their belief in this hadith and other teachings.
Masussuka, who had two wives and seven children, began preaching at the age of 13 in Quranic schools.
He later attended Al-Azhar University in Egypt and later went to Oman for further studies.
At his home, he had a studio where he would record videos of his teachings for broadcast on social media for his followers.
The cleric was also outspoken about violent extremism, radicalisation and openly advocated for interfaith dialogue and peaceful coexistence between Muslims and Christians, who make up nearly equal parts of Nigeria's population.
Thousands of Christians and Muslims have been killed in ethnic and religious violence here over the past 25 years.
For Masussuka's efforts, Nigeria's Network for Good Governance and Transparency honoured him with a Peace Ambassador Award last year.
Six other prominent Muslim preachers have been murdered over the last two decades in northern Nigeria - several targeted by Boko Haram for criticising the jihadist group that began its insurgency in 2009.
Founded in north-eastern Nigeria, it opposes Western culture, education, the secular government - and its political goal is the creation of an Islamic state.

The story so far: Hundreds of women gathered outside Polish Parliament (Sejm) in Warsaw on Thursday (October 22, 2026), braving heavy rain to demand access to free and legal abortion, as demonstrations spread across more than 20 cities in Poland. Signalling rejection of the government’s record, protesters raised pro-choice slogans in a show of anger at Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s failure to deliver on his promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws.
The demonstrations came just two days after the lower house, the Sejm, passed two bills seeking to ease the country’s restrictive abortion laws. The proposed changes seek to roll back some of the restrictions on the rights of abortion imposed under the previous government, but their passage into law remains uncertain, with President Karol Nawrocki expected to veto the measures.
What does Poland’s abortion law say?
Poland has some of the most restrictive abortion laws in Europe. Since 1993, abortions has been allowed in Catholic Poland only on specific grounds. The restrictions tightened in October 2020, when the country’s Constitutional Tribunal ruled that abortion on the grounds of severe foetal abnormalities was unconstitutional. The ruling came into force in January 2021, effectively establishing a near-total ban on abortion. Since then, and under the current law, legal abortion is when a pregnancy threatens the woman’s life or health, or when a pregnancy results from a criminal act, like rape or incest. In cases involving rape or incest, termination is permitted up to the 12th week of pregnancy.
Abortion on request is not permitted in Poland, and women seeking such terminations outside the legal grounds face major barriers to accessing healthcare. The law also criminalises assistance in pursuing an unlawful abortion, with penalties of up to three years’ imprisonment. However, the woman undergoing the abortion is not criminally liable. The restrictions have prompted repeated nationwide protests, including demonstrations in 2016 and after the 2020 ruling, with activists accusing the authorities of curtailing reproductive rights and restricting access to abortion care.
When Mr. Tusk’s coalition, comprising parties ranging from the left to the centre-right, came to power in December 2023, replacing the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to liberalise abortion laws. However, disagreements between the coalition’s more conservative and liberal factions stalled reform efforts, fuelling criticism that the government had failed to honour its electoral commitments.
What do the two bills propose?
The issue has now returned to the parliamentary agenda, a year ahead of the next parliamentary election. On October 20, the Sejm passed two bills seeking to ease abortion restrictions.
The first bill seeks to partially decriminalise abortion by removing criminal penlties for terminating a pregnancy with a woman’s consent outside the grounds currently permitted by law, as well as for helping or encouraging such an abortion. It also proposes protections from criminal liability for doctors, nurses and midwives who terminate a pregnancy to avert a threat to the woman’s life or health, or in circumstances involving a high probability of severe and irreversible foetal abnormalities or an incurable condition threatening the foetus’s life.
The second bill seeks to restore abortion as a legal option when doctors identify a severe and irreversible foetal abnormality or an incurable condition threatening foetal viability. This would reverse the effect of the 2020 Constitutional Tribunal ruling, which removed foetal abnormalities as a legal ground for termination.
Both bills would need to clear further legislative and presidential hurdles before becoming law. Even if enacted, they would not legalise abortion on request and would leave Catholic Poland’s near-total ban unchanged. Protesters have dismissed the new measures, calling it token gestures rather than a genuine effort to reform the law, arguing that the government is seeking to demonstrate progress on an issue that could influence its prospects in 2027 parliamentary elections.
How do Europe’s abortion laws compare?
Abortion laws vary widely across European Union, with countries setting different gestational limits and conditions for access. While several countries permit abortion on request during the first trimester, others maintain restrictive legal frameworks.
France became the first country in the world to explicitly enshrine the freedom to have an abortion in its Constitution in 2024. Abortion is permitted on request up to 14 weeks of pregnancy and is covered by the public healthcare system. In Sweden, abortion is permitted on request up to 18 weeks, with medical abortions available at home under approved arrangements and costs covered by the state healthcare system. The Netherlands permits abortion until the foetus is considered capable of surviving outside the womb, generally around 24 weeks in practice, subject to legal and medical requirements.
Spain permits abortion on request up to 14 weeks of pregnancy, while Ireland allows it up to 12 weeks. Finland also permits abortion on request during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, following a reform that took effect in 2023. Portugal permits abortion on request up to 10 weeks.
Ireland legalised abortion following a referendum in 2018, while Spain’s 2023 reforms removed the requirement for parental consent for 17-year-olds seeking an abortion.
Malta has historically maintained one of the world’s most restrictive abortion laws, criminalising the procedure in almost all circumstances. Before 2023, doctors who performed an abortion to save a woman’s life could face up to four years in prison, while women could face up to three years. In 2023, the country introduced a narrow exception to the near-total ban, allowing doctors to terminate a pregnancy when a woman faces an immediate risk to her life or when her health is in grave jeopardy that could lead to death. In non-immediate cases, the decision must be confirmed by a panel of medical specialists. The reform did not legalise abortion on request

Hearts vs Rangers; Scottish Premiership
Hearts 2-2 Rangers: Olwethu Makhanya's late equaliser rescues draw on Derek McInnes' Tynecastle return
Report as Rangers score late to draw 2-2 with Hearts; Kevin Kelsy opened the scoring for Rangers; goals from Claudio Braga and Calvin Miller gave Hearts the lead; Olwethu Makhanya headed in to rescue a point with Dujon Sterling missing a brilliant chance to snatch a win
Wednesday 28 October 2026 23:08, UK
Rangers snatched a point on Derek McInnes' Tynecastle return as Hearts held onto their formidable unbeaten home record.
The Gers boss was loudly booed by the home support as he emerged from the tunnel for his first match back in Gorgie since leaving for Ibrox in June, just weeks after the Edinburgh side were pipped to the Premiership title.
But his team silenced a pumped-up home crowd when Kevin Kelsy scored a 16th-minute opener following a lapse from Laurent Mendy.

The hosts emerged with renewed impetus after the break and drew level three minutes into the second half when Caludio Braga rushed in to force the ball over the line from close range.
With Rangers rattled, Hearts went ahead in the 57th minute. Tomas Magnusson nicked possession off Kim Minsu and sent Braga racing down the left. The Portuguese drove into the box and his angled shot broke off Manny Fernandez into the path of Calvin Miller, who drilled home a low finish from seven yards out.
McInnes sent on Bouanani for Gassama, and the Algerian winger helped give the visitors an increased threat in attack before he delivered the free-kick from the left which was headed home by Olwethu Makhanya with stoppage time approaching.
Dujon Sterling had a brilliant chance to be Rangers' hero in the dying seconds, only to chest the ball straight to Hearts 'keeper Beau Reus.
Rangers remain four points behind Celtic, who drew with Dundee United, and four above Hearts, who are unbeaten in 26 league games at home.
The key moments from Tynecastle Park
2: CHANCE! Kerjota sends in a cross and Fagan-Walcott is just inches from getting his head to it.
11: CHANCE! Minsu sends in a cross as Rangers start to find a way into the game, Raskin gets to it but Hearts clear.
16: GOAL RANGERS! Rangers jump on slack Hearts play. Naderi slips a pass to Kelsy to finish past Reus.
26: SAVE! Kerjota has a shot blocked with Miller's follow-up saved by Pandur.
27: CHANCE! A rash challenge from Fernandez sees Hearts with a free-kick in a dangerous area. Miller whips it in, but Mendy heads over the bar.
48: GOAL HEARTS! Rangers are punished for conceding another free-kick and Braga is the one to get it over the line.
57: GOAL HEARTS! Braga drives into the Rangers box and his deflected strike falls to Miller to smash in.
68: SAVE! Kelsy's header reaches Bouanani, who curls an effort towards goal. It's saved by Reus.
76: SAVE! Pandur is called into action again as Braga is given so much space to shoot from distance.
79: SAVE! Neil whips a shot to the far post, which is stopped by Reus.
83: WIDE! Hearts break but Williams sends fires wide from distance. What a chance to wrap things up.
89: GOAL RANGERS! Makhanya heads in from Bouanini's free-kick to pull level heading into stoppage time.
90+4: CHANCE! Curtis sends in the cross to Sterling who looks certain to knock in a winning goal only to hand Reus a simple save.
'Rangers have stolen a point'
Sky Sports' Kris Boyd at Tynecastle Park:
"Rangers will actually be delighted to leave here with a point tonight.
"Hearts, the amount of games they've had, running on empty, the amount of injuries they've got, they were the better team tonight and that would be worrying.
"Rangers will leave here with a point and I'd be absolutely delighted that they've got that point.
"I saw a team out there tonight, Hearts, that have got a style of play. There's nothing wrong with it, but when it doesn't work, you're going to be criticised.
"You see that team that was going long, trying to play for second balls, get up on that. When it doesn't work, it looks so disjointed. Towards the end Rangers got that equaliser and then they had the chance to win it, but they didn't deserve that tonight.
"They wouldn't have deserved the three points. Hearts were by far the team who you felt as if were in control of the game, looked as if they were a team that had been coached in terms of patterns of play, especially the second half.
"Rangers really struggled to deal with Hearts. Emmanuel Fernandez, he looked so at unease with the Hearts attacking players. The amount of times that he caused problems for his own team-mates, again.
"I'll say it, Rangers have stolen a point here tonight. They've stolen a point because, especially that second half, it's got to be better."
Vrancken: 'We lost two points'
Hearts head coach Wouter Vrancken speaking to Sky Sports:
"It was a really good performance against a really good side on full strength.
"Actually, we lost two points. I think we had to win here.
"I'm pleased with the reaction because the moments they got was through a mistake of us.
"The first goal was a mistake for us. The performance afterwards makes up for a lot of things there.
"We were good in organisation. We were good at the ball. We were winning second balls, duels.
"We know they were aggressive or they want to be aggressive man but we played through their pressure.
"I'm really happy with the performance today. A pity that we couldn't take the three points."
McInnes: 'Winner would have been unjust'
Rangers manager Derek McInnes speaking to Sky Sports:
"I think we deserve our point.
"If we'd scored a winner there, possibly it would have been unjust.
"I liked how my team kept going, but there was a lot about tonight that I thought we looked very naive at times.
"We've got a young team and this ground can do that to you at times. Sometimes you've just got to stem the tide and sometimes you've just got to stay in the game and do the basics really well.
"I thought the game was a bit topsy-turvy. For us, there was loads we can do better."
Genuine handshake?
There appeared to be some tension between Vrancken and McInnes at full-time, with both telling Sky Sports what happened...
"I think you have to be like a genuine handshake among colleagues for me. Win, draw, lose," said the Hearts head coach.
"At the end everybody fights for his own team, works hard for his own team and in their way of working so I think it's normal and this is also how it has to be but at the end it has to be a genuine handshake.
Asked if he thought McInnes' handshake was genuine, he added: "I don't think so but afterwards we spoke so I think it's okay."
McInnes had less to say: "I was just telling him how fortunate it is to have such a good squad that I left him," he said. "All good."

Advocate Asmi, 23, was elected unopposed as a member of the Bar Council of Punjab and Haryana on Tuesday, becoming the youngest-ever member of a State Bar Council in India and the first Generation Z representative to be elected to any State Bar Council, according to the announcement. Her election was declared by Returning Officer Pardeep Parmar after no other nomination was received by the closing time on Monday, October 26, The Tribune reported. Asmi filed her nomination for the post of member of the Bar Council of Punjab and Haryana against a casual vacancy that arose following the elevation of Minderjeet Yadav as a judge of the Punjab and Haryana High Court. No other nomination was received by the deadline on October 26. After the period for withdrawal of nominations expired, Returning Officer Pardeep Parmar declared Asmi elected unopposed on Tuesday. Her election marks a milestone for young advocates entering leadership roles in the legal profession. At 23, she is the youngest-ever member of a State Bar Council in the country and the first Gen Z member to be elected to any State Bar Council, according to the announcement. Several members and office-bearers of the legal fraternity were present to congratulate Asmi on her election. Those present included Amit Rana, Chairman, Bar Council of Punjab and Haryana; Sharmila Sharma, Vice-Chairman; Karnajit Singh, Member, Bar Council of India; Dr Vijender Singh Ahlawat, former Chairman; Gurtej Singh Grewal, former Vice-Chairman; Partap Singh, former Chairman; Rajni Nanda and Dr D.P.S. Randhawa, Members, Bar Council of Punjab and Haryana; Harinder Pal Singh Ishar, Additional Advocate General, Punjab; and Niharika Singh, Advocate. With Asmi's election, the Bar Council of Punjab and Haryana now has the highest representation of women members among all State Bar Councils, according to the announcement. Her election marks a milestone for women's representation in the legal fraternity and highlights the participation of younger advocates in the governance of the Bar. As the first Gen Z member of a State Bar Council, Asmi's election also marks a generational milestone for the legal profession and may serve as an inspiration to aspiring lawyers across the country.
