Big companies are still cutting jobs in 2026.
So far this year, dozens of major brands have laid off employees, continuing a trend of significant workforce reductions across a broad range of industries, including tech, media, finance, and retail.
While prominent brands continue to announce cuts, the broader economy shows that unemployment hasn't spiked. Economists frequently describe the environment as low-fire, low-hire.
The big change is AI.
Several companies, including Block, Coinbase, and Standard Chartered, have cited the impact of artificial intelligence as a key reason for the layoffs.
A World Economic Forum survey last year found that some 41% of companies worldwide expected to reduce their workforces in the next five years because of the rise of artificial intelligence. The survey also found that jobs in big data, fintech, and AI are expected to double by 2030.
Last year, Business Insider tracked layoffs at around 65 major companies, including Amazon, Meta, Paramount, and Starbucks. In 2026, we'll continue to track additional job cuts based on company announcements, WARN notices, and our own reporting.
Here are the companies with job cuts underway in 2026, listed in alphabetical order.
Amazon is laying off thousands of employees
Amazon said in January that it would eliminate around 16,000 corporate roles globally.
Beth Galetti, senior vice president of people experience and technology, described the January move in a company memo as part of broader efforts to cut back on bureaucracy inside the company.
The cuts followed mass layoffs from October 2025, when the tech and retail giant shed 14,000 roles.
In May, Amazon's Selling Partner Services team slashed additional jobs as it continued to reshape its organization.
"Following a recent review, we've made the difficult decision to eliminate a relatively small number of roles in our Selling Partner Services team," a spokesperson told Business Insider.
American Express is cutting 5% of its workforce
American Express took a $336 million restructuring charge as it plans to cut around 5% of its workforce, the company announced during its third-quarter earnings call.
It employed around 77,000 people by the end of 2025, meaning the layoffs could impact between 3,000 and 4,000 employees.
On the earnings call, the company also highlighted how AI has changed its internal structure.
"There's been a lot of talk about how companies are using AI to increase productivity, automate processes, and generally make their organizations more efficient," Stephen Squeri, Amex's CEO, said during an October earnings call. "We're using AI to do all of those things too."
Angi is cutting 350 jobs
Angi, the popular contractor listing site once known as Angie's List, said in January that it was cutting around 350 jobs "to reduce operating expenses and optimize the organizational structure in support of long-term growth." The company also said it's making the cuts "in light of AI-driven efficiency improvements."
In a January 7 SEC filing, Angi said that the cuts would save between $70 million and $80 million in annual spending. The layoffs will cost the company between $22 million and $30 million, according to the filing.
Atlassian is cutting 1,600 employees
Atlassian, the enterprise software company and maker of Confluence, said on March 11 that it will be cutting about 10% of its workforce as it invests in AI to reshape its organization.
CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes said in a statement that about 1,600 employees will be affected by the cuts.
"We fundamentally believe people and AI create the best outcomes. Our approach is not 'AI replaces people,'" Cannon-Brookes said. "But it would be disingenuous to pretend AI doesn't change the mix of skills we need or the number of roles required in certain areas. It does."
The company expects to incur $225 million and $236 million in restructuring charges, according to an SEC filing.
Barclays cuts 5,000 jobs
Barclays, the British financial institution, disclosed plans to cut around 5% of its workforce.
Anna Cross, the Group Finance Director of Barclays, said on an October 22 earnings call that the company expects more than GBP 1 billion in efficiency savings in 2027, which will involve reducing its head count by 5,000 full-time employees.
Cross said that 60% of affected workers are related to "support functions, including fewer developers as AI makes our people more productive."
The company reported Q3 pretax profit of GBP 2.3 billion — about $3 billion — up 12% from the same quarter a year earlier.
Barclays CEO, C.S. Venkatakrishnan, said that the company is moving to "drive even greater cost efficiency through deep technological transformation, reducing the unit cost of product, manufacturing, service and innovation."
British American Tobacco cuts 9,000 jobs
British American Tobacco said it will cut 9,000 jobs by the end of the year, about one-fifth of its workforce. The cuts will not impact the US arm of its business.
"We are building a future-ready organisation that is more agile, cost disciplined and technology enabled," CEO Tadeu Marroco said in the statement.
The company, whose cigarette portfolio includes brands like Lucky Strike and Dunhill, has stepped up its push in recent years into smoke-free alternatives, such as nicotine pouches and vapes.
Citi's job cuts continue this year
Citi will cut more jobs this year as part of its plan to reduce its workforce by 10%, or 20,000 employees.
In a statement on January 13, the bank said that it will continue to reduce head count in 2026.
"These changes reflect adjustments we're making to ensure our staffing levels, locations and expertise align with current business needs," a spokesperson for Citi said.
The plan was detailed in the company's January 2024 earnings report and could save the bank as much as $2.5 billion.
Cloudflare lays off 20% of its global workforce
Cybersecurity company Cloudflare on May 7 said it plans to cut roughly 20% of its global workforce, affecting more than 1,100 employees.
In an internal memo, Cloudflare executives said the company's use of AI has climbed more than 600% over the past three months, and that the rapid shift has forced the company to reconsider its structure.
"We want to be clear that this decision is not a reflection of the individual work or talent of those leaving us," Cloudflare executives wrote in the May 7 memo. "Instead, we are reimagining every internal process, team, and role across the company."
The company's shares fell more than 14% in extended trading following the announcement.
Coinbase is cutting 14% of staff
The CEO of Coinbase, Brian Armstrong, said in a letter to staff on May 5 that 14% of its staff would be cut, largely because of AI.
"AI is changing how we work. Over the past year, I've watched engineers use AI to ship in days what used to take a team weeks," wrote. "The pace of what's possible with a small, focused team has changed dramatically, and it's accelerating every day."
Armstrong said this would mean fewer layers and faster decisions in the company. No pure managers, he said — all leaders will now be required to get stuck in and "get their hands dirty."
"AI is bringing a profound shift in how companies operate, and we're reshaping Coinbase to lead in this new era," he added.
Crypto.com laid off 12% of its workforce
Crypto.com CEO Kris Marszalek said in March that the company laid off 12% of its workforce, including "roles that do not adapt in our new world."
"Companies that move immediately and pair the best AI tools with top-performers will achieve a level of scale and precision that was previously impossible," Marszalek wrote in a post on X. "This is where we must go."
Dell cut 10% of its workforce
Dell cut its workforce by 10% for the third year in a row, the company said in its annual filing with the SEC.
As of January 31, 2026, the company had 97,000 employees, down 11,000 from the same time last year. The decline includes both layoffs and attrition, Business Insider reported.
eBay is expected to lay off 6% of its employees
eBay is set to eliminate about 800 jobs globally, making up 6% of its workforce. The company told Business Insider that it's taking steps to better align with its strategic priorities.
"We are grateful for the contributions of the employees impacted and are committed to supporting them with care and respect," a company spokesperson said in a statement.
Epic Games is cutting 20% of its workforce
Epic Games, the company behind Fortnite, said in March that it would lay off more than 1,000 people — about 20% of its workforce — as engagement with the game declined.
CEO Tim Sweeney said in a memo that the layoffs "aren't related to AI."
"To the extent it improves productivity, we want to have as many awesome developers developing great content and tech as we can," Sweeney said.
Estée Lauder is deepening its cuts, now to as many as 10,000 roles
Estée Lauder said in its May earnings report that it will deepen its previously announced cuts, which are now expected to affect up to 10,000 jobs.
More than two-thirds of the reductions are in cashier and demonstration roles at lower-performing retail and department stores.
Etsy
Etsy said August 5 that it is laying off about 220 employees, roughly 12% of its workforce.
"We will be saying goodbye to approximately 220 colleagues across the company, with most of the changes concentrated in Product & Engineering," the company's CEO, Kruti Patel Goyal, told staffers in a memo.
The company also reported its second-quarter financial results on Wednesday.
While Goyal's memo made no mention of AI or its potential threat to jobs, she said that the cuts were a preemptive move.
"The answer is that today's decisions aren't a reflection of this quarter or even this year, but of where Etsy needs to go next," she wrote.
Expedia laid off some employees
Expedia confirmed to Business Insider that it had laid off some employees on January 26 and had also posted new job openings. It's unclear how many of its workers were affected by the cuts.
"We are eliminating roles as well as opening some new roles as we remain disciplined about assessing the skills we need for the future," an Expedia Group spokesperson said in a statement. "We are also simplifying our structure and reducing organizational layers to move faster and with more accountability. These are not easy decisions, and we are grateful for the contributions of our colleagues who are impacted."
Freshworks is cutting 11% of staff
The San Mateo, California-based software company said in its early May earnings report that it would cut 11% of its staff in the second quarter. The company had about 4,500 employees at the end of 2025.
The cuts aim "to streamline the Company's organizational efforts and product development process" and increase AI across the company, according to the filing.
On an earnings call, CEO Dennis Woodside said about half the company's code comes from AI.
"Like many other software companies, that is definitely changing how we build products, how fast we can build products, and the amount of people that we need to build products," he said.
The company's stock slumped 35% from May 2025 to May 2026.
General Motors is axing 600 salaried employees
General Motors is cutting 600 salaried employees from its global IT division.
A spokesperson said the layoffs would enable it to "better position the company for the future," by ensuring GM has employees with expertise in AI-native development, data engineering, analytics, cloud engineering, prompt engineering, and AI workflows.
GoPro is laying off 145 employees
On April 7, GoPro said it would lay off about 145 employees as it tries to cut operating costs and restructure operations.
The layoffs make up 23% of its global headcount of 631 employees, the camera maker said in a regulatory filing.
The cuts will start in the second quarter of the year and will largely be completed by the end of 2026. The restructuring is expected to result in a charge of $11.5 million to $15 million.
The company cut about 15% of its staff in August 2024 to cut costs.
Groupon is reducing up to 400 positions globally
Groupon said on May 21 that it would cut up to 400 roles globally as part of a restructuring plan, according to a financial filing. It previously said it planned to rebuild as an "AI-native company."
The cuts are expected to happen by the end of the third quarter of 2026. Groupon is looking to generate $10 million to $12 million in gross savings in 2026.
"Up to half of this year's savings will be reinvested into AI infrastructure, talent density, and the tools and teams building the next version of the company," a spokesperson told Business Insider.
Groupon had 1,734 employees worldwide at the end of 2025, according to its annual report.
Heineken has a multi-year plan to reduce its workforce
Heineken is cutting 5,000 to 6,000 roles over the next two years to boost productivity and bring down costs, according to its latest full-year earnings report.
The company told Business Insider that the divisions and regions where the layoffs are due to take place are yet to be confirmed.
Heineken said in its 2025 report that it faced "subdued consumer sentiment" in the Americas, alongside a "challenging year" for brewers in Europe.
Intuit is laying off 17% of its workforce
Financial software company Intuit announced on May 20 that it would be cutting 17% of its full-time workforce.
The company shared a memo from CEO Sasan Goodarzi to employees that listed five reasons for the culling, including reducing management layers, focusing roles on "high impact work," and closing down two of its offices.
"These changes are a necessary evolution to reduce complexity and architect an organization that operates with the velocity required to fuel our growth engines," Goodarzi wrote in the memo, shared in a blog post on Intuit's website.
Laid-off employees in the US would receive 16 weeks of base pay, plus two additional weeks of pay for every year they have worked at Intuit.
The company said in a May 20 earnings report that restructuring costs from the layoffs would be about $300 million to $340 million.
Kenvue cuts 3.5% of workforce
Consumer healthcare brand Kenvue, which produces Tylenol, plans to cut 3.5% of its staff. Kenvue had about 22,000 employees globally, per its latest annual report.
The company wrote in a mid-February SEC filing that its board aimed to reduce complexity and drive operational efficiencies.
The company's layoffs and restructuring efforts are expected to cost $250 million in 2026, per the filing.
LinkedIn is laying off staff and 'scale back' other investments
LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero told employees on May 13 that it was laying off employees, and those in affected roles would receive a calendar invite. The jobs included positions in the Microsoft-owned company's Global Business Organization, marketing, engineering, and product teams.
"We need to reinvent how we work, with agile teams focused on our highest priorities, and by shifting investments toward areas such as infrastructure to fulfill our mission and vision over the long term," Shapero said in the memo.
Shapero also said LinkedIn would "scale back" investments in areas like marketing campaigns, customer events, and underutilized office space.
Lululemon laid off 100 part-time employees at its customer service center
The athleisure giant said it laid off 100 part-time employees to "strengthen the business." The affected roles are in the company's North American contact center.
"After careful consideration, we have made the decision to transition our North America GEC to a full-time employee staffing model. As a result, approximately 100 part-time positions in our GEC have been impacted," a Lululemon spokesperson said.
Meta lays off workers at Reality Labs and other divisions
Meta began laying off employees across multiple teams on March 25, including Reality Labs, Facebook, recruiting, sales, and global operations.
The cuts come as the company ramps up spending on AI infrastructure and talent, alongside broader cost-cutting efforts. Meta said the changes are part of ongoing restructuring to better align teams with company goals, while exploring other roles for affected employees where possible.
Meta first began preparing to slash jobs within its Reality Labs division, the unit responsible for Mark Zuckerberg's metaverse ambitions, in January, three people familiar with the matter told Business Insider at the time.
Two employees said that teams working on virtual reality headsets and Horizon Worlds, the company's VR social network, would be disproportionately affected.
Meta has shifted away from virtual reality in recent years in favor of spending hundreds of billions of dollars on beefing up its AI capabilities.
Nike laid off workers in two rounds
Nike is cutting roughly 1,400 jobs, mostly from tech, as part of a broader push to streamline operations and revive growth.
In a memo to staff on April 23 obtained by Business Insider, Chief Operating Officer Venkatesh Alagirisamy said the layoffs are tied to the company's "win now" turnaround plan, which focuses on improving culture, product, marketing, marketplace strategy, and in-person retail. He described the effort as entering its "final stretch."
This is Nike's second layoff in 2026. Nike said on January 26 that it planned to lay off 775 employees across Tennessee and Mississippi, citing efforts to "streamline" its distribution center operations.
"We are sharpening our supply chain footprint, accelerating the use of advanced technology and automation, and investing in the skills our teams need for the future," Nike said in a statement to Business Insider.
Oracle's headcount fell 13% in a year
Oracle's workforce shrank by roughly 21,000 employees, or 13%, over the past year, bringing its headcount to 141,000 as of May 31, according to a 10-K filing released on June 22.
"The adoption and deployment of AI technologies across our operations have resulted, and may continue to result, in reductions to our workforce," Oracle wrote in the filing.
Oracle also disclosed that restructuring costs surged in fiscal 2026. The company spent $1.84 billion on severance and other exit costs, up from $374 million in the prior year.
The reduction in workforce comes as Oracle continues to invest heavily in AI infrastructure.
Papa Johns is restructuring
Papa Johns said it is laying off 7% of its corporate staff amid a broader restructuring.
The pizza chain said it will also close 300 locations in North America through 2027, starting with 200 this year.
"Optimizing our restaurant portfolio and strategically closing underperforming restaurants are among the most impactful actions we can take to improve restaurant profitability and fleet health," Papa Johns CFO Ravi Thanawala said during the company's fourth quarter earnings call on February 26.
Patreon, a creator economy company, laid off 20% of staff in July
Patreon announced layoffs in July.
The creator economy company is laying off 93 employees — roughly 20% of the company — per a memo its CEO, Jack Conte, shared publicly.
Conte wrote that the "market in which we operate has undergone profound change over the last 6 months," and that Patreon needs to cut costs to "remain a stable, dependable rock for our creators."
Pinterest is expected to lay off 15% of its workforce
Pinterest announced a global restructuring plan that includes layoffs affecting less than 15% of its workforce, according to a January securities filing. The cuts come with reductions in office space.
"We are making organizational changes to further deliver on our AI-forward strategy, which includes hiring AI-proficient talent," a Pinterest spokesperson said.
"As a result, we've made the difficult decision to say goodbye to some of our team members. We are grateful for their service and supporting them with separation packages and benefits," they added.
Saks laid off 16% of its corporate staff, among other job cuts
Saks Global, the beleaguered parent company of Saks Fifth Avenue, Neiman Marcus, and Bergdorf Goodman, conducted several rounds of layoffs as it closed stores and trimmed its corporate staff
In April, the company cut about 16% of its corporate staff, representing less than 4% of its total workforce.
"Following the strategic actions we've taken to secure long-term financial stability, sharpen our focus on luxury and full-price selling, optimize our operational footprint, and exit non-core businesses, we are right-sizing our corporate organization to align with our go-forward strategy," a Saks spokesperson told Business Insider.
The cuts followed Saks's closure of dozens of stores and fulfillment centers in the first quarter, resulting in layoffs.
Saks filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in January.
Sprout Social cut 20% of staff — about 260 employees
Sprout Social — a social media management program — announced on July 15 that it will cut 260 jobs, or about 20% of its workforce.
In a letter about the reduction in force, CEO Ryan Barretto said the cuts were due to rapid industry changes.
"This decision is not a reflection of their talent or commitment," Barrett said. "We made this decision because we believe it was the right one for Sprout's future. Our industry, and software more broadly, is changing quickly, and the way companies need to operate and invest has changed with it."
Affected staff will be offered a 12-week severance package, plus an additional week of pay for every year of tenure, fully-paid health benefits for six months, and a cash payment equal to the value of their equity shares that would have vested in the next 90 days.
Standard Chartered plans to eliminate 15% of corporate functions over the next 4 years
Standard Chartered plans to cut 15% of corporate function roles over the next four years, the company said on May 19.
The bank, headquartered in London, credited AI as a driver for the reductions.
"It is not cost-cutting, but it is replacing, in some cases, lower-value human capital with the financial capital and the investment capital that we are putting in," CEO Bill Winters said in a media briefing, Reuters reported.
The company added in a statement: "We are combining the best human talent with AI, investing to support our people into higher-value roles."
T-Mobile cut some jobs
T-Mobile cut some staff in early 2026, though the scope of the layoffs is unclear. Some workers posted on LinkedIn saying they'd been affected by the changes in January.
"As the next step in our evolution, we're making some changes while continuing to hire to ensure we have the right focus, structure, and momentum to keep changing the industry through innovation and our long-standing focus on customers," T-Mobile told Business Insider in a statement.
Tailwind cut 3 of its 4 engineers
Tailwind, a popular web tool, said it cut three of its four engineers in January, citing an AI-driven decline in revenue.
"75% of the people on our engineering team lost their jobs here yesterday because of the brutal impact AI has had on our business," CEO Adam Wathan wrote in a GitHub comment on January 6 that made waves in the tech community.
Target is cutting 500 roles from its distribution and regional offices
Target confirmed to Business Insider in February that it would cut 100 district office roles and 400 supply chain positions. It plans to invest instead in additional labor hours at stores to improve the shopping experience and return to growth.
The store improvement effort is a signature priority of the retailer's new CEO, Michael Fiddelke, who started on February 1.
In November, Fiddelke said the company intends to invest an additional $1 billion in capital expenditures for 2026, an increase of 25% from 2025.
TikTok lays off 250 employees
TikTok is laying off 250 employees and closing an office in Nashville, according to documents filed with the Department of Labor and Workforce Development in Tennessee.
A spokesperson for TikTok US Data Security, a joint venture established in January 2026 to oversee TikTok's US operations, said closing the office will "streamline our operations and better align our teams for long-term growth."
The Nashville office will close in October, according to the documents.
UPS said it will eliminate 30,000 jobs
UPS CEO Brian Dykes told analysts during the company's fourth-quarter earnings call that the company plans to reduce its operational workforce by 30,000 in 2026.
"This will be accomplished through attrition, and we expect to offer a second voluntary separation program for full-time drivers," Dykes said.
He told analysts that the company has identified 24 buildings for closure in the first half of 2026 and will continue to evaluate additional buildings for closure.
Verizon is selling 274 retail stores, affecting about 3,000 workers
Verizon said in July that it would transition 274 retail stores into franchise locations as part of ongoing changes at the telecom giant.
The company said about 2,500 retail workers and 500 corporate roles would be cut, and that typically around 70% of store employees accept jobs under the new franchisees.
The move comes two months after Verizon laid off several hundred corporate employees, or about 1% of its head count, as the company reallocates workers across its overall business.
Volvo is cutting 2,500 global jobs
Volvo's CEO, Håkan Samuelsson, said the luxury automaker is facing "a very tough environment with strong external challenges," including a fierce Chinese car market, US tariffs, and continued high-priced investments in a new lineup of electric vehicles.
The company said it is cutting 2,500 employees globally — including 2,000 in Sweden — to save around $530 million in response to those headwinds.
Volvo is also ending consultant contracts and planning some targeted employee exits, the company said in a press release.
Walmart said it would cut or relocate 1,000 corporate jobs
Walmart told employees on May 12 that it would cut or relocate about 1,000 corporate jobs to address redundancies and duplicate roles.
Suresh Kumar, Walmart's chief technology and development officer, and Daniel Danker, executive vice president of AI acceleration, product, and design, announced the changes in a memo.
"We've made changes to simplify how the work is organized, make ownership clearer, and better align roles to the work and skills we need going forward," the memo said.
The move follows Walmart's May 2025 decision to cut 1,500 corporate roles as part of an effort to "remove layers and complexity."
The company employed 2.1 million people as of January.
WiseTech is cutting 30% of its workforce
Logistics software maker Wisetech is cutting 2,000 jobs, or 30% of its staff, citing AI-driven efficiency gains.
In a conference call on February 25, CEO Zubin Appoo embraced AI and said that it means more productivity, in less time, and from fewer employees. The Sydney-based company employed about 7,000 people, according to its annual report released in October.
"I am prepared to say this clearly: the era of manually writing code as the core act of engineering is over," Appoo said. AI is "unlocking levels of efficiency gains across WiseTech that were previously out of reach."
Wix CEO said the company is set to cut 20% of its workforce
Wix, which provides website-building software, is reducing its workforce by 20%, the CEO told employees in a memo published on X on May 28.
The Israel-headquartered company employs about 5,300 workers.
CEO Avishai Abrahami cited the "fast evolution of AI capabilities" as a reason for the cuts and said the company needed to become a "faster, leaner, and flatter organization."
Workday is cutting jobs
Workday is cutting about 400 jobs, and said on February 4 that the move will help the enterprise software company redirect resources toward priority areas.
The layoffs will primarily affect customer-facing roles that are "non-revenue generating," Workday said in a regulatory filing.
The cuts represent roughly 2% of its workforce and are expected to result in about $135 million in charges in the fiscal fourth quarter, which ended in January.
Workday announced a larger round of layoffs about a year ago, citing the need to invest more heavily in strategic areas such as AI. The company reported about 20,600 employees as of late October.
Visa is cutting roughly 7% of its workforce
Global payment technology company Visa confirmed to Business Insider that it's cutting about 2,600 jobs.
That's roughly 7% of the company's employee footprint.
"To capture the opportunities ahead and best position Visa to lead this transformation, we must continue evolving how we work," CEO Ryan McInerney wrote to staff in an internal memo, according to Bloomberg. "AI is also helping to accelerate this evolution and shape the way work gets done at Visa."
Zillow cut 500 employees
Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman announced on August 4 that the company was cutting 500 employees as part of "organizational changes."
As of December, Zillow had around 7,000 employees, so the changes are affecting about 7% of its workforce.
"These changes are about ensuring we have a disciplined cost structure and getting more efficient, with the right people in the right positions," Wacksman said in a blog post.

Dropbox is cutting roughly 200 workers
Dropbox announced on October 28 that it is cutting roughly 200 roles, or 9% of its global workforce.
"Delivering on that strategy requires concentrating our resources on the priorities that will have the greatest potential for customer impact and growth," Dropbox co-CEO Ashraf Alkarmi wrote in an email to employees.
Alkarmi said while Dropbox was profitable, it had to make "hard choices."
The affected roles are in the company's Engineering, Product, Design, and G&A teams. Alkarmi also wrote in the email that Dropbox's chief technology officer, Ali Dasdan, would be spending down.

A jet carrying the far-right Brazilian senator Flávio Bolsonaro has left Guayaquil in Ecuador and is on its way to Miami, Florida, where it is expected to arrive mid-morning on Wednesday.
After losing Sunday night’s election to the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Bolsonaro disappeared for more than 24 hours, until Argentina’s migration authorities said he had entered the country by land on Tuesday night.
There, he boarded a Gulfstream IV registered as LV-JQW. The aircraft had been parked at Puerto Iguazú airport since the early hours of the previous morning, when the first reports emerged in Argentinian media that he intended to flee on it.
Bolsonaro, the son of the jailed former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, boarded the jet with his wife and two daughters at about 11.30pm, bound for Guayaquil, reportedly to avoid Brazilian airspace. They made a brief stop in Ecuador, and have continued to the Miami-Opa Locka executive airport. The senator is expected to hold a press conference in the US at some point on Wednesday.
A senior US state department official told media outlets that visas would be granted to Bolsonaro and his family, and on Tuesday night the US president said he would approve their move to the country.
“They’re fine people. The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible,” Donald Trump said, as he returned from a campaign event in Texas. “I didn’t take sides, you know. I know them both. I know Lula. I know Flavio a little bit. I know the father very well.”
Lula called Bolsonaro’s flight “shameful”. “This is what the Bolsonaro family are like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as they’ve become accustomed to doing,” he said at an event celebrating his 81st birthday in Brasília.
Some in the Brazilian government suspected Bolsonaro allies had spent Tuesday privately telling the press he was already on his way to the US to distract from his real plan through Argentina. The federal police are facing criticism for failing to prevent him leaving the country.
There is a gap between the last time he was seen by allies at about 6pm on Monday and the moment he entered Argentina late on Tuesday. It remains unclear how or when he travelled to the border, or where he was during that time.
Footage from a television channel there shows two vans crossing the border checkpoint and then being escorted by airport security officers to the airport.
Shortly after the election result, police asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s passport to be retained over concerns he could flee, citing an interview given last Friday by his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro.
Speaking on a podcast in the US, where he is in self-imposed exile and lobbying the Trump administration against Lula, Eduardo said if his brother were to lose the election, he should not concede and should go to the US.
O Globo newspaper reported that the escape had been planned for weeks as a contingency in case he lost, and that Eduardo had been its main organiser, holding talks with US officials about receiving the senator.

Online astrology platform Astrotalk reported a 895% increase in its consolidated net profit to ₹222 Cr in FY26 from around ₹22 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its operating revenue rose 55% to ₹1,823 Cr from ₹1,176 Cr in FY25, driven by growth in consultations, international markets, and ecommerce, according to the audited consolidated financial statement. Profit before tax nearly quadrupled to ₹296 Cr from ₹75 Cr a year earlier. International Markets Drive Growth Astrotalk’s international revenue rose 2.6X to ₹621 Cr in FY26 from ₹236 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Overseas markets contributed 34% of operating revenue, up from 20% in FY25. Meanwhile, domestic revenue grew 28% to ₹1,202 Cr from ₹940 Cr in FY25. The company said it has been investing in marketing to expand internationally. Its overall marketing spend jumped 144.2% to ₹823 Cr in FY26 from ₹337 Cr a year earlier. Ecommerce Outpaces Consultation Growth Consultations delivered through chat, calls, and video remained Astrotalk’s largest revenue source, generating ₹1,657 Cr in FY26, up 45% from ₹1,139 Cr a year earlier. The business accounted for about 91% of operating revenue. Meanwhile, ecommerce revenue more than quadrupled to ₹166 Cr from ₹37 Cr in FY25. Its share of operating revenue increased to 9.1% from 3.1%. Astrotalk Store sells spiritual products, including rudraksha, gemstones, crystals, and Vastu products, through its own platforms and third-party marketplaces such as Amazon, Flipkart, and Blinkit. Launched in November 2024, the ecommerce business forms part of Astrotalk’s push beyond consultations. Gupta previously told Inc42 that the startup had invested ₹40 Cr in building inventory, strengthening supply chains, and adding product categories after an initial investment of ₹30 Lakh. The startup has also outlined plans for offline stores and a separate gemstones offering. “We set out to build a diversified, global business from India, and FY26 shows it is working. A third of our revenue now comes from outside India, and Astrotalk Store has grown into a real second business,” said Puneet Gupta, founder and CEO of Astrotalk. He further added, “The reason we are growing rapidly is that we are able to create a positive impact in the lives of our customers.” Cash Reserves Strengthen Astrotalk’s cash flow from operations increased 21% YoY to ₹229 Cr in FY26. Its year-end cash and investments rose 41.1% to ₹917 Cr from ₹650 Cr. This included cash, bank deposits, mutual funds, and bonds. The startup said it funded its FY26 investments through internal cash flows, supporting its expansion into international markets and new business lines without relying on fresh external capital. Founded in 2017 by Puneet Gupta and Anmol Jain, Astrotalk connects users with astrologers and charges for consultations on its platform. It has raised $34 Mn to date from investors including Left Lane Capital and Elev8 Venture Partners. In August this year, Astrotalk joined the unicorn club following an ESOP buyback at a $1 Bn valuation. The startup competes against the likes of InstaAstro, Astroyogi, AstroSage Kundli, among others.

Jamia Millia Islamia alleges campus vandalism amid protests
The university said the incidents raised serious concerns about the safety of students, faculty and staff
Jamia Millia Islamia on Wednesday alleged widespread vandalism on its campus through Tuesday night, claiming that groups of protesting students and locals damaged university gates and boundary walls, brought down Gate 4C, threw stones, and damaged CCTV cameras and their control room amid an ongoing protest.
In a statement on Wednesday, the university said the incidents raised serious concerns about the safety of students, faculty members and non-teaching staff. It alleged that a group of masked protesters reached the university’s boys’ hostels to mobilise additional support.
The allegations came amid protests against the university administration’s decision to restrict access to the campus, with hostel residents particularly angered by the closure of Gate 4C, which they use to enter the university.
A protesting student, not wishing to be identified, said, “The university administration had sealed Gate 4C, which is used by hostel students to reach the university campus. There are two halls - Zakir Hussain Hall and Jauhar Hall -- that house eight hostels. Residents of these hostels were angry about the administration’s decision to close the entry. They broke the gate to gain entry to the campus.” He said they will chalk out the further course of action on Wednesday.
The university said its proctorial team and teachers rushed to the campus after receiving reports of the attacks. It alleged that the scale and intensity of the damage were particularly concerning, with videos, CCTV footage and social media posts indicating that heavy iron rods, hammers and other tools had been used to damage university infrastructure.
The administration alleged that women faculty members, wardens and provosts were threatened when they attempted to reason with female protesters. It said the vandalism began shortly after another attempt by the university to hold dialogue with the protesting students.
The statement said the university administration had made seven attempts to engage with the protesters, including negotiations with committee members and teachers on Tuesday evening. The university expressed dismay at what it described as a contradiction between the students’ participation in discussions and the destruction that followed.
The incidents, it said, came after a week of repeated instances of university gates and boundary walls being scaled, damaged and broken. The university has shifted to online mode, as notified on October 24.
The administration said damage to classrooms, laboratories, libraries, entrances, exits and security systems could compromise the safety of the university community, apart from causing significant financial losses.
Ebin Basil, a National Students’ Union of India (NSUI) leader, who has been on an indefinite hunger strike, accused the university administration of restricting access to essential supplies and medical assistance for protesters.
In a video message, he said, “The Jamia administration has fortified the campus. They are not even letting food and water reach protesters. They are not even allowing the doctor who came to visit me to check my blood pressure. They are deliberately trying to kill me and the others on hunger strike. I request students to sustain this movement for a few more days. We will definitely win. I request students not to indulge in defacement or any kind of violence because the administration will tarnish this movement.”
The university said the damage to its infrastructure and security arrangements left faculty members and non-teaching staff distressed, adding that the safety and well-being of the entire campus community were at stake.
Delhi Police said that they have not yet received any complaint from the university and they did not enter the campus.

Varun Dhawan and Janhvi Kapoor revisited their fallout with Karan Johar during the latest episode of Koffee With Karan Season 9. The actors opened up about the disagreement that followed Bawaal being scheduled around the release of Johar's Rocky Aur Rani Kii Prem Kahaani in 2023, with the conversation revealing how the professional disagreement turned into a personal fallout.
Koffee With Karan 9: Janhvi Kapoor says she lost 6 kg after fallout with Karan Johar, Varun Dhawan recalls calling him a ‘child’; says, “You became Amitabh Bachchan from Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham”
Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, Bawaal stars Varun and Janhvi and was originally scheduled to premiere on Amazon Prime Video on July 27, 2023. Rocky Aur Rani Kii Prem Kahaani, directed by Karan Johar, was scheduled for a theatrical release the following day, July 28.
Varun Dhawan says Karan Johar ‘ghosted’ them
Recalling the disagreement, Varun said, “He just ghosted us and stopped talking. She knew you were fighting with her. I didn’t know you were fighting with me. For one week, I don’t think Karan was capable of fighting with me in my head.”
Janhvi then reminded Varun that Karan had called him a “child” during the disagreement. Varun responded that he had also described Johar as a child and said he still stood by his comment. “I said he was a child, which is nothing to get so offended about. I still stand by that,” Varun said.
Karan Johar explains why he was upset
Karan explained that he felt hurt because he was releasing his own film while Bawaal was initially coming close to its release date. “I was releasing a film of mine and you came on that same date. I am not supposed to be upset,” Karan said.
Varun pointed out that he had informed Johar that Bawaal might have to be released on that date. Karan, however, said the situation became difficult because the date had not been formally announced and he had limited options. “You weren’t announcing your date and I had to come because there are no dates. And then you come on a date and I was quiet. I didn’t reply. I didn’t pick up your call. I just didn’t reply to your messages,” Karan recalled.
He said he was particularly upset after receiving a message from Varun telling him to stop “acting like a child.”
Varun compares their equation to a family relationship
Varun explained that his use of the word “child” came from the paternal equation he shares with Karan. “There is a paternal relationship. I tell my dad also, ‘Dad, you are behaving like a child.’ I tell my mother also,” Varun said.
Karan responded that Varun could speak that way to his parents, while Varun maintained that he viewed their relationship similarly.
Karan also described the fallout with Janhvi as resembling a breakup, saying there had been genuine hurt involved. “Janhvi and I, I behaved like it was a breakup,” Karan said.
Varun described his own disagreement with Karan differently, calling it “a one-sided fight.” Karan, however, maintained that there had been real pain involved.
“There was pain. There was a proper fight. I was hurt with both of you,” Karan said.

NEW DELHI: Congress faced a major setback in the legislative council elections on Wednesday, failing to secure a victory in the seats declared so far across Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Maharashtra, even as counting continued in several constituencies.The BJP-JD(S) alliance swept all four seats in Karnataka, where the ruling Congress drew a blank despite having a majority in the state Assembly. The RJD also scored a victory in Bihar, wresting the Patna Teachers’ seat from the BJP.Counting for 28 legislative council seats across Uttar Pradesh (11), Bihar (8), Maharashtra (5) and Karnataka (4) began on Tuesday following polling on October 23. The elections were held for graduates’ and teachers’ constituencies, with results declared for several seats and counting continuing in others.
Here is a state-wise look at the latest results and counting trends.
Karnataka (4 seats): BJP-JD(S) alliance sweeps all four, Congress draws blank
The BJP-JD(S) alliance swept all four legislative council seats in Karnataka, dealing a setback to the ruling Congress.

Sitting BJP MLC S V Sankanur retained West Graduates’, defeating Congress candidate Mohan Limbikai by 9,323 votes.The results marked a clean sweep for the opposition alliance, with the Congress failing to win a single seat despite campaigning by chief minister D K Shivakumar, former chief minister Siddaramaiah and other senior leaders.However, the results are not expected to affect the stability of the Congress government or significantly alter the balance of power in the 75-member Legislative Council.
Uttar Pradesh (11 seats): BJP wins four seats, SP secures two
The BJP won four of the 11 Uttar Pradesh legislative council seats, while the SP secured two, according to the latest confirmed results.The BJP retained the Bareilly-Moradabad Teachers’ seat, where Hari Singh Dhillon defeated SP’s Danish Akhtar by 17,676 votes. SP candidates were also leading in the Varanasi and Lucknow Graduates’ constituencies.BJP candidate Manvendra Singh was leading in the Agra-Aligarh Graduates’ constituency.In the Gorakhpur-Faizabad Teachers’ seat, BJP candidate Dhruv Kumar Tripathi received 11,881 votes against independent candidate Rajiv Yadav’s 11,415 after the final round, though disputes arose over the counting process. Maharashtra (5 seats): BJP's Sudhakar Kohale leads Congress in Nagpur

Dozens are dead in a high-speed train crash in Spain
URDA, Spain — One high-speed Spanish train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks Wednesday, killing at least 68 people and shredding carriages in the country's second deadly rail collision this year.
The regional government for Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people needed medical treatment in hospital. Rescue workers continue to search in the wreckage for survivors and bodies.
The accident comes with memories still fresh of another crash between high-speed trains in southern Spain in January involving trains from the same two companies.
Spain's rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo, involving two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain.
One train, run by the state-owned RENFE company, ran into the tail of the other train owned by private company IRYO that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track in a rural area between two villages.
David Gómez, a construction worker, was working with his brother and another colleague nearby when they heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El País.
"People were trying to get out through the windows ... We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought," until emergency services arrived, he said. "As I was trying to pull a young woman out, there was a piece of a leg."
Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Until this year, there had been no fatal crash on Spain's dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992. It was a source of national pride.
Transport minister says crash was due to "inexplicable" decision
Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said that the accident was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command center for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Puente said they were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph (124 mph) for that stretch of the track.
"I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts," Puente said.
Everything went flying when the trains collided, a passenger said
The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left one car torn into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
Spanish Health Minister Mónica García said that emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and bodies from the two most damaged train cars. She said that the injured are being sent to different hospitals in the area.
"It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said.
Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.
"We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact," he said. "The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook."
Another passenger recounted to Cadena Ser radio how she felt the train slam on the brakes and was thrown forward in her seat, breaking the small table in front of her. She said she saw body parts and trapped people covered in blood.
Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.
IRYO, an Italian-owned company, said in a statement that it has "activated its security protocols and is closely working with authorities."
The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, said civil protection authorities had asked his officials to prepare a sports pavilion to receive injured passengers.
A military emergency brigade was deployed to help emergency services, firefighters and police. Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while unscathed survivors were put on buses.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez canceled his agenda to focus on the crash. He wrote on X that he was "dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo."
"Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers," wrote Sánchez, who faces a national election next month. "All my thoughts are with the victims and their families."
Spain's King Felipe VI visited the crash site. He and Queen Letizia said in a short statement on X that they were following news of the accident.
"We are deeply saddened and concerned by the train accident in Urda (Toledo)," the royal couple said. "We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said "My heart goes out to the victims' families and loved ones. Today, Europe mourns with you."
Spain's soccer federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled on Wednesday.
Spain already suffered a devastating train crash this year
The wreckage of Wednesday's crash reminded many of the aftermath of another train collision in January, when 46 people died in southern Spain when a IRYO train jumped the track and hit an oncoming RENFE train. That sent the first two cars of the impacted train plummeting down a four-meter (13-foot) slope.
That crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people.
The January incident shook confidence in the European country's extensive high-speed rail service.
Spain is a leader in high-speed rail
Over recent decades, Spain has invested heavily in high-speed rail — which the country's railway union defines as rails for trains going 250 kph (155 mph) and over — turning it into a world leader.
Spain has laid some 3,900 kilometers (2,400 miles) of such tracks over more than three decades for its 49 million residents. Only China, with 45,000 kilometers (28,000 miles) for its 1.4 billion people, has more high-speed track, according to the International Union of Railways.
Only recently did Spain open its rail network to private companies to compete against RENFE. IRYO started operating in Spain in 2022.
A spokesperson for Spain's train workers' union, Joan Rodríguez, said that the increased traffic brought by privatization has put extra strain on rail infrastructure.
"We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines," Rodríguez told TVE. "I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind."

Subsea cable projects owned by US companies such as Google and Meta face some of the greatest risks from the threat of deep-sea sabotage in the Pacific Ocean, according to a new report. That coincides with Chinese research ships spending an extraordinary amount of time apparently surveying undersea cables—not to mention Chinese commercial ships being investigated for cutting cables in both European and Asian waters.
Most damage to the undersea cables that form the Internet’s backbone is the result of accidents involving bottom-trawling fishing nets and ship anchors dragging on the seabed, with storms and undersea landslides also factoring in. But the recent rise in international tensions and open conflicts have placed new scrutiny on more suspicious instances of cable-cutting damage, with analysts warning about Russia and China in particular engaging in cable sabotage or tampering as “gray zone” tactics that fall short of direct military confrontation.
One of the newest risk assessments of China’s gray zone tactics targeting the Internet’s undersea infrastructure comes from a research report published by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, an independent government commission that advises Congress. The report was contracted to the London-based think tank China Strategic Risks Institute and published in September 2026.
Mapping the risks
The report authors created an interactive Trans-Pacific Cable Gray Zone Vulnerability Index that ranks the undersea cables considered most at risk and displays a map of their routes spanning the Pacific Ocean. Such an index could help identify which cables should get highest priority in terms of placing underwater sensors or setting up patrols to monitor for threats.
Risk factors used in the vulnerability index include the undersea depth of the cable routes, nearby shipping traffic, cable ownership, China’s exclusive economic zone and broader territorial claims, and whether each cable connects to Taiwan. Taiwan is considered a geopolitical hotspot as a self-governing island democracy that is also claimed by China, with the latter ramping up military maneuvers involving warships and aircraft around Taiwan in recent years.

Despite significant economic progress and sustained public health efforts, anaemia — driven significantly by iron deficiency — continues to be one of India’s most pressing public health challenges. Affecting over half of Indian women and almost three-fourths of children, anaemia contributes to maternal mortality, an intergenerational cycle of malnutrition, impaired cognitive development, reduced productivity and substantial economic losses. The Government of India’s 7X7X7 Anaemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategy, which was launched recently, rightly recognises the multifactorial nature of anaemia through a comprehensive approach spanning prevention, screening, treatment, dietary diversification and behaviour change. Yet, one proven preventive intervention remains significantly underutilised.
The promise of fortification
That intervention is Double Fortified Salt (DFS) — salt fortified with both iodine and iron. Salt offers an unparalleled opportunity to address iron deficiency. Consumed daily by virtually every household across India, in predictable quantities regardless of income or geography, it is uniquely suited to deliver a preventive nutrition intervention at population scale. DFS also addresses one of the fundamental challenges of anaemia control — sustained compliance.
Delivering iron through an everyday food complements interventions such as iron supplementation and dietary diversification, whose effectiveness depends on regular adherence. India already has one of the world’s most successful public health platforms in Universal Salt Iodisation, with around 95% of households consuming iodised salt. Building on this existing infrastructure, DFS is already distributed to an estimated 76 million people across four States through government safety-net programmes. Global and Indian evidence strongly support DFS. A global review has shown that DFS can reduce anaemia by up to 21%. Randomised controlled trials in Bengaluru, Darjeeling, and Punjab, along with large-scale implementation in Uttar Pradesh, have shown improvements in iron status and confirmed that, when manufactured to validated specifications, DFS is acceptable to consumers, reduces iron deficiency, and is highly cost-effective. A DFS standard has been issued by the Government of India’s Food Safety and Standards Authority (FSSAI), and the Government of India actually mandates DFS’ inclusion in the national school feeding programme (PM POSHAN and the national early childhood development programme- Integrated Child Development Scheme, or ICDS).
At an estimated cost of ₹14-₹20 per person annually, DFS represents one of the most affordable population-level nutrition interventions available, with a benefit-cost ratio of 4.2:1 for national DFS introduction, primarily driven by improved health outcomes and subsequent increases in labour productivity. India also possesses the manufacturing capacity to produce high-quality DFS at scale. Established fortification technologies, centralised salt production and existing laboratory infrastructure make quality assurance and regulatory monitoring simpler than for many other fortified foods.
What the barriers are
What has limited DFS from wider adoption? The barriers are now primarily institutional rather than technical. The next imperative is to accelerate its nationwide adoption and ensure last-mile access, particularly the Public Distribution System apart from social safety-net programmes, across all States through a central flagship scheme. Although DFS is recommended under PM POSHAN and ICDS, its integration into the largest safety net programme i.e., the Public Distribution System (PDS) — which reaches around 800 million beneficiaries — remains uneven because implementation depends largely on State governments. Greater policy commitment, dedicated financing, stronger quality assurance, wider commercial availability and consumer awareness are now needed to accelerate nationwide scale-up. These are implementation challenges — not technological ones — and are well within India’s capacity to address.
Like all public health nutrition interventions, DFS should be implemented within a robust regulatory framework. It should complement existing strategies under Anaemia Mukt Bharat, align with India’s sodium reduction goals, and continue to be accompanied by screening for haemoglobinopathies such as thalassaemia and sickle cell disease. These safeguards are well recognised through experience of rice fortification programme and can be readily integrated into implementation and monitoring systems.
The launch of the revised AMB strategy provides renewed momentum to strengthen the preventive pillar of India’s anaemia response and advance the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.
Potential to be a global model
India has already shown the world how science, policy, public systems, and public awareness can transform nutrition through Universal Salt Iodisation. By scaling DFS nationally, India can not only accelerate progress towards Anaemia Mukt Bharat but also contribute to global efforts to reduce iron deficiency by demonstrating an affordable, scalable model for other low- and middle-income countries.

A recent review of international clinical practice guidelines published in The Lancet Rheumatology highlights a shift in the management of non-specific low back pain towards clinical assessment, patient education, physical activity, and exercise, while discouraging routine imaging when there is no suspicion of serious disease.
Examining guidelines issued between 1994 and 2026, the review underscores the importance of assessing symptoms and identifying warning signs before deciding on investigations or treatment. Bengaluru-based specialists said the approach reflected a growing emphasis on restoring function and avoiding unnecessary investigations and interventions.
Ravikumar Mukartihal, senior consultant orthopaedic and robotic joint replacement surgeon at SPARSH Hospitals, Bengaluru, said the approach had moved from investigation-driven care to one focused on clinical assessment and restoring function.
“Most cases of non-specific low back pain do not indicate a serious structural problem and can be managed without extensive investigations or invasive procedures,” he said.
Treatment should focus on understanding symptoms, reassuring patients, maintaining normal activities, prescribing appropriate exercises and physiotherapy, and using medication judiciously, he said.
Treat the patient, not the scan
Karuna Kabadi, neurosurgeon at Apollo Speciality Hospital, Jayanagar, said a disc bulge or prolapse described in an MRI report was an observation about the disc, not necessarily a diagnosis explaining the pain. “Many of us may be having disc bulges but do not have symptoms and feel perfectly fit,” she said.
Back pain can arise from muscles, ligaments, and joints, and may also be associated with systemic diseases. A disc bulge may cause symptoms when it irritates or compresses a nerve, resulting in shooting pain in the buttock or leg, commonly known as sciatica. A detailed history and clinical examination help doctors assess the likely cause, with imaging supporting the diagnosis where necessary, she said.
Ravikumar T., Head and Consultant of the Department of Orthopaedics at Ramaiah Memorial Hospital, said incidental findings on scans could cause unnecessary anxiety if patients interpreted them as proof that their spine was damaged.
“Treat the patient and not the scan,” he said, noting that disc bulges and mild degenerative changes were also seen in people without back pain.
Non-specific back pain can involve several factors, including muscle strain, weak core muscles, poor movement patterns, sedentary habits, stress and inadequate sleep. Clinical examination helps assess pain, movement limitations and neurological signs before treatment is decided, he said.
Movement over prolonged rest
The review found that most guidelines recommended taking a patient’s history, conducting a physical examination and assessing psychological factors, including risk-stratification tools where appropriate. Routine imaging was generally discouraged without indications of serious pathology.
For acute low back pain, recommendations commonly included self-management, heat therapy, spinal manipulation and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). For chronic pain, they included exercise therapy, psychological interventions and multidisciplinary care, with acupuncture and spinal manipulation recommended in some guidelines as part of broader treatment programmes.
Dr. Ravikumar T. said treatment had moved away from prolonged bed rest and early reliance on strong painkillers towards reassurance, education, continued activity and structured physical therapy.
“Movement is medicine,” he said, warning that avoiding activity out of fear of scan findings could cause muscle deconditioning and prolonged disability.
Dr. Kabadi said sitting for long hours and reduced daily movement contributed to mechanical back pain. Staying active, avoiding prolonged sitting and following guided physiotherapy and muscle-strengthening exercises could help, although consistency was essential.
When is a scan necessary?
Doctors stressed that discouraging routine imaging did not mean scans were unnecessary. Imaging remains important when there are warning signs of serious disease, progressive neurological deficits or persistent symptoms for which the findings could change treatment.
Surgery also has a role in selected patients, but decisions should be based on clear clinical indications rather than an MRI finding alone, Dr. Mukartihal said.
The specialists said the focus should be on appropriate clinical assessment and treatment tailored to each patient, with the aim of restoring movement and function while avoiding unnecessary investigations and procedures without overlooking serious underlying conditions.

Amgen's Imdelltra used in combination with AstraZeneca's immunotherapy Imfinzi reduced the risk of death by 58% compared to the Astra drug alone in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, according to data from a study presented at a major medical meeting on Saturday.
Imfinzi is currently the standard of care following chemotherapy for patients with this very aggressive and hard-to-treat disease whose cancer does not worsen after initial chemotherapy.
The study found that those given both drugs lived for a median of 21.1 months, compared with 12.7 months for those treated only with Imfinzi.
"If you give Imdelltra earlier and earlier, you get bigger clinical benefit," said Paul Burton, chief medical officer at California-based Amgen. He called the results "unprecedented in advancing the treatment of extensive-stage small cell lung cancer."
Imdelltra's U.S. list price is about $30,000 per cycle, or over $390,000 a year. Wall Street analysts have estimated annual sales reaching more than $2.5 billion by 2030, according to LSEG data.
The Amgen drug is currently approved for adults in the advanced stages of small cell lung cancer that has worsened despite chemotherapy, based on data showing that Imdelltra reduced the risk of death by 40%.
Full results of the 563-patient trial were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology meeting in Madrid and published in the New England Journal of Medicine. Amgen had previously announced that the Phase 3 study was successful.
Imdelltra belongs to a dual-target class of drugs called bispecific antibodies designed to pull immune system T cells into contact with cancer cells to destroy them. Imfinzi is an older type of immunotherapy that essentially blocks the mechanism tumors use to hide from immune-system assault.
Most lung cancer cases are non-small cell, while up to 15% are the small cell variety targeted by Imdelltra. About 250,000 new cases are diagnosed worldwide each year, according to the U.S. National Institutes of Health.
Very few people diagnosed with small cell lung cancer are candidates for surgery, and most are initially given radiotherapy and chemotherapy, Burton said.
Survival rates depend on when the cancer is diagnosed, but the overall 5-year rate is only around 9%, according to the American Cancer Society.
Amgen said that nearly 80% of trial patients treated with the combination were alive after one year, compared with 53% of those on Imfinzi alone, as patient follow-up continues.
Serious side effects, including low white blood cell counts, occurred in 20.9% of patients on the dual therapy and 10.8% with the single therapy. A potentially dangerous condition known as cytokine release syndrome, an aggressive inflammatory response, was reported in 49.6% of patients who received Imdelltra. But only one case was serious and there were no CRS-related deaths.
Adverse events led to discontinuation of the combination therapy in 5.7% of trial patients and 5.8% of patients given only Imfinzi.

Are you an organ donor? Here are some rule changes you may want to know
Organ donation conversations are changing. Critics worry families may feel pressured
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
The U.S. organ transplant system is making a controversial change to a long-standing rule that was designed to protect potential donors. The revision aims to boost donations and reduce errors. But critics worry that the move may endanger patient care.
Under the change, the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network, which runs the transplant system, will relax a strict firewall between the doctors and nurses trying to save patients in the hospital and the transplantation team standing by to procure patients' organs.
Previously, no one from that team was even supposed to talk to family members until after they had made the heart-wrenching decision to let a loved one go. The rule was intended to prevent pressure that could change the care patients receive. It was also in place to dispel any doubts that doctors aren't doing everything they can to save patients.
But the board of directors for the transplant system voted Aug. 20 to modify that rule as part of a new set of guidelines governing donation following circulatory death. That occurs after life-sustaining care has been withdrawn and now accounts for about half of organ donations.
The new rules, which go into effect Nov. 18, "allow discussions for organ donation to take place once end of life discussions are taking place with the potential deceased donor's agent," according to the new policy.
Why is the firewall previously barring these conversations coming down?
"I think the best way to think about it is that insisting on a bright line without focusing on what's happening on either side of that line is a false sense of security," Dr. Raymond Lynch, the director of transplantation at the Health Resources & Services Administration, the federal agency that oversees the organ network, told NPR in an interview.
The new rules aim to prevent disturbing mistakes that have occurred in the past. Those errors have included patients being wheeled into operating rooms to remove their organs when they were still alive.
"That specific line in the policy is part of a suite of improvements to the coordination and communication between the organ procurement organizations and the healthcare team that is caring for these patients in hospitals and the families of the patients themselves. And that really is a marked improvement over the policy that was in place before," Lynch says.
A balance of safety and speed
In addition to allowing donation teams to approach families sooner, the new policies include making it easier to pause organ retrieval if anyone becomes concerned that something is amiss and standardizing other patient protections, including testing for determining death.
"Documentation, clear coordination, deference to the primary healthcare team and consequences — that's what keeps patients safe," says Lynch.
The change in policy is also designed to make sure the organ retrieval team isn't brought in too late to conduct the tests and preparation necessary for families to honor their loved one's desire to be a donor.
When that happens, "the family loses out on that memory" of helping their loved one donate their organs, "the patient loses out on the choice that they made, and the people on the waiting list lose out on the chance to receive a lifesaving organ," Lynch says.
More than 109,000 Americans are waiting for an organ transplant, according to the Health Resources & Services Administration. About 12 die every day because of a chronic organ shortage.
Does the change cross an ethical line?
Critics, however, say the change is dangerous. It could subtly pressure families and caregivers to discontinue care and create confusion about who's in the intensive care unit to try to save their loved one and who's there to obtain their organs, which could deepen distrust in the organ donation system.
"It's a very important bright line," says Dr. Lainie Ross, a bioethicist at the University of Rochester. "Our primary responsibility is that patient's well-being and care. And we need a bright line. That's where our focus is, and we're not even going to start thinking about whether those organs are usable until death is inevitable and imminent."
She adds: "When my family member is in that hospital bed, I want to know that we're all on Team Mom and not worried the reason the doctor's really suggesting the treatments aren't working is because they want your organs for someone else."
Ross says she's "horrified to think that families will feel pressured. They'll feel manipulated."
Others also see problems with the change.
"I don't disagree with the desire to have more transplantable organs. I think transplants provide great benefit to many, many people," says Dr. Claire Morgan, a transplant surgeon who serves on the transplant network's Patient Affairs Committee. "But people may be pressured to make that decision too quickly. I don't want to interfere with a family's grieving process, and I don't want to interfere with a family's ability to make a decision for their family member at a time when it's correct for them."
Some critics say the change is the latest worrisome development for organ donors.
"This is part of a number of things that are going on in organ donation that are blurring lines," says Lois Shepherd, a professor of law and bioethics at the University of Virginia who opposed the change as a member of the working group that developed the new guidelines. "A lot of safeguards for patients are weakening. And that's a concern to me."
But the change was endorsed by the Association of Organ Procurement Organizations (AOPO), a trade group.
"Families/agents who are considering [withdrawing life support] must be informed about donation and how the donor evaluation process may affect the timing of the [withdrawal of life support]," the group said in its public comments. "Many families have expressed frustration with learning about this timing impact after planning for other family members to be present at the time of [withdrawing life support]. Waiting until the family has made the decision is too late."
The AOPO declined to make someone available for an interview with NPR. But AOPO President Allison Erickson said in a written statement: "Donation depends on public trust, and it is our responsibility to respect and maintain it. Any time there is confusion or concern, [organ procurement organizations] clarify and improve the process. Donor families deserve to fully understand each stage of the end-of-life and donation processes, as well as that their loved ones are cared for by all involved."

Sara Ali Khan has returned to Kedarnath for prayers amid the ongoing discussion surrounding a proposed affidavit requirement for non-Hindus visiting the shrine. The actor reportedly reached the temple by helicopter around October 25 and joined the regular queue to offer prayers, waiting for approximately 30 minutes despite snowfall and cold weather.
Sara Ali Khan visits Kedarnath amid Sanatan affidavit debate

Her trip has drawn attention as it comes months after the Badri-Kedar Temple Committee (BKTC) said that non-Hindus wishing to visit Kedarnath and Badrinath could be asked to submit a written affidavit affirming their faith in Sanatan Dharma.
No public confirmation exists on whether Sara submitted an affidavit before entering the temple. Her visit alone does not establish whether the proposed requirement has been implemented or what arrangements were followed in her case.

(Bloomberg) -- New World screwworm was found in Arizona for the first time, detected in a dog, as cases of the deadly parasite accelerate.
The US Department of Agriculture confirmed the infection late Wednesday in a dog in Cochise County, Arizona. 
The spread of the parasitic fly, whose larvae burrow into the wounds of animals, had remained relatively contained since the pest was first detected in the US in June. Most of the early cases were limited to Texas. However, the pace of infections has increased this month, particularly in New Mexico. 
There have been a total of 71 cases of screwworm in the US since the outbreak began, according to the USDA. Eighteen are still active, with 10 located in New Mexico. 
The increase in October comes after screwworm, which can be deadly to livestock if left untreated, was discovered for the first time in wildlife last week. Spread among wildlife has been a key concern for cattle ranchers since the animals travel through the same terrain that their herds graze on. 
The spread also comes as the USDA has reopened ports in Arizona and New Mexico to shipments of cattle from Mexico. The US had halted livestock shipments from the country, and largely maintained that ban until late August when it began a phased reopening of the ports. 
The US had previously eradicated screwworm, pushing the pest south of Panama. But the fly began spreading north again after the pandemic, reaching Mexico in late 2024. 
While screwworm is a major threat to the US cattle herd, the parasite has also infected animals from goats to horses. The most recent five cases involved four dogs and one cat.

Artiva Biotherapeutics said Tuesday that it’s winding down after two patients died in a trial testing its cell therapy for autoimmune diseases, the latest in a series of safety events that emerged in a promising research field.
One participant in the Phase 2 study died from a neurological complication after receiving the treatment, an NK cell therapy. Researchers, however, determined the death was likely not related to the cell therapy itself, but to a chemotherapy that was given before the cell therapy, Artiva said. It’s standard to give patients chemotherapies before infusing cell therapies to lower the patients’ white blood cell count and make room for the new cells.
A second participant experienced sudden death about two months after treatment. Researchers determined that this was not related to any component of the treatment process, but the cause of death has not been determined, the San Diego-based company said.
