The Netherlands reaffirmed its position as a key supporter and strategic partner of WHO and a leading donor of flexible and predictable resources to WHO. In picture: WHO Director-General Dr Tedros and Dutch Minister of Health, Welfare and Sport Ernst Kuipers. ©WHO
The Netherlands strengthened its longstanding engagement with WHO on Monday with the renewal of the multiannual contribution of the Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to WHO for €13.34 million for 2024–2028 and for €6 million to the technical partnership with Dutch WHO collaborating centres.
With the new contribution, the Netherlands reaffirmed its position as a key supporter and strategic partner of WHO and a leading donor of flexible and predictable resources to WHO.
"Amid increasingly complex and connected threats, from pandemics and climate change to conflicts, the Netherlands remains an essential supporter of WHO and global public health," said WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus during the agreement signing.
"The Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport's new contribution reflects the Netherland's commitment to its long partnership with WHO, and its support of the sustainable financing for WHO that Member States have agreed. This will enable WHO to respond quickly to global health challenges, and strengthen public health worldwide, including in the Netherlands."
Dutch Minister of Health, Welfare and Sport Ernst Kuipers added that “the Netherlands values our strong and long-standing relationship with WHO. Given the global challenges we collectively face, and the added value the Netherlands can deliver, we believe this renewed arrangement with long-term flexible funds well represents our commitment to advancing health worldwide. These funds will be used to achieve our shared priorities in the WHO’s General Programme of Work, facilitate the secondment of Dutch experts, and to support the Dutch WHO collaborating centres.”
The Netherlands recently recommitted to its role as a leading voice for global health through its Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030. The strategy aims to strengthen health systems at home and worldwide, better prepare for pandemics and address the impact of climate change on public health.
The Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport has provided for many years critical financial and technical support to WHO’s efforts to strengthen health security, improve the capacities of countries to address health emergencies, fight antimicrobial resistance, promote access to medicines, and support food safety, tobacco control and mental health.
The renewed partnership expands the joint work of the Netherlands and WHO into new global health challenges, such as those posed by climate change.
The interconnection between the health of the Earth and human health makes climate change a fundamental threat to decades of progress on health. The joint work of the Netherlands and WHO aims to make healthcare more climate resilient and sustainable while mainstreaming health into internal climate policies.
***
The Netherlands also funds crucial activities in sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care and antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.
Between 2022 and 2023, the Netherlands provided US$ 80 million to WHO, including over US$ 66 million in voluntary contributions.
The Netherlands also contributed over US$ 20 million in flexible and thematic funding to WHO, making it the third-largest flexible contributor to the Organization. Such support allows WHO to be agile and strategic in its efforts to help countries improve the health and well-being of their populations.

Bolsonaro claims he is Brazil's true leader after fleeing to US
"I am the elected president, and the criminals who stole Brazil's election are part of a criminal organisation that has established a tyranny," Flavio Bolsonaro said as he slammed "electoral fraud".
MIAMI: Brazil's defeated right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro insisted on Wednesday (Oct 28) he is his country's rightful leader after arriving in the United States to start a self-imposed exile.
Bolsonaro's defiance on fleeing to Florida signaled continued upheaval for Brazil, where leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won a dramatic runoff election on Sunday.
"I am the elected president, and the criminals who stole Brazil's election are part of a criminal organisation that has established a tyranny," Bolsonaro said in the statement published on his X account, slamming "electoral fraud".
"I will lead the opposition from here," he said. In a subsequent statement, he revised his claim, saying he is the "leader", rather than "president".
Bolsonaro, 45, touched down earlier on Wednesday in a private jet at Opa-Locka Executive Airport near Miami.
President Donald Trump's hard-right administration has strong links to Bolsonaro and his father Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest in Brazil after attempting to overturn his own electoral loss to Lula in 2022.
Trump reiterated his stand that Brazil's election was "very strange" but told reporters he "won't get involved" in Flavio Bolsonaro's claim to the presidency.
Details of how Bolsonaro, accompanied by his wife and daughters, made it to US soil are still emerging.
He is under investigation in his home country over alleged corruption and money laundering. With his current parliamentary immunity about to expire, he was ordered to surrender his passports but left anyway, reaching the United States via Argentina and Ecuador.
A police source told AFP that Bolsonaro's Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been canceled, but the senator has also held Italian nationality since 2023, according to Italian documents seen by AFP.
The US Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that the Bolsonaro family members were inspected and cleared "with applicable immigration laws and procedures".
The travel ban was issued by powerful Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who led the case against Flavio Bolsonaro's father and is a controversial figure hated by the Brazilian right.
Flavio Bolsonaro had vowed to seek the justice's impeachment if he were elected - which up until Lula's comeback in the runoff had looked increasingly likely.
"SHAMEFUL" ACT
Lula, who won the election with 51.8 per cent of Sunday's vote, called Flavio Bolsonaro's departure a "shameful" act.
"A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide," he said in Brasilia during his 81st birthday celebration on Tuesday.
But Brazil police issued a statement on Wednesday saying that he was not considered a fugitive.
There was controversy in neighbouring Argentina, where opposition lawmakers demanded to know how Bolsonaro had managed to transit through the country.
While Argentinian authorities said he was carrying valid travel documents, officials have requested chief of cabinet Diego Santilli to provide details to parliament, according to opposition lawmaker Agustin Rossi.
FRAUD CASES
The most high-profile fraud case against Flavio Bolsonaro in Brazil centres on the unreleased biopic "Dark Horse" starring US actor Jim Caviezel as Flavio's father Jair.
In May, the outlet Intercept Brasil revealed audio recordings in which Flavio Bolsonaro negotiated approximately US$24 million to finance the film with banker Daniel Vorcaro, who is jailed over one of Brazil's biggest-ever fraud cases.
Before the leak, Flavio Bolsonaro had denied knowing Vorcaro, or that he had financed the movie.
In July, the Supreme Court ordered a probe into the financing of the film, and whether it involved corruption, money laundering or the illegal movement of currency.
Flavio Bolsonaro acknowledged Vorcaro had funded the film, but insisted it was a private business deal that was "completely legal".
In another probe, police are investigating whether Flavio Bolsonaro laundered money and moved funds out of the country in collaboration with his close friend, the lawyer Willer Tomaz.
Flavio's father Jair Bolsonaro also never conceded defeat after losing to Lula and left the country on the eve of his rival's inauguration, before returning to Brazil three months later.

US-based Innodata has become the latest company to lay off a big chunk of its staff in India. The AI services company reportedly axed nearly 550 jobs in the country, nearly 5% of its global workforce. Reflecting on how Saani Kaayidham influenced Dharmaraj’s decision to consider her for a character, Keerthy recalled their first meeting and his response to the film. Serbian police say an unidentified assailant attacked a guard with knives outside the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade and was killed just after midnight Wednesday
BELGRADE, Serbia -- Serbian police said on Wednesday that an unidentified assailant attacked a guard with knives outside the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade and was killed just after midnight.
Interior Minister Ivica Dacic said that police were treating the incident as a “terrorist attack” and had raised the terror threat to the highest level and stepped up police presence at key locations.

But Vucic and his allies still control the police as the new government is yet to be formed.
Israel also held its parliamentary vote Tuesday that exit polls said produced no clear winner.
In June 2024, an attacker with a crossbow wounded a Serbian police officer guarding the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade. The assailant was shot and killed by a guard.

A zookeeper who spent nearly all of her 40-year career at the Beekse Bergen Safari Park in the Netherlands has died from wounds suffered following a leopard attack.
The woman, whose name has been withheld in accordance with Dutch privacy law, passed away on Tuesday, the park in the southern Dutch town of Hilvarenbeek said.
She had suffered serious wounds to her head and neck on Saturday while working in an enclosure with two male Persian leopards. The woman began working at the zoo when she was 17.
“Her passing deeply affects us all, and we sympathise intensely with her family, friends, and loved ones,” the zoo said in a statement, which was made together with her family.
An investigation is underway to determine why the woman was in the enclosure with the leopards. Zoo staff are typically not permitted to be in the same space as predatory animals.
According to the zoo, the woman was able to alert colleagues via a walkie-talkie that she had been hurt.
An ambulance and a trauma helicopter were dispatched to the park at around 11am local time on Saturday.
The woman underwent emergency surgery, but her condition worsened on Sunday evening and the zoo had said they did not expect her to survive.
The death of the Dutch zookeeper comes a little over two weeks after a man was mauled to death by a tiger in Yorkshire, England, after entering an enclosure at a wildlife park.

A hacker stole a trove of personal information from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The breach exposes the names, job titles, phone numbers, email addresses, and office locations of more than 41,000 employees, including those in US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), according to TechCrunch and Wired. The data also linked the agencies to specific surveillance tools.
A hacker stole more than 40,000 DHS employee records
The names, job titles, phone numbers, and emails of thousands of ICE, CBP, and other DHS employees were compromised in a massive hack.
As reported by TechCrunch, a hacker known as “Department of Peace” gained access to the data through Okta, an identity and access management service used by the DHS. Around 21,000 records pertain to CBP employees, and nearly 7,000 belong to staff at ICE. The data also includes records from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI).
The DHS has worked to conceal the identities of CBP and ICE agents, who have carried out anti-immigration raids around the US, while also tracking down online critics. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” the “Department of Peace” hacker said, according to TechCrunch. This leak comes just weeks after hackers stole data from the FBI on its employees and job applicants.
The leaked DHS information was reportedly given to cybersecurity researcher maia arson crimew, who shared it with Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), a nonprofit organization that’s now hosting the leaked “Icepick” dataset. The leak also reportedly includes information about DHS groups that have access to tools that can be used for surveillance, such as the facial recognition app Mobile Fortify and PenLink, which can collect and analyze data from phones and online services.
The DHS didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

FCC chair wants to let prisons jam illegal cellphones
The agency will vote next month on relaxing its long-standing opposition to jammers.
The US Federal Communications Commission announced today that it will vote on a new rule that would allow state prisons and jails to use cellphone jammers. The goal of the change would be to block use of illegal cellphones by inmates, since having outside contact could allow them to continue engaging in criminal activity.
The planned vote during the agency's open meeting on November 19 would consider allowing state and local incarceration facilities to opt in to using jammers; use of the tech would not be required. Any tech that interferes with communications signals is illegal for non-federal parties to use. In 2018, the Federal Bureau of Prisons began testing "micro-jamming" in federal prisons as a way to block unauthorized cellphone use by inmates. This move would potentially open up similar tools at the state and local levels, and provide a formal pathway for federal facilities to jam signals as well.
It's a reversal from previous policies where the FCC has not allowed implementing jammers as a method of reducing illegal cellphone use in prisons. Previous concerns about jammers suggested the tech could interfere with emergency and public safety communications, as well as creating new security risks by putting more jamming tools into the wild where they could be exploited by bad actors. The bulletin today notes that if the new rules are adopted, correctional facilities would need to meet some standards, including proving "that the jamming solution does not cause harmful interference outside of the designated geographic areas."
Today's move isn't the first time the FCC has changed its approach toward prisons under the current administration. In July 2025, the department said it would delay implementing a cap on the rates charged for prison phone calls.

The recent conversation over the merchant discount rate on select UPI transactions raised the question of who pays for the digital convenience that millions of people enjoy. Hospitals may soon face a similar problem for strengthening their privacy even if no separate “privacy charge” appears on a patient’s bill.
Protecting digital patient information will require secure systems, trained personnel, and continuous compliance. Parliament enacted the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act 2023 in response to this need. The Act consists of 44 sections in nine chapters plus one Schedule. The government notified its Rules on November 13, 2025, with the Sections pertaining to provisions for consent managers set to kick in from November 13, 2026. The rest of the substantive obligations will start to apply from May 13, 2027.
Unusually difficult places
The Act is a general framework to protect digital personal data across sectors, including healthcare. In healthcare, the Act recognises that clinical consent and data consent are different. For example, a person agreeing to undergo a medical scan does not automatically mean they have agreed to every later use of the same scan, no matter how useful the hospital or doctors deem the scan data to be. While facilitating this distinction, the Act also makes room for data-processing during emergencies and specific medico-legal and public health situations.
Under the DPDP Act, the patient is the data principal (or owner) and the hospital — which usually decides why and how some information will be used — is the data fiduciary. Some external software, cloud, and/or data-processing company will serve as the data processor.
That said, hospitals are unusually difficult places in which to ensure compliance with a general data-protection law. Unlike banks or regional transport offices, hospitals continuously create information of an intimate nature. For example, healthcare workers record a patient’s clinical notes, nursing observations, diagnostics and laboratory results, ventilator readings, and prescriptions — all within hours.
At the same time, several professionals will need to access different parts of that record at different times. If access is too tightly controlled, patient care may suffer; on the other hand, unrestricted access can result in significant breaches of privacy. So the Act needs to facilitate the lawful processing of consent with reasonable security safeguards, grievance handling processes, and of course the correction or erasure of data where permissible.
Failure to take reasonable safeguards can attract a penalty of up to ₹250 crore.
Compliance costs
In the same vein, compliance requires hospital information systems with role-based access, facility to encrypt or mask data as necessary, systems to generate and preserve audit logs, backups, vendor contracts, breach response protocols, staff training, and a clearly identified person who is responsible for data governance.
Entities designated data fiduciaries must also appoint a statutory data protection officer, and smaller hospitals will need a privacy or data management lead in practice.
Further, information rarely stays within the hospital, since a cashless claim can send diagnoses and reports to an insurer or a third party administrator. Laboratories, radiology platforms, cloud vendors, and telemedicine services will create additional routes for the same record. Even low-cost WhatsApp-based workflows that became popular because they were convenient will have to be examined for compliance and security.
Healthcare may therefore need specific DPDP provisions, either explicitly or eventually as a separate Act, to cover sector-specific uniqueness, such as small hospitals and large hospitals separately, as clinical care is more than a commercial transaction.
Lesson from Chandigarh
U.S. estimates show the cost of complying with the famed Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, or HIPAA, to be around $5 per patient a year in 2008. Estimates for 2025 suggest the cost of $498 per affected record.
In a 2023 study, researchers from India and Norway estimated that adding an integrated information and communications system to an urban primary health centre (PHC) would expand the centre’s annual economic budget by 17.7%. But when the researchers applied the same model across 400 PHCs, the incremental cost fell to about 6% per PHC. The reason: common development and infrastructure costs were shared.
The finding offers an important policy clue: the government should not expect every small hospital, diagnostic centre, and/or PHC to independently purchase the same privacy tools, legal templates, and so on.
That said, the harder problem is that India has legislated faster than it has trained the people who must make the law work. Medical education teaches confidentiality and ethics, but there is no uniform DPDP-oriented National Medical Commission curriculum or standard course materials that span medicine, nursing, allied health, hospital administration, and healthcare IT training.
The vendor side faces the same problem: behind every software workflow is a human being who configures access, checks claims, handles support or views data. And an untrained person handling data in a hospital can pave the way for a major breach due so little as to one leaked password. So data literacy has to become a core healthcare competency.
Building an ecosystem
The National Health Accounts 2022-23 released this year estimated the out-of-pocket expenses on healthcare to be 43.4% of total health expenditure. There is a nontrivial chance that the new costs of complying with the DPDP Act will be passed on to patients as well.
Ahead of the November 13 date, the Indian government should step in by enabling a shared infrastructure through the Unified Health Interface of the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission. It could provide model consent and vendor agreements with affordable cybersecurity support, and healthcare-specific implementation standards.
User data is routinely commoditised today, and passing a law assuming compliance and waiting for complaints or litigation will not suffice. As the DPDP Act comes into effect, the government must finance, build, and sustain an ecosystem that allows every health worker to comply and patients to be able to better access care.
Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. Views expressed here are personal.

Top Vatican official says pope's cancer diagnosis a 'game-changer' for the papacy
A top Vatican official says that Pope Leo XIV's lung cancer diagnosis is “a bit of a gamechanger” for the Vatican
ROME -- Even though Pope Leo XIV is recovering well from lung cancer surgery and is going ahead with a big trip to Latin America next week, the diagnosis is “a bit of a game-changer” for the Vatican and Leo’s still-young papacy, a top Vatican official said Tuesday.
Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, the Holy See’s foreign minister, said there had been a temptation to think that Leo was a “Superman, a Superpope” after he was elected in 2025 and “hit the ground running” following the drawn-out illness and death of Pope Francis.
“The fact that he has fallen ill with, in many ways, one of the most common illnesses of our age means that he is a poor mortal like the rest of us. And I think that that is going to change how we see him and possibly how he sees himself as well,” Gallagher told reporters at the Italian foreign press association.
“Even if the operation has gone well, and everybody (says) there are grounds for considerable optimism, I think it is a bit of a game-changer at the same time,” Gallagher said.
Leo, 71, had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Oct. 13 after doctors found a tumor, later diagnosed as adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. Subsequent tests indicated no further treatment is necessary, and Leo has been slowly resuming his daily activities.
The Vatican this week confirmed Leo would go ahead with his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, without any changes to the program. The published trip itinerary is challenging even for a healthy pope, with a dozen flights and two helicopter rides covering 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles), the longest of Leo’s pontificate.
Asked why Leo didn’t postpone the trip so he could recover further, Gallagher said the pope simply wanted to go. Leo spent two decades as a missionary priest in Peru, where he has citizenship, and has made clear his close attachment to its people and his former diocese of Chiclayo.
“All of the medical advice is very positive, from a clinical point of view, so he feels he can go,” he said.
Gallagher, a British veteran of the Vatican's diplomatic service, also predicted that the Chicago-born Leo would in the “not-too-distant future” visit his native United States. But he said the outcome of next month’s midterm elections might influence whether the trip comes in 2027 or later.
The Vatican generally tries to avoid papal trips to countries in the throes of national election campaigns to avoid allowing the governing powers to use the pope for political benefit. U.S. presidential elections are scheduled for November 2028.
Preliminary discussions on an eventual U.S. trip have included timing it to coincide with the U.N. General Assembly gathering in the fall, or alongside a possible stop in Mexico, though Gallagher stressed that no firm plans are in place.
“He’s, I think, quite keen to visit the Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe at some point,” Gallagher said, referring to the immensely popular pilgrimage destination where past popes have visited.
Gallagher also said it was “highly likely” that Leo would travel to Australia in 2028 to close out a big church meeting in Sydney, the International Eucharistic Congress. Other big trips expected are to South Korea in August 2027 for World Youth Day.
Gallagher, who served as foreign minister under Pope Francis as well, shared some insights about working with Leo after the sometimes turbulent Francis pontificate, which was characterized by the Argentine pope's spontaneity, grand gestures and occasional diplomatic gaffes.
Leo, he said, is pensive, thinks things through and is “not impetuous.” The math major pope can read a spreadsheet and is extremely well-informed, asking follow-up questions, such that when Gallagher meets with him each Wednesday evening to brief him on pressing foreign policy issues, “nearly everything I say he knows already.”
At the same time, Leo is tight-lipped and holds his cards close. Gallagher revealed he didn’t know about Leo’s planned surgery until the pope announced it to the world on Oct. 11 at his weekly Sunday blessing. He said he still doesn’t really know what the pope is thinking down the line.
“I think he’ll stick to his plan. And he will stick to revealing his plan, because he’s not the sort of personality who shares a lot in what he’s thinking of doing in three or four years’ time,” he said.
Gallagher said what has struck him most working with Leo is his serenity, focus on preaching the Gospel and dealing with issues as they come along. And he rejected speculation that the Italian-centric Vatican bureaucracy would eventually have its way and thwart his agenda.
“I don’t think the Curia will eat him up. I think if there’s any indication of that, he will demonstrate that he too has an appetite,” Gallagher said to laughs.

While plant-derived kababs may still struggle to replicate the taste and texture of meat from a tandoori joint, they may contain relatively more protein in a form that the body can absorb, according to a study presented on Monday (October 26, 2026).
In a collaboration between the CSIR–Institute of Himalayan Bioresource Technology (CSIR-IHBT), Palampur, and the Good Food Institute (GFI) India, a non-profit that promotes alternative proteins such as plant-based, fermentation-derived and cultivated meat, scientists investigated whether protein bioavailability (meaning protein in a form that’s nutritively useful to the body) of traditional meat was the same as that of plant-based meat.
Tests on five cooked plant-based products — two burger patties, a nugget and two seekh kebabs — showed higher bioavailability percentages than their chicken counterparts, according to the findings presented at a press conference on Monday (October 26). The plant-based kebabs scored 80.8% and 86.1% against 38.8% for chicken. The nugget scored 61.2% against 43.4%, and the patties recorded about 57% and 58% against 21.2%.
The findings do not mean plant-based meat is healthier, but only that they are nutritively comparable, as ‘healthier’ is a subjective term, Dr. Padma Ishwarya, senior scientist at GFI India, told The Hindu. “It’s too much of a vague term. It’s too broad a term…for health, we need to do further studies.”
The chicken products held more crude protein and released more amino acids, the building blocks of protein, during digestion, and Dr. Ishwarya said more products and samples would be tested in the next phase.
The work has not yet been published as a journal paper. “It is a report that is hosted on our website, but it is very much peer-reviewed,” Dr. Ishwarya said in a conversation with The Hindu. Two experts reviewed it, she said, and it was an overview and that detailed manuscripts would follow.
The team used an in vitro method that simulated digestion in a laboratory. Samples went through a two-minute salivary phase, then a stomach phase with digestive enzymes at pH 2 to 3, and then an intestinal phase. The method follows INFOGEST, an internationally harmonised protocol, Dr. Ishwarya said.
The team added an ultrafiltration membrane chosen to mimic the pore size of the human intestine. Whatever passed through the membrane was deemed bioavailable, and only free amino acids were measured. Each sample was adjusted to start with 40 milligrammes of protein.
Animal studies remain the gold standard, she said, but are tedious and require ethical clearances. The simulated method is faster and more reproducible. The team plans to conduct tests across laboratories next year so that NABL-accredited labs can use the method.
Plant-based meat, Dr. Ishwarya said, is made “specifically for biomimicking animal-derived meat”, unlike crisps or cereals, which are plant-based foods. It is made from soya, pea or wheat gluten, mostly soya, and shaped by extrusion, a process in which material is pushed through a die under heat and pressure. She said it contains no synthetic chemicals beyond ingredients such as spices and texturisers.
The study examined only protein. An earlier analysis in 2024 of about 120 products in the Indian market, she said, found that saturated fat and sodium levels were comparable to those in animal-derived products, leaving room for reduction. Plant-based products also supplied dietary fibre, which animal-derived products do not.

Albertsons is curbing health care benefits for employees due to rising healthcare costs.
Starting next year, the grocery giant will no longer offer medical insurance plans to employees' spouses and domestic partners who have jobs that provide such coverage. The grocery giant detailed the change in an open enrollment guide posted to its website.
Albertsons said it expects its healthcare costs to increase 9.5% next year due to inflation, higher prescription drug costs, provider consolidation, and shortages in the healthcare workforce.
"We are making changes to our benefits in 2027 to reduce the projected cost increase while still maintaining a quality benefits program that meets the needs of our associates at a cost sustainable for the company going forward," it said.
The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Other changes this year include higher weekly paycheck contributions from employees, the elimination of two network plans, along with higher deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums for some other plans.
Large companies Disney, Starbucks, and Deloitte have also introduced cost-saving changes to their benefits packages for 2027. Disney is also dropping coverage for partners and spouses who can get insurance from their own jobs.
"We've seen employers reducing their contribution toward the spouse's coverage, but not eliminating the coverage option for those people," Capitol Benefits CEO Joshua Lavine told Business Insider in August, regarding Disney's decision.

A group of 21 news publishers has reportedly challenged India’s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act in the Supreme Court (SC), arguing that the law could undermine investigative journalism and expose journalists’ sources. The lawsuit, filed on October 6, argues that the law’s provisions on consent, data erasure and government access to information could restrict news reporting and force publishers to remove factual stories. The case is scheduled to be heard on October 27, according to a Reuters report. The challenge comes nearly a year after the Centre notified the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 in November last year. The broader DPDP Act, 2023 and the Rules establish a framework governing how organisations collect, process and protect individuals’ digital personal data. The Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), which represents the publishers, has argued that the law does not provide a specific exemption for journalistic activities. According to the confidential filing, the association reportedly said that the absence of such safeguards could compromise press freedom and investigative reporting. The DNPA’s members include Mukesh Ambani-owned Network18, Gautam Adani-owned NDTV, the Indian Express and Times Internet, which is part of the Times of India group. Publishers Vs The DPDP Act A key concern raised by the publishers is the requirement to obtain consent before processing personal data. The DNPA has argued that requiring journalists to notify the subjects of investigations and seek their consent could allow them to destroy evidence or intimidate witnesses. The association has also flagged provisions allowing individuals to withdraw consent and request the erasure of their personal data. According to the filing, the absence of a public-interest safeguard could force publishers to remove or substantially redact factual news reports. The publishers have further raised concerns about provisions empowering the government to seek information from organisations handling personal data. They argue that these powers could expose confidential journalistic sources and discourage whistleblowers from sharing information about corruption, corporate wrongdoing and electoral malpractice. The filing also challenges the government's power to restrict access to information in the public interest, arguing that the provisions could curtail press freedom. The DNPA has sought the quashing of several contentious provisions of the law, most of which are scheduled to come into effect from May 2027, Reuters reported. The association has also argued that the government has granted broad exemptions to the state without extending corresponding protections to the press. What The DPDP Framework Provides The DPDP Act, enacted in August 2023, establishes obligations for processing digital personal data. The later DPDP Rules, notified in November 2025, provide a phased implementation framework, giving organisations up to 18 months to comply with specified requirements. The framework requires platforms to obtain consent for processing personal data, provide clear information about its use and implement security safeguards. It also gives individuals rights to access, correct, update and seek the erasure of their personal data, subject to the applicable provisions. The latest case marks one of the most prominent challenges to the DPDP framework so far, raising questions about how India’s data protection requirements will interact with press freedom and investigative reporting. The Act provides for financial penalties of up to ₹250 Cr for failing to implement reasonable security safeguards. Other violations, including certain breaches of obligations relating to children’s personal data, can attract penalties of up to ₹200 Cr. However, the publishers argue that the framework does not adequately account for the requirements of investigative journalism, particularly when reporting involves personal information collected in the public interest. The government has maintained that the framework protects citizens’ privacy while supporting responsible data processing.

- The claim that rapper Nicki Minaj is not a United States citizen is still under investigation.
- The rumor stems from X and TikTok posts claiming that even though Minaj is expressing her support for U.S. President Donald Trump and encouraging voters to support Republicans in the midterm elections, she herself cannot vote.
- In January, Minaj — who was born in Trinidad and Tobago — stated that she was not a citizen, but was "finalizing" her citizenship application. In the same post, she suggested she was instead a lawful permanent resident, commonly known as a green-card holder, writing "Residency?" She has not given any more updates on her status since then. Noncitizens, including permanent legal residents, cannot vote in federal or state elections and most local elections.
- Since a person's immigration record is not publicly available, we were unable to confirm Minaj's immigration status using primary evidence as of this writing.
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We have reached out to Minaj's record label, the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, and await responses.
As rapper Nicki Minaj expressed her support for U.S. President Donald Trump and joined him at a Republican campaign rally in late October, many people questioned (archived) her own citizenship status.
Numerous posts (archived) claimed that while Minaj called on voters to support Republican candidates in the midterm elections, she herself cannot vote because she isn't a citizen.
One X user wrote, "The GOP is telling people to 'vote red' with Nicki Minaj as the messenger. Problem is, she can't even vote. She's not a U.S. citizen."
Minaj wrote in a Jan. 28 X post that she was "finalizing" her citizenship paperwork. In the same post, she suggested she was a lawful permanent resident, commonly known as a green-card holder. Noncitizens, including permanent legal residents, cannot vote in federal or state elections and most local elections.
Since a person's immigration record is not publicly available, we were unable to confirm Minaj's immigration status using primary evidence as of this writing.
We also reached out to her record label, the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to learn more, and will update this story if we receive responses. Until then, we leave this claim unrated.
On Jan. 28, Minaj wrote on X:
Residency? Residency? The cope is coping. 😅
Finalizing that citizenship paperwork as we speak as per MY wonderful, gracious, charming President. 
Thanks to the petition. 📋 
I wouldn't have done it without you. 
Oh CitizenNIKA you are thee moment
Gold Trump card free of charge
Minaj was referring to the Trump administration's "gold card" visa, which guarantees foreigners U.S. residency for a $1 million fee. In January, The New York Times reported that, per a Department of Homeland Security official, Minaj has been a legal permanent resident in the U.S. for over two decades, meaning she likely would not need to apply for a gold card.
In a 2024 TikTok livestream, Minaj said she was "not a citizen" despite paying "millions of dollars" in taxes.
In 2018, while posting about children in immigration detention centers, Minaj said on Facebook that she "came to this country as an illegal immigrant @ 5 years old." She was born in Trinidad and Tobago. In the same post, she wrote, "Please stop this. Can you try to imagine the terror & panic these kids feel right now?" 
Citizenship applications can take around 12 months to process and timing varies based on the applicant's primary city of residence. Assuming Minaj uses Los Angeles as her primary residence, where she has a home, the process could take more than a year, according to processing times on USCIS website. Given that she has a close relationship with Trump, it is possible her application could be expedited.
On Oct. 25, White House communications director Steven Cheung posted a video of Minaj in Air Force One, pretending to be the new White House press secretary and praising Trump.
For further reading, Snopes has reported on the unsupported rumor that Minaj was the only "Trump gold card" visa recipient, and the claim that her husband is a registered sex offender.

Russell Brand denies all charges as he takes the stand at rape and sex assault trial
Russell Brand says allegations of sexual misconduct have had a “devastating” impact on his life
LONDON -- Actor-comedian Russell Brand said allegations of sexual misconduct have had a “devastating” impact on his life, as he testified in court Wednesday at his trial on charges of rape and sexual assault.
Brand entered Southwark Crown Court alongside his wife, Laura Gallacher, telling reporters that “today is the day for truth and justice.”
Brand, 51, stood in the witness box and took the oath, then gave his full name: Russell Edward Brand. He answered “no” to each of the charges: three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Questioned by his lawyer, Ian Winter, Brand said the allegations had a “devastating” impact, with friends and colleagues abandoning him. He said no one with relevant evidence had been willing to testify in court on his behalf.
“My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations,” he said.
Brand said he even was forbidden from staying with his baby son in hospital after anonymous allegations of sexual misconduct were made against him in a newspaper and a TV documentary in 2023.
“The reason given by Great Ormond Street Hospital when my son was receiving open heart surgery and subsequent treatment was due to the material published,” he said.
Over the past two weeks of the trial, prosecutors have set out their case and the jury heard from six women who accuse Brand of sexual misconduct between 1999 and 2009.
Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones told jurors that Brand was “ruthless, he was calculating, he was manipulative. And, the prosecution say, he was a sexual predator.”
As the defense attorney asked Brand about each of the alleged incidents, which his accusers said took place in locations including a hotel room, the offices of MTV and the toilet of a London bar, he denied forcing women to do anything against their will.
“Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary, and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself,” Brand said.
Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek” and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.
In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.

China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in party
- Published
A major political gathering is under way in the Chinese capital, with a closed-door meeting of senior figures that could shape the look of the ruling Communist Party in the years to come.
The Fifth Plenum brings together around 300 members of the Central Committee and state media said it would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the Party's ranks.
The four-day session that started on Monday will give Xi Jinping an opportunity to further consolidate his grip on power following recent purges.
The normally annual plenums are highly secretive, but a summary of decisions and a more detailed document will be made public after.
What is a plenum?
They are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year.
There are usually seven plenums during each five-year Central Committee term and they are watched from afar because they are meant to signal the leadership's priorities.
The timing for this year's gathering is important because it is a year away from the next Party Congress, where a new set of priorities is set up and a new central committee appointed.
Officially, the Central Committee selects the Party's top leadership but the real processes leading to the selection are kept secret within the Party elite.
The next Party Congress will almost certainly reappoint Xi as the country's leader, following the abolition of term limits.
What is on the agenda this year?
Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy – branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" – to the same level as Chairman Mao.
This year's plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.
Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.
According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.
This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.
Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled.
"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".
The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.
The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.
This plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

Ecommerce major Meesho reported a 68% decline in its consolidated net loss to ₹132.5 Cr in the September quarter (Q2 FY27) from ₹411.4 Cr in the year-ago period as its revenue growth outpaced increase in expenses.However, net loss remained largely unchanged from ₹132.8 Cr in the June quarter.
Operating revenue rose 34% YoY and 11% QoQ to ₹4,131.6 Cr. Including other income of ₹127.4 Cr, Meesho’s total income stood at ₹4,259 Cr in Q2 FY27, up 31% from ₹3,254.9 Cr a year ago.
Meesho incurred exceptional expenses in the last year quarter which it didn’t incur this year, leading to the sharp annual reduction in loss. In Q2 FY26, Meesho incurred exceptional expenses of ₹45 Cr towards a business combination and a vendor dispute settlement, besides a ₹64.4 Cr tax charge related to the business combination. Neither charge recurred in the quarter under review.
Before exceptional items and tax, its loss narrowed by 57% to ₹123.3 Cr from ₹285.5 Cr a year earlier.
Meanwhile, Meesho’s total expenses increased 24% to ₹4,382.3 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹3,540.4 Cr. (The story will be updated soon)

The 2026 US midterm elections are shaping up to be a significant test of Indian-American political representation.
Four Indian-origin Democrats — Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam — are seeking re-election to the House of Representatives. Meanwhile, Vivek Ramaswamy is locked in a high-octane race for governor of Ohio, and physician-turned-politician Amish Shah is attempting to capture an open Arizona congressional seat.

The contests extend beyond Congress. Indian-American candidates are competing for attorney-general positions, mayoralties and seats in state legislatures across the country.
The elections on November 3 will take place against the backdrop of a closely divided Congress and a national debate over the economy, immigration, healthcare, technology and Trump's policies. The outcomes could determine not only which party controls Capitol Hill but also how much influence Indian-American lawmakers exercise in Washington and state governments.
Indian-Americans in key congressional races
1. Ro Khanna
Ro Khanna, one of the most prominent Indian-American Democrats in Congress at the moment, is seeking a sixth term from California’s 17th Congressional District, which covers much of Silicon Valley, including parts of Santa Clara and Alameda counties. 
He faces Republican Ritesh Tandon in the midterms, after comfortably finishing first in California’s June 2 nonpartisan primary with 62.3% of the vote. Tandon advanced with 14.8%.
The district, home to major technology companies and a large population of technology workers, has consistently favoured Democrats.
First elected to the House in 2016, Khanna has established himself as a progressive voice on economic policy, technology, foreign affairs and the role of American power overseas.
Khanna has been a vocal critic of President Donald Trump, particularly over his economic policies
Born in Philadelphia to Indian immigrant parents, he studied economics at the University of Chicago and earned a law degree from Yale University. Before entering Congress, he taught economics at Stanford University, practised law and served as deputy assistant secretary of commerce under President Barack Obama.
He now sits on the House Armed Services Committee and has been an influential voice on issues ranging from artificial intelligence and semiconductor manufacturing to US competition with China.

US midterms 2026: Meet Ro Khanna, Indian-American Congressman behind Epstein files push
Khanna has been a vocal critic of President Donald Trump, particularly over his economic policies, immigration crackdown and approach to democratic institutions. He has challenged the administration’s priorities on taxation and economic inequality, arguing that government policy should benefit working families rather than disproportionately favour wealthy individuals and corporations. His opposition to Trump also extends to the president’s use of executive power and his approach to foreign policy, where Khanna has advocated greater congressional oversight of military action and a stronger emphasis on diplomacy.
At the same time, Khanna has sought to distinguish himself from the Democratic establishment by championing a more populist economic agenda, including investment in manufacturing, clean energy, education and healthcare.
His views on technology, economic inequality and America’s global role frequently place him at the centre of the party’s policy debate.
2. Pramila Jayapal
Pramila Jayapal is seeking re-election from Washington’s 7th Congressional District, which includes much of Seattle and surrounding communities. She faces Republican Nirav Sheth in the midterms after dominating the state’s nonpartisan primary, securing 84.4% of the vote against Sheth’s 9.8%.
The result underlined her strong standing in a heavily Democratic district, where she has built a substantial political base through her advocacy on immigration, healthcare and economic inequality.
Elected to Congress in 2016, Jayapal made history as the first South Asian American woman elected to the House of Representatives.
Pramila Jayapal serves on House committees that give her influence over debates on immigration.
Born in India, she moved to the United States at 16 to attend Georgetown University and later earned an MBA from Northwestern University. Before entering electoral politics, she founded OneAmerica, a Washington-based immigrant-rights organisation, and became a prominent campaigner for immigration reform and civil liberties. Her experience as an activist has shaped her legislative priorities, particularly on deportations, detention, family separation and pathways to legal status.
Jayapal has championed Medicare for All, stronger labour protections, affordable housing, climate action and expanded access to education. She has also held leadership positions in the Congressional Progressive Caucus and serves on the House Judiciary, Foreign Affairs and Budget committees, giving her influence over debates on immigration enforcement, federal spending and American foreign policy.

A vocal critic of President Donald Trump, Jayapal has repeatedly challenged his administration’s immigration crackdown, deportation policies and restrictions on legal immigration. She has argued that the administration’s approach threatens civil liberties and undermines protections for immigrant communities. Her opposition also extends to Trump’s economic agenda and broader use of executive power, with Jayapal advocating stronger social protections and greater accountability for the administration.
Her politics frequently put her to the left of the Democratic leadership, although she has worked within the party to advance progressive priorities.
3. Ami Bera
Ami Bera, one of the longest-serving Indian-American members of Congress, is seeking another term in California’s 3rd Congressional District, which covers Sacramento County and surrounding communities. He faces Republican Robb Tucker in the November 3 midterm elections.
In the state’s nonpartisan primary, Bera secured 34.3% of the vote against Tucker's 29.9%.
His re-election bid comes as Democrats seek to regain control of the House, with the Sacramento region offering a test of whether his established local support can withstand the broader national political climate.
Bera has supported stronger US engagement with India.
First elected in 2012, Bera has represented the Sacramento area in Congress since January 2013. The son of Indian immigrants, he grew up in California and earned his medical degree from the University of California, Irvine. Before entering politics, he worked as a physician and served as Sacramento County’s chief medical officer.
His background has helped shape his political identity as a pragmatic Democrat who emphasises healthcare, public services and evidence-based policymaking rather than the more sweeping economic agenda associated with the party’s progressive wing.

Healthcare remains a central part of Bera’s political profile. He has advocated improving access to medical care, reducing prescription drug costs and strengthening Medicare, while also focusing on education, infrastructure, veterans’ services and economic development. His approach generally favours targeted reforms and bipartisan cooperation, positioning him closer to the Democratic Party’s moderate wing on several policy questions.
Foreign affairs, however, have become one of his defining areas of influence.
Bera has served on the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, with a particular interest in the Indo-Pacific. He has supported stronger US engagement with India and closer cooperation with regional partners, while emphasising the strategic challenge posed by China. His work has given him a prominent role in debates over US-India relations, regional security, intelligence oversight and the future of American engagement in Asia.
4. Suhas Subramanyam
Suhas Subramanyam is seeking a second term in the US House of Representatives from Virginia’s 10th Congressional District, which includes Loudoun County and parts of the surrounding Northern Virginia suburbs. He faces Republican Dave Beckwith and independent candidate Ahsen Mujeeb Malik in the midterms.
The district, home to technology professionals, federal employees and government contractors, has generally favoured Democrats, but the Trump administration’s cuts to the federal workforce and changes to government spending have made these issues particularly consequential for local voters.
Suhas Subramanyam served as a technology policy adviser in the Obama White House.
Subramanyam entered Congress in January 2025 after defeating Republican Mike Clancy in the 2024 election. His victory made him one of the newest Indian-American members of the House. Born in Houston to Indian immigrant parents, he studied at Tulane University and earned a law degree from Northwestern University. Before entering electoral politics, he worked with technology startups and served as a technology policy adviser in the Obama White House. He was elected to Virginia’s House of Delegates in 2019, becoming the first South Asian American elected to the state legislature, and later served in the Virginia Senate before moving to Congress.
His political profile combines technology policy, economic affordability and a focus on practical local concerns. During his time in the Virginia legislature, he worked on issues including utility bills, prescription drug costs, education and gun safety. In Congress, he has emphasised support for small businesses, infrastructure investment, healthcare access and protecting federal workers. His background in technology has also shaped his attention to the rapid expansion of data centres in Northern Virginia, where new developments promise investment and jobs but raise concerns about electricity demand, water consumption, land use and higher infrastructure costs.

Subramanyam has been critical of Trump’s policies on federal employment and government restructuring, arguing that abrupt cuts and uncertainty can harm public services and communities that depend on government jobs. His district is particularly exposed to such changes because of its concentration of federal agencies, contractors and defence-related businesses. He has also advocated reproductive healthcare protections, stronger gun-safety measures and policies aimed at lowering household expenses.
New entrants
- Amish Shah is running as the Democratic nominee in Arizona's 1st Congressional District. He previously contested the seat in 2024, losing to Republican David Schweikert. Schweikert is now running for governor, leaving the congressional seat open. Shah won the July 21, 2026, Democratic primary with 39.4% of the vote, defeating Marlene Galán-Woods, who received 34.4%. He faces Republican Jay Feely, a former NFL kicker, in November. The district is competitive, making this one of the more consequential races involving an Indian-origin congressional candidate. A FirstStrategic poll conducted on October 1 found Shah at 44.4% and Feely at 41.6% among registered voters, with a margin of error of 5.4 percentage points. A forecast updated October 23 projects Shah at 63% to win.

Indian-American politicians not on the ballot

- Shri Thanedar lost the Democratic primary for Michigan's 13th Congressional District and is not the Democratic nominee in the November race.
Gubernatorial race attracting national attention: Vivek Ramaswamy
Vivek Ramaswamy, the Indian-American entrepreneur who emerged as a prominent voice in the Republican Party during the 2024 presidential race, is seeking to become governor of Ohio, the state where he was born and raised. The Republican nominee faces Democrat Amy Acton, a physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health. The contest has become a closely watched test of Ramaswamy's transition from conservative political outsider to candidate for executive office.
Born in Cincinnati to Indian immigrant parents, Ramaswamy studied biology at Harvard University and law at Yale. He made his fortune in biotechnology and investment management, founding Roivant Sciences in 2014. His 2021 book, 
Woke, Inc.
, established his political identity as a critic of corporate diversity initiatives, environmental, social and governance investing and what he considers excessive ideological influence over business.
Ramaswamy's political relationship with Trump remains a defining feature of his campaign
During the 2024 Republican presidential primary, he advocated cutting government bureaucracy, restricting federal spending and challenging established political institutions. Although he withdrew from the race and endorsed Donald Trump, his combative campaign style helped establish him as a nationally recognised conservative figure.
Trump subsequently selected Ramaswamy to co-lead the Department of Government Efficiency initiative alongside Elon Musk, although he left before the initiative's major restructuring efforts as he turned to the Ohio governor's race.
His gubernatorial platform centres on reducing government costs, deregulation, education reform and expanding economic opportunity. His political relationship with Trump remains a defining feature of his campaign, even as he seeks to establish an independent record as a candidate for state leadership.
The campaign has recently been embroiled in controversy over an advertisement featuring Acton's estranged mother criticising her daughter.

Trump, however, defended the advertisement and encouraged Ramaswamy to continue running it, while Vice-President JD Vance also criticised Republicans who opposed it. Other statewide contests
- Nirav Shah, a physician and public-health administrator, is the Democratic nominee for governor of Maine. He previously served as director of the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention from 2019 to 2023 and as principal deputy director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from 2023 to 2025. Shah won Maine's June 9 Democratic gubernatorial primary with 26.9% of the vote.
- Aruna Miller, Maryland's lieutenant governor, is seeking to continue in office on the Democratic ticket led by Governor Wes Moore. Born in India, Miller immigrated to the US as a child and built a career as a transportation engineer before entering politics. Her career includes service in Maryland's House of Delegates and election as lieutenant governor in 2022. Miller's political position differs from that of a standalone gubernatorial candidate: the lieutenant governor runs on a joint ticket with the governor. Her electoral prospects therefore depend on the performance of the ticket as a whole as well as her own profile.

Nithya Raman: Running for Los Angeles mayor
Raman is a Los Angeles City Council member and urban planner seeking to unseat Mayor Karen Bass. Her campaign focuses on housing, homelessness, city services and the cost of living. She has become a prominent figure in the city's progressive political movement.
Raman advanced to the November 3 mayoral runoff after the June 2 primary. Certified results gave incumbent Bass 34.3%, Raman 29.0% and Spencer Pratt 25.5%. Raman's advance to the runoff turned the race into a direct contest between two Democrats.

A McLaughlin & Associates/California Post poll conducted October 15–18 put Raman ahead by 7.9 percentage points. An Impact Research poll conducted October 2–7 put her ahead by 10 points, while a UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies/Los Angeles Times poll from September 15–20 showed an 11-point lead.
Raman's candidacy is significant beyond her own electoral prospects: a victory would make her the first South Asian woman to serve as Los Angeles mayor. Her campaign will test whether her progressive coalition can expand sufficiently to defeat an incumbent in a city facing persistent housing and homelessness challenges.
What's at stake for Indian-Americans
For the Indian-American community, the November 3 midterms are about more than individual victories. They are a test of how far a once-underrepresented community has come in American politics — and whether its growing presence can translate into greater influence in Congress, state governments and the national debate.
The stakes are particularly high for the so-called ‘Samosa Caucus’, the informal label for Indian-American lawmakers in the US Congress.
November 3 mideterms will shape the scale and reach of Indian-American representation in American public life.
Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam are fighting to retain their House seats, while challengers such as Amish Shah and Dandiya are seeking to expand the community’s footprint on Capitol Hill. Their outcomes will help determine whether Indian-origin representation in Congress consolidates, grows or faces a setback at a time when immigration, technology, healthcare, economic opportunity and America’s role in the world are fiercely contested.
The stakes extend beyond Washington. Vivek Ramaswamy’s bid for governor of Ohio could take an Indian-American politician from national prominence to one of the country’s most powerful state offices. Nirav Shah’s campaign in Maine adds another dimension to the contest for statewide leadership. Success in races such as these would signal that Indian-origin candidates are competing not just in safe districts or within established political networks, but for executive power and leadership across the political map.
Yet there is no single Indian-American political story. The candidates span the ideological spectrum — from progressive Democrats to more centrist lawmakers and conservative Republicans — and are campaigning on sharply different visions of government. Their fortunes will reflect not only the strength of their personal brands and local coalitions, but also how voters respond to their parties, their policies and the national political climate. Representation, in other words, does not automatically translate into a common agenda.
Ultimately, November 3 will test whether Indian-American candidates can turn growing political visibility into electoral power. The results will shape not only the careers of individual candidates, but also the scale and reach of Indian-American representation in American public life — and the influence the next generation may be able to wield in setting the country’s political priorities.

Former Bengal minister Indranil Sen arrested in Kolkata over alleged financial irregularities in Durga Puja preview shows
The investigation centres on alleged financial irregularities involving the Mass Art Society, an organisation headed by Indranil Sen’s wife.
Former West Bengal tourism minister Indranil Sen was arrested by Kolkata Police on Wednesday after being questioned by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) in a case linked to alleged financial irregularities involving Durga Puja preview shows.
The probe centres on massArt (Mahanirban Road Mass Art), an organisation associated with Sen’s wife, Madhuchhanda Sen, which organised Durga Puja preview shows at selected pandals in Kolkata. The ED has alleged that the organisers sold tickets priced between ₹1,749 and ₹5,499, with more than one lakh tickets issued in 2023 and 2024.
ALSO READ | Durga puja 'preview shows' probe suggests ex-minister's firm sent ₹30 lakh to Mamata's accounts: ED
According to the ED, the proceeds were allegedly siphoned off through cash withdrawals or recorded as miscellaneous expenses. The agency has also alleged that more than ₹3.8 crore in cash was deposited into the bank accounts of Sen and his proprietorship concern, Octave Records, during his tenure.
The ED further said nearly ₹30 lakh was transferred from Octave Records to former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee through banking channels. Sen reportedly described the payment as “royalty”. However, the agency did not specify what the payment was for or allege any criminality in the transaction.
The case is being investigated under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). The ED had questioned Sen for around 10 hours and searched 15 premises in Kolkata linked to him and his associates as part of the investigation.
