US Fed holds interest rates steady despite surging inflation
The move comes just days ahead of the US midterm elections, in which the rising cost of living has been a key issue
The US Federal Reserve on Wednesday held interest rates steady, in line with market expectations, days ahead of crucial midterm elections where surging inflation has been a key issue.
The 12-member Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to hold rates at a target range between 3.75 to 4.00 per cent, citing the need for more data in the fight against inflation, after having hiked for the first time in three years at its previous meeting in September.
“The accumulation of more information will help the committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the committee’s 2 per cent goal,” the Fed said in a statement announcing its decision.

NASA’s Mars Odyssey spacecraft has been operating for so long, it can rent a car without any fees. The spacecraft arrived at the Red Planet on October 24, 2001. It, along with its 20-year-old sibling, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), have operated longer than anyone watching their launches could have dreamed possible.
Having such a long record of observations from above the Martian surface has rewritten the story of water on the planet, past and present alike. Keeping the wizened orbiters going for so long has been possible only thanks to great engineering and constant problem solving—and a little luck. But scientists wonder whether, despite their storied legacies, Odyssey and MRO will be the last of their kind, at least for the Red Planet.
“Both Odyssey and MRO are some of the most productive spacecraft that have ever existed,” says Briony Horgan, a planetary scientist at Purdue University who isn’t affiliated with either mission, calling them “critical” to NASA’s overall Mars research program. Odyssey’s observations of the planet’s ice, for example, and MRO’s ability to see surface features change over time have each given scientists unprecedented insight into Mars as a vibrant planet rather than a lump of rock. Odyssey and MRO also connect humans to every NASA rover, which can’t communicate with Earth directly. It’s an impressive legacy for a pair of orbiters that were only meant to last just a few years.
Space is a notoriously harsh environment that takes luck and resilience to survive for decades. Particularly tricky is the barrage of high-energy particles hitting machinery; a powerful enough strike to a delicate enough apparatus can be fatal. And whereas engineers can keep constant tabs on satellites orbiting Earth, bandwidth to Mars is more limited—science spacecraft might only check in once or twice a week, says Rob Lillis, a planetary and space physicist at the University of California, Berkeley, who has worked on a range of more recent Mars orbiters.
“A Mars craft has to be able to manage by itself,” he says.
Losing an instrument is bad, but losing the power or computing systems can brick the whole craft. NASA often doubles up on vital parts of a spacecraft to ensure that if something important fails, the mission can run off the spare until engineers can troubleshoot a problem.
In the MRO’s case, one challenge it’s faced is ironically due to its staying power. The orbiter determines its precise location and orientation by comparing what its cameras see with a stellar atlas onboard—with just one hiccup. “MRO is actually old enough that some of those stars have moved across the night sky—very slightly, but they have moved,” says Paul Fieseler, an engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and chief engineer for MRO. The tiny misalignments confused the spacecraft, and last year, engineers had to send up an updated map to keep MRO oriented into the future.
Odyssey’s greatest risk right now is simply running out of propellant it uses to make tiny adjustments to maintain its orientation in space. The spacecraft doesn’t have a fuel gauge–without gravity to push the fuel down, there’s no volume to measure–so NASA can’t be sure how much juice it still has. Engineers have improvised new ways to fully operate the spacecraft on just a few drops at a time in a bid to extend its life.
Experts say both spacecraft benefited from failures during NASA’s infamous “faster, better, cheaper” era. In 1999, NASA lost two missions arriving at Mars: First the Mars Climate Orbiter burned up in the atmosphere, and then, just months later, the Mars Polar Lander botched its arrival and slammed into the surface. Each catastrophe, investigations determined, was caused by what might in more pedestrian realms be dubbed careless mistakes. The first was due to miscommunication between a ground system relying on imperial units and the flight system using metric, while the second was due to a software error not caught during testing.
“Those failures were very much on the mind of the team pulling together the Odyssey spacecraft,” says Glen Havens, an engineer at JPL and project and mission manager of Mars Odyssey. With those losses stinging, NASA invested more in perfecting the Odyssey and MRO spacecraft before launch, designing each to be as resilient as possible and testing every tiny component and every system configuration.
One key principle is what NASA calls “margin”—the spacecraft equivalent of carrying a snack, just in case.
“Unexpected things might happen, and you want to make sure the spacecraft will survive,” says Nilton Renno, a spaceflight engineer at the University of Michigan who hasn’t worked on either mission. MRO launched with a larger battery and more propellant than it strictly needed, Fieseler notes, and that margin is now keeping the mission going, with NASA hoping to operate it for another decade.
But orbiting Mars, it’s wise not to take anything for granted. Just last year, NASA lost the 11-year-old Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution—its youngest Red Planet orbiter—after the spacecraft unexpectedly lost power on the far side of the planet. As Odyssey and MRO continue to age, questions linger about what Mars orbiters come next for NASA.
The agency has hired Blue Origin to build a dedicated communications satellite to beam scads of data back to Earth for at least five years—but unlike its forebears, which began as science missions before turning to communications work, this orbiter will only relay signals for other spacecraft.
NASA’s Mars science agenda includes only relatively limited projects. One mission, which Lillis leads, features two orbiters currently on their way to study how the planet responds to the constant stream of charged particles flowing off the sun. But even he calls the mission “right on the edge of being too small to do good science.” Then, there’s Skyfall, the trio of small helicopters meant to launch aboard the first nuclear-propelled spacecraft within just two years—a shockingly rapid timeline, and for a mission with minimal ability to answer meaty research questions.
To scientists, none of these initiatives quite build on the legacy of Odyssey and MRO and may even raise the specter of the infamous Mars failures that came before. “Certainly they’re pushing for faster, cheaper,” Horgan says. “It’s going to be a lot more challenging to do good science in that environment.”

The Indian Patent Office has rejected a patent application filed by the U.S.-based Global Alliance for TB Drug Development (TB Alliance) for the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL), a six-month, all-oral treatment regimen for drug-resistant tuberculosis.
The Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+), Sankalp Rehabilitation Trust and Third World Network (TWN) welcomed the development.
Recommended by the WHO for eligible people, BPaL offers a shorter course of treatment than older, longer regimens, reducing the burden of treatment on patients and their families.
“Only those who have been treated for TB know what it feels like to go through more than a year of antibiotics with painful injections. Access to a shorter, oral and effective treatment can mean returning to work, caring for their families and rebuilding their lives”, explained Loon Gangte of DNP+.
The decision follows two pre-grant oppositions filed in 2020—one by Eldred Tellis (Sankalp Rehabilitation Trust) and Ganesh Acharya, with support from the Lawyers’ Collective and Médécins Sans Frontières Access Campaign, and the other by the Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+), with support from TWN.
The opponents challenged the patent application on the grounds that the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid, as well as its use in a shorter treatment regimen, had already been disclosed in scientific research and clinical trials dating back to 2015. They argued that combining these known medicines did not constitute an inventive step warranting a new patent monopoly.
The Opposition invoked key safeguards under India’s Patents Act, including Section 3(d), which restricts patents on new uses of known substances, Section 3(e), which excludes mere admixtures, and Section 3(i), which excludes methods of medical treatment. The opponents further argued that the application failed to sufficiently disclose the claimed invention. All four grounds were upheld by the Indian Patent Office.
India has the world’s largest tuberculosis burden. According to WHO estimates, approximately 2.71 million people developed TB in the country in 2024, accounting for a quarter of global cases, with an incidence rate of 187 per 1,00,000 people. Civil society groups are also demanding that the TB Alliance stop the pursuit of proprietary rights over BPaL in other countries.
“Having received public and philanthropic support to develop pretomanid, one of BPaL’s components, they should not be applying for a patent, let alone over frivolous secondary patents on its combination with the other two known medicines,” said Mr. Tellis.
In light of the weak claims by the TB Alliance, Prathibha Sivasubramanian, senior researcher at TWN, endorsed the call for the waiving of patents. “The Indian Patent Office’s decision should serve as a clear signal to the TB Alliance to voluntarily surrender granted patents and to withdraw all corresponding pending applications in other jurisdictions. TB Alliance should also publish its pretomanid licence agreements,” she said.
Patents on the BPaL combination have been granted in 11 countries and are set to expire in 2036: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Bulgaria, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, South Africa, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.

Serrano to end career in Puerto Rico in January
- Published
Seven-weight world champion Amanda Serrano will face Australia's Skye Falzon in Puerto Rico on 9 January in the final fight of her illustrious professional boxing career.
The 38-year-old will defend her WBA and WBO featherweight titles on home soil at the Coliseo de Puerto Rico in San Juan.
Serrano, who boasts a fight history of 50 wins, four defeats and one draw, will be seeking to break the all-time women's knockout record in her farewell bout.
"Boxing has been my life, and I never could have imagined the journey it would take me and my family on," said Serrano, who turned professional in 2009.
"To close my career at home in Puerto Rico, in front of the people who have supported me from the beginning, means everything. I'm going to give the fans one final night to remember."
Serrano's farewell bout, labelled The Last Walk, will be contested over 12 three-minute rounds against 37-year-old Falzon, who has won 12 of her 14 professional fights, including seven by knockout.
In her previous outing, Serrano edged a majority decision victory over Argentina's Lucrecia Manzur to claim her 50th professional win.
The contest was the first world title fight to be broadcast live on TikTok, generating 3.4m views.
But Serrano was unable to secure the knockout she needed to surpass American boxing pioneer Christy Martin's record of 32, leaving her with one final opportunity to make history.
'I'll continue fighting for the next generation'
Serrano is the only Puerto Rican boxer, male or female, to become an undisputed world champion.
Her profile reached new heights after she became the first fighter to sign with Most Valuable Promotions (MVP) in 2021.
Founded by YouTuber-turned-boxer Jake Paul and Nakisa Bidarian, MVP has invested heavily in women's boxing in recent years.
"Nakisa, Jake and MVP believed in me and in women's boxing, and together we've helped change what's possible for women in this sport," Serrano said.
"We've fought for respect, equal opportunities, fair pay, and the choice to compete under the same rules as men.
"There's still more work to do, and I'll continue fighting for the next generation long after I hang up my gloves."
Serrano's career will perhaps be best remembered for her historic rivalry with Ireland's Katie Taylor, who won all three of their encounters.
The pair became the first women to headline a boxing event at the iconic Madison Square Garden in 2022, before meeting again in a hugely watched rematch on Netflix in 2024.
Taylor completed a clean sweep of the trilogy in July 2025, headlining an all-women's card in New York, before retiring in September this year following victory over Flora Pili at Dublin's Croke Park.
Paul and Bidarian said Serrano had "changed the entire landscape of women's boxing".
"Amanda Serrano is the MOAT. The Most Of All Time. The most accomplished female boxer of all time, the most watched, the most paid, and one of the most influential athletes this sport has ever seen," they added.

The Delhi High Court has asked the Centre and Meta to respond to a plea against withholding the Instagram handle ‘Bring Back Ballot’, which published content advocating the use of paper ballots for elections.
Justice Amit Mahajan, on October 27, issued notice on the petition by the account operator, organisation Mission Save Constitution, and its founder lawyer Mehmood Pracha, and listed the case for hearing on November 6.
The petition said that on the day the organisation proposed to hold a peaceful protest, called “Bring Back Ballot - EVM Hatao Desh Bachao”, at Jantar Mantar, it discovered that its ‘Bring Back Ballot’ handle was not available in India.
The petition alleged that withholding the entire account with over 50,000 followers was disproportionate, unreasoned and without any notice.
‘Called for peaceful protest’
“The handle advocated, peacefully and lawfully, a return to paper ballots in Indian elections under the slogan “EVM Hatao Desh Bachao”, and mobilised citizens for the peaceful protest at Jantar Mantar, New Delhi on October 10, 2026, of which prior intimation had been given to the Delhi Police on September 10, 2026,” the plea said.
“On October 10, 2026, the very day of the Petitioners’ peaceful protest at Jantar Mantar, the Handle began displaying the message: ‘Account not available in India. This is because we complied with a legal request to restrict this content’,” it added.
The notice displayed by Instagram, the petition added, does not disclose any order, the issuing authority or the content objected to, and afforded it no means to contest the decision. The petitioner said it works toward promoting constitutional values, democratic participation and the integrity of the electoral process.

- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,

“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

Israelis vote in their highest numbers in decades in pivotal elections
Israeli voters turned out in their highest numbers in decades in a tense national election on Tuesday to decide whether to stick with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right coalition or change course.
Netanyahu is in a tight race with his top rival, Gadi Eisenkot, a center-right former military chief of staff, according to early exit polls after voting ended at 10 p.m. local time.
But the final tally won't likely be known until Wednesday. Even then, if no bloc wins an outright majority, it may take days or weeks to find who will be Israel's next prime minister as party leaders try to assemble a governing coalition.
Israelis consider this one of their most consequential votes in history — the first parliamentary election since the October 2023 Hamas-led attack and years of war in Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East.
Election officials said it was set to be the country's highest voter turnout in nearly 40 years.
There is especially high enthusiasm among voters seeking to replace Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, with almost two decades in office across multiple tenures.
" Important is an underestimation, because it's much more than important. It's crucial," voter Naama Aaronsohn said of the election. "I'm worried. ... What's going to become of our country if there's not a major change?"
Netanyahu voiced alarm throughout the day, commenting in a number of social media posts about the high number of Arab citizens of Israel who turned up at the polls. There are two predominantly Arab parties in the elections. Netanyahu urged his right-wing supporters to vote.
"This government it's not good for us and ... not good for anyone," said Nur Abu Na, a 30-year-old Arab voter.
Another voter, Itamar Ariel, said there are problems in Israel but no one can replace Netanyahu. He said his choice is about security for Israel.
President Trump publicly endorsed Netanyahu. After going to war together against Iran, in June 2025 and again this February, the two leaders plan to launch major attacks against Iran after the Israeli and U.S. midterm elections.
This is a developing story and will be updated.
Daniel Estrin reported from Tel Aviv, Israel. Ruth Sherlock reported from Jerusalem. Samantha Balaban, Itay Stern, Shir David and Alon Avital contributed reporting in Israel.

When Xi Jinping came to power in 2012, he pledged to stamp out corruption all through the ranks of the Communist party. More than a decade later, the pace of investigations has not slowed. Last year, China’s disciplinary authorities opened investigations into more than 1 million people, including more than 100 officials at or above ministerial or provincial level.
As Chinese Communist party (CCP) officials prepare for an important meeting this week discipline – and party loyalty – is high on the agenda. For those who try to read the tea leaves of elite Chinese politics, concern about the apparent lack of discipline is dominating CCP discussions.
The “fifth plenum” starts on Monday and is set to focus on “major issues on advancing the party’s full and rigorous self-governance”, according to a Chinese state media. In party-speak, “governance” is a byword for discipline, loyalty and anti-corruption.
As Xi continues to crack down on corruption, the fact that investigations nearly always result in a conviction begs the question over whether targets are truly guilty of corruption, or are they just political rivals to the people in charge.
Kerry Brown, director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London, explained that in Xi’s worldview, which is obsessed with discipline and loyalty, there may not be much difference between the two. “If you’re corrupt, you’re not politically loyal. If you’re politically loyal, you’re not corrupt,” Brown said.
He added that in the CCP system, “corruption is not just material things”, but also “spiritual corruption”, which includes political disloyalty.
Some analysts argue that the reason that the anti-graft drive is so enduring is because corruption is a feature rather than a bug of an authoritarian, top-down political system with a sprawling bureaucracy that governs 1.4 billion people.
Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, said: “Xi has made the party less corrupt and strengthened his control, but he knows that tougher punishment cannot fully resolve the problem of officials putting their own interests ahead of the party’s.
“Xi’s answer is to keep tightening discipline, making anti-corruption a permanent method of governing with no obvious point at which he can declare the job done,” Thomas said.
The job may be never ending, but the plenum is an opportunity to refocus the party’s energy on discipline. The fifth plenum is the fifth of seven gatherings that normally happen in every five-year cycle between CCP congresses. The plenums bring together more than 300 members of the CCP’s Central Committee, the most senior officials in the party hierarchy.
The upcoming meeting is particularly significant because it is likely to be the last substantive meeting before next year’s 21st Party Congress, where a new Central Committee will be chosen, and where Xi is expected to be anointed for a fourth term as the head of the CCP.
Eliminating anyone who poses a risk to his authority or to the party’s credibility is a key priority for Xi. And potential threats are everywhere. Nearly 15 years after Xi took office, according to CCP proclamations and a host of recent investigations, the problem is still not stamped out. “It is a deeply ingrained part of [Xi’s] worldview,” said Brown. “Everyone else is corrupt”.
In the past, Xi has warned that the party could “lose its ruling status and inevitably be eliminated by history” if it could not get its house in order. “This is by no means an exaggeration,” he said.
The current focus on party governance comes amid a host of high-profile investigations against senior party and military leaders.
In January, Zhang Youxia, China’s top general and a man second only to Xi in the military hierarchy, was placed under investigation; he was expelled from party last month, having already been removed from the military’s top ruling body, the Central Military Commission (CMC)
A host of other purges means that the CMC, which normally has seven members, has been reduced to just two: Xi and Zhang Shengmin, the CMC’s head of discipline.
Other recent scalps include Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang, and Huang Qifan, the former mayor of Chongqing.
Huang had long been known as the ultimate survivor in Chinese politics because of his connections to the scandals in the early 2010s in which Xi’s political rival, Bo Xilai, the former Party boss for Chongqing, was embroiled in the death of the British businessman Neil Heywood. Bo was ultimately convicted of bribery and embezzlement, for which he is serving a life sentence, but Huang survived. No longer.
Some China analysts have asked whether the recent purges, which have reached the highest echelons of the Party and military ranks, indicate instability in the regime. But Xi likely sees it differently. Corruption investigations demonstrate who is in charge. Plus, Brown added, they are “the most easy and natural tool by which to enforce unity and discipline”.

Data centers’ reliance on private natural gas plants is a key near-term risk to Anthropic. In the company’s IPO filing on Monday, it warned that the data center gas buildout could drive prices higher in some regions, affecting its AI ambitions and other data center operators around the country.
As America’s data center boom keeps growing, the facilities are set to consume a staggering amount of natural gas, with many companies opting to build their own plants rather than wait years for grid connection. Energy analyst company Cleanview estimates that behind-the-meter gas projects in development as of October 2026 at 110 gigawatts, up from just 20 gigawatts in July of 2025.
Competition from other natural gas-fired data centers could leave Anthropic exposed to “fuel price volatility and supply disruptions that are outside of our control,” the company wrote in its IPO filing, and “could drive up the price of natural gas in such areas and may adversely affect our ability to contract for firm fuel supply.”
The surge in demand for gas comes on top of an already tight market for natural gas. US export terminals are sending more gas abroad for a variety of reasons, including geopolitical conflicts and federal support for exports. Export demand is expected to double over the next decade.
Still, data centers could add a hefty chunk of demand, even if just some of what’s in the pipeline is built. BloombergNEF estimates that grid-connected data centers alone could add an additional 15 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas demand by 2035, a 15 percent increase in overall demand. Adding on a conservative estimate of onsite gas capacity in the pipeline would add another 3 billion cubic feet per day by the next decade.
Anthropic has traditionally relied on renting compute from major cloud service providers. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and SpaceX are specifically named in the IPO. (Anthropic is renting server space from the latter’s Colossus data centers in Memphis, Tennessee, which is facing a lawsuit for relying on unpermitted gas turbines.)
But the company has moved in recent months to directly lease and develop data centers, in a bid to lessen its reliance on other tech giants and more directly control its own data centers. In the IPO, it singles out its $50 billion partnership with Fluidstack, announced last year, which “provides data center development and operations services” for the company. It has announced data center sites in Texas and New York.
Doing so, though, exposes it to more risks, including the rises in natural gas prices. The company has also been tied to developing data centers with major on-site gas projects in states as spread out as Louisiana, Texas, and West Virginia. The latter could eventually be among the largest gas plants in the US, according to developer Nscale’s own IPO filing.
The geographical dispersion of its data centers opens Anthropic up to regional gas supply shocks and markets. That’s particularly true in the Southeast, where projects will have to compete with LNG exports.
“It wouldn’t be surprising if you start to see gas start to get more expensive in Louisiana and Texas, where all the LNG projects are concentrated,” says Enrique Gonzalez, BNEF’s head of gas research for the Americas.
Texas is also the national hotspot for behind-the-meter data center development, putting multiple developers in competition for the same, potentially limited gas supply. Anthropic acknowledges this risk in its IPO filing, writing that “we expect increased competition among users for the same natural gas supply and pipeline capacity in those areas. This competition could drive up the price of natural gas in such areas and may adversely affect our ability to contract for firm fuel supply.”
Any strain on gas supply could have knock-on prices for home energy bills. Gonzalez thinks that natural gas producers learned their lesson from the energy crisis of 2022, when high gas prices caused production to increase, in turn knocking down prices. While markets are unlikely to be that extreme in the coming years, “if hub prices rise, there’s a chance—unless you have legislation—that it goes to consumers,” he says.
One solution for this is, of course, to look at renewables, which also have the added climate benefit of being carbon-free. But Anthropic mentions them once in its IPO filing, and only to dismiss them. “Newer sources of generation, such as solar, wind, battery storage, nuclear, and geothermal power, may not be available in the quantities or on the timelines we require, or may be available only at higher cost,” the prospectus states.

A stroke is an urgent situation where either the flow of blood to the brain is cut off, or there is a rupture of the blood vessels in the brain. Oxygen and glucose are the two elements essential for brain activity. Interruption of their supply results in impairment of brain activity and eventual damage of brain tissues -- and this damage occurs in minutes. The first few hours of a stroke, therefore, determine how damaged the brain can become.
Types of strokes
Strokes can be categorised into ischemic strokes and haemorrhagic strokes. In ischemic strokes, the stroke occurs due to the blocking of an artery by a blood clot. In haemorrhagic strokes, there is a rupture of the blood vessel, which leads to blood in the brain tissue. Regardless of the type of stroke, the result is damage to the brain tissue, which can result in vital body functions including speaking, movement, vision, memory and coordination becoming impaired.
An ischemic stroke is accompanied by oxygen starvation of the affected brain tissue. Due to insufficient energy resources, brain cells cannot function normally. The chemical composition of the brain cells, therefore, changes, which results in the accumulation of toxic substances that harm brain cells and other structures. With continued oxygen starvation, cells continue to deteriorate. The damage, however, does not occur uniformly. In the central area of the brain (core) where oxygen starvation is critical, damage can occur rapidly and irreversibly. Around this area, there is a zone called the ischemic penumbra. Here, even if blood flow is low, brain cells can survive for a certain period of time. They can be saved if blood flow is restored promptly.
The effect of bleeding in a haemorrhagic stroke is brought about by the leaking of blood into the brain when there is a rupture of a blood vessel. This may lead to injury of brain cells, and also interfere with proper blood and cerebral spinal fluid flow in the brain.
The first few hours
There are only so many minutes that the brain can withstand interrupted blood flow. Brain cells (neurons) begins to undergo irreversible damage within 3 to 5 minutes of interrupted blood flow. With each minute that goes by, 1.9 million neurons, i.e. 32 neurons per second, die due to lack of oxygenation, which is why we emphasise that ‘time is brain’. The first few hours are critical since at this point, one needs to assess what kind of stroke it is and start appropriate treatment.
In some cases of ischemic stroke, intravenous thrombolysis, the administration of drugs that dissolve the clot within the blood vessels, might be given in the first 4.5 hours after symptoms develop. In some patients with large vessel blockage, there might be indications for mechanical thrombectomy. In simple terms, a mechanical thrombectomy involves the removal of the clot using special equipment, and it might be done up to 24 hours after the patient was last seen without symptoms. In cases of haemorrhagic strokes, others strategies must be employed: this includes blood pressure control, correction of the consequences of taking blood thinners, management of intracranial pressure, and surgical procedures, where necessary.
Not all patients automatically qualify for all interventions. There are other issues that have to be taken into account, including the patient’s medical status, imaging studies, timing of stroke symptoms, and dangers involved in the therapy. Even some of those who come after these time windows, can still be eligible for certain treatment procedures after imaging is done.
How brain function is affected
The effects of a stroke vary, depending on the site and degree of damage within the brain. Movement centres can be damaged leading to weakness or paralysis that usually affects one side of the body. Speech centres could be damaged causing speech problems and comprehension difficulties or trouble reading and writing. A stroke involving the visual pathways leads to a sudden loss of vision or partial visual fields. If the cerebellum or the brainstem is involved, there could be a problem with dizziness, poor coordination, problems swallowing, double vision or loss of balance. There could also be memory, attention and decision-making problems and problems with emotional regulation.
It is important to know and understand these symptoms since sometimes a stroke occurs without the characteristic facial drooping or arm weakness of the disease.
Recognising warning signs
The BE FAST method is an effective means of identifying the symptoms of a stroke:
- B – Balance: Sudden loss of balance, dizziness or difficulty walking
- E – Eyes: Sudden blurred vision, double vision or loss of vision
- F – Face: One side of the face is drooping or numb
- A – Arms: One arm is weak or dropping down
- S – Speech: Slurred speech
- T – Time: Call for help immediately
Sudden changes in vision, lack of balance, confusion or even a severe headache without apparent reason might be symptoms of a stroke as well. Disappearing symptoms within a minute or two shouldn’t be considered harmless and require immediate medical examination.
After the golden hour
The ‘golden hour’ is significant to preserve as much of brain function as possible and to ensure best possible outcomes, but this does not mean medical professionals cease working after this window is over. Medical teams will continue monitoring the condition of the patient, controlling blood pressure and preventing additional harm to him or her. In case the condition of the patient becomes satisfactory, it is likely that he or she will be offered physiotherapy, speech and language therapy, occupational therapy and cognitive therapy.
It is worth noting that every stroke patient has his or her own path to recovery, which depends greatly on the level of injuries, the affected area of the brain, timely assistance and the patient’s health in general. For all individuals, however, it is important to understand how the brain functions, remember the signs of a stroke and seek timely help for oneself or a loved one.
(Dr. B. K. Madhusudhan is lead consultant – neurology, Aster RV Hospital, Bengaluru. madhusudhan.bk@asterhospital.in)

Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders
"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."
That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.
From the outside looking in, his career was flying.
By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.
But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.
Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.
After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.
It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.
The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.
But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.
BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.
REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.
Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.
"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.
"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."
Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".
Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off".
For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.
The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".
But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.
"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.
"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."
Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.
Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.
So why is REDs so common?
One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.
For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.
And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.
"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.
"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."
Initially, the strategy can work.
When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.
It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.
But eventually, the luck runs out.
Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.
Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.
"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.
"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."
Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".
"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."
It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.
Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.
The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.
"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.
"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.
"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."
As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.
After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.
Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".
"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.
"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"
Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.
For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.
Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.
"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.
"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."
Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.
Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.
"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.
"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.
"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."
While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.
"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.
"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.
"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.
British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.
Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.
The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.
"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.
"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."
With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.
But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.
Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.
The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.
"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.
"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."

Passengers on a live-aboard round-the-world cruise say they were abruptly asked to leave the ship and given only hours to disembark.
Villa Vie Residences, which operates the residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey, said on Tuesday it had halted operations due to surging fuel costs.
The ship was docked at the port of Sihanoukville in Cambodia when the announcement was made, with passengers saying they were given only eight hours to disembark.
"On October 27, 2026, we received notice from the CEO at around 6 a.m. that all residents had to disembark by 2 p.m. that day," passengers Lanette Canen and John Bodin told Business Insider by email.
Canen and Bodin have been on the Odyssey since it first set sail in September 2024 and run a YouTube channel called Living Life on a Cruise about their experiences on board.
"We knew leaving was a possibility, but the eight-hour notice still surprised us," they said.
The couple shared a video on their YouTube channel that appears to show the moment a staff member announced that passengers must leave the ship.
"Unfortunately, they were unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations," a male voice says in the video.
A notice on the Villa Vie Residences website says the company is working with residents to arrange temporary living arrangements and that it is evaluating restructuring options over the next 60 days.
Mikael Petterson, executive chairman of Villa Vie Residences, told Business Insider he understood residents' feelings of shock and sadness.
"I get it. I get it. I feel awful," he said in a phone interview. "They're counting on me to make the decisions here and there's nothing else I'm focused on. I'm the villain in the story, but I'm doing everything I can to support the residents on a solution forward."
Petterson said that until last week, he was in talks with a potential investor and was expecting a new infusion of cash. When the deal fell apart, he said, the company was out of options.
Villa Vie Residences Chief Executive Kathy Villalba didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.
Soaring fuel costs
Villa Vie Residences said in a statement Tuesday that the surging cost of fuel since the beginning of the Iran war had made operating the cruise liner increasingly difficult.
The company said its monthly fuel expenses per cabin, which had previously averaged about $1,800, had risen as much as 344% in parts of Asia, to an estimated $6,000 to $8,000.
"Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port," Villa Vie Residences said.
"Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses."
On August 1, Villalba, the CEO, sent residents a message titled "Urgent operational update" on an internal messaging platform. In the message, she referenced a "fuel contribution" that had been previously requested of residents. Business Insider has viewed a screenshot of the message.
"When the fuel contribution was requested several months ago, participation was not universal," she wrote in the message. "The contributions received helped some, but they covered only part of the extraordinary increase in fuel costs."
Villalba wrote that the "cash-flow" challenge had continued, and the Odyssey needed 650 metric tons of fuel, adding that fuel prices had almost doubled.
"We have now reached a critical point. The lack of full participation, combined with the unprecedented increase in fuel costs, means we must make immediate and creative operational decisions to preserve the voyage," her message said.
It continued, "We are asking every Resident who did not previously contribute to please do so now. We are also asking those who are able to provide additional support to consider helping with this immediate fuel requirement."
Villalba described the financial need as "real, immediate, and necessary to keep Odyssey moving." It went on, "This is a moment when preserving our home and continuing the voyage requires support beyond contractual minimums from those who are able to provide it."
Residents scrambled to leave their cabins
Among the passengers asked to disembark on Tuesday with only a few hours' notice was Barbara Fiegel, 62, who has lived with her partner aboard the ship since December 2024.
"Everybody's just shocked, everybody's just saddened by this whole issue," she said. "We're still processing, trying to debate what we're going to do."
Fiegel said she and her partner booked a hotel room in Cambodia, then returned to the ship Tuesday evening and Wednesday afternoon to empty their safe and pack their belongings. "Today, as we approached, as we went back on the shuttle back to the ship, I couldn't stop crying," she said.
They plan to return on Thursday to collect their remaining items. Fiegel described the atmosphere on the Odyssey as a “ghost town.”
Joel Greiff, 57, moved aboard the ship at the start of the month and planned to live on the ship for 10 or 20 years or more. “I don’t think that will be happening,” he said.
When residents were told to disembark, Greiff emptied his cabin. “I personally grabbed everything,” he said.
He said he would like to return if Villa Vie Residences resumes operations. If not, he is planning to move to Thailand. In the meantime, he has rented an apartment in Cambodia for a month.
Greiff said he plans to return to the Odyssey on Thursday to assist other residents and “help with their luggage, help them find a place, and just start getting them and all their stuff off the ship.”
Jacob Shamsian contributed to this story.

A recent debate over investors’ lack of interest in India’s hardware and deeptech bets has brought some longstanding challenges in the ecosystem back into focus. These include a lack of patient capital, pressure from limited partners (LPs) for early distributions, consensus-driven investing, and the difficulty of underwriting long development and qualification cycles. As AI infrastructure moves beyond a pure compute race to focus on the layers that determine how efficiently systems run, India stands at the cusp of a significant opportunity. However, simply adding more computing power will not be enough for the country to establish itself as a global AI leader. Instead, opportunities are emerging in the supporting infrastructure. Data centres, for instance, need more efficient power delivery, better cooling systems, and faster connections between processors and memory. These layers are becoming increasingly critical as they directly influence real-world performance and the total cost of ownership of AI infrastructure. For India, the debate and the technical opportunity converge. Rather than trying to compete across the entire AI hardware stack, the country can develop specialised technologies. To understand which of these layers offer the strongest multiplier effects and what it will take for India to own them, we spoke to VCs tracking the homegrown deeptech ecosystem. Let’s unravel what they said in this edition of The AI Shift... The Need To Power Data Centres A consensus among VCs pointed to power delivery as the first major opportunity. As AI systems become more power-dense, improving power efficiency becomes an increasingly important engineering challenge. Natasha Malpani, founder and general partner of Boundless Ventures, sees an opportunity in power electronics, grid-edge systems and cooling designed for hot and humid environments. Data centres operating in Indian cities must manage local temperature and humidity conditions, potentially creating demand for technologies that can also serve other tropical markets. “The multiplier here is integration,” she said. Power semiconductors can serve AI data centres, electric vehicles and energy infrastructure. The opportunity, therefore, is to develop components that address multiple markets instead of relying on demand from one category. Cooling is also closely connected to this opportunity. Liquid-cooling systems help manage the heat generated by high-density computing equipment, creating demand for coolant distribution units, heat exchangers and direct-to-chip cooling technology. The second opportunity lies in moving data between processors and memory. Debraj Banerjee, general partner of F2A (Fundamentum Frontier Advisors), which recently closed a ₹3,000 Cr fund for deeptech, argues that India should target the interconnect and memory layer of AI chips. This includes high-speed SerDes circuits, PCIe and CXL controllers, chiplet interconnects, and memory expansion silicon. These technologies help processors exchange data and access memory efficiently. Banerjee’s argument is that standards-based technologies can give new entrants a route into multiple chip ecosystems without requiring them to challenge established GPU platforms directly. “India shouldn’t try to win the fab race. It should own the plumbing of AI chips, the interconnect and memory layer, because that’s where the bottleneck is moving and where one design earns on every chip shipped worldwide,” he recommended. The multiplier here is the business model. Companies that own valuable semiconductor IP could license it to multiple manufacturers and potentially earn royalties across global shipments, rather than relying entirely on engineering fees. Pranav Pai, managing partner of 3one4 Capital, added a third dimension: India’s established semiconductor and systems-design talent can support demand for custom embedded-system design, verification and testing. But he argues that value capture requires moving beyond services. "The opportunity is to move deeper, into components, advanced materials, proprietary process equipment, and finally product and system IP, which is where value capture will concentrate," Pai said. For AI infrastructure, this means turning engineering capabilities into products that global customers repeatedly buy. Who’s Taming The AI Infrastructure Layer Some Indian startups are already building in these areas, although their commercial maturity and ownership of technology differ. Bengaluru-based C2i Semiconductors developed power-management technology for AI data centres, including multiphase controllers and smart power stages. Then, German semiconductor company Infineon completed its acquisition of C2i on October 5, 2026, strengthening its power-management capabilities and expanding its research and development footprint in India. The deal demonstrates how Indian-developed technology can attract a global strategic buyer. Ahmedabad-based KuhlTherm is addressing the thermal-management problem. It develops liquid-cooling systems for high-density computing, including rear-door heat exchangers and coolant distribution units. Its next test is to demonstrate reliability, secure customer deployments and scale beyond early stage development. In data movement, LightSpeed Photonics is developing optical interconnect technology for AI and high-performance computing. The company raised $6.5 Mn in a funding round led by pi Ventures last year. Its work highlights an emerging opportunity in using light to transmit data, although commercial adoption will depend on integration with existing systems, manufacturing readiness and customer qualification. Government support is also building the broader semiconductor design ecosystem. Earlier this year, 24 chip-design projects were supported under the Design Linked Incentive scheme, producing 16 tape-outs, six fabricated chips and 10 patents. The projects had engaged more than 1,000 specialised engineers and developed over 140 reusable semiconductor IP cores. These figures show growing design activity. However, chip-design progress is not the same as a proven position in the global AI hardware supply chain. What Comes Next? India’s challenge is to turn early technical progress into commercially competitive products. Semiconductor development involves long design and testing cycles, while cooling and power systems must demonstrate reliability under demanding operating conditions. Global customers are unlikely to switch suppliers without evidence that new products can meet performance, safety and service requirements. Banerjee of F2A said the biggest gaps are not necessarily engineering talent, but patient capital and a lack of willingness to work with first-time chip companies. His thesis points to a need for investors who understand hardware development timelines and can support businesses through product qualification, rather than expecting rapid commercial returns. Access to manufacturing and advanced packaging is another constraint. India’s design ecosystem is expanding, but startups still need to establish where their IP resides, which components can be produced domestically and where they depend on overseas suppliers. The government’s Design Linked Incentive scheme provides financial incentives and design infrastructure support, but moving from prototype to volume production is still a challenge. The next phase should be judged by commercial milestones: customer qualification, repeat orders, manufacturing scale and licensing revenue. For instance, for power and cooling startups, the test is whether their products can deliver measurable efficiency improvements and win deployments. Similarly, for semiconductor IP companies, it is whether global manufacturers adopt their designs and generate recurring revenue. Overall, VCs agree that Indian startups need to choose where their engineering strengths can translate into proprietary technology, then build the capital, manufacturing and customer relationships needed to commercialise that technology. The opportunity is visible. Whether it becomes a lasting advantage will depend on how many Indian startups can move from promising designs to products that global infrastructure providers cannot easily do without. Flag any mismatch first. Judge it on one metric: total revenue per user who saw the test, across every product, and 6 month LTV projection. Not just the product we changed. (Bloomberg) -- Veteran federal judge Alvin Hellerstein, who oversaw cases against Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, Archegos Capital Management family office founder Bill Hwang and litigation over the 9/11 terrorist attack, died at 92.
The Jewish Center, a synagogue in Manhattan, notified congregants that Hellerstein, a longtime member and trustee, had died. The US District Court for the Southern District of New York said the the judge passed away Wednesday morning, surrounded by family.
“Judge Hellerstein was an insightful and dedicated lawyer who, following a distinguished career in the private sector, served with distinction for over 25 years as a distinguished jurist of this court,” Chief Judge Laura Swain said in a statement. “His energetic and dedicated service to this court continued until his death.”
Hellerstein, a native New Yorker, served in the Army’s Judge Advocate General’s Corps before joining New York City law firm Stroock & Stroock & Lavan LLP in 1960. He was appointed to the bench by President Bill Clinton in 1998.
Since then, he has overseen high-profile white collar prosecutions and complex litigation. Most recently, he was overseeing the narco-terrorism case against Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores.
The couple are scheduled to face trial in June. New judges will be assigned at random to the Maduro case and the other cases Hellerstein was overseeing.
During his early years on the bench, Hellerstein built his reputation overseeing yearslong litigation related to the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. In 2010, he rejected a settlement for 10,000 rescue and cleanup workers who fell ill working at Ground Zero because the payouts may have been too small after attorney fees were taken out. Months later, Hellerstein approved a $712 million pact well over the original proposal.
In a separate case, he ruled against families seeking to recover human remains from the 9/11 debris.
In the courtroom, the Columbia Law School graduate was famous for interrupting lawyers who weren’t questioning witnesses to his satisfaction or losing the jury’s attention.
In the 2024 criminal trial of Hwang, whose family office meltdown caused chaos across Wall Street, Hellerstein interrupted the questioning of a witness to announce the birth of his great-grandchild. “It’s a gorgeous baby,” remarked Hellerstein as he turned his phone to bemused lawyers in the courtroom. The jury erupted in applause.
In the same trial, he chided a lawyer for boring the jury to tears.
‘Just and Measured’
He sentenced Hwang to 18 years in prison, a decision that the judge never took lightly.
In rare public comments, Hellerstein, an Orthodox Jew, has spoken about how his faith intersected with his work. He told a podcast in 2020 that he held sentencing hearings on Fridays so he could used Sabbath to reflect on the consequences of his decisions.
“I never ever have had the feeling that my punishment was just and measured,” he said. “And that’s good. I think a judge should be disconcerted with what he does. I’m taking away the liberty of someone.”
In recent years, Hellerstein oversaw trials involving Charlie Javice, the start-up founder convicted of defrauding JPMorgan Chase, as well as a human rights case against BNP Paribas.
Roger Stavis, the head of Mintz & Gold’s white collar defense practice, who’s tried cases before Hellerstein, recalled him having a sense of humor that made him likeable even when Stavis was losing.
‘Dayenu’
In one hearing in Hellerstein’s courtroom in lower Manhattan, Stavis recalled objecting to the prosecution introducing the same evidence over and over. The judge shot back at Stavis, asking him to identify the legal precedent on how many times is too many.
“I said ‘United States v. Dayenu’ — the Hebrew term for it would have been enough — and he started cracking up,” Stavis said.

'He could be happier' - why is Estevao becoming Chelsea's forgotten man?
- Published
The last time Chelsea beat Liverpool, Estevao was the talk of the Premier League.
The Brazilian was still in his first couple of months at Stamford Bridge when his name hit the headlines after he scored the winner against the Premier League champions with practically the final kick of the match last October.
Fast forward 12 months, and Estevao is beginning to attract attention for all the wrong reasons as he struggles to force his way into Xabi Alonso's side.
The 19-year-old, who joined Chelsea from Palmeiras last summer, was conspicuous by his absence on Wednesday night as Chelsea were knocked out of the Carabao Cup following a penalty shootout loss to Liverpool at Anfield.
The Blues had taken the lead in the first half through Morgan Rogers, but they failed to kick on after Cody Gakpo quickly restored parity for the hosts.
Most concerning for Estevao, though, was that as both teams pushed for a winner in the second half, Alonso never appeared to consider the forward.
The clearest indication of just how low Estevao sits in Alonso's pecking order came midway through the second half, when Alonso made a triple substitution in an attempt to turn the game in his side's favour.
One of the three changes was Emanuel Emegha, who had yet to feature for the Blues since his summer move from Strasbourg.
Just moments after that triple change, which brought Chelsea's total number of substitutions to five, Estevao could be seen ending his warm-up and retreating to the bench.
It was another night of no action for the Brazilian.
'I'm sure Estevao will have his moment'
Sadly for Estevao, Wednesday night's situation at Anfield was nothing new for him.
The Brazilian has failed to make the starting XI in any of the eight Premier League matches since Alonso took charge of the Blues in the summer.
His total minutes for the campaign so far stand at an underwhelming 172, with 125 of those coming in the victories over Luton Town and Leeds United in the earlier rounds of the EFL Cup.
Yet even in the thrilling 6-3 win against Daniel Farke's side, which remains one of only two games he has started this campaign, he was withdrawn at half-time with Chelsea trailing 1-0.
After the fourth-round defeat by Liverpool, Alonso defended his decision not to play Estevao, hinting that the forward is still coming to grips with the physical demands of English football.
"We started with Pedro [Neto], Morgan [Rogers] and Danny Welbeck, and the game had very intense moments," said Alonso.
"We knew it was going to be physical, and Malo [Gusto] had cramps, so we were a bit forced with substitutions. The season is going to be very long, and there will be moments for everyone."
When asked directly about the Brazilian, Alonso added: "He could be happier. He wants to play. I'm sure Estevao will have his moment, it is my responsibility.
"We know the game in England is really intense, and you need to be up for it. Estevao is in his second season. The season is going to be long."
Neto's revival and attacking firepower limit Estevao's chances
One of the main reasons behind Estevao's exile has been the form of Pedro Neto.
It was only a couple of months ago that Portugal international Neto looked destined to leave Chelsea, only two years after joining from Wolverhampton Wanderers.
The 26-year-old was linked with a move to Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli, but he ultimately remained at Stamford Bridge.
That decision appears to have been influenced by Alonso, who has underlined his faith in Neto by handing him seven starts in eight Premier League matches this season.
His success out on the right - which also happens to be Estevao's favoured position - has meant opportunities have been few and far between for the Brazilian.
He has primarily been deployed as a right-sided wing-back in Alonso's 3-4-2-1 system, with his Premier League experience and greater defensive solidity compared to Estevao seemingly winning over the Spaniard.
After an impressive start to the campaign, in which he has scored four goals in 11 matches, Neto was rewarded with a new six-year deal at Stamford Bridge.
"He's a player who is a little bit of a victim of the system," former Reading midfielder Jobi McAnuff told Sky Sports.
"Alonso tends to play Neto in that hybrid wing-back role, expecting him to get high up the pitch as well. Maybe he doesn't feel that suits Estevao, and I don't feel it does either."
One area that has not been a problem for the Blues this season is attack, with the forward positions firmly in the hands of Joao Pedro, Cole Palmer and Rogers, who has made a spectacular start to life at Stamford Bridge following his £117m move from Aston Villa.
Against Liverpool, though, Estevao couldn't even get a look-in despite Chelsea being without the suspended Palmer and the injured Joao Pedro.
"How Estevao has not got on the pitch tonight, I do not know," said former Crystal Palace forward Clinton Morrison.
"He must be thinking, 'What do I have to do? We have injuries to two of the star players up front, and I'm still not getting on the pitch'."
Estevao will be hoping he can follow in the footsteps of Neto and revive his Stamford Bridge career.

Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition 2026 review: Nice, but doesn't justify the price
$320 is a lot to pay for a well-balanced device in an aluminum case with pogo pins.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
I'll be honest. I don't have much to say about the new Kindle Colorsoft. It doesn't feel like that long ago that Amazon introduced its first-ever color ereader, but that was in October 2024. At the time, the product was novel for the company, as it presented a technical challenge. How was Amazon going to offer a paper–like color reading experience while preserving the quality of a black-and-white ereader? The company used nitride LEDs and custom algorithms to finetune how lights were beamed through individual pixels to maintain contrast levels, and also made sure that pages turned faster than previous devices. The original Colorsoft only came in one color, which felt like a staid container for its relatively vibrant contents.
Cut to October 2026 and Amazon has a new Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition for the world. It's a bit thinner than before, with edge-to-edge color and a new color option: Fig. With this variant, the Colorsoft's front bezels also match the rest of the case, so you won't see unsightly white or black bars like on previous models. This Kindle Colorsoft generation starts at $290, but if you pay $30 more, you can get the Signature Edition, which is what I'm reviewing here.
What's new (or not so new) in the Kindle Colorsoft 2026?
Everything else about the Kindle Colorsoft is basically the same as its predecessor. You're still getting a screen with 300 pixels per inch (ppi) for black-and-white reading, or 150 ppi for color. Nothing has changed about the color representation here – you still get the "vibrant" mode in addition to the standard rendering to get a bit more saturation out of your pages.
I'm not a huge graphic novel reader, and most of the pops of color in my Kindle Colorsoft experience are in the book covers in my Library or when I highlight particular sentences or passages. They were pleasant little touches, but for me, the novelty of paperlike color E Ink displays has largely worn off. If I'm not reading something where the colors are actually integral to the storytelling, I don't need an ereader to deliver a broad spectrum of shades.
All that is to say – the reading experience on the Kindle Colorsoft this year is largely the same as last year, minus the early troubles our reviewer (and some other people online) encountered with yellow bands on their devices. Since Amazon resolved to fix the issue, it should not impact current and new Colorsoft models, and I did not notice this during my testing. I didn't experience any obvious issues when reading on the Colorsoft either.
Pricing is a bit confusing to compare, so bear with me. At launch in 2024, Amazon only made a "Signature Edition" of the Colorsoft available, and it started at $280. This year, the Colorsoft starts at $290 for the base configuration with 16GB of RAM and goes up to $320. That additional spend will get you the Signature Edition's aluminum case, pogo pins on the back, twice the storage and the choice of black or maroon. So you can say the Colorsoft costs between $10 and $40 more than before, and for that money you're mostly getting a slightly more refined flush-front design and thinner chassis.
In real life, much as I appreciated the aesthetic tweak, it didn't have a huge impact on my reading experience. I never struggled to hold the previous Colorsoft (or many other recent Kindles) so the thinner body, while nice, wasn't a huge change. The new Fig finish was a nearly identical match for my Burgundy iPhone 18 Pro, though, so if you love matching your gadgets to each other, this might be worth considering.
More importantly, I liked the sturdiness and premium vibe of the aluminum housing. My Kindles live in my cluttered purses, and their ability to withstand scratches is crucial. In my two weeks with the new Kindle Colorsoft, I've thrown it in my backpack with no regard for its safety, and it's still managed to remain pristine. I did decide to put a case on it midway through my testing so as not to tempt the review Gods, though, to ensure I could get a good photo of it before my recklessness marred it forever.
Charging and battery life
I haven't had a chance to connect the Colorsoft to any new accessory that's compatible with its new pogo pins in the real world yet. But I can at least say that based on a short demo ahead of Amazon's launch, I enjoyed how easy it was to snap the Signature Edition Colorsoft onto a magnetic case and use page turning buttons on a cover that connected via the pogo pins. I'll need more time to judge the responsiveness, consistency and ease of use, but for now, color me intrigued. I do wish Amazon hadn't removed the ability to wirelessly charge the Colorsoft. It's so handy to just drop the tablet onto a charging stand, and those who have already bought those accessories might be miffed at the omission.
That said, I never worried about charging the Kindle Colorsoft, because like most other Kindles, its battery lasts forever. I mean quite genuinely, because every time I pick up one of the many abandoned Kindles lying around in my house, they always still have juice left. I was slightly concerned when, after a day or two of focused reading, the Colorsoft's battery dipped by 10 percent to 90 percent. But then I remembered I had the same experience with the larger, more energy intensive Kindle Scribe Colorsoft. And that thing remains alive on my couch without me even thinking about plugging it in.
I won't say that I've had enough time to properly evaluate the Kindle Colorsoft's battery performance, but suffice it to say that nothing in my two weeks with it has been a real cause for concern so far.
The competition
Like I said, I don't read a lot of stuff that's better in color. But I can tell you that the Kindle Colorsoft is not your only option out there – Signature Edition or no Signature Edition. Our favorite ereader overall is the Kobo Clara Colour, which costs just $150. It has a slightly smaller 6-inch screen, so if that's too small and you have more money to spare, the Kobo Libra Colour is also a solid offering. It has a 7-inch screen that's a respectable color E Ink display, and costs $260 on Kobo's website. As a bonus, it has physical page-turn buttons onboard so you won't have to spend even more money on a case for that feature. However, it does only come in black or white options. At that price, the Kobo Libra Colour comes in at $30 under the Kindle Colorsoft's starting fee, and still manages to offer 32GB of storage and stylus support.
The thing is, Kobo's interface and library simply can't hold a candle to Amazon's, which isn't just vast, but is easy to use across various platforms. You can browse for books through the Amazon store on your Kindle, and for anyone that's already amassed a library in one place or subscribed to Kindle Unlimited, then leaving presents a lot of friction. I also like how I can read on my phone, tablet or Kindle and my progress is synced anywhere I leave off and wherever I decide to pick back up.
Wrap-up
The Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition feels like an unnecessary splurge for me. But for anyone who regularly reads color ebooks, the Colorsoft might be a treat. Plus, if you are also a fan of the Fig color option, are locked into the Amazon ecosystem and might want to use your Kindle Colorsoft with the page-turn cover one day, the Signature Edition is a capable ereader that won't disappoint.

Koffee With Karan 9: Varun Dhawan says he feels “ashamed of himself” seeing Ranbir Kapoor as a father, recalls Alia Bhatt wanting kids at 19

Varun Dhawan says Alia Bhatt spoke about having children at 19
