Varun Dhawan praises Ranbir Kapoor’s parenting
Karan also asked Varun whether any awkwardness from the past resurfaced when he met Alia and Sidharth, given their history of working together and the time that had passed since their debut.
Varun said he and Sidharth get along well whenever they meet. He added that his interactions with Alia and Ranbir are also warm, with plenty of conversation. Speaking about Ranbir’s relationship with Raha, Varun praised the actor’s parenting. “When I see Ranbir as a parent, he’s amazing. He’s so good as a father,” he said, adding that it made him feel “really ashamed”.
Alia Bhatt and Ranbir Kapoor welcomed Raha in 2022
Alia Bhatt and Ranbir Kapoor married in April 2022 and welcomed their daughter, Raha, on November 6 that year. The couple have occasionally shared glimpses of their life as parents, while generally keeping their daughter’s life away from the spotlight.

United Launch Alliance announced Wednesday it plans to return its Vulcan rocket to service on November 13, nine months after a solid rocket booster anomaly threw the company’s 2026 launch schedule into oblivion.
The return-to-flight mission will launch 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation, the first of 38 Vulcan flights Amazon has booked to deploy the bulk of its network. The mission will lift off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, and ULA said the launch date is pending range approval.
The launch is critical for ULA after its new flagship rocket suffered nozzle failures on its solid rocket boosters on two of its first four missions, most recently during a flight in February. In both cases, the rocket overcame the nozzle failure and completed its mission, but officials at the US Space Force, ULA’s primary customer, lost confidence in Vulcan.
Space Force officials will closely scrutinize Vulcan’s return-to-flight mission. The Pentagon has entrusted ULA’s Vulcan rocket for roughly half of its major launches through the early 2030s. The Space Force certified the Vulcan rocket for national security launches in 2025, then flew two missions on Vulcan before its grounding after the February booster incident.
Making strides
In a statement, United Launch Alliance said engineers “made great strides” in understanding the booster anomaly that occurred in February. Engineers “have identified several potential contributors, which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle,” ULA said.
“To support our customers, this upcoming launch will utilize the improved nozzle design, and additional testing and analysis will continue in parallel with the mission,” ULA said. “By flying the improved design, ULA gains valuable flight data that validates these improvements and is the most beneficial path in support of all our customers.”

The Osmania General Hospital (OGH) in Hyderabad has established a dedicated gender-affirming surgery service in the government healthcare sector in Telangana, marking a step towards improving access to specialised healthcare for transgender persons.
The Department of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery has introduced the service through a multidisciplinary team of specialists from plastic surgery, anaesthesiology, endocrinology, urology, gynaecology and psychiatry, along with nursing staff and other healthcare professionals. The initiative has been developed over the past eight months, said doctors.
The team has successfully performed several procedures for transgender people, including frontal bossing reduction, autologous fat grafting for breast augmentation, breast augmentation using implants, penile inversion vaginoplasty and bilateral nipple-areola complex-sparing mastectomy. Breast implants have also been facilitated through letters of credit under the Chief Minister’s Relief Fund (CMRF).
The initiative aims to provide safe, accessible and affordable gender-affirming surgical care within the public healthcare system, particularly for individuals who face financial and logistical barriers to accessing specialised procedures.
The service follows a multidisciplinary approach, with emphasis on patient evaluation, individualised surgical planning, perioperative care and post-operative follow-up. The hospital has also received support from the Queer Badhu Parents Association, whose president, Mukunda Mala, helped facilitate the renovation of a three-bed ward for transgender patients recovering from surgery, said Dr P. Lakshmi, Professor and Head of Department of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery.
The hospital plans to expand the range of gender-affirming procedures offered and further strengthen the multidisciplinary programme. The initiative is expected to help more transgender people access specialised surgical care through the government healthcare system while promoting inclusive, dignified and comprehensive healthcare.

Indore (Madhya Pradesh): A young sub-adult male leopard, estimated to be between 2 and 2.5 years old, was rescued by forest department personnel from the Choral forest range under the Indore division following reports of its lethargic and unresponsive behaviour.
According to sub-divisional officer (SDO) Subhash Sharma, who oversees Ralamandal and led the rescue operations, villagers first raised the alarm after attempting to drive the big cat away from peripheral fields. Despite aggressive efforts by locals to shoo the animal, it remained unnaturally motionless, refusing to budge.
"Villagers reported that they weren't able to shoo him off, and he would not move - staying still no matter what people did," said Sharma, detailing the initial alerts received from the ground.
Suspecting severe illness, physical trauma, or internal organ compromise, a specialised team dispatched by the forest department moved into the Choral area and successfully secured the big cat.
However, forest officials observed alarming clinical signs immediately following the rescue. Sharma stated that the young leopard "seems to get unconscious after a few minutes again and again," indicating recurring episodes of syncope or neurological dysfunction.
A comprehensive veterinary check-up was initiated immediately after the rescue. Sharma confirmed that the animal will be kept under strict, round-the-clock medical observation throughout the night to monitor its vital parameters and stabilise its condition before deciding on further diagnostic tests or rehabilitation protocols.
Pattern of big cat movements across Indore division
The rescue in the Choral range is the latest in a series of big cat encounters across the forest fringes surrounding Indore:
The Umariya Khurd search: Just days prior, panic gripped Umariya Khurd village near Crescent Water Park along the Indore Bypass after an injured, limping leopard bearing facial and head wounds was spotted resting near a residential veranda.
The Crescent Water Park trap: Forest search teams deployed multiple bait cages across the Umariya Khurd belt. A healthy adult male leopard was trapped inside a cage set up near Crescent Water Park and shifted for assessment, while field teams maintained traps and search grids to track the remaining injured cat.
Urban fringe encounters: Earlier this year, forest teams handled similar emergency rescues across the division, including the capture of a leopard in Sanawadiya village near Devguradia and another operation near the Asrawad grid premises.
Wildlife officials attribute the spike in fringe encounters to seasonal movements, shrinking buffer corridors near Ralamandal Wildlife Sanctuary, and water availability along irrigation channels. The Choral range leopard remains under active veterinary care as medical officers evaluate the cause behind its repeated loss of consciousness.

Girija (name changed) spent years working as a domestic worker before her failing knees made it difficult for her to continue. Hoping to find a more manageable way to earn a living, the 60-year-old borrowed money from acquaintances and set up a roadside vegetable stall. But another health problem emerged, making it difficult to keep the business running.
“She learnt that she was suffering from urinary incontinence. Taking frequent loo breaks while managing the stall was not practical, and she eventually decided to shut shop, losing her source of income in the process,” says Gurajada Sobha Pernidevi, founder-president of Telangana Stree Seva Samstha, a voluntary organisation working for the welfare of women.
For older people with limited financial means, a health problem can do more than cause physical discomfort; it can take away their livelihood, independence and opportunities to socialise. Conditions that are difficult to discuss, such as urinary incontinence, are often endured in silence because of embarrassment and the cost of managing them.
Unlike ailments that call for joint replacement surgery or a cardiac stent, these less visible difficulties of ageing often receive scant attention, despite their potential to disrupt daily life. However, as Telangana’s share of elderly population grows, addressing such overlooked needs will become increasingly important.
Telangana’s population aged 60 and above is projected to rise from 12.5% in 2026 to 17.1% in 2036, according to the Reserve Bank of India’s report, ‘State Finances — A Study of Budgets of 2025-26: Demographic Transition in India — Implications for State Finances’.
The State is expected to join the category of ageing ones, where senior citizens account for at least 15% of the population. The projected demographic shift raises questions about how healthcare, caregiving and community support can keep pace with the needs of older people, particularly those who live alone or cannot afford private services.
Associations working with senior citizens say the challenges range from obtaining medicines and reaching hospitals to finding dependable caregivers and accessing mental health support.
P. Shyam Kumar, State project coordinator at HelpAge India, says doorstep medical services, including palliative care, could make healthcare more accessible. Nutritional supplements and the delivery of medicines through Accredited Social Health Activists could also help older people manage their health.
“Without adequate support, their condition may deteriorate, leading to more hospital visits, additional expenses and greater dependence on family members. So, supplying medicines through Accredited Social Health Activists may work in this direction,” he adds.
The pace mismatch
Access to healthcare is not simply a matter of getting an appointment or obtaining medicines. Older people who depend on younger family members for hospital visits may have to wait until someone can take time off work and accompany them.
Members of several associations say a family member’s availability often influences whether and when an older person seeks medical attention. Those with limited mobility may need transport, a wheelchair or stretcher. In a multi-storey building without a suitable lift, even getting someone downstairs can require additional assistance and planning. Hospital visits can involve long walks between departments, diagnostic tests and consultations, making them particularly difficult for those without someone to accompany them.
The problem does not end at the hospital gate. For older people who cannot leave home, finding a doctor willing to make a home visit can be equally difficult. “This is a crucial requirement of those who are unable to step out of their house,” says Sobha.
For older couples whose children have moved away for work, one partner falling ill can leave the other struggling to coordinate treatment, travel and follow-up visits. The absence of accessible transport and medical services at home can turn routine healthcare into an exhausting exercise.
Shanti, trustee and volunteer at Roshni Trust, which has organised mental health camps in bastis, says Hyderabad’s urban spaces do little to encourage inclusion and social interaction among older people. “The city is designed for isolation and does not promote inclusiveness,” she says.
Shanti calls for government centres at the basti level, on the lines of Anganwadis, where older people can access basic facilities, attend health camps and receive nutritious food. Such centres could also offer a place to meet others, reducing isolation among those who spend much of their time at home.
The search for dependable care
For older people who need help with daily activities, finding a caregiver presents its own difficulties. Volunteers point to the need for people who understand the physical and emotional needs of senior citizens, as well as concerns about safety when elderly couples live alone and their children live elsewhere. Sobha recalls the case of an elderly woman who sleeps during the day and stays awake at night to keep an eye on her caregiver, fearing for her safety.
“This fear weighs on many older people who live with hired help,” she adds.
Through Telangana Stree Seva Samstha, she along with 80-plus volunteers, distributes adult diapers, commode converter seats, walking sticks, books and other resources to those who need them.
S. Bhooma Reddy (78), editor of Voice of Senior Citizens magazine, says the demand for caregivers is substantial, with some families hiring them even when their children live in the same building. “The caregivers are paid a monthly salary of around ₹25,000, apart from being provided food and accommodation,” he adds.
Such arrangements, however, remain beyond the reach of many households. Families from financially disadvantaged backgrounds often live in cramped homes and juggle work, household responsibilities and the care of parents or in-laws with limited resources.
V. Manjula, president of Gruha Karmikula Union-Telangana, says opening community halls where older people are provided regular meals and medicines would be a significant source of support for those from poor backgrounds.
The consequences of inadequate family support can be more severe than the absence of daily assistance. Associations report cases of older people being abandoned at hospitals, railway stations and bus stops. They also cite instances of elderly parents being neglected after transferring property to their children. Physical ailments are not the only problems that can go unnoticed as people grow older. Depression and dementia, too, may remain undiagnosed because their early signs are mistaken for normal aspects of ageing.
K. Chandra Sekhar, 70, founder-director of ASHA Hospitals, says families often seek specialist help only after symptoms have worsened. Forgetfulness, which can be an early sign of dementia, is frequently dismissed as a natural consequence of growing old. Such assumptions can delay diagnosis and prevent older people and their families from accessing appropriate support.
“Early diagnosis can improve quality of life and help caregivers prepare for the support that may be required as a condition progresses,” he says.
A loss of interest in activities once enjoyed, reduced appetite and weight loss, less social interaction and multiple physical complaints can be signs of depression, Dr. Chandra Sekhar points out. Older people experiencing forgetfulness can consult neurologists or psychiatrists.
While health camps often screen for physical illnesses, camps focused on identifying mental health problems are rarely organised, he says.
Aarathi Bellary, consultant physician and co-founder of Aayu Geriatrics, says some older people overlook age-related health problems even when symptoms become apparent.
“While physiological issues get attention, mental health issues in old age are barely discussed. One should not dismiss every problem as an inevitable part of ageing. It is important to consult the relevant medical specialists,” she says.
Dr. Bellary also encourages older people to pursue hobbies, maintain an active social life and take part in activities that allow them to share their knowledge and experience. Such engagement can help them remain socially connected rather than being defined solely by their health needs.
Planning for assisted living
For those who need more sustained support, assisted living and other residential care options could fill a gap between hospital treatment and independent living. Hyderabad, however, has only a few such facilities.
Ambati Rampapa Rao, chairman of PACCS Healthcare Pvt Ltd, which has a subsidiary, Ucchvas Transitional Care Centres, says longer life expectancy has made it necessary to plan for the changing needs of older people, particularly when their children move out of their hometown.
Ageing can bring a range of difficulties, including reduced physical strength, tremors, weight loss, malnutrition and emotional or psychological problems, affecting one’s ability to carry out everyday activities.
Dr. Rao outlines three broad categories of elderly care. Transitional care provides support immediately after hospital discharge, ranging from a few weeks to several years, with some degree of medical supervision; assisted living caters to those whose age and medical history call for monitoring and preventive care; and elderly living facilities serve people who remain mobile but have minor health problems.
“Social and aspirational security has to be factored in while designing spaces for the elderly, to meet their emotional and intellectual aspirations. This has to be planned for people of all financial segments,” he says.
With corporates exploring investments in the sector, the number of facilities could increase. But affordability remains central to whether these services can reach those who need them the most.
Care beyond the family
The Telangana government has sanctioned 37 multi-service daycare centres for senior citizens, of which 32 are operational. Run by non-governmental organisations with full financial support and monitoring from the government, the centres encourage social interaction and provide nutritious food, indoor games and basic medical check-ups once a week.
For older people who depend on regular meals or monitoring of health conditions, however, the reliability of these services matters as much as their availability. One elderly woman says she worries that health problems could jeopardise her access to the centre.
“My sugar levels shoot up if I don’t have food on time. Someone else may develop other health problems. If we fall ill at the centre, our children may consider taking us there a hassle and ask us to stop going,” she says.
Her concern points to a larger dilemma: services intended to support older people may not be enough if families view the time and effort involved in accessing them as a burden.
As Telangana’s elderly population grows, the challenge will be to make care accessible not only to those who can afford paid assistance, but also to people whose health problems, limited mobility or financial circumstances threaten their independence.

A Bengaluru consumer commission has directed Samith Chits Pvt Ltd to pay ₹4,07,940 to a subscriber who received only ₹20,000 after winning a bid in a ₹5 lakh chit fund scheme. The commission has also ordered the company to pay interest at 6.5% per annum on the outstanding amount and ₹3,000 towards proceedings costs, the Times of India reported. The order was pronounced on September 28, 2026, by the Bangalore 1st Additional District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, comprising President Syed Anser Khaleem and two members. It followed a complaint filed by Vishnuprasad against the chit fund company. According to the complaint, Vishnuprasad subscribed to a ₹5 lakh chit scheme operated by Samith Chits. Under the scheme, he was required to pay ₹12,500 every month for 40 months. The chit period ended in June 2025. Vishnuprasad had successfully bid for the chit in May 2025, making him eligible to receive the prize amount under the agreement. However, the company did not pay him the full amount due. It subsequently issued two cheques towards the payment: one for ₹1 lakh, dated July 5, 2025, and another for ₹3,27,940, dated July 15, 2025. Both cheques were drawn on a private bank's Rajajinagar branch in Bengaluru. Vishnuprasad presented the ₹1 lakh cheque through his bank account at the Ramamurthy Nagar branch on July 17, 2025. The cheque was returned unpaid with the endorsement "Funds Insufficient". He presented the second cheque, worth ₹3,27,940, on July 24, 2025. That cheque was also dishonoured due to insufficient funds. The commission's order records that Samith Chits eventually paid Vishnuprasad ₹20,000 after he followed up over the unpaid amount. However, the company did not clear the remaining dues of ₹4,07,940. Vishnuprasad then issued a legal notice under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, which deals with cheque dishonour. He also initiated proceedings before the Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate court in Bengaluru in two cases, numbered CC No. 72718/2025 and CC No. 72660/2025. He subsequently approached the consumer commission seeking relief for the unpaid chit prize money. The documents submitted by Vishnuprasad included the company's brochure, a statement issued by Samith Chits, copies of both cheques, records showing their dishonour and proof of the ₹20,000 payment. Samith Chits did not appear before the commission despite being issued notice. It was placed ex parte on July 24, 2026, leaving Vishnuprasad's allegations and supporting evidence undisputed in the consumer proceedings, the TOI reported. Based on the material on record, the commission concluded that the company had failed to pay the amount due after the subscriber successfully bid for the chit. It held that the conduct amounted to deficiency in service as well as an unfair trade practice. The commission also considered the separate proceedings initiated under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. It observed that proceedings for cheque dishonour and a consumer complaint serve different purposes. The existence of the former did not prevent Vishnuprasad from pursuing a remedy under consumer protection law. The commission relied on Section 100 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, which provides that remedies under the Act are in addition to, and not in derogation of, remedies available under other laws. It also referred to the Supreme Court's decision in Shriram Chits (India) Private Limited v. Raghachand Associates (2024). The commission cited the ruling to support its position that a chit subscriber can qualify as a consumer and a chit fund operator as a service provider under consumer protection law. On this basis, it held that Vishnuprasad was entitled to seek relief before the consumer commission despite the separate cheque-dishonour proceedings. The commission allowed the complaint and directed Samith Chits, through its managing director, to pay Vishnuprasad ₹4,07,940 with interest at 6.5% per annum. The interest will be calculated from the date of filing the consumer complaint until realisation. The company must also pay ₹3,000 towards the cost of the proceedings. The order directs Samith Chits to comply within 30 months from the date of receipt of the order and submit a compliance report to the commission within 45 days from the date of receipt. The ruling provides relief to the subscriber for the unpaid chit amount while separately addressing the costs incurred in pursuing the consumer complaint. Israel's Arab parties appear to secure a record number of seats in parliament and could emerge as kingmakers after strong turnout in Tuesday's election. Vote tallies show the two main Arab parties on course to win around 19 seats, nearly double their current representation in the Knesset. The two main parties are Yousef Jabareen-led Joint List and Ra'am, led by Mansour Abbas.
Yousef Jabareen, the leader of the Arab-dominated Joint List, said his party would seek to use its projected 12 seats "to facilitate getting rid of Netanyahu's govt and hopefully helping to change the political situation in Israel". Jabareen said the Joint List could not join an Eisenkot-led govt because of its support for Israel's military campaign in Gaza and occupation of southern Lebanon. But he left open the possibility of bolstering Eisenkot's bloc from the outside, propping up a minority govt that could survive confidence votes. "We have our demands to protect our community, to advance the rights of our community and to promote equality for our community," said Jabareen, speaking from his home in the Arab town of Umm al-Fahm.
The second main Arab party, Ra'am, is led by Mansour Abbas. He has sought to make Ra'am a more attractive coalition partner, adding a Jewish former police official to its slate and saying he would join an Eisenkot-led govt.
Speaking to Israeli television after voting wrapped on Tuesday night, Ra'am chief Mansour Abbas said: "I believe we can overcome the difficulties ... and I think that most voters for the (Eisenkot) bloc do want to see (a) govt with the Ra'am party." He said senior members of Eisenkot's bloc had discussed a possible deal with him even before the election. "Everyone is talking to us, not just the change bloc. A few days ago, a very, very senior member of the right approached me."
Eisenkot ruled out forming a govt with any of the Arab parties during the campaign, citing what he called a lack of shared values, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state.
Netanyahu's Likud party confirmed it would not negotiate with any Arab party to try to form a govt. "Not a chance," spokesman Guy Levy said at the party's headquarters in Jerusalem. "It's not even a question that should be asked."
Who is Mansour Abbas?
Mansour Abbas (52) is an Arab-Israeli politician, dentist and leader of Ra'am. Elected to Knesset in 2019, he reshaped Arab politics by advocating a pragmatic, domestic-focused approach. Instead of making engagement conditional on the wider Israeli-Palestinian conflict, he prioritises civil gains for Arab citizens, focusing on crime, socioeconomic inequality, infrastructure and municipal funding. He also briefly served in an Israeli ruling coalition from 2021 to 2022.
What is Joint List?
Joint List is an alliance of Arab-majority parties in Israel, formed in 2015 to unite the vote of Arab citizens. It includes Ahmed Tibi's Ta'al and has historically brought together secular, nationalist and left-leaning parties such as Hadash. It campaigns on civil equality, tackling crime in Arab communities and ending the occupation, and has backed govts from outside rather than joining them.
How are Arabs placed in Israel
Arab citizens of Israel, who often identify as Arab Israelis or Palestine citizens of Israel, comprise 20% of the population, or roughly 2.1 million people. They are central to the medical sector. Data from Israeli ministry of health and Taub Center for Social Policy Studies in Israel show Arabs account for over 20% of physicians, nearly a quarter of nurses and almost half of licensed pharmacists. Two Arab citizens have served as Supreme Court judges, while Arab engineers, scholars, writers and athletes, have visible public roles.
Arab parties' past support
For decades, Arab parties provided outside support to governments. Cabinet representation was limited to individual appointments, including Druze lawmaker Salah Tarif in 2001, Labor's Raleb Majadele in 2007, and later Issawi Frej and Ayoob Kara. A significant change came in 2021 when Abbas's Islamist Ra'am joined Naftali Bennett-Yair Lapid's ruling coalition.

India’s only international bullion exchange is seeing a revival in activity, driven by silver imports after a regulatory change made licences mandatory for certain categories of the metal.
The India International Bullion Exchange (IIBX) recorded trades of 570 metric tonnes of silver in the three months since August, after seeing no trades over the preceding year, while spot gold imports stood at just 0.3 tonnes.
The surge follows a May decision by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) to move certain categories of silver to the restricted list, requiring importers to obtain authority's licences. As licences began to be issued, importers turned to IIBX to source the metal, with industry estimates suggesting that approvals covering about 400 tonnes of silver had been granted by mid-August, and some may have been approved after that.
“As licences began to flow, imports followed. Industry estimates suggest around 400 tonnes of licences were approved by mid-August,” said Anindya Banerjee, head of commodity and currency research at Kotak Neo. The 400 tonnes refers to the quantity of silver that could be imported under the approved licences, not the volume already imported.
India imported 1,017 metric tonnes of silver in the current fiscal year through September, according to Department of Commerce data. Of this, 283 metric tonnes, or about 27%, came through IIBX. Silver prices have fallen 11.7% since August to ₹1.92 lakh per kilogram.
What's prompting silver imports via the IIBX is how nominated banks allocate silver. Working with limited quotas, banks often favour a single large order over several smaller ones, according to officials.
“If a nominated bank has a 200 kg quota, and one client asks for the full 200 kg while 20 others ask for 10 kg each, the bank will typically give the entire amount to the first buyer,” said an industry official, who asked not to be named. “The exchange model solves this allocation issue, which is why so many importers are switching to IIBX,” the person added.
The government’s move to restrict certain categories of silver imports was aimed at curbing non-essential imports and easing pressure on the rupee, the official said. It also sought to prevent importers from exploiting a duty differential that had emerged following changes in import duties.
In May, the Centre raised the import duty on silver to 15% to curb imports. However, the India-UAE trade agreement allowed eligible importers to bring in silver at lower duty rates, creating an incentive to source the metal through the UAE. Moving certain silver categories to the restricted list made imports subject to government licensing, giving authorities greater control over the flow of silver into the country.
Second growth engine
IIBX, launched as India’s first exchange through which eligible jewellers and other buyers can directly import bullion, was expected to build its business around gold. However, a legal dispute over the allocation of quotas for importing gold at lower customs duty rates, which began in early 2025, has disrupted gold imports through the exchange. Gold and silver imports into India have traditionally been routed primarily through nominated banks.
IIBX expects silver to become a more significant part of its business. “We are hopeful of recording silver trading volumes of over 2,000 tonnes in the current financial year, subject to the availability of import licences issued by the DGFT,” said Ashok Gautam, managing director and chief executive officer of IIBX.
“We see silver becoming IIBX’s second growth engine. The exchange has already handled silver at scale, with about 1,127 tonnes in calendar 2024, roughly 16% of India’s silver imports. The market is large, with India’s silver import bill at a record $12 billion in FY26,” Banerjee said.
Sustainability
For the exchange to sustain those volumes, however, it may need to attract importers even when they can use banks and other permitted channels, according to experts.
“Traditionally, bullion imports have been concentrated among a relatively small group of banks and intermediaries. Allowing a wider range of eligible participants to import directly from the exchange can improve competition, reduce intermediary premiums and potentially deliver better pricing to end consumers,” said Hiren Chandaria, managing director for the Middle East and Asia at Monetary Metals.
Some industry participants argue that regulation could help secure a more durable flow of business for IIBX by requiring a portion of imports under each licence to be routed through the exchange.
“The DGFT could specify that a certain percentage of imports under each licence must be routed through IIBX. Suppose an importer receives a licence to import 50 tonnes of silver. The DGFT could stipulate that 10 tonnes must be imported through IIBX, while the remaining 40 tonnes could be sourced through other permitted channels like banks,” another official said.

Leh, Oct 28: Northern Army Commander Lt Gen Pratik Sharma on Wednesday visited Kargil and Batalik sectors of Ladakh and reviewed the operational preparedness of troops deployed in the strategically important areas.
Lt Gen Sharma, General Officer Commanding-in-Chief of the Northern Command, visited the Forever in Operations Division on October 28-29 and reviewed the operational preparedness of troops deployed in Kargil and Batalik Sectors, Northern Command said on X.
The two sectors, characterised by challenging terrain and adverse weather conditions, are guarded by battle-hardened troops of the Indian Army.

This story was produced by Grist and copublished with WIRED. It is part of Distorted, a Grist series exploring the spread of misinformation in the wake of extreme weather, and is published with support from the CO2 Foundation.
Earlier this month, after Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the Gulf Coast as a Category 3 hurricane, the emergency management expert Laura Myers got a call from a meteorologist in Alabama. Myers is director of the University of Alabama’s Center for Advanced Public Safety, and she talks to state and local emergency managers around her region all the time. The meteorologist told Myers that a local emergency manager had published a graphic showing where Isaias might threaten the Alabama coast with a “sting jet” of high winds.
The problem? The emergency manager had generated the graphic using an artificial intelligence chatbot, and it wasn’t accurate.
“That county emergency manager was trying to get his stakeholders to focus on the risk in that county, and so he had asked AI to help him,” she said. “It did what he wanted it to do, but it was not meteorologically accurate.”
Most emergency management agencies don’t permit employees to use generative AI, but Myers and most other emergency management experts agree that its usage is likely already pervasive at state and local disaster departments. There are hundreds of companies that are marketing AI tools to emergency managers for tasks like flood damage assessment and resource coordination, but public communication is one of the areas where government employees and startups have the most interest.
The reason? Most emergency managers aren’t very good at sending out alerts and quickly communicating about disasters with the public. That’s not because they’re emergency managers, but because they are human beings. They tend to write in jargon that non-experts might not understand, leave out information on the assumption that the public already knows it, and include irrelevant details that could distract people from what they actually do need to know.
“A lot of agencies are really limited in resources and the number of people that they have,” said Jeannette Sutton, a disaster researcher at the University of Albany who has created a comprehensive dashboard that provides templates for disaster alerts. “I think they recognize it as a priority, but they don't prioritize it until they realize they should have. They're just trying to get their job done without screwing something up.”
Emergency managers are the government officials who are in charge of disaster response and recovery. At the state and local level, It is these officials and their agencies, not the Federal Emergency Management Agency, that make up the first line of defense after an extreme weather event. As such, emergency managers often like to say that “trust is our currency,” and it’s in their communication with the public that they build and lose this trust.
As climate disasters become more frequent and widespread, there have been numerous examples of flawed human communication scrambling an emergency response. In 2016, for instance, adjacent counties in California issued a “voluntary evacuation” and a “mandatory evacuation” for the same wildfire. In Australia in 2019, officials warned about wildfires by using the phrase “Watch and Act,” which the government later said caused “significant confusion” because no one knew what it meant.
In some cases, inadequate communication can mean the difference between life and death. This happened in Montecito, California, after the 2017 Thomas Fire. A few weeks after the fire, a heavy rainstorm produced a deadly mudslide. The government of Santa Barbara County struggled to communicate the risk to residents still traumatized from the blaze and experiencing a phenomenon that Sutton calls “warning fatigue.” The county sent alerts to everyone in the “voluntary evacuation zone” for wildfires, telling residents to “stay alert to changing conditions and be prepared to leave immediately.” Most of those residents should have left immediately, but to many the evacuation notice was optional; others just didn’t want to evacuate for a second time in a month. The mudslide killed 23 people and injured more than 160 others.
Governments that put out bad warnings are apt to lose the public’s trust, said Sutton. “They're losing the opportunity to be that voice to help people to be safe.”
In theory, alerts are a perfect use case for artificial intelligence, and in particular for the generative AI systems that have developed at a dramatic pace over the past few years. FEMA provides training sessions for emergency managers to learn best practices for synthesizing and sending alerts, but many officials don’t remember all their training when an emergency arrives. A large language model is different. It can read hundreds of thousands of alerts in mere minutes, digest all the research on what works in similar scenarios, and then apply that to edit a human alert in seconds.
“If you’ve only sent one [alert] in your life, and that was 15 years ago, and you need to remember all your training, and you’re thinking ‘Hey, there's a chemical plume coming my way, the phone's ringing, the radio's blaring, I need help,’ the AI is probably gonna do a better job than you are,” said Rob Dale, a former meteorologist who now runs the emergency management department in Ingham County, Michigan.
Dale has already used AI to draft a few practice alerts behind the scenes, but he’s never had to send one out. Ingham County is a small county in central Michigan, and it’s immune from major weather events like hurricanes and fires. If such an event did happen, Dale said he would have no issue allowing a chatbot to draft his incident communication, but he’d still want control over sending the alert out.
Some experts believe the technology is already good enough to deploy. EM1, a startup that produces AI software for emergency managers, has used Sutton’s research to train a model that its executives say is already better than almost any human emergency manager. The company has tested this in-house model on a number of scenarios including wildfires and tsunamis. It can already match or exceed human capabilities on most benchmark tests.
Sutton gave Grist an example of how the software works: Grist provided her with a recent alert sent by a New Mexico county that was trying to warn residents about flooding on the San Juan River.
The original alert read, “Breeched banks. The water is rising. EVACUATE NOW. McGee Park open for people and pets, RV.” Sutton asked the EM1 model to evaluate and revise the alert. In a few seconds, it produced what she said is a far better alert, one that checks all the main boxes of disaster communication.
The new alert read: “San Juan County: Floodwater is rising near [location]. People in [evacuation area]: LEAVE NOW for higher ground. Do not walk or drive through floodwater. McGee Park is open for people and pets. Check [official update source] for updates.” The model identified and fixed several problems with the original text, which does not say who is sending the alert, name the specific location where flooding is happening, or clarify who needs to evacuate and give advice on how to do so safely. It misspells the word “breached,” and it doesn’t provide any guidance on where residents can seek further information.
EM1 has contracts with around a hundred government agencies and school districts, but none are using it to automate their extreme weather alerts just yet. For the moment, they’re only using it to workshop plans and internal preparations. Even so, all the experts interviewed for this story said they are certain that many emergency managers are already using chatbots to write messages, even if they won’t admit it. Sutton said that the emergency managers who take her alert training sessions often present her with high-quality alerts they have drafted in seconds using ChatGPT or Gemini.
“Official adoption is pretty low, but people are unofficially using it, absolutely,” said Sarah Miller, a professor of emergency management at Pierce College in Florida and a longtime instructor at the National Disaster Preparedness Training Center. “They're using their own personal accounts, or they're using free ones.”
It sounds like an easy trade-off: if AI is better and faster than humans, and the difference between a good alert and a bad alert can be life and death, we should be using AI for every heat wave and wildfire. Yet even researchers who are bullish on chatbot technology say that making the switch could backfire. Members of the public who are skeptical of AI or who don’t trust the government in the first place may spurn agencies that publish AI-generated graphics or social media posts. In Syracuse, New York, for instance, a union of public employees sued the local government for using an AI service to answer non-emergency 911 calls.
“We trust things that we perceive [are] authentic and care about us,” said Ginny Katz, the founder of HazAdapt, a consultancy that helps disaster officials figure out how to use technology. “AI-generated content does not feel authentic.” There’s also a risk that chatbots could allow emergency managers to send out more alerts, and faster, which could increase the risk of warning fatigue.
As is the case in other areas where AI is being deployed, disaster experts say that for the moment the software is only as capable as the person using it. A seasoned emergency manager might be able to speed up their communication with the public by having a chatbot draft a series of alerts, but an inexperienced one rushing to create an urgent alert won’t know how to evaluate the output of a model like ChatGPT or Claude.
Even though the technology is a ways off from being able to perform without a human expert in the loop, that hasn’t stopped many understaffed emergency management departments from using it. As for how the proliferation of AI-generated content is affecting public trust in government, experts say it’s too early to tell.
“If you had a human sending you a text message versus a computer sending you a text message, which one would you believe is being more accurate?” said Justin Snair, the founder of Preppr, another company that offers AI software to emergency managers.
The answer, he said, depends on the person receiving it.

Minister's comments show attempt to get ahead of growing anger over rail infrastructure - snap analysis
Gwyn Topham
Transport correspondent
The speed with which Spain’s transport minister has laid out the broad circumstances of the crash appears unusually fast for the aftermath of an accident, where politicians and industry leaders are anxious not to pre-empt investigations.
That may be due to the scale of the crash and the nature of the findings – but also owe much to the growing anger and concern about the state of the nation’s railway infrastructure. And perhaps a desire to demonstrate that, for this second horrific crash this year on the Madrid-Seville line, the circumstances were apparently very different.
Although the official investigation is yet to come, Óscar Puente has pointed towards human error as the predominant cause (15:01) – an “inexplicable decision” to tell trains to continue operations when the outage of the signalling system had brought services to a standstill.
That makes the crash – on one level – move from the narrative where the trains are literally coming off the rails, and the country metaphorically so, as elections approach.
But questions will remain. The recent collision in Bedford in Britain was similar in its rarity: a train likewise hit the back of another stopped on the same line, albeit at a lower speed and with only one fatality. That crash continues to be investigated, but first findings show that while human error may have been the biggest cause, it arose from a set of unusual circumstances and a technical failure in the automated warning system which has yet to be fully explained.
Spain has identified individual culprits in past disasters: prosecuting the train driver who sped recklessly round a corner in 2013 in Galicia, killing 79 people. Police are apparently questioning the line controller today.
But the public will want to know what led to the initial outage of a signalling system that was due to be phased out – and what circumstances or daily experience could have pressed someone to urge the trains to continue regardless, however tragically wrong that decision proved to be.

A high-speed passenger train rear-ended another and caused a derailment on Wednesday morning near Toledo, Spain, killing at least 30 people, according to the regional government.
The fatal accident, which sent multiple carriages down an embankment, comes after another deadly crash involving the same carriers on a southern line in January that killed 46 people, stunned Spain and created deep doubts about the security of its once-vaunted rail system.
At least 30 people were killed in the Wednesday crash, though that number could rise, said Emiliano García-Page, the president of Castilla-La Mancha. He added that about 80 people were injured, 50 of whom had severe injuries.
The cause of the crash was not clear.
In Spanish news reports, passengers who were in the crash described an awful impact that tossed people from a dining car, broke limbs and piled passengers atop one another. People crawled out of windows and lay in a nearby field, where local workers, who had heard the crash, rushed to help them with first aid kits and saw the first bodies.
The Adif, Spain’s rail authority, said the trains involved were a “Renfe train and another from the Iryo company, both covering the Madrid-Sevilla route.” Renfe, the national rail provider, reported that high-speed service from Madrid, the nation’s capital, to the southern region of Andalusia was suspended.
Initial reports suggested that the Iryo train was stopped on the tracks, and that the Renfe train barreled into it. Local news outlets reported that there were 397 passengers aboard the Renfe train and about 150 aboard the Iryo train.
Isaac Barrientos, a spokesman for the government’s transportation ministry, said initial reports indicated that two carriages of the Iryo train had derailed.
With early national elections set for the end of November, the crash had the potential to become an issue in an already bitter campaign about the competence of the left-wing government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
“Shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo,” Mr. Sánchez, whose office canceled all scheduled meetings, wrote on social media. “Emergency services are working on the ground to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations. My affection, solidarity and support to all the victims and their families.”
The conservative opposition leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, quickly voiced his own concern as well.
“I am very concerned about the information we are receiving regarding another train accident,” he wrote on social media. “The priority now is to assist the victims and support their families. My full support goes to the emergency teams working on the ground.”
His Popular Party canceled all its campaign events around the country.
José Bautista contributed reporting from Madrid.
Spain’s Civil Guard said on social media that it had set up offices in Madrid, Seville, Córdoba and Toledo for family members of potential victims. The primary goal is to identify missing persons through the collection of DNA samples, the agency said.
The president of Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano García-Page, confirmed that at least 30 people had been killed in the train crash, a number that may rise. About 80 people were injured, 50 of them, according to Mr. García-Page, with severe injuries.
Blood donation groups in the area of the train crash are urging donors to come to hospitals in Toledo and Ciudad Real to “urgently replenish the reserves. Blood of all types will be needed.”
The fatal train crash near Toledo on Wednesday comes months after a deadly collision in southern Spain that involved the same carriers. In that accident, in January, 46 people were killed when two high-speed trains collided near Adamuz, in the country’s worst rail disaster since 2013.
The crash in January occurred when a train belonging to the private company Iryo derailed as it traveled toward Madrid. The train had been traveling north from Málaga when two of its rear cars fell into the opposite track. Seconds later, a southbound train operated by Spain’s national rail company, Renfe, slammed into the carriages.
The two trains were carrying hundreds of people when the collision occurred. An official report on what caused that accident is not yet available, but preliminary investigations pointed to a broken rail as the likely cause.
The accident shocked Spain and led to deep uncertainty about the safety of the country’s rail system, which contains the world’s second-longest high-speed rail network.
The deadly crash on Wednesday was the third in Spain this year. Days after the accident in January, a commuter train near Barcelona struck a collapsed retaining wall and derailed, killing one person.
Videos shot by passengers after the crash show parts of the derailed carriages pulverized, with charred wheels, and bags and seats strewn across an embankment. Emergency workers tend to the injured or hover over people covered in Mylar blankets. The arid field outside the small towns of Los Yébenes and Urda has become a parking lot of emergency vehicles and tents.

The footage was first shared by the Spanish radio station Capital Radio, which said an employee had been on one of the trains at the time of the crash.

Olympic and World Championships marathon gold medallist Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for EPO.
Kenyan Jepchirchir provided the sample prior to winning the Sydney Marathon on 30 August 2026.
The 33-year-old clocked a time of two hours, 18 minutes and 31 seconds to win in Sydney.
EPO, or erythropoietin, is a natural substance produced within the kidneys that stimulates the creation of new red blood cells.
If injected, it is only detectable in the urine or blood for a short window of time, and increases the amount of red blood cells, which carry oxygen to the muscles, in the blood stream.
Jepchirchir became the Olympic women's marathon champion at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics and returned to the Japanese capital to win the World Championships in September 2025.
She broke the women's half-marathon world record in 2017 and on three occasions in 2020.
In addition to Sydney, her other major wins came at the New York Marathon in 2021, the Boston Marathon in 2022 and the London Marathon in 2024.
Jepchirchir won the Sydney race, which became the seventh world major in 2025, by more than three minutes from compatriot Irene Chepet Cheptai.
She provided the sample which tested positive for EPO while in Kenya prior to the race.

Chirping, chewing and, with bat in hand, often appearing to idolise and mimic his team-mate Steve Smith.

Without him, Australia wanted their number three to feast at last chance saloon, where he has been perched for an eternity, on day two in Cape Town.
The 32-year-old lasted five deliveries and did not score a run.
Labuschagne failed to scored a Test century for the 48th time in a row - a new record for the number of innings an Australian top order batter has waited to raise his bat at three figures.
"That will never be broken," said former Australia quick Jason Gillespie on ABC.
"I say that because, respectfully, I don't think anyone will be given that length of time again."
There was a time when, from his insertion into the 2019 Ashes as a concussion substitute until the end of England's next quest to win back the earn, Labuschagne averaged 65 in Test cricket.
Repeat that over a Test career and only Sir Donald Bradman's mark of 99.94 would be ahead.
Instead, since his last Test century at Old Trafford in 2023, he averages 24.77.
Labuschagne may get one more chance in this Test, should Australia not progress from their position of 330-4, leading by one run, and dismiss South Africa before needing to pad up again.
Even that may not be enough.
"I just feel it is too far gone now," Gillespie added. "It is a very big sample size. Australia are at a point where they need to look elsewhere."
Labuschagne's technique has been poured over again and again as his slump progressed.
In August, the great Ricky Ponting, one of his predecessors as Australia's number three, called for the axe to fall.
"He can't score off the back foot," was Ponting's cutting remark.
Having batted nicely in three or four innings in this series only to give it away after reaching 30, here he was stuck on the crease, playing back to a full ball and nicking spinner Simon Harmer to slip.
"That's nerves and the pressure the selectors have put him under for an extended period of time," said former Australia batter Simon Katich on SEN Radio.
"They put him in this position by not making the decision to give him a breather."
It felt like all of Labuschagne's issues collapsing into one.
But if his pained stare down the pitch signalled the end of something, what followed hinted at their future.
With Travis Head already out and Labuschagne following, the score 58-2 in reply to the Proteas' 329, there was no Smith to steer Australia out of this tricky spot.
Matt Renshaw, Cameron Green and Josh Inglis, three of the junior members of this side, instead made fifties and put their side in the ascendancy.
Renshaw is one of those who has been kept out by the selectors in the hope Labuschagne could rediscover his best form.
Had he been picked to open in the World Test Championship final against South Africa in 2025, rather than Australia's decision to try Labuschagne as opener, he may have spent the following 17 months ending the debate over who should replace David Warner.
Having got his chance in this series, initially as number five before the Nic Maddinson experiment was cut short after two Tests, the Middlesbrough-born Renshaw looks like being a fixture for this winter and beyond.
His 74 here, which followed a career-best 190 in Durban, suggests a return to England next summer awaits.
Green is one who has not lacked opportunity. Long viewed as Australia's golden boy, the 27-year-old has flicked across 39 previous Test without ever truly appearing comfortable.
In making 65 below Table Mountain, the towering all-rounder played with the composure and authority he has often lacked.
Most impressive, though, was Inglis - another Aussie who spent his early years in Yorkshire.
He had not faced the red ball since March, has had his preparations limited by a broken finger, and came in with South Africa buoyed by Marco Jansen dismissing Renshaw and Green in successive overs before tea.
The 31-year-old finished 85 not out in an unbroken partnership of 145 with Alex Carey. There would be no late-evening South Africa fightback, like the one Mitchell Starc inspired on day one to bowl South Africa out.
This is not to say everything has fallen into place for Australia. Smith will return, meaning Green and Inglis would likely move from their current batting positions of four and five for their next Test against New Zealand in December.
Smith has avoided batting in Labuschagne's position before, and a four-Test trial of Green in that spot in 2024 and 2025 was aborted after he returned 188 across eight innings.
Leeds-born Inglis, meanwhile, has three first-class matches worth experience at number three, in which he averaged 12.66 and has a best score of 29.
But if ever a day showed Australia there is merit in moving from one generation to another it was this.
Three of their less experienced players, albeit two of them have celebrated their 30th birthdays, stood up to take Australia to a position from which they can control this Test.
Labuschagne did not. His days look numbered.

Prosecutors in Japan have filed formal charges against a US marine suspected of murdering and robbing a woman while stationed on the country’s island of Okinawa, according to Japanese media.
Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal assigned to Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, is charged with fatally strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the city and stealing from her a backpack containing a wallet, the public broadcaster NHK reported.
Ballard had initially been arrested in Yagi’s killing on 4 October, about a day after she was found dead in Naha, Okinawa’s capital. Prosecutors indicted him in the case on Sunday, and he has reportedly denied the charges.
NHK and other Japanese media outlets had previously reported that Ballard was arrested after surveillance camera footage from near the scene of Yagi’s killing showed a man entering a room with a woman and later leaving the scene with her belongings.
Ballard evidently matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage, was confronted and agreed to accompany investigators voluntarily to a local police station, Japanese media reported.
While being questioned by police, Ballard denied having a hand in Yagi’s killing, saying, “I don’t know anything about it,” NHK reported. But during subsequent questioning Ballard was alleged to have “made statements that partially hinted at his involvement”, the broadcaster reported.
A statement reported by NHK and reported to Yagi’s family on Sunday expressed a hope that Ballard “will confront what he has done and make amends commensurate with what he has done”.
“She lost her life at the young age of 39,” the statement from Yagi’s family added. “She … wanted to live much, much longer.”
Yagi’s killing prompted protests in Okinawa and the Japanese capital of Tokyo, with political leaders publicly condemning her killing. It also triggered a curfew and alcohol ban for US military members stationed in Okinawa, where most of the 54,000 US troops in Japan are based.
Crimes committed by US troops in Japan – including rape, assault, hit-and-run and drunk-driving – have long strained relations between the countries, which are close military allies.
A Japanese court in June 2025 sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton, then 22, to seven years in prison after he was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.
In 2017, a former US marine and civilian military base worker named Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local Okinawa woman.
US military forces in Japan that same year banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing a local driver, age 61.
The Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper reported that about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since the US returned Okinawa to Japan after the second world war in 1972.
There were 80 such arrests in 2024, constituting a 20-year high.
After Ballard’s arrest, Shinjiro Koizumi, Japan’s defense minister, said: “Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen.”

Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.
A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.
The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.
During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.
The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.
Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.
Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.
Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.
A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.
A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”
During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.
The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

Mbappé sorry for 'ill-judged' Mao remark after backlash in China
- Published
Kylian Mbappé has apologised for "ill-judged" comments he made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong which led to him being dropped by several Chinese brands.
Mbappé had reportedly told French talk show The Bridge the meme "that makes me laugh the most, it's the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator..." He then laughs as the clip cuts to a meme showing his face superimposed on an image resembling Mao.
The meme is part of a running joke about the Real Madrid forward being called a "dictator" because of his huge influence in football.
"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappé said in a statement.
"I apologise to everyone my words have upset."
Spain's La Liga also apologised, saying it "deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé's recent comments have caused among Chinese fans".
The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his chaotic and often violent rule that left millions dead.
A few people came out in support of him on Chinese social media, but that is a rare response given China's tightly controlled internet, where people are expected to toe the party and government line on sensitive topics.
Few topics are as sensitive as Mao, which may explain why brands were so quick to terminate partnerships with a global sports star like Mbappé.
The original video is not available on the show's YouTube channel, and it's unclear when the interview hosted by Real Madrid's Aurélien Tchouaméni first aired. In clips that have been circulating online, Mbappé does not identify Mao by name. He says he "uses [the meme] with friends all the time".
The furore appeared to kick off on Monday night after Chinese football forum Dongqiudi drew attention to the comments in a statement, saying they were "inappropriate" and "hurt the feelings of Chinese people".
Screengrabs of the clip and meme have since spread quickly on Chinese social media, with people echoing this sentiment and even calling for a boycott of both the French striker and his club, Real Madrid.
But some have blurred the meme itself as well as the part of the comment they found offensive, when Mbappe refers to "a Chinese dictator".
Dongqiudi said in its statement that it was "unable to translate" his comments because they were "offensive to China and the Chinese people".
Many people are therefore also wondering what exactly Mbappe said and have responded to the angry posts and comments with questions, wanting to know more.
What is the reaction in China?
Chinese fans have been criticising Mbappé – who is popular in China and has huge brand endorsements – of "profiting from the Chinese market yet making remarks that offend the Chinese public".
"International public figures, in particular, should show greater respect and sensitivity, as national sentiment must never be taken lightly," reads another comment on Weibo.
As the anger online grew louder, Chinese brands began to cut ties, although they did not explicitly refer to the video.
The country's largest dairy producer, Mengniu, said it "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people".
Drinks giant Dongpeng issued a similar statement: "Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments."
According to state-owned newspaper The Global Times, state broadcaster CCTV's news apps will not feature content related to the French striker. CCTV will also stop showing La Liga matches, Chinese media reported on Tuesday. Real Madrid is one of 20 clubs that play in the Spanish football league and is the most decorated team with 36 league titles.
China's foreign ministry has also weighed in, with spokesperson Lin Jian saying: "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."
China is a major market for international sports stars and homegrown brands have signed multimillion-dollar endorsement contracts with Mbappé, Norwegian striker Erling Haaland, and NBA player Stephen Curry.
By 14:00 local time on Tuesday, five of the top 10 trending topics on Weibo centered on Mbappé, with the hashtag "multiple brands terminate partnerships with Mbappé" topping the list.
"Don't ever come to China," read one of the top comments on Weibo.
Why is Mao a sensitive topic?
Mao founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled through tumultuous decades in the 1960s and 1970s.
His attempt at rapid industrialisation, which he called the Great Leap Forward, led to a famine that killed tens of millions. Then came the Cultural Revolution: a violent purge of anyone seen as a threat to Communism, which included Chinese intellectuals, landowners, artists and often rivals within the Party.
His death in 1976 brought a new era for China, which began to open its doors to the global economy. Even as the country moved away from Mao's rule, he continued to be hailed by the party as a national icon whose legacy was beyond reproach.
So jokes or memes about Mao are seen not just as an insult to the party but also its closely-guarded narrative about the country's past.
It's unclear when the Mbappé meme involving Mao began but his nickname, "the dictator", has made the striker the subject of many memes and jokes online.
Mbappé is widely regarded as one of the best footballers in the world and has wielded significant influence at the clubs he has played for. His extraordinary speed, goalscoring ability and worldwide popularity have made him a global icon, attracting millions of fans, major sponsorship deals and media attention, with his influence extending into fashion, culture and business.
In 2024, he sued a French influencer and kebab shop owner for using his name in the description of one of the shop's sandwiches, leading to more jokes about the nickname.
France teammate Ousmane Dembele jumped on the trend during the 2026 World Cup, calling Mbappé Mobut – a reference to Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator who ruled the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, for three decades.
In an interview with France Football in September, Mbappé acknowledged the light-heartedness behind many of these memes, but said they "sometimes reveal a lack of political and human awareness among people".
"There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history," he said.
"Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life."
Additional reporting by Fan Wang and Osmond Chia

Special ed diaries: Teachers tell NPR about their most joyous, most difficult moments
One of Kathleen Tejeda's students began freshman year just trying to get by. High school can be tricky for any teenager, but she was navigating it as a blind person.
By the end of her junior year, with support from Tejeda and other school staff, the student had gone from getting by to going big: She made the cheerleading squad and the school choir. She even sang the national anthem in front of the whole school.
Tejeda, who has been a special educator for 20 years in Riverside County, Calif., said that kind of advocacy is just as much a part of her job as teaching her students. But teachers like her can be hard to find.
There is a shortage of special educators in 45 out of 50 states, according to the Learning Policy Institute, an education research organization. That shortage is growing because the number of special education students is climbing: It's now more than 8.2 million — about 1 out of 6 public school students.
While turnover worsened sharply after the COVID-19 pandemic, the shortage isn't new. It has existed since special education became embedded in federal law with the passage of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act in 1975. Half a century later, a fundamental question remains: Why is this shortage of special education teachers so persistent?
Myths and realities about teaching special education
Let's start with a common misconception: The kids are hard to work with, so teachers don't want to do the job. "That is not the case," said Liz Bettini, a former special education teacher who is now a researcher and professor at Boston University. "That has not borne out in our research at all."
Loading...
What Bettini's research does show: Special educators can feel isolated from other school staff and feel they have too many student needs to manage. The volume of required paperwork can be crushing. These educators are often responsible for teaching across several subjects and grade levels. Many feel they don't get paid enough to do this essential work.
"That's a very heavy weight to carry as a teacher," Bettini said.
NPR set out to hear directly from about a dozen special educators from around the United States' public schools to learn what it takes to do their jobs day to day. They have been sharing snippets of their lives through voice memos since the start of the school year, and some will open their classroom doors to NPR in the coming months.
"No teacher does this for the paycheck," said third-year high school teacher Diana Swanson, who works in Vail, Ariz., as she sat at her desk the day before her school year began in July. "Just the students, that fulfillment, seeing them fill their cup a little bit, seeing them smile, be a member of society and part of their community. That's what fulfills me."
"I feel like I was coming into this school year more prepared this time around," fourth-year elementary school teacher Danalyn Garcia said late one school night from her living room in Chicago. "Yet, I feel the needs are even greater than the year before."
"Honestly, I had no life outside of school and outside of being a teacher," said Kaori Anderson-Walker, looking back on his first year of teaching middle school in Philadelphia. Now in his fourth year, he said he has finally learned to manage his time more effectively but said the work is still never-ending. "When my students aren't performing where I want them in the classroom, my mind is just constantly moving."
Much of the day isn't spent on teaching
Being an educator of any kind is demanding and requires immense skill. Research shows that burnout among all kinds of public school teachers is high, but it's even more acute for special educators. These teachers work with students who have an incredibly diverse set of needs, including those with autism, learning disabilities such as dyslexia, developmental delays and physical disabilities.
Special educators also do a lot more than teach — in fact, one study found that they spent only about a third of their day on instruction. They spend the rest of their time tracking student goals, coordinating specialized services for students (say, speech therapy or extra reading help), training support staff and writing individualized education programs (IEPs), which are legal documents that track each special education student's needs at school.
In many states, that means teachers must have specialized certification and training, but they typically aren't paid more. In 32 states, teachers get no extra pay for the hardest-to-staff positions, including in special education, according to a recent study.
While all 13 special educators NPR has spoken to said building relationships with students is their favorite part of the work, they also described the realities of those students' needs being more complex than those of many general education students.
"Special educators have reported, 'I can't teach this kid and respond to the student's crisis simultaneously. So I'm abandoning instruction because the crisis has to take priority,'" Bettini said.
For example, Grace Fitzgerald, who teaches elementary school in Peoria, Ill., shared on a drive home from school that one of her students had an emotional crisis that forced her to evacuate the rest of her class for their safety. "It's been challenging mentally and emotionally to kind of go through that at the very end of the first quarter, my first year of teaching," she said. "No one gets a road map to deal with that kind of situation."
Several teachers shared that behavioral challenges with individual students can make it harder to meet the needs of their many other students.
Loading...
"Our school doesn't have walls. So we have six classes per grade level in one ginormous room, and it's separated by dividers," Garcia, in Chicago, said. "So when one kid is screaming and crying and begins to escalate, it disturbs the whole pod and then other kids react to it." Getting students back on track can be difficult in these kinds of situations, she said.
Essential but time-consuming paperwork
Individualized education programs are a key part of special education. These written plans, required by federal law, are managed by teachers and other school staff and serve as a kind of road map for each special education student. IEPs outline the student's unique needs and their annual goals. For example, a goal of a student with autism may be to maintain eye contact for a certain period of time.
IEPs help families hold schools accountable, and they also help enforce a primary aim of special education: to teach students in the "least restrictive environment," meaning students with disabilities are taught alongside students without disabilities as much as possible. But IEPs also require regular meetings with families, an understanding of special education law and time spent away from teaching students — time that teachers often don't have.
Then there's the work of putting the IEP into practice in the classroom. Tejeda, of Riverside County, said when she's "pushing in" to other teachers' general education classrooms, she provides targeted support without singling out special education students. "We're going to walk the classroom and check in with everybody, but at the back of our minds, we know that we need to make sure we're [making] accommodations for that particular student."

For Anderson-Walker, in Philadelphia, "the biggest struggle" was feeling like he had to juggle IEP paperwork with teaching duties. Then, last year, his school, Boys' Latin of Philadelphia, hired staff members who are responsible for the paperwork part of IEPs, leaving teachers more time for the classroom. "Not having that stress is amazing," Anderson-Walker said.
Searching for solutions
In addition to the workload, at the core of the special education teacher shortage are pay and the sheer number of qualified people. Research shows that paying teachers more can help attract and retain them.
For example, in 2020, Hawaii raised special education teacher salaries by $10,000 annually. That cut the state's vacancies by 35%, but it wasn't enough to keep many special education teachers in their jobs. Seventeen states now pay teachers additional money to work in hard-to-staff subjects, including special education. That's down from four years ago, when 22 states did so.
The pipeline of qualified special educators is another big problem. According to education policy researcher Chad Aldeman's analysis of federal data a few years ago, about 46,000 special ed teachers leave public schools every year, while teacher preparation programs train fewer than 30,000 annually to replace those teachers.
Aldeman calls it a crude estimate but said that the rapid increase in demand for special education teachers is outpacing the supply of people trained to do those jobs. Many schools end up resorting to hiring teachers who aren't fully qualified for the work.
But research has found that "grow-your-own" programs that focus on recruiting people who already live in the community may be effective at filling special education jobs. Bettini and her research partners also found that supportive administrators and adequate planning time can help make the work feel more sustainable for teachers.
For example, Fitzgerald, the first-year teacher in Illinois, said she was feeling overwhelmed by her workload at the start of the year. So she worked with her school leadership to build more dedicated planning time into her day.
"I think that's going to be very beneficial and will hopefully lead to a decrease in time spent after school," Fitzgerald said. She uses that time to focus on lesson plans, logging data and writing IEP goals.
It allows her to be more present in the classroom, working with her students.
